1|28.c: Graduating into the dot-com crash and losing jobs made her willing to bet on an unloved, early Baidu.
1|28.e: She graduated from UCLA in 2001, right as the internet bubble burst and big companies froze hiring. She landed at a router startup of about a dozen people, which failed to raise money and shut down a year and a half later, leaving her jobless again. After that, she stopped chasing choices that merely looked safe. In late 2002, fellow alumnus Ming Lei invited her to join Baidu, then under 100 people. Her family thought the company was too shabby and pushed back hard, but she went anyway. She says she found her path by feeling her way in the dark, with no clear plan.
ex: Many Silicon Valley companies lost about 98% of their value; jobless, she cooked at home daily
Baidu went public in 2005; people joked she'd angel-invested, but she calls the money trivial
Became Baidu's VP of technology at 35, running search and apps for up to 4,000–5,000 people

items.d: Bubble bursts; big companies stop hiring

1|28.c: A slump weeds out weak companies, and recovery usually takes two to two and a half years.
1|28.e: She sees a financial winter as a normal part of the cycle. When a bubble bursts, companies that can't stand on their own are cleared out, and the strong survivors get resources again. That is how a market economy corrects itself. Her timeline comes from recoveries she watched firsthand: stocks that hit bottom took over two years to get back to normal, and the U.S. needed two to three years to recover after the 2008 crisis. So she doesn't treat a slump as the end of the world, but as a stage you have to get through, with a roughly known length.
ex: NetEase stock fell to about $1 and took 24 to 28 months to recover
Google once considered selling to Yahoo; Yahoo passed, and Google went on to rise
After the 2008 financial crisis, the U.S. took two to three years to recover

items.d: Valuations and funding turn cold fast
Usually two to two and a half years
Like Google after the dot-com bust

1|28.c: Over 20 years she's seen three eight-year cycles. This one runs downhill from a peak, in changed conditions.
1|28.e: She splits her career into three crisis cycles of about eight years each, and marvels at how much upheaval she has witnessed. She admits her generation grew up during two or three decades of steady growth, so they may overreact to a downturn. Still, she warns that old lessons can't simply be reused this time, because the wider environment has changed deeply. Drawing on Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio's theory of cycles, she thinks we are now heading down from a peak of prosperity. Even so, she is staying in China: it may not get another golden twenty years, but there is still plenty of room.
ex: Some 20 years ago, she and her husband decided against emigrating, fearing an idle life abroad

items.d: First cycle, after the bubble burst
Second cycle, after the financial crisis
Where we are, per Dalio's cycle theory

1|28.c: This winter isn't short on money. Investors don't know what to back or how they'd cash out.
1|28.e: She thinks "capital winter" has become an overused phrase, and that the gloom and caution among investors is mostly a state of mind. Unlike past downturns, most top firms have plenty of cash this time. Two things are holding them back. First, companies are now valued lower on the stock market than in their private funding rounds, so it's unclear how investors would ever exit their deals. Second, nobody is sure which industries are worth backing. So she expects firms to mostly sit on their cash and wait until the direction becomes clearer.
ex: Her only chances to practice cooking in 22 years: jobless in 2000, homebound in May 2022

root.d: Top firms have money but hold back

items.d: Unclear how to get the money back out
Unsure which industries are worth backing
The winter is mostly a state of mind

1|28.c: Founders should crouch through the winter: stay alive, and save enough strength to jump when things improve.
1|28.e: Her advice to founders comes as a posture. Lying flat means giving up entirely. Lying face-down means just trying to survive. She rejects both. Crouching means keeping the company alive while saving the strength to leap, so you can move the moment conditions warm up. This fits her view of the cycle: if a slump usually heals in a little over two years, what matters is that you come out of it with energy to spare.

marks.d: Stay alive with strength to jump

1|28.c: Her ideal hard-tech founder is someone who is both smart and honest.
1|28.e: Talking about what she wants to invest in next, she described her ideal founder in hard tech, meaning fields built on tough core technology: smart enough to crack hard problems, yet honest and steady, never showy. The written notes on the episode only list this point without laying out her reasoning. At the end of the show she also talked about startups through Dream of the Red Chamber. She picked Tanchun, a daughter born to a concubine, as the most founder-like, because she had the drive to change her fate.

2|51.c: Humanoid robots aren't new. Getting them to walk almost like people took forty to fifty years.
2|51.e: He points out that humanoid robot research began in the late 1960s and early 1970s, so it's hardly Musk's invention. Early robots walked slowly and stiffly. Only with Boston Dynamics did walking rhythm and speed get close to a human's. Walking on two legs is the hardest way to move, and there's a clear technical gap between slow and fast two-legged walking. So when he watches a launch, he first checks whether the real robot can support the body shown in the demo. That depends on materials, balance design, walking algorithms, even the size of the feet.
ex: Japan's Waseda University began humanoid robot research in the late 1960s and early 1970s
Optimus looks decent and walks unremarkably, he says; carrying boxes and bags is already impressive
If it could slice watermelon or embroider, it would be beyond today's technology

items.d: Rhythm and speed close to a human's

2|51.c: Tesla can reuse its self-driving navigation skills, but not the fine force control robots need.
2|51.e: He breaks a humanoid robot's abilities into perception, decision-making, control, and interaction. Tesla says its robot uses the same chips and camera-only vision software as its cars, so walking through messy environments, mapping in real time, and finding its own way can largely build on self-driving work. But driving barely needs precise force control, while fine household tasks depend on it. People also sense the world through hearing, touch, and smell, which robots lack today. Interaction with people matters just as much, and he has doubts about how far Tesla can get there.
ex: Reusable foundation: the Dojo supercomputer, D1 chip, and camera-only vision software
What won't carry over: peeling an egg or a crayfish takes fine force control

d.verdict: Navigation transfers; fine handling is a brand-new problem

2|51.c: A robot's shape should come from the job it does. Saying humanoids will upend everything is wrong.
2|51.e: He sees robots as built to solve a specific problem in a specific setting, and their shape settles only after ten, twenty, even fifty years of iteration on that problem. A human shape is the best answer only when the job truly requires it. Many factory jobs don't need legs at all. Everyday services like housekeeping, babysitting, cleaning windows, and folding clothes suit humanoids better. On the show he also predicted that the best service-robot companies will break out of their category and look more and more like consumer electronics companies.
ex: A forklift moves several TVs at once. 500 robots each carrying one box makes no sense.

items.d: Most factory work doesn't need one
Housework and care suit humanoids better

2|51.c: The uncanny valley is a trap humanoid robots will hit when they try to enter homes.
2|51.e: He cites the uncanny valley effect from research: as a robot looks more human but not quite human enough, people find it creepier. Only when it becomes nearly indistinguishable from a person does liking come back. If humanoids enter homes during this stage, buyers may not want them. Experts disagree on how long the valley will last, from ten or twenty years to longer. He thinks Optimus, with no eyes and a flat panel for a face, already sits in that half-human zone. In science fiction, I, Robot is stuck in the valley, while Westworld is nearly fully human.

marks.d: No eyes, flat face; already in the valley

2|51.c: Musk's humanoid bet mixes sci-fi dreams with a hunt for Tesla's next source of growth.
2|51.e: Half joking, he guesses Musk may be a Westworld fan who wants a world where people and robots are hard to tell apart. Add brain-computer interfaces, which link the brain directly to computers, and Musk might even imagine moving human consciousness into robots to live on. From a business view, though, the growth story and valuations of electric-car makers are under pressure. Humanoid robots are a fresh story that can run for a hundred years, and could become Tesla's second growth engine beyond cars.

items.d: A new story to prop up the carmaker's valuation

2|51.c: With certain demand and a strong industry base, China has a broad opportunity in robotics.
2|51.e: He sees global demand for robots as highly certain, since rich countries face falling birth rates and labor shortages. China's case is even stronger: a fast-aging population, young people who don't want manual jobs, and factories short of workers. China is already the world's largest buyer of robots, with many universities in related fields, active founders and investors, a full supply chain, faster product iteration than other countries, and clear long-term industrial policy. The real risk is pacing: companies that last thirty years will be valuable, but many will stall and fall along the way.
ex: A downside he imagines: robots could replace some relationships between people

terms.d: Largest buyer; active talent and capital

result.d: The risk is losing control of pacing

3|53.c: Humanoid robots are like the Moon landing: maybe not the final form, but a great rallying goal.
3|53.e: He estimates mass-produced humanoid robots may still be 10 to 20 years away or more, and that public imagination runs about 50 years ahead of real technology. He doesn't think that makes them pointless. The Moon landing's direct value may not have been huge, but the goal was simple and inspiring, drew in huge numbers of talented people, and threw off technology and in-between products along the way. As for the end state, he leans toward the WALL-E picture: lots of specialized robots. Some jobs are beyond humans anyway, and people already rely on tools to work.
ex: Cleaning air ducts calls for a snake-like robot; a humanoid would be a poor fit

3|53.c: Musk frames near-term engineering as part of a grand vision, winning talent and patience for failure.
3|53.e: He breaks down SpaceX's story. To build a self-sustaining city on Mars, you'd need to move hundreds of thousands of people on thousands of rockets, so rockets must be cheap, reusable, and mass-produced. What SpaceX actually does today is launch satellites into low Earth orbit on low-cost rockets, far from colonizing Mars. Tying today's work to a distant goal attracts more talent and money, and makes people more forgiving of short-term failures. He jokes that if he did the same, he'd just call it a cheaper reusable rocket, and one failed launch would have people doubting him.

3|53.c: Home robots are harder than self-driving cars, and throwing money at them won't fix it.
3|53.e: He compares how much each has to see. A self-driving car only needs to roughly recognize cars and people. A home robot has to spot the pits on a potato and tell scissors from pliers, recognizing more kinds of things at higher precision. In space programs, money is the obvious limit. But for robots working in a kitchen, nobody even has a complete approach yet, so more funding won't help. He even says anyone who can get today's robots to tie shoelaces well, or shake out and hang up washed clothes, deserves to be a top professor or academician.
ex: Chang'e phase one cost about 1.4 billion yuan; Apollo once took about 3% of U.S. GDP

items: Fewer kinds of things to recognize
See the pits on a potato

d.verdict: Housework is harder than driving; money isn't the only bottleneck

3|53.c: Robots today are where computers were in 1980; mass adoption is still ahead.
3|53.e: He sees robots as the next big wave and uses computer history to place where we are. By 1972 humans had already been to the Moon, and by 1980 large American companies were using computers, but small businesses and individuals were not yet. Robots are at that same stage now, with only big customers on board. On the show he noted that industrial robots started in car factories before spreading to other industries. He also points out that Czech writer Karel Čapek coined the word robot, meaning slave or forced laborer, so the Chinese term, literally "machine person," doesn't quite fit.

items.d: Computers reach big U.S. companies by 1980
Small businesses and individuals adopt them

3|53.c: Robotics founders usually get one shot. If they miss, they're out.
3|53.e: He contrasts it with the internet, where software changes fast and mistakes are cheap. Robots span mechanics, electronics, control, optics, reliability, software, and algorithms, a very long chain, and one product can take three to five years. So if you bet on the wrong direction, you rarely get a second chance. He uses the movie Pacific Rim to make the point that there are no shortcuts: you grind through one engineering problem after another, and it's go big or die. His own company's product took three or four years of polishing to mature.

items.d: Miss, and it's hard to try again

3|53.c: Lei Jun is about as far as most founders can learn from; Musk and Jobs can't be copied.
3|53.e: At the end of the show he sorted entrepreneurs into those you can learn from and those you can't. In his view, Xiaomi founder Lei Jun is the ceiling for what ordinary founders can learn, and his methods and path are worth borrowing. Elon Musk and Steve Jobs are so exceptionally gifted that trying to imitate them is more likely to land you in a ditch. The written notes only outline this part without details.

4|57.c: Vietnam is now living through the kind of golden decade China once had.
4|57.e: He left China to study abroad in 2003 and missed the decade when China grew fastest. Vietnam's real boom has come in the last ten years, and it is the last emerging market deeply shaped by Confucian culture, so he feels that history is repeating there. That's why he moved to Vietnam in 2021. The home he bought in Ho Chi Minh City has more than doubled in price.

items.d: His Ho Chi Minh City home more than doubles

4|57.c: Vietnam has real strengths, but it won't become the world's next factory floor.
4|57.e: He doesn't expect Vietnam to become the next factory of the world, and he uses the paths the Asian Tigers chose decades ago as a reference for where Vietnam could go. Still, Vietnam has its own strengths. Outside India, it is the world's second-largest hub for IT outsourcing, where foreign companies send software and tech work. Women's employment there is also about 10% higher than in China.

root.d: But hard to copy the factory-of-the-world path

4|57.c: Vietnam's north and south are so different that the gap felt like culture shock.
4|57.e: His biggest culture shock in Vietnam came from the differences between north and south. Northerners tend to save money, for example, while southerners don't save much. By talking with locals, he has tried to understand the historical roots of this divide.

d.verdict: The north-south gap is big enough to be a culture shock

4|57.c: Life in Vietnam is noticeably happier, and he plans to stay for the long haul.
4|57.e: He says he has been clearly happier since moving to Vietnam. He plans to live there long term, and is even thinking about marrying a Vietnamese woman and having his kids go to school there. The feeling rests on concrete details of daily life: the country is safe, living costs are low, and people treat each other warmly.

terms.d: Dating in Hanoi costs very little

result.d: Plans to settle and start a family

5|65.c: A country has to hold together politically before its economy can really grow.
5|65.e: He argues that Southeast Asian countries must first achieve political integration, meaning a central government that can actually run the whole country, before their economies can develop. The harsh part is that Indonesia and Vietnam, the economies with the most potential today, are also the countries with the most killing in their history. In his view, stable regimes are often built on bloody conflict.

items.d: Indonesia and Vietnam have the most potential
A system that controls the whole country
Killing laid the base for stable rule

5|65.c: Indonesia's 1965 September 30 Movement ended up giving the country a system to govern all its islands.
5|65.e: Indonesia is an archipelago, which makes it extremely hard to govern. He points out that beyond the humanitarian condemnation it deserves, the 1965 September 30 Movement, a coup attempt followed by mass killings, had another side. Founding father Sukarno fell, the U.S.-backed Suharto took power, and Indonesia built a system of control that reached the whole country. That is one reason he is upbeat on Indonesia. In the second and third quarters of 2022, its foreign direct investment rose 39.7% and 63.6% from a year earlier.

items.d: Strong central rule over the islands
Regional balance and fast-growing foreign investment

5|65.c: The Philippines swings between strongmen and revolutions, so it struggles to build a strong central government.
5|65.e: When it was founded, the Philippines was Asia's most developed country. He sees Marcos-era martial law and the People Power Revolution as the two ends of a pendulum. The country keeps swinging between them, and its economy moves three steps forward, two steps back. Add tangled family dynasties and presidents limited to a single six-year term, and building a strong central government becomes its biggest challenge.

items.d: Clans carve up power; orders don't reach the south

5|65.c: Thailand escaped colonization, but the government's reach has never really extended beyond Bangkok.
5|65.e: Squeezed between British Burma and French Indochina, Thailand served as a buffer zone, kept its history intact, and never went through a crisis of decolonization. But he thinks Thailand is weak at holding the nation together. The king reigns while the military rules, and more than 20 coups and constitutional rewrites have thrown it into turmoil every few years.

items.d: Between British Burma and French Indochina
More than 20 coups and constitutional rewrites

5|65.c: To understand a country, start with its episodes of violence and its founding fathers.
5|65.e: Colleagues call him a "butcher journalist" because he pays special attention to violence within a nation and what it reveals about national character. He believes you study a country through its most extreme events and its founding fathers. Sukarno, Tunku Abdul Rahman, Ho Chi Minh, José Rizal, and Aung San share one qualification: they led the fight against colonial rule. Singapore officially has no single founding father; instead it lists 11 founding leaders.

root.d: Look at the extremes to see its nature

items.d: One test: leading the anti-colonial struggle

6|69.c: After a layoff, workers with green cards and those without face completely different challenges.
6|69.e: He points out that laid-off employees with green cards, meaning U.S. permanent residency, face very different challenges from those without. Without a green card, your right to stay in the U.S. is often tied to your employer, so after losing your job you must find a new one within the visa grace period. Meta even arranged for immigration experts to help, as part of its layoff notice.

items: Time to find the next job
Status at risk when the job ends
Must find a new employer within the grace period

d.verdict: Immigration status makes the layoff hit very differently

6|69.c: Layoff severance is concrete math you can work out ahead of time.
6|69.e: The episode works through the numbers for laid-off staff. Under the package Meta announced, U.S. employees get 16 weeks of base pay, plus two more weeks for every full year of service, with no cap. Meta also covers six months of health insurance, and stock scheduled to vest on November 15 still vests.

terms.d: Two more weeks per year, no cap

result.d: Plus six months of health coverage and vested stock

6|69.c: Silicon Valley's tech job market has gone into a deep freeze.
6|69.e: The episode was recorded on the Friday night after Meta's layoffs were finalized. The company cut more than 11,000 people, about 13% of its workforce. He believes the tech job market has frozen, offers what he calls his "cold-blooded advice," and compares how this downturn feels with 2008.

items.d: A black week comes to an end

7|70.c: Freezing her eggs, a step that felt like a stand against marriage, made her more open to it.
7|70.e: Before freezing her eggs, she felt women were the ones being chosen in dating and marriage, like sitting through a job interview. After doing it in Silicon Valley in 2019, she felt she had taken control as a woman. Something with an anti-marriage flavor ended up making her more open to marriage and intimacy. She also notes that egg freezing is already an employee benefit at Silicon Valley tech companies and Wall Street firms.

items.d: Being chosen, like a job interview
No longer pushed by the clock

7|70.c: Globalization hasn't ended. It has just moved into a different arena.
7|70.e: Over six months she visited more than ten cities across the U.S., Europe, and Asia, hauling three big suitcases. She sees Web3's most passionate believers as a hippie-style rebellion in an age of retreat from globalization. In her view, industrial-era globalization may have stalled, but globalization itself hasn't ended. It continues in new arenas of the intelligent age.

items.d: Goods and supply chains cross borders
Globalization continues in a new arena

7|70.c: Unlike the first two generations of the internet, Web3 moves value, not just information.
7|70.e: She thinks the core difference between Web3 and earlier generations of the internet is that the old web moved information, while Web3 moves money, and it could become infrastructure for public services. She recommends the book The Network State, and believes Web3 has the potential to change how society is organized.

d.verdict: Web3 is about value flowing over the network

7|70.c: Web3 is where the internet was in 1995–98; finance projects are closest to product-market fit.
7|70.e: She compares today's Web3 to the internet of 1995 to 1998: still very early. Among all the directions, she focuses on finance-related projects, because they are the closest to product-market fit, the point where a product truly meets real demand.

items.d: First to match product and market

8|81.c: Venture capital follows a power law: a tiny number of huge winners decide a whole fund's returns.
8|81.e: Mallaby sees the power law as the key to understanding venture capital. Returns on most assets roughly follow a bell curve: gains and losses cancel out and drift toward the average. Venture is the opposite. Most investments fail, but a few return ten to twenty times the money, enough to cover every loss. So what makes or breaks a fund is the handful of extreme successes, not the average deal.

8|81.c: Venture capital funded people with ideas, so quitting to start a company went from betrayal to normal.
8|81.e: He traces Silicon Valley venture capital back to eight young researchers at Shockley Semiconductor. Fed up with its high-pressure management, they walked out together. Arthur Rock found them money and in 1957 backed Fairchild Semiconductor, which is why Mallaby calls Rock the father of Silicon Valley. Venture capital let people with ideas leave big companies and strike out on their own. Quitting to found a startup stopped being seen as treason and became an ordinary choice. That fundamentally changed the Valley's business culture.
ex: The Valley didn't win on Stanford (MIT had better engineering) or defense contracts (Boston had more)
What mattered was money willing to back ideas with no customers and unproven products

items.d: Young Shockley researchers are fed up

8|81.c: Sequoia endured and Kleiner Perkins faded because only Sequoia's leaders invested in building the firm.
8|81.e: He sees Kleiner Perkins' John Doerr as brilliant and charismatic, but uninterested in internal management. Strong partners left one by one until he was the only big boss left. Sequoia's second-generation leaders, Michael Moritz and Doug Leone, instead thought hard about hiring, training people, and shaping culture, even studying behavioral science to make better investment decisions. Senior partners joined boards alongside newcomers, took the blame for failures, and gave young partners credit for wins. Sequoia also kept reinventing itself and expanding.
ex: Around 1995 Sequoia did only Valley Series A; it later added growth, China, even hedge-fund ideas

items: Veterans take blame, newcomers get credit

d.verdict: In venture, building the firm decides who wins long term

8|81.c: Giant growth-stage checks are really a bet on whether the whole tech sector goes up or down.
8|81.e: Masayoshi Son and Yuri Milner's innovation was to skip early bets and instead pour huge sums into companies just when they could have gone public, letting them keep growing while private. That created growth-stage investing. Mallaby calls it a double-edged sword. A giant check is really a bet that tech stocks as a whole will rise: a powerful money machine in good times, a source of huge losses in a downturn. He also notes that two outsiders could rewrite the Valley's rules, proof of how open it is to outside talent.
ex: Goldman Sachs sold its early Alibaba stake to Son, who made billions from it over time
About two in five Silicon Valley companies were founded by people born outside the U.S.
Son committed huge sums after half an hour with founders; Mallaby calls him the craziest

items.d: Son briefly tops the global rich list
His gains perhaps second only to Musk's

8|81.c: Top VCs share high emotional intelligence, the opposite of what hedge fund managers need.
8|81.e: He concludes that the very different stars in his book share one trait: emotional intelligence. VCs have to meet founders constantly, build trust, and even spend weekends with discouraged founders to help them bounce back. Hedge fund managers can work like islands, analyzing markets alone. Distinctive firms take very different approaches, which shows there is no single right way to do venture. Age isn't a hard barrier either: older investors who understand people and build relationships can still win over young founders.
ex: Bill Gurley was far older than Uber's founder, yet still won the deal
Founders Fund backs crazy people doing crazy things and accepts that most companies fail
Benchmark does only early Series A deals, with partners deeply involved in building companies

marks.d: High EQ, stays close to founders

8|81.c: Silicon Valley's many weak ties let information move faster, which is how it overtook Boston.
8|81.e: He borrows sociologist Mark Granovetter's idea of "the strength of weak ties" to explain how Silicon Valley differs from Boston. People in Boston tend to stay at one company for a long time and form deep but narrow networks with a few close friends. People in Silicon Valley switch jobs often and build up lots of loose connections, so information, talent, and money flow faster, and creativity takes off. VCs act like bees in a garden, carrying pollen, and information, from flower to flower.

items.d: No lifelong loyalty to one company

9|81.c: Outsiders struggle to climb inside big institutions, so they're more inclined to disrupt them.
9|81.e: Mallaby noticed that many VC legends had hard childhoods or lived on the margins. People outside the elite rarely realize their ambitions by climbing the ladder at a big company, so they start their own companies or funds. Unusual backgrounds lead to unusual choices. He stresses that the point isn't a blue-collar upbringing but an unusual set of experiences. Nor does everyone need to build an institution that lasts decades; being a natural solo boss is neither right nor wrong.
ex: Rock had childhood polio, faced antisemitic bullying, was a loner, and clashed with both partners
Son, a poor ethnic Korean in Japan, changed course after high school in California
Kathy Xu turned down a partnership at Qiming and started her own firm instead

items.d: The path inside big institutions is blocked

9|81.c: Modern venture capital grew out of inventions by Arthur Rock and the founders of Sequoia and Kleiner Perkins.
9|81.e: He walks through a few foundational designs. Arthur Rock created the limited partnership fund with a life of about seven years, raised in advance so he could back a great company right away instead of lobbying investors one by one. The seven-year limit also pushed funds to move fast. Sequoia's Don Valentine and Kleiner's Tom Perkins invented staged investing: give only enough money for six to nine months, then add more once milestones are hit. They also got deeply involved, installing or replacing CEOs when needed, and Perkins, an engineer, dug into the technology.
ex: Valentine's first bet, Atari, held hot-tub board meetings; his Navy water-polo build kept him in control
Perkins was deeply involved in shaping Genentech in its early days

items.d: Rock's design: about a seven-year life
Ready to back a great company fast
Enough cash for 6–9 months at a time
Board seats, replacing CEOs if needed

9|81.c: Venture capital turned joining a startup from a one-time gamble into a game you can play repeatedly.
9|81.e: He uses Eric Schmidt's move to Google to show another side of venture capital. Schmidt worried that the young founders, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, would push him out. John Doerr promised that if things failed, he'd line up another software CEO job for him. Mallaby calls venture capital "a machine for making wagons": founders and early employees can't build the wagon themselves, so VCs supply the capital and show them how to build a company. Joining a startup is no longer a one-shot bet, so talented people dare to take more risks.

9|81.c: Venture capital is a team sport, and picking the wrong successor can destroy a firm.
9|81.e: He stresses that Sequoia wasn't built on individual heroics. Don Valentine didn't name the fund after himself, deliberately spoke little in meetings, and handed power to the younger Michael Moritz and Doug Leone before he truly had to retire, aiming to build a lasting institution. Successful deals are usually relays involving several people, and after exiting an investment Sequoia lists everyone who contributed. If Sequoia ever fails, he thinks the biggest risk is choosing the wrong next leader, someone who alienates colleagues, so talent walks out to start rival firms.
ex: Accel's Facebook deal: a student spotted it, a 30-year-old investor ran it, a senior partner helped
Sequoia China is the exception: Neil Shen has always been its undisputed sole leader

items: Talent leaves to start rival firms
Hands power to the next generation early
Credits every contributor after an exit

d.verdict: Lasting firms depend on choosing the right successor

9|81.c: China's late start in venture capital became an advantage: it caught the software wave and included more women.
9|81.e: Chinese venture capital began in the late 1990s with Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent, and in about 15 years matched Silicon Valley's count of unicorns, startups worth over $1 billion. Fast economic growth helped, and firms like Sequoia imported American practices such as stock options. U.S. venture moved from chips to PCs and hardware before software; China started right in the software wave, so it focused on apps. Starting later also meant growing up in a more equal era, so noticeably more of China's top investors are women. He expects hardware and deep tech to regain favor over the next decade.
ex: Goldman Sachs' Shirley Lin was Alibaba's first investor; he calls her China's Arthur Rock
His top Chinese investors include many women: Kathy Xu, Anna Fang, Xiaohong Chen

items.d: Matched the Valley's unicorn count in ~15 years

9|81.c: Today looks like the 2000 Nasdaq crash; after a year or two of pain, venture will come through.
9|81.e: As a historian of finance, he compares the 2022 downturn to the 2000 Nasdaq crash. Back then, internet companies that burned cheap money on advertising went under in droves, the IT firms serving them went bankrupt too, and even Amazon nearly failed. He thinks the painful phase may last a year or two, but the combination of venture capital, entrepreneurs, and new ideas has made it through cycle after cycle. So his advice is to stay optimistic.

items.d: Many companies burn cash on ads

10|82.c: Plan your career around the job after next, not just the next one.
10|82.e: She believes the key to career growth isn't your next role but the one after that, and about two years in a role is a natural checkpoint. It echoes a line the host quoted from former Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg: a career is a jungle gym, not a ladder.

items.d: About two years is a checkpoint
What you should really aim for

10|82.c: A good career path comes from creating your own role, not waiting for an opening.
10|82.e: Her career spans IBM (which she left quickly), Box (which went public), Twitch (acquired by Amazon), and a top-tier U.S. investment firm. She advises joining fast-growing "rocket ship" companies and taking on fuzzy work nobody has clearly defined, creating a role for yourself instead of just filling an existing opening.

d.verdict: In Silicon Valley, opportunity comes from roles you create

10|82.c: When Chinese founders struggle to raise money in the U.S., what's often missing is storytelling.
10|82.e: Asked why Chinese founders struggle to raise money in the U.S., she says the problem sometimes isn't the business itself but a lack of storytelling skill. The pitch deck doesn't need to be long, either: ten slides is enough.

terms.d: The product and the business itself
Made clear in a 10-slide pitch deck

10|82.c: Going global means going local: Chinese companies abroad succeed by fitting into each market.
10|82.e: She says Americans have mixed views of Chinese companies like TikTok, SHEIN, and Wish, with Wish especially controversial. Temu, PDD's overseas app, leads with low prices but has done a great job fitting into American culture. Her conclusion: going global means going local.

10|82.c: Silicon Valley is optimistic and accepting, so you can be completely yourself, however weird.
10|82.e: She describes Silicon Valley as an optimistic place that embraces individuality, where you can be "totally weird." She lists successful U.S. companies founded by Asians, including Zoom, DoorDash, Deel, Twitch, YouTube, Lime, Airtable, and Scale AI, to show that outsiders can do big things there too.

11|85.c: Singapore won't become the center of Web3. At most, it will be a hub people pass through.
11|85.e: He has lived through several gold rushes in Singapore: a wave of U.S.-dollar capital around 2014, the spillover from China's mobile internet in 2016 to 2018, and the Web3 boom, built on blockchain, that started in late 2021. After a string of blowups, raising money for Web3 projects went from easy to hard, and the government shifted from open to cautious. So he expects Singapore to be a hub for Web3, not its center.

items.d: Many industry people move to Singapore
The rich and industry insiders flood in
Funding dries up; government turns cautious

11|85.c: Singapore's government puts real money behind local startups.
11|85.e: He uses his own experience as an example. For his first startup, the government gave him 2.5 million yuan with no strings attached. For his second, it invested 1.5 million yuan for a 15% stake, and any investor could buy that stake out at the investor's own valuation. He thinks knowing these policies can sharply cut the cost of starting a company.

11|85.c: Singapore manages its officials the way a company manages its staff.
11|85.e: In his view, the Singapore government runs its officials much like a business. It judges them on performance targets, values efficiency, and expects quick replies at any time. Pay is benchmarked to the private sector, and policies are enforced strictly and based on data.

items.d: Expected to reply at any time

11|85.c: Once the boom faded, the tables turned: investors no longer want, or dare, to meet founders.
11|85.e: This wave brought mostly wealthy people and internet workers to Singapore, and rents at one point rose about 10% a month. But as the Web3 craze cooled, things flipped. Founders used to chase investors everywhere; now investors neither want to meet founders nor dare to.

items: Investors won't, or don't dare, meet them
Fundraising goes from easy to hard

d.verdict: With the boom over, the balance of power has flipped

12|65.c: Small states caught between big powers either pick a side or hedge, depending on how strong they are.
12|65.e: He borrows the business idea of hedging, using one investment to reduce the risk of another, to make sense of small countries' diplomacy. Facing great-power rivalry, small states broadly choose between two strategies: bandwagoning, which means siding with one big power, or hedging, which means spreading their bets. How well a country can hedge politically depends heavily on its national strength.

items: Follow it for protection and benefits
Lower the risk of backing the wrong side

d.verdict: The stronger the country, the more room it has to hedge

12|65.c: Southeast Asia is where the strategic interests of China, the U.S., and Japan meet.
12|65.e: He sees Southeast Asia as the meeting point of Chinese, American, and Japanese strategy. In investment terms, China and Japan are the biggest investors in the region, while the U.S. shows up more through involvement in all kinds of regional affairs.

items.d: One of the region's biggest investors
One of the region's biggest investors

12|65.c: Laos has many mountains and few resources, so it survives by connecting with its neighbors.
12|65.e: Laos is Southeast Asia's only landlocked country. It sits in a geographic transition zone, with lots of mountains and few resources. He thinks a country like this can only survive by staying connected with its neighbors, which makes it a bit like Afghanistan. Its economic aid comes mainly from China, Vietnam, and Thailand.

items.d: Mainly from China, Vietnam, and Thailand

12|65.c: Cambodia has fallen from the glory of Angkor, and today its economic potential ranks in the second tier.
12|65.e: Cambodia was once home to the glory of the Khmer Empire and Angkor civilization. It later declined, and in the 20th century went through the horror often called a "self-genocide," in which Cambodians killed Cambodians on a mass scale. Today its monarch has almost no real power, and he puts Cambodia's economic potential in Southeast Asia's second tier.

13|90.c: A cruise ship is a utopia at sea, far removed from land and everyday life.
13|90.e: Having boarded more than 100 cruise ships over a decade-plus, he compares cruising to a utopia at sea, cut off from land and routine. On board he has seen original Picassos. At night he has watched a volcano erupt and lava pour into the sea, and he recently sailed to Antarctica. He hopes people can find comfort in ships and the ocean, along with an unusual spiritual experience.

items.d: Lava flowing into the sea at night
Sunrises, sunsets, stars, arrivals and departures

13|90.c: To judge a cruise ship, look at staff per passenger and space per passenger.
13|90.e: He offers two key measures for judging a cruise ship: how many crew members there are for each passenger, and how much space each passenger gets. These two ratios directly determine the quality of the experience on board.

result.d: The key measures of the experience

13|90.c: Small luxury cruise ships and mass-market ones offer completely different experiences.
13|90.e: He sorts cruise ships into mass-market ships, river cruises, expedition ships, and small luxury ships, with huge price differences between them. On small luxury ships he has seen original Picassos hanging on board, entire walls made of gold and copper, and unlimited caviar. Still, he also recommends mass-market cruises to listeners.

14|65.c: Singapore's language policy scrubbed it clean and uniform, while Hong Kong kept its complexity and ambiguity.
14|65.e: He compares the two cities. Singapore once gave two languages equal weight, then made English the main language of schooling and pushed hard to squeeze out Chinese dialects. The change met resistance and had costs. It reshaped the whole country and brought some downsides. To him, the remade Singapore is neat and uniform, as if it had been disinfected. Hong Kong, by contrast, still keeps its own complexity and ambiguity.

items: From two equal languages to mainly English
Met resistance, came at a cost
Two written, three spoken languages, highly mixed

14|65.c: Hong Kong's mix of languages leaves learners in a bind that is both a blessing and a curse.
14|65.e: Hong Kong runs a "two written, three spoken" policy: Chinese and English in writing, and Cantonese, Mandarin, and English in speech. The result is a very mixed language environment. He discusses whether the policy should change, and argues that language learning in Hong Kong is caught in a paradox. That is both the city's luck and its misfortune. He also jokes that if someone's Chinese and English are truly equally good, it probably means they aren't very bright.

14|65.c: Hong Kong's young people feel lost, and even top exam scorers now choose medicine over finance and law.
14|65.e: He believes Hong Kong's economy is trying to find a new role, a process full of myths and confusion, and young people have become disillusioned along with it. One surprising sign: the city's top scorers on the university entrance exam no longer choose finance or law. Almost all of them now go into medicine.

items.d: The way ahead is clouded by myths
No clear sense of the future
No longer finance or law first

15|101.c: Going abroad really means running your company as a local American business.
15|101.e: She reframes going global. The question isn't how to do cross-border business, but how to run a local company in the U.S. From there, the product, the team and the marketing all have to be rebuilt around the rules of the American market. You can't just take your Chinese product and methods and run them remotely from home.

marks.d: Run it from China, export the product

15|101.c: Globalization has entered a "3.0" phase, so startups can target the U.S. from day one.
15|101.e: The guests don't think globalization is simply going into reverse. They call this stage "globalization 3.0," and one new feature is that it's more even. Over the past three years, remote tools like Zoom have made working across distances more equal. So going global is no longer just for big companies. A startup can set itself up as a global company from the start and plan for the U.S. as its first market.

items.d: Zoom makes cross-border work more equal
No longer just for big companies
Build a global setup from day one

15|101.c: To make it in the U.S., local marketing and good storytelling matter enormously.
15|101.e: Chinese companies entering the U.S. often stumble on go-to-market, meaning how to bring a product to customers, and on cultural details. Americans are sensitive about topics like age, photos and having children in ways that differ from China. The guests stress that the U.S. market puts huge weight on marketing and storytelling. Add a solid product and service and a local team, and a company can hold its ground. They point to Zoom's Eric Yuan and Otter.ai's Sam Liang as Chinese founders who built global companies.

items.d: Leaders who know the local culture
Care around age, photos and having children

15|101.c: Cold emails, 996 work hours and leaning on connections, common in China, often fail in America.
15|101.e: The guests list Chinese habits that often don't work in the U.S.: finding customers through cold emails, the 996 or even 007 schedule (9am to 9pm six days a week, or nonstop), and relying on ties to government and big companies. America is a capitalist society, they say, but it's also built on people and relationships. Tech companies there can find hiring harder than fundraising. Even a Chinese giant may be a small fish overseas and has to adapt.

items: Relying on government and big firms
Chinese giants are small fish here

d.verdict: Copying what works in China often fails in the U.S.

15|102.c: Think globally when setting strategy, but act locally when executing in each market.
15|102.e: Joyce has visited more than 100 countries. Drawing on that, she argues for using the global market as the frame for strategy, while digging deep into each market's culture and rules when it comes to execution. This complements the idea that going abroad means becoming a local company. A global view without local execution, or local work without a global frame, won't produce a truly global company.

result.d: Scale plus a fit for each market

16|105.c: Nearly two-thirds of internet managers have left, because companies grew bloated during the boom years.
16|105.e: He estimates that close to two-thirds of mid- and senior-level internet managers have left. For 20 years the industry grew fast on new technology and a flood of new users. That didn't demand much management skill, so organizations ballooned. Once growth turned into cutthroat competition and companies had to reinvent themselves, the bloat turned into infighting. He sees this round of cuts as a necessary self-correction. He also argues the so-called age panic isn't about age: fast growth hid some people's weaknesses, which show up once real innovation is needed.
ex: Baidu: under 100 directors when he joined in 2013, 200+ at the peak, later trimmed below 200

items.d: Driven by new tech and new users

16|105.c: Those leaving are either financially free or still restless, and they head down three main paths.
16|105.e: He splits the leavers into two groups. Some have made enough money and choose to rest or invest. Others haven't, or still feel unfulfilled in their careers, and keep looking for new ground. They head in roughly three directions. Some become angel or venture investors. Some go deep into traditional industries such as cross-border e-commerce, new consumer brands and smart cities. Others chase next-generation tech like AR/VR, Web3 and AI-generated content. As for when to step off, he says there's no absolute right or wrong. It depends on each person's mission and path.

items.d: Cross-border e-commerce, consumer brands, smart cities

16|105.c: Over 20 years there were four good times to join the internet industry, with very different outcomes.
16|105.e: He walks through four good moments to join. Around 2000, as the PC internet began, Tencent or Baidu was the place to be, but most people picked foreign firms, consulting or finance. After the 2008 financial crisis, the PC internet found better business models and pulled in consultants. Then came the shift to mobile in 2012–13, and mobile merging with AI and other industries in 2015–16. The first wave mostly became bosses or got rich. The second became VPs at big firms. Some of the third moved into consumer brands and smart manufacturing. The fourth is mostly still remaking industries with new tech.

items.d: Join Tencent or Baidu; many became bosses
Some later moved into consumer brands, manufacturing

16|105.c: The internet hasn't run out of chances. It's become a slower train with many more stops.
16|105.e: As easy growth fades, he sees the internet as a train that has slowed down but stops at more stations, because internet thinking can be grafted onto more industries. At its core, that means deciding with data and technology, innovating constantly, and shipping something imperfect, then improving it fast. Traditional product development is a straight chain of steps. The internet approach spirals upward on real-time user feedback. The hard part: internet people who join traditional firms lack a platform behind them, their grasp of the industry can stay shallow, and bosses often give them only three to six months to fit in.
ex: New products take Nike 18 months to launch, Zara about a month, SHEIN 7 days
SHEIN also uses algorithms to predict trends, win customers and choose suppliers

d.verdict: SHEIN blends the two better than anyone

16|105.c: Many founder-led Chinese firms face a succession crisis, and Midea's horse-race method is worth copying.
16|105.e: He notes that many first-generation Chinese companies face a succession crisis. Founders' children may not want the job or be able to do it, so professional managers need grooming early. Midea ran a long "horse race": before stepping down, the founder gradually handed management power to several candidates. In 2012 he passed the company to Fang Hongbo, who had joined in 1993, and the family now attends just two board meetings a year. In traditional industries with complex value chains, he thinks insiders have the edge. A successor needs strategy, an eye for innovation, a grip on operational detail, and the ability to pull the organization's resources together.
ex: He calls Fang Hongbo one of China's most successful professional managers
He mentions BCG is studying how founder-led firms transform and pick successors

items.d: Gradually share power among several candidates
Knows the whole chain and a huge organization
2012; the family steps back to the board

16|105.c: Now, while people are still unsure, may be a better time to get on board than ever.
16|105.e: He thinks now is a good time to get in, maybe better than any moment before. His logic is that rewards will rebalance. Pay for internet managers is falling. Returns are rising where traditional industries adopt internet thinking. And people who truly master next-generation tech and innovate can still earn huge rewards. He likes three areas: new consumer brands backed by real tech and R&D; smart manufacturing, industrial internet and SaaS (software sold by subscription) that bring big data and AI into traditional industry; and new AI, metaverse and Web3 products tied to concrete industry needs.
ex: Traditional-industry managers usually earn millions of yuan a year, rarely 10M+, but stars reach 100M+

items.d: Traditional firms using internet thinking earn more

17|113.c: Family offices, which manage wealthy families' money, boom at a certain stage of growth, and China is there.
17|113.e: Her logic: once a country's GDP reaches a certain size and a middle class forms, families want to move part of their assets out of the local currency and invest globally. Japan and South Korea went down this road. Citing consulting-firm figures, she says roughly 15% of GDP ends up invested globally. China is at that stage now, and more and more of its global investing will run through family offices. Singapore, Hong Kong and Dubai are all competing for these clients.

items.d: Japan and Korea went this way

17|113.c: Hong Kong stocks move on money flows with nothing to anchor them, so every swing gets amplified.
17|113.e: She sees Hong Kong as a trading floor for global hot money, the fast-moving speculative kind. Money chases prices up when it floods in and dumps stocks when it leaves, so valuations and company fundamentals can't hold prices steady, and swings are huge. She has lived through several rounds: within a few years the Hang Seng Index lurched between just over 10,000 and over 30,000. Her rule of thumb: daily turnover is usually about HK$100 billion, and a jump above HK$200 billion may signal a top. She is also extra careful every October.
ex: Tencent: about HK$240 in May 2017, 400+ by early 2018, a peak near HK$711 in 2021
Mainland A-share turnover above 1 trillion yuan a day signals overheating

items.d: Peak of the tech-driven bull market

17|113.c: Hong Kong stocks will likely trade in a range in 2023. The big risk is a geopolitical shock.
17|113.e: She credits the rally since late 2022 to several pieces of good news arriving at once: COVID controls lifting faster than expected, support for property developers' financing, the internet crackdown largely ending, easing geopolitical tension, and U.S. rate hikes nearing a peak. The pullback after Lunar New Year came from profit-taking, plus strong U.S. data reviving rate-hike fears. Valuations are still below their five-year MSCI average, and foreign money is returning, with hedge funds first and long-term investors waiting. So she expects range trading for the year, unless a geopolitical black swan hits.
ex: India, Vietnam: 20-plus times earnings. Chinese and Hong Kong stocks: 11–12, a five-year low
State-owned firms can yield about 12–13% in dividends; China Mobile, CNOOC and big banks top 5%

items.d: Hedge funds first, long-term money waits
A black swan is the biggest unknown

17|113.c: Hong Kong capital moved from British to local to mainland to tech firms, and now toward wealth management.
17|113.e: She divides Hong Kong's financial history into four eras: British trading houses in charge; local family conglomerates rising in the 1970s and 80s; mainland Chinese firms arriving around the 1997 handover; and, after 2017, new-economy companies such as internet and tech firms listing in Hong Kong, cashing out and reinvesting in new startups. That last wave drove the 2017 bull market, as these firms did IPOs in Hong Kong or second listings after U.S. ones. The host suggested the next stage is wealth management. She agrees Hong Kong is becoming a wealth management hub, and the rise of family offices is the sign.

items.d: The four big British trading houses
Mainland firms arrive around the handover

17|113.c: Once you have real wealth, set up a trust with insurance to pass down both money and values.
17|113.e: Without a plan, she notes, a death means splitting assets under inheritance law, and parents, children and even ex-spouses may all stake claims. It gets very messy. A trust, where assets go to a trustee who manages and pays them out by set rules, shields risk, clarifies ownership and names beneficiaries. With terms written in advance, children don't need prenups that make partners feel distrusted. She suggests putting insurance in the trust to lock in an entrepreneur's value at their peak, and insurance and loans inside a trust can add leverage. Passing on values matters as much as passing on assets.
ex: Terms can reward marrying, having kids, getting into an Ivy, or doing charity work
Most detailed clause: money only after a yearly grave-visit photo with headstone and newspaper

terms.d: Locks in the founder's personal value

17|113.c: Setting up a family office is too easy. There are more family offices than families.
17|113.e: In Hong Kong, a single-family office only needs to register a company to manage its own family's money. There's no license and no minimum capital. A multi-family office that manages other people's money needs a Type 9 asset-management license, and the rules are being tightened. Because the bar is so low, many middlemen stitch together a few small clients and call themselves a family office. She compares it to China's earlier P2P lending and private equity startup crazes. Hong Kong, she says, has tax, legal and proximity-to-China advantages. Singapore is more like a box for parking money: lots of it, mostly sitting idle in private banks.
ex: A Hong Kong investment promotion official joked there are more family offices than families
Singapore's trading volume in Hong Kong stocks is only about a tenth of Hong Kong's

d.verdict: Low barriers make quality wildly uneven

18|119.c: Brand management trains you better than consulting, because the real skill is getting close to users.
18|119.e: He studied semiconductors at Tsinghua, then sociology at Columbia, where he found the field had shifted to small-scale studies of organizations and psychology, so he moved into consulting and marketing. Consulting teaches you an unfamiliar industry fast, he says, but being a brand manager at P&G trained him more. He interviewed customers himself and used what he learned to push Pringles toward break-proof packaging, less oil and more flavors. It's hard for Chinese people to make cultural products in America, he thinks, but understanding users can break through. His advice: after 40, play to your strengths; before 40, there's still time to fix weaknesses.
ex: For Sun Hung Kai's 50-year strategy at McKinsey, he mapped China's pace onto U.S. industrial history
Ping An in Shenzhen hired McKinsey early, for about $1 million with a small team

items.d: Brand manager, interviewing users in depth

18|119.c: Yahoo lost its founders' soul, focused on making money, and missed the shift to search.
18|119.e: He and Qi Lu worked in Yahoo's search and platform group, he on marketing and Lu on engineering, for about four and a half years. He thinks Yahoo's core problem was that its founders stepped back too early. The professional managers who took over lacked the nerve for technical innovation and bold change. They focused more and more on making money and forgot Yahoo was meant to be an innovative company. Users were moving from browsing directories to searching directly, and Yahoo didn't keep up. His lesson: founders shouldn't leave the helm lightly.
ex: He and Qi Lu weighed buying Google but passed; Yahoo later outsourced search to Google, feeding it
P&G likewise underrated Starbucks-style coffee culture and missed buying it
Richard Liu left JD.com and came back, which he cites as why founders shouldn't step away

items.d: Users moved from directories to search

18|119.c: Bet big on acquisitions that matter, then hold back and leave the acquired team alone.
18|119.e: He believes acquisitions succeed or fail on company culture. Forceful, operations-heavy companies always want to remake what they buy right away. Google was willing to bet big where it counted, then left the original team alone for a long time before slowly finding ways to fit it in. Its failures were mostly small deals. Yahoo did the opposite. It spent money where no bet was needed and rushed to integrate where it should have gambled, so most of its acquisitions failed.
ex: Google bought YouTube in one go for $1.9 billion
Keyhole, which became Google Maps, kept running much as before for ten years after the deal

items.d: Keep the team's way of working

18|119.c: Google has the algorithms and computing power. What it lacks is data on what users do next.
18|119.e: He breaks AI competition into algorithms, computing power and data. Google has plenty of the first two. Its weak spot is real-world use cases and closed-loop data: it sees what people search for, but not how much they spend on the takeout they then order, or whether they liked it. Google Maps is one of the few places it sees the whole loop. Microsoft invested in OpenAI and opened up data from search, Word and more, building a pipeline to feed the model. ChatGPT also keeps improving from huge numbers of user conversations. Add Google's tense relations with several governments, and losing round one isn't surprising.
ex: He likes Amazon's staying power: many use cases and a top smart-speaker maker's conversation data
He expects China and the U.S. to build separate AI ecosystems, sharing no data or algorithms

18|119.c: Meta's problem is organizational: Zuckerberg never sorted out roles with his number two.
18|119.e: He thinks Meta lacks a mature organizational structure, and Zuckerberg wasn't deft in handling his relationship with Sheryl Sandberg, Meta's former COO. Google, by contrast, set up Alphabet so founders and professional managers could split duties and hand over gradually. When Sandberg left Google years ago, her number two in sales stepped in smoothly. His advice: Zuckerberg should step back to chairman, make Sandberg CEO, and focus on new bets like the metaverse. He puts both Meta and Twitter among today's laggards.

d.verdict: Zuckerberg should become chairman and focus on new bets

18|119.c: This AI revolution is bigger than the steam engine and at least as big as the internet.
18|119.e: He was there when Netscape and Google were just starting, and he vividly remembers how a revolution feels. He thinks the change ChatGPT brings is at least on par with the internet, which itself was bigger than the steam engine. In the future, people's jobs will center on highly original creative work, companies will compete on efficiency and how much AI they use, and midsize companies will get their chance. A startup that isn't thinking about AI hasn't thought hard enough. He also thinks Chinese teams have decent computing power but slightly weaker algorithms, and the key is how many talented people they have.
ex: Google's early employees worked in a converted railway car
He thinks Qi Lu could become China's Sam Altman

marks.d: The earlier revolution he compares to
Bigger than the steam engine, he says
At least as big as the internet

19|119.c: The Fed's choice was clear: protect depositors and let shareholders take the losses.
19|119.e: He sees clear priorities in the rescue. Depositors get all their money back, so the startups and venture funds that banked with SVB are safe, while shareholders are left out. That shows regulators care most about keeping confidence in the deposit system, not about protecting the bank's investors.

d.verdict: Keeping faith in deposits beats protecting investors

19|119.c: The crisis isn't over. The real danger is a loss of confidence in banks.
19|119.e: Depositors have been made whole, but he thinks risk could still spread along three paths, and all of them come down to a crisis of confidence in the banking system. Until that confidence is repaired, a run on one bank, where depositors rush to pull their money out, could happen again somewhere else.

19|119.c: SVB failed, but at heart it's still a good asset.
19|119.e: He stresses that SVB was a landmark bank built to serve innovation. What went wrong was how it handled its assets as interest rates rose, and how badly it handled the crisis. Selling Treasury bonds turned paper losses into real ones and set off the run. Its mission of serving innovative companies wasn't the problem. So even after the collapse, it remains a good asset.

terms.d: The run spiraled out of control

19|119.c: This is not a 2008-style Lehman doomsday.
19|119.e: He compares this crisis with the collapse of Lehman Brothers in 2008, and from the start judged it would not turn into a doomsday collapse of the whole financial system. But he also warns that not being doomsday doesn't mean it's over. Whether the risk spreads further still needs watching.

20|124.c: Brazil lacks local growth-stage funds, and its midsize companies are missing.
20|124.e: She noticed that Brazil's complex tax system and strict labor laws leave a gap in its business landscape: there's no real layer of midsize companies. There's a gap on the money side too. No local venture funds invest in growth-stage companies. SoftBank was once very active but has pulled back, most active investors are U.S.-dollar funds, and the ways for investors to cash out are limited.

20|124.c: Brazil today looks a lot like China did seven or eight years ago.
20|124.e: Based on basic data like population, age structure and GDP, she thinks Brazil is at roughly the stage China was seven or eight years ago. Food delivery and ride-hailing already have players such as Rappi, iFood and 99, which Didi acquired. Chinese internet companies like Kuaishou, Didi and ByteDance have moved in too. There are opportunities and challenges alike.

items.d: The basics resemble China's earlier years

20|124.c: In Latin America, business runs through introductions. Cold emails don't work.
20|124.e: She found Latin America has a strong culture of go-betweens. Cold emails from strangers get almost no reply. When she first arrived in São Paulo, she built her local network bit by bit using her reporting skills. The takeaway: to get into the local market, you first have to get into local networks of relationships.

d.verdict: Get into the network before the market

20|124.c: Brazil is slowly climbing out of crisis, while Argentina is still stuck in inflation.
20|124.e: She thinks Brazil is gradually recovering from its political and economic crises. One local investor even told her that their political instability is itself a kind of stability. Argentina is a different story. Inflation is out of control, and changing money means handling thick stacks of cash.

items: Thick stacks of cash to change money

21|28.c: Generative AI is a decade-long trend, and it's improving faster than Moore's law.
21|28.e: She sees the move from AI 1.0 to AI 2.0 as a fundamental shift in approach. After the image generator Stable Diffusion came out, Qingliu began focusing on AI-generated content, because users can see and use the output directly. Earlier AI, mostly sold to businesses, rarely managed that. It's also improving faster than Moore's law, the rule that chip power doubles roughly every two years. So she sees AI as a solid, long-term direction for the next ten years.

items.d: Qingliu starts focusing on AI content

21|28.c: OpenAI won because it had conviction, money, resources and people all at once.
21|28.e: Google owned the underlying technology but didn't make the first breakthrough. Her explanation is that OpenAI had conviction, money, resources and talent at the same time. It was born from the industry's worry that Google would dominate AI. Then Sam Altman secured Microsoft's investment and huge amounts of computing power, which showed real foresight. She also thinks Google's talent is strong and it will catch up.

root.d: Not Google, which had the tech

items.d: Born to keep one firm from dominating AI
A dense pool of top talent

21|28.c: General-purpose models belong to big tech. Startups should go after narrow, industry-specific uses.
21|28.e: Building a large model takes heavy capital, a dense team of top talent and a long runway. Burning $50 million to $100 million a year is normal, so small venture checks don't help much. That's why she bets on giants like Baidu and ByteDance, and Qingliu doesn't actively invest in large models. Startup opportunities lie in narrow vertical niches protected by hard-to-copy data, like healthcare with its strict privacy rules. A general writing tool like Jasper will see most of its use cases covered by ChatGPT.

d.verdict: General models go to giants; startups go vertical

21|28.c: Prompt engineering is a passing phase, like the search tricks people once had to learn.
21|28.e: She compares it to how search engines evolved. Early users had to learn search techniques, and Baidu's Yu Jun even wrote a book about it. As the technology improved, any phrasing would find results. Prompt engineering, the craft of wording instructions for AI, is the same kind of transition. In the future, people will be able to ask in whatever way they like.

21|28.c: China will have a second major model, and the U.S. won't stop at OpenAI.
21|28.e: She disagrees with the claim that China doesn't need a second large model. She expects China to have one, and the U.S. won't have only OpenAI either. She also warns that relying on someone else's model through their API turns a company from attacker into defender.

marks.d: More than one in both countries

22|140.c: No need to spend $50 million on a new company. Building on the existing business is more realistic.
22|140.e: Over dinner with Wang Huiwen and others early in the year, he estimated a Chinese OpenAI would need at least $50 million, a separate company and a year of heads-down work. A month later he changed his mind. Too many people were building large models, and opinions had converged too fast. If you aren't pushing the frontier, open-source models and Nvidia's computing platform have lowered the bar a lot. So he's building on Mobvoi, working on core model capabilities and applications at once, iterating on feedback from the existing business, and not raising money for now. He hasn't given up on AGI. A gradual path just suits him better.
ex: Original estimate: $20M for compute, $20M for hiring, $10M for labeling data
Mobvoi began in Aug 2020, paused after ~8 months over an unclear business model, restarted last September
Its model has tens of billions of parameters, easier to manage than trillion-parameter ones, he says

d.verdict: Not chasing the frontier means no costly fresh start

22|140.c: This wave's real breakthrough is that one general model can handle all kinds of tasks.
22|140.e: He recalls his time on Google Translate. From 2005 to 2012, Google trained statistical speech recognition and machine translation on huge datasets, but by around 2012 adding more data and machines had hit a ceiling, and accuracy sometimes even dropped. Deep learning has more capacity and can learn abstract patterns in data. ChatGPT's key is generality. Speech and translation used to have separate teams, data and code. Now one system unifies many abilities. And the model teaches itself by predicting the next word, with no need for human labeling.
ex: Training data grew from tens or hundreds of millions of tokens to about ten trillion
He agrees GPT-4 shows sparks of AGI, splitting general intelligence into generality, abstraction and planning
His wow moment: ChatGPT follows a conversation and banters, rather than just retrieving matching text

items.d: More data and compute stop helping
One self-taught system for many tasks

22|140.c: OpenAI won on conviction, a product feedback loop and its talent mix. Google lost on organization.
22|140.e: In Silicon Valley he found that even people inside OpenAI can't fully explain why it works. But it has three advantages. It has believed in artificial general intelligence since GPT-2, while many at Google didn't. After GPT-3 opened up in June 2020, it used user feedback to gather data and improve models, a loop that has run for about two and a half years. And its research, product and engineering people work well together. Google has plenty of compute, data and talent, but research and business units are siloed, so moving resources and shipping products is hard. His conclusion: on highly uncertain bets, being ten times stronger doesn't guarantee a win.
ex: Academic teams switch topics after each paper; DeepMind works project by project, as with AlphaGo

root.d: Google had more resources but fell behind

items.d: Improved on user feedback for 2.5 years
Research, product and engineering work together
Research and business units are siloed

22|140.c: What protects large models is computing power, years of accumulated skill and endless trial-and-error experiments.
22|140.e: He sees three layers of barriers. At the bottom is computing power: without enough chips, you can't train a model. Next come model design and data collection and cleaning, which take years of accumulated experience. On top, this is a highly experimental science that needs lots of machines to tune settings and test results over and over. He compares building large models to building hardware, with each cycle taking at least six to eight months. Even a rival like Google can't skip that.

items.d: Many machines tuning and testing repeatedly
Design and data cleaning take years

22|140.c: China's large-model race will be ten times as intense as America's, with 50-plus companies entering.
22|140.e: He sees large models as more like the post-iPhone moment than the browser moment. Phones are everywhere, intelligence has just broken through, and within five to ten years almost no field will be untouched. The last generation of AI companies struggled because their business models didn't work: high cost, low return. Demand this time may be ten or a hundred times bigger, but supply has exploded too, and everyone reached the same view too fast. His math: China has about twice as many startups as the U.S., while U.S. customers pay about five times as much each. Multiply them and you get 10x. Within a year or two, 50-plus companies will be building large models.

22|140.c: Most people shouldn't rush into general models. Figure out the use case and business model first.
22|140.e: He doubts China will produce an organization like OpenAI, thinks OpenAI itself may not repeat its success, and is somewhat pessimistic about its business model. The winners will more likely be vertically integrated: pick one main use case, collect user data, train your own model and keep improving it. Companies relying purely on third-party models will struggle to build a lasting edge. So he urges peers not to leap into general models. He admits that two months ago he wanted to copy ChatGPT himself. Ten years of startup life have been hard, and now he leans toward the long game, adjusting as his thinking changes.

items.d: Pouring in within a year or two
A real use and business model first
Use case, data and own model in a loop
Third-party models alone give no edge

23|142.c: Large AI models will move from an elite tool for a few to something everyone can use.
23|142.e: He sees large language models as, at heart, a capacity for logic and reasoning. He sees two paths ahead: a handful of "Einstein" top-tier models, and widely available everyday models. He expects the technology to shift from high-end and proprietary to broadly accessible, with lots of everyday large models appearing.

d.verdict: Large models will go from exclusive to everywhere

23|142.c: This AI revolution compares to the steam engine. The internet is too small a comparison.
23|142.e: He says this is the first time humans have stopped putting machines at the center and instead made machines revolve around people. Because it changes the relationship between people and machines itself, its scale should be measured against the birth of the steam engine. It's a revolution in productivity, not just another internet-style wave.

marks.d: Like the birth of the steam engine

23|142.c: Expertise built for the old approach is now a burden. Put applications first.
23|142.e: Under the new approach, the knowledge graphs and word-splitting techniques that older language AI built up are no longer advantages. They have become baggage. He comes from interaction design and has always put applications first, so he cares most about use cases that can really ship, like search, office work and social.

root.d: Drop old baggage like knowledge graphs

23|142.c: Large models finally make it possible for robots to enter people's homes.
23|142.e: He has been building robots for several years and lived through AI's slump of the past two or three years. GPT changed how people interact with machines, making it possible for robots to truly enter homes. He discusses when that might happen, what robots would cost and what form they'd take, and suggests robots could be the "next Tesla" of the large-model era.

items.d: The past two or three years
When, at what price, in what form
A hardware opportunity in the model era

24|151.c: The valuation premium for business software will fade, with price-to-sales falling below 10x.
24|151.e: He admits enterprise software has carried a valuation premium for the past two or three years. Judging by many signals, from the second half of this year to the first half of next, the sector's price-to-sales ratio, a company's value as a multiple of its yearly revenue, will drop below 10. Valuation is also shifting from revenue alone to revenue plus profit, as the industry returns to normal.

items.d: The past two or three years

24|151.c: Business software firms are heading for break-even, setting up a wave of IPOs in 2025.
24|151.e: Most of the enterprise software companies he has backed plan to break even on a monthly basis by the end of this year, and for the full year next year. On that basis, he expects a wave of enterprise software IPOs in 2025. Beisen's listing was a test run in this cycle.

items.d: First software IPO after the pandemic

24|151.c: This cycle of Chinese business software companies is healthier than the last one.
24|151.e: Compared with the last cycle in 2015–2017, he sees real change in Chinese enterprise software companies. They have customers who actually pay, they're closer to the public markets, and the industry is consolidating instead of staying fragmented. That's one reason he has stuck with the sector even as it cooled.

24|151.c: Large models have had their iPhone moment. Their Android moment hasn't arrived yet.
24|151.e: He thinks closed products like ChatGPT will be around for a long time, like the Mac and iPhone. But cheap open-source AI will surely appear too, like Android. Tesla opening its patents sparked the electric-vehicle wave, and open-source Android sparked the mobile internet. So open source plays a decisive role in shaping the ecosystem, and the foundations of the large-model landscape are still unsettled.

d.verdict: The landscape is unsettled; open source is the key factor

25|119.c: The race for general foundation models is over. A second company will struggle to get in.
25|119.e: He thinks OpenAI and Microsoft are already moving like monopolists. Emergent abilities, skills that suddenly appear as models grow, arrived 5 to 8 years earlier than Sam Altman expected. Large models are an opportunity, but the competition is brutal and many will be squeezed out. He doubts a second company will earn a ticket to the general-model game. A possible path for China is combining several small industry-specific models so they work like one large model.

items.d: Likely no room for a second

25|119.c: Foundation models belong to the young. Industry AI copilots belong to seasoned veterans.
25|119.e: The foundation models were built by young researchers under Sam Altman, backed by Microsoft. But the industry copilots built on top, AI assistants that help professionals do their jobs, require industry experience and connections. So they're more likely to belong to seasoned veterans. What he finds interesting is that the internet era shut out people over 35, while in the AI era people over 35 are thriving.

d.verdict: The real business is in industry copilots

25|119.c: In industry-specific AI, what protects you is data, relationships and your business model.
25|119.e: He thinks ChatGPT itself may swallow half, two-thirds or even more of the demand in many industries. So what protects the rest? In his view, the barriers for industry-focused companies aren't algorithms, or even computing power. They are data, social relationships and the business model.

25|119.c: OpenAI open-sourcing a model and Amazon entering the race will reshape the field.
25|119.e: He expects Amazon to release two models, one large and one small, within about a month, and thinks that's worth watching. He also predicts OpenAI will open-source a model, letting anyone use it freely, and walks through the knock-on effects. In his view, search is only the first battlefield in the large-model fight.
