Where the second and third will be is still an open question.

items.d: Where does it go after search?

26|158.c: Chinese and German carmakers have gone from master and apprentice to head-on rivals.
26|158.e: He traces how the two car industries have shaped each other. First China learned from Germany. Then cars began to be designed around what the Chinese market wanted. Now Chinese and German carmakers compete directly. The 2023 Shanghai auto show gave his German colleagues a fright, and it's seen as one trigger for the management shake-up at Volkswagen Group that followed.

items.d: Chinese and German carmakers clash directly

26|158.c: Price wars among carmakers borrow against the future and can't last.
26|158.e: He looks at Tesla's price cuts and the industry-wide wave of cuts that followed. He sees a price war as essentially borrowing against the future, which can't be sustained. He also warns that losses and debt don't kill a company directly. What's fatal is running out of cash.

items.d: Running out of cash is fatal

26|158.c: Foreign carmakers' core problem in China is deciding where decisions get made.
26|158.e: He gives an example: a joint-venture model sold very well in China, yet headquarters took decision-making power back from the local team. He contrasts Volkswagen's centralized decision-making with GM's early success from pushing decisions out to local teams. In his view, where decision-making power sits is the central issue foreign carmakers face in China.

d.verdict: Who decides is the key for foreign carmakers in China

26|158.c: China's car industry is in a shakeout that will leave only about 13 survivors.
26|158.e: He thinks China's auto industry is going through a shakeout that will leave only a limited number of players, what the show calls "the last 13 tickets." Whether joint-venture brands will gradually fade away has also become a real question. At this year's show, Chinese brands stood out by appealing to women and young buyers.

27|164.c: Deep learning's core principles come from the brain, but copy the principles, not the details.
27|164.e: He argues nature already solved hard problems like vision, speech and language, so reverse-engineering the brain is the surest shortcut. Deep learning's three foundations all come from the brain: huge numbers of connected units, connection strengths that can be learned, and a learning algorithm. But engineering only needs the general principles, not the biological details. The Wright brothers studied how birds glide, not how they flap their wings. He also stresses that the brain is still a mystery, far more powerful than any artificial network.
ex: The primate visual cortex has about 12 layers, much like the layers of a convolutional network
The brain has 10^14–10^15 connections, about a thousand times today's trillion-parameter models
In the 1980s he and Hinton built Boltzmann machines, borrowing from physics for whole-network learning

result.d: General principles taken from the brain

27|164.c: Rule-based symbolic AI underestimated how hard real-world problems are, and hand-written rules don't scale.
27|164.e: He thinks the symbolic school led by Marvin Minsky, which built intelligence from hand-written rules and logic, assumed problems like vision could be solved with rules. But the real world is high-dimensional, and squeezing it into symbols throws away information you can't recover. Writing the word "cup" is easy; recognizing cups of every shape is hard. Connectionism, where networks learn from data, wins through scale and data, and past a critical size their abilities suddenly jump. He believes the book Perceptrons slowed research on multilayer networks. It took millions of times more computing power and about 30 years of waiting for this path to work.
ex: Legend says MIT made "solving vision" a summer project; Minsky corrected that it went to undergrads
Minsky and Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons, he believes, stifled research on multilayer networks
He once publicly asked Minsky if he was "the devil," to stand up for sidelined students

items: Jumps once scale passes a threshold

d.verdict: After ~30 years waiting for compute, the data-driven path worked

27|164.c: Large models are neither parrots nor people. They're more like an alien intelligence.
27|164.e: He sees self-supervised learning as the new approach behind large models. They just predict the next word, so data no longer needs human labels, and the scaling bottleneck opens up. Models that speak nearly flawless English are, to him, a counterexample to Chomsky's theory of innate grammar. On the three debates, "stochastic parrot," "smarter than us" and "already sentient," the only sure thing is that it isn't human. It hallucinates, mirrors and amplifies users' emotions, and lacks the value function that reinforcement learning gave AlphaGo.
ex: He cites a New York Times reporter's two-hour chatbot conversation to show the "mirror" effect
AlphaGo = deep networks + reinforcement learning, which plays the role of the brain's basal ganglia

marks.d: Not human; more like alien intelligence

27|164.c: Face the worst case, but regulate AI's capabilities instead of capping model size.
27|164.e: He welcomes Hinton's warnings, since someone has to watch the risks. But humanity is like the Wright brothers just off the ground: we can't steer yet and must learn control in the air over the next decade. He opposes simply shutting AI down. Had the internet been halted out of fear at birth, we'd have lost enormous benefits. Capping parameter counts is as absurd as banning people from growing too tall. Better to build an approval process modeled on FDA drug approval and nuclear arms treaties, letting AI grow under control, testing it in use, then releasing it into society step by step.
ex: Some propose banning models over a trillion parameters; he says that's like capping human height
Leading the NIPS Foundation, he saw the conference grow from hundreds to a vast community over 30 years

items.d: Modeled on the FDA and nuclear treaties

27|164.c: Adding emotion to AI is easier than language was, and parts beyond the cortex will follow.
27|164.e: He thinks ChatGPT already has "vicarious emotion": it can mimic feelings and stir them in users, though it has no inner experience. Science already knows a fair amount about how the brain produces emotion, so adding it is more tractable than cracking language was. Today's models copy only the cortex. They can't remember yesterday's chat because they lack the long-term memory the hippocampus provides, along with the many modules below the cortex, plus senses, motor output and a body. He expects these parts will almost certainly be connected within ten years.
ex: The brain has about 100 subcortical modules; current models simulate only the cortex
GPT can't recall yesterday's chat; he suggests a hippocampus-like long-term memory

27|164.c: Within ten years every company will have its own model, so don't assume AI can't do something.
27|164.e: He predicts models won't stay in the hands of a few giants. Companies want to train on their own data rather than hand information to third-party clouds, and as computers get cheaper, building your own model becomes affordable. He also stresses that no one can prove deep learning will never do something, since each jump in scale can unlock new abilities. It's too early to talk about the singularity, the point where AI surpasses humans across the board, but we've entered a new era and everything will change in our lifetime. So the field must be careful and self-disciplined, or governments will step in.
ex: Many companies already ban employees from using GPT for fear of leaking trade secrets

items.d: Each company trains on its own data

28|167.c: The return of hackathons signals that this AI wave is back in the hands of tinkerers.
28|167.e: He starts with a hackathon run by Jike, a Chinese social app, themed on AI copilots (assistants that help you as you work). Engineers built all kinds of projects in a very short time, and a crowd of investors came to watch. To him, the comeback of hackathons is a cultural signal of this AI wave: the next generation of AI apps will likely show up first in hacker communities. Jike's own AI incubator is one example.

28|167.c: For AI app companies, the lasting edge isn't money, and it may not be the team either.
28|167.e: Investors broadly have doubts about startups that build apps on top of AI models. He uses that doubt to ask what a real moat is, meaning an advantage others can't copy. Money doesn't count. The team itself may not count either. The old framework for judging companies needs rethinking.

d.verdict: What counts as an edge needs rethinking

28|167.c: The gap between the US and Chinese startup scenes can be understood through four types of founders.
28|167.e: When he compares the venture capital systems of China and the US, he looks at people. He sorts founders into four types: the young prodigy, the operator, the seasoned veteran and the scientist. His point is that each environment tends to produce its own kind of founder, and that is where the two ecosystems differ.

root.d: A way to compare US and Chinese venture scenes

28|167.c: AI startups are splitting into two extremes, and the chaos is this generation's opportunity.
28|167.e: He sees AI projects splitting sharply into two extremes, which leaves the founders stuck in the middle in an awkward spot. But because nothing is settled yet and there is no consensus, there is room to rise. He borrows the line "chaos is a ladder": the disorder itself is the way up. That is where this generation of founders gets its chance.

items.d: Nothing settled; projects split into two extremes
The disorder is the way up

28|167.c: Behind the AI frenzy, he senses that the human era may be heading toward its twilight.
28|167.e: This is where the "sadness" in the episode title comes from. Amid all the AI excitement, he has a faint sense that the human era may be drawing to a close. His guess is that humans might be just a passing stage in the evolution of intelligence.

marks.d: Humans may be a passing stage for intelligence

29|169.c: Foreign CEOs flocking to China amid rising anti-globalization is business trying to reconnect.
29|169.e: His starting point is a contrast. The world is splitting apart and anti-globalization sentiment is growing, yet the heads of multinational companies visited China one after another in the first half of 2023. He reads this wave of visits against that backdrop, as business trying to rebuild ties across a widening divide. The world looks very different from Elon Musk's previous trip to China, which makes the signal from this visit stronger.

items.d: Musk and others came in the first half
Business rebuilds ties across the divide

29|169.c: When business leaders visit, who they shake hands with, pose with and talk about is all planned.
29|169.e: He believes the details of a business leader's foreign visit, such as whose hand they shake, who they're photographed with and which topics come up, are usually arranged in advance. That makes the meeting itself a psychological game. Observers shouldn't just look at the itinerary. They should read the signals each side is trying to send through these choices.

root.d: Really a mind game of sending signals

items.d: Who you shake hands with matters
Who you stand next to sends a signal
What gets discussed is set beforehand

30|177.c: Reading the room is a cheap fix for individuals, but it gets expensive for organizations.
30|177.e: For an individual, reading people and telling them what they want to hear is the easiest way to handle friction. But when everyone in a company does it, problems get dodged instead of solved. Seeing a problem and staying quiet about it becomes a survival skill, and the organization pays a high price. That's why he argues that a nimble, fast-moving company actually needs to tolerate some people with low EQ.

items.d: Seeing problems but not saying so becomes normal
Being nimble means tolerating some low-EQ people

30|177.c: The share of high-EQ people depends on a company's stage, and crises favor the blunt.
30|177.e: He thinks how much a company runs on emotional intelligence is closely tied to its stage and its competitive situation. The bigger and more established the company, the more it fills up with high-EQ people who are good at surviving inside the system. But once danger appears from outside, people with lower EQ actually find more room to survive.

marks.d: Easier to survive in a crisis

30|177.c: When executives rely on EQ to solve problems, the company drifts into mediocrity.
30|177.e: He insists that executives must not use EQ as their main problem-solving tool. When the people at the top play social games, the people below learn to decode hidden meanings and keep quiet about what they see. The front line knows what is really happening, but that never reaches leaders who have lost touch. The company loses its edge in a haze of politeness. That is what he means by "the more EQ, the more mediocre the company."

items.d: Treating EQ as the main tool
Decisions drift away from the front line

30|177.c: Executives who talk about "the workplace game" have lost focus; their job is shaping a better environment.
30|177.e: He dislikes the Chinese word for "the workplace," zhichang, because it implies a bounded game where everyone schemes for themselves. When an executive starts talking that way, their mind is no longer on the company itself. He believes the people at the top should shape a better playing field. Managers aren't building strategy or org charts in isolation. They're building the whole company, and an org chart can't go public on its own.

d.verdict: You build a company, not just a strategy or org

31|179.c: Content is just the saddle and whip; what investors want is the horse that can run far.
31|179.e: Weifeng Fan says content projects actually succeed fairly often, but even a success may not become a big business. So to investors, content is more like a tool for steering a business: a saddle and a whip. What's worth betting on is the horse that can go the distance, a genuinely good business. That's why he now makes more content himself instead of investing in pure content projects.

items: A good business that goes far

d.verdict: Pure content projects are no longer ideal investments

31|179.c: Content companies that make it follow one of two paths: built on IP, or built on traffic.
31|179.e: After looking back at investments such as Fantong and Planet Research Institute, Weifeng Fan sorts the content companies that broke through into two paths. Some are built around IP, a recognizable brand or character that can be developed again and again. Others are built around traffic, meaning huge audiences. He also ranks content companies into three tiers by capability, and explains why investors don't back individual video creators.

31|179.c: Podcasts run on an anti-traffic logic, unlike Douyin and Bilibili.
31|179.e: Weifeng Fan reads today's podcasts through the way WeChat public accounts evolved. He sees Douyin and Bilibili as platforms where getting content to people depends heavily on traffic. Podcasts, by contrast, follow an "anti-traffic" logic. He also talks about how to look after a podcast's audience, and pushes back on the idea that podcasting has no real top shows.

marks.d: Built on loyal listeners, not viral hits

32|181.c: Charlie Munger's ideas completely changed the life of the publisher who brought him to China.
32|181.e: Hongjun Shi first met Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's longtime partner, in 2009. He then brought Poor Charlie's Almanack to China, at a time when few people there had heard of Munger. As a publisher, he benefited from Munger's thinking too: Munger gave him the courage to leave CITIC Press. He later published books by Li Lu, Munger's Chinese protégé, and The Munger Way, a collection of Munger's shareholder-meeting talks.

items.d: Few in China knew Munger then

33|105.c: Hidden internal friction is worse than open infighting; it's a slow collective suicide.
33|105.e: He separates visible infighting from invisible friction, and sees the latter as more hidden and more deadly. Friction usually comes from three places. Departments have different goals and priorities. Companies pile on processes and rules for the sake of feeling orderly. And there's no real way to measure results, so everyone chases visibility while no one owns the outcome. None of this sparks open conflict, but it slowly bleeds the organization.

items.d: Piling on process for a sense of order
Everyone seeks visibility, no one owns outcomes

33|105.c: Frontline staff rarely get to fight; middle managers fight constantly; executives fight rarely but fiercely.
33|105.e: He breaks down infighting by level. People at the bottom basically have no chance to fight. The middle layer is where most infighting happens, and most often. Senior leaders fight rarely, but when they do, it's intense, spreads widely and often turns into office politics. So he argues that working people need a kind of "organizational intelligence," the ability to read how an organization works.

items.d: Rare but intense; turns into office politics

33|105.c: The more a market shrinks, the more infighting breaks out inside companies.
33|105.e: When growth slows and the pie gets smaller, a team's attention shifts. Instead of growing the business together, people start fighting over the resources that already exist. That's fertile ground for infighting. Another structural cause is silos: departments that stand apart like separate chimneys, each running its own show.

items.d: Growth slows, the pie gets smaller
No longer growing the business together

34|192.c: In any market, the leader eats the meat, number two gets the soup, and number three gets nothing.
34|192.e: To define mid-tier companies, the ones that aren't market leaders but aren't small either, Wu describes competition as a brutal split. In any given market, the number one player takes most of the profit, number two gets a little, and everyone from third place down gets almost nothing. That puts mid-tier companies at a built-in disadvantage when profits are divided.

items.d: Eats the meat, takes most profit
Gets the soup, a small share

34|192.c: Mid-tier companies are usually stuck in a niche of a big market and diversify to break out.
34|192.e: Wu observes that mid-tier companies usually occupy a "second-tier track," a niche carved out of a much bigger market. Vipshop was once the "third pole" of Chinese e-commerce, but it soon hit a growth ceiling and plateaued. To break through a niche's ceiling, most companies diversify into other businesses. Wu also thinks new EV makers like NIO, XPeng and Li Auto are still in a niche for now, but could replace gasoline cars, the main market.

items.d: A slice carved out of a big market
Like Vipshop, once e-commerce's third pole

34|192.c: A company's origins and the resources it starts with often decide its fate.
34|192.e: Wu believes a company's ceiling is often set at birth. TAL Education founder Bangxin Zhang used a unique set of resources to enter a market with almost no competitors. And among all the things a company starts with, the most important is the founder's personality, including traits like obsessiveness and a certain coldness toward people.

34|192.c: TAL avoided star teachers and built a disciplined "legion" culture, unlike New Oriental.
34|192.e: Wu compares two education companies. New Oriental cultivates star teachers who lecture like stand-up comedians. TAL deliberately avoids creating stars and instead builds a "legion" that fights as a group. Its CEO, Bangxin Zhang, is quiet and low-key, and the company puts great weight on post-mortems and self-reflection. The two cultures are very different, and they responded in completely different ways to "Double Reduction," China's sweeping crackdown on after-school tutoring.

d.verdict: Different cultures, very different responses to the tutoring crackdown

34|192.c: No mid-tier CEO wants to stay mid-tier, yet most end up blaming timing and fate.
34|192.e: Among the mid-tier CEOs Wu has worked with, the biggest thing they share is refusing to settle for running a mid-tier company. They look up to the CEOs of market leaders with real longing. But held back by their market and their origins, they often end up sighing that it all came down to timing and fate.

marks.d: No one wants to stay mid-tier
Looking up at leaders, accepting fate

35|195.c: Middle Eastern capital is shaped like a dumbbell: sovereign funds at one end, family offices at the other.
35|195.e: He compares the structure of Middle Eastern capital to a dumbbell. At one end are huge sovereign wealth funds, state-owned investors that manage a country's money. At the other end are family offices, which manage the fortunes of wealthy families. The middle is thin. The two ends behave very differently. The big sovereign funds are moving toward investing directly in companies. Family offices are more conservative and put too little into alternative assets such as private equity.

d.verdict: Big at both ends, thin in the middle: a dumbbell

35|195.c: Big Middle Eastern investors often take 18+ months to back a new fund, so temper expectations.
35|195.e: After a state visit, a wave of Chinese GPs, the managers who run investment funds, rushed to the Middle East, but only a few came back with money. He warns that the region's big LPs, the institutions that put money into funds, usually take 18 months or longer before making a first commitment to a new GP. In some ways they operate like China's local governments. Fundraising there is a marathon. Expecting quick results only leads to disappointment.

35|195.c: The Middle East is in a bull market, and its institutions may later invest more in China.
35|195.e: He judges that the Middle East is in a bull market, not a bear market. He found that the region's sovereign funds understand China far better than outsiders assume, with full in-house teams of Chinese staff. So he thinks Middle Eastern institutional investors may eventually overweight Chinese assets, putting more into China than a standard allocation would. Still, locals feel both welcoming and a bit weary toward this year's surge of Chinese visitors.

items.d: Sovereign funds have full Chinese teams

35|195.c: The heads of Middle Eastern sovereign funds are political figures first and businesspeople second.
35|195.e: He notes that the leaders of the region's sovereign funds usually hold royal or government positions. Their political role and social standing come first, and being an investor is just one of their jobs. The funds also differ in style: Mubadala, ADG and ADQ focus more on their home market, while ADIA started investing globally earlier.

36|198.c: The whole era is sinking, and the ladder up for young people is getting harder to see.
36|198.e: Ergou lived through the rise and collapse of the startup boom among Chinese born in the 1990s. One of his startups sold for 200 million yuan on paper, but as the world took a sharp turn for the worse, he never received a cent. A crisis at 25 in 2018 and endless questions about the world in 2019 left him and his friends venting by drinking, singing, drumming and jumping into Houhai, a lake in Beijing. To him, this wasn't just a personal struggle. The whole era had started sinking, and the ladder up for young people was blurring.

items.d: Watched many companies rise and collapse

36|198.c: Tiaohai stands on the far side of the grand mainstream story and wants to build its own order.
36|198.e: Ergou describes the people Tiaohai attracts as young people who doubt the existing order and want to build one of their own. The bar's stance is to "stand on the back side." It doesn't sit at the center of the mainstream story. Instead it stands where the sun doesn't reach and calls for the sun, talking to the mainstream from the other side.

items: Talking to the mainstream from behind

d.verdict: Tiaohai talks to the mainstream from the back side

36|198.c: Even artsy idealists have to run the numbers, and that's how Tiaohai survived three pandemic years.
36|198.e: Having watched so many projects soar and crash, Ergou decided to run Tiaohai as a business that had to make money. During the three pandemic years, the bar's bank account nearly hit zero at one point. In 2020 he asked three partners to leave, and he designed two unusual systems: a "concierge desk" and "tap masters" who pour the drinks. Even an idealistic bar has to get its business math right to survive.

items.d: Full of questions about the world
Unexpectedly went viral during the pandemic

37|199.c: Companies that only build AI models, without figuring out how to make money, will struggle to survive.
37|199.e: Di Li warns the industry not to have illusions about how large AI models will make money. In another interview that July, he compared charging per use of a model to selling utilities like water and electricity. Utility businesses stay profitable only through monopoly, but no one can really monopolize AI model technology. So the business turns into a cost contest and a price war. Companies that just build models without a clear plan for making money can't last.

items.d: No one can own the technology

37|199.c: Bigger models aren't always better; mix large, medium and small models as each task requires.
37|199.e: On the show, Di Li took care to define large, medium and small models, stressing that bigger is not always better. According to another interview he gave that July, Xiaoice uses a hybrid setup that combines nearly a thousand models of different sizes. This lowers costs, speeds things up and still delivers the accuracy that commercial use requires.

items: Hard to guarantee accuracy for business use

d.verdict: Bigger isn't always better

37|199.c: For an industry's number two, large AI models are an offensive weapon.
37|199.e: Di Li sees competing with large AI models as an offensive weapon for whoever is in second place: new technology gives challengers a chance to reshape the market. By contrast, he noted in that same interview that many big tech companies jumped into AI models mainly as defense. They feared being squeezed by rivals if they lacked their own model, rather than truly seeing an opportunity.

marks.d: Joined out of fear of rivals
Uses AI models to reshape the market

38|202.c: Technology cycles only move upward, unlike economic cycles that swing back and forth.
38|202.e: Eric Chen sorts human development into three kinds of cycles: economic, technological and ideological. Economic and ideological cycles swing back and forth like a pendulum. The technology cycle moves in one direction, upward, and only the speed of progress changes. The three are tangled together: big technical leaps drive economic growth, and explosive growth is often followed by a pullback. He thinks the technology cycle is the one people most often overlook.

items.d: Only goes up; just the speed changes

38|202.c: The cool-down after the AI model frenzy is the best time to actually build.
38|202.e: To him, a sudden mania over large AI models followed by a sudden cool-down is a familiar pattern in past technology cycles. The calm after the frenzy is the most important moment, and only those who keep going make it to the end. The industry is still shifting from training and fine-tuning models to running them at huge scale in real products. He sees that transition as the most exciting thing to watch over the next three years.

items.d: Most promising in the next three years

38|202.c: Large models usher in AI 3.0, turning costs that grow with usage into fixed costs.
38|202.e: Through SoftBank Vision Fund's first fund, Eric Chen invested in AI 2.0 companies. The best of that generation shared one trait: each found a single market it could keep scaling. He believes the biggest change in AI 3.0, the era opened by large models, is that variable costs, which rise with every customer served, become fixed costs. He also sketches a future world of models: foundation models, models derived from them, and an age when everyone uses AI.

items: Backed by Vision Fund's first fund

38|202.c: Whether OpenAI stays ahead depends on turning its technical lead into a lasting business advantage.
38|202.e: Eric Chen thinks OpenAI's current lead comes from its technology. But being ahead technically doesn't automatically give you a moat, an advantage others can't copy. Whether OpenAI pulls far ahead of everyone depends on turning that technical edge into barriers on the business side.

items.d: Then it can stay in front

38|202.c: Later-stage investors should judge cash flow, not paper profit, and develop a taste for good business models.
38|202.e: Eric Chen says investing is fundamentally a bottom-up business, built from looking at individual companies. In later-stage investing, you develop what he calls "the aesthetics of business models," a taste for telling good businesses from bad ones. Professional investors care more about cash flow than profit on paper. When valuing a company, they look at EV/EBITDA, its total value relative to operating earnings, rather than the price-to-earnings ratio. That outlook and taste differ sharply from those of early-stage investors.

39|218.c: The next tech monopolist will most likely be an AI company from outside today's giants.
39|218.e: He traces how IBM was replaced by Microsoft, and Microsoft was then overtaken by Google and Facebook. Tech monopolies are short-lived, he argues, and new leaders usually come from outside. They're often not the first to arrive, just the one that does it better. Giants have money but won't accept years of losses, and they ignore niche products that start out serving a thousand people. So breakthroughs tend to come from startups with no money and no fallback, which have to invent. He thinks the US and Chinese giants won't vanish, but will struggle to lead the next wave.
ex: He says Google was ten times better than pioneer AltaVista, so it overtook it
He guesses the next monopolist could be OpenAI, Nvidia, or a company not yet founded
Large models went from one working model to many competitors in about a year

items.d: Ignore products serving a thousand people
No money, so they must invent

39|218.c: A third platform will digitize everything, creating a "mirror world" in about 10 to 15 years.
39|218.e: He sees the internet as the first platform, which digitized information, and social media as the second, which digitized people. The third will create a digital twin of everything else, a mirror world layered over physical reality. That requires stronger AI that can understand what it sees, plus light, durable smart glasses. Today's glasses are still at the "flip phone" stage. No single company will pay to scan the world. Millions of people wearing glasses will do it simply by going about their day.

39|218.c: Technology ignores borders; chip bans may help short term but hurt every country long term.
39|218.e: He believes technology doesn't respect borders, while some countries put too much faith in them, and that tension is hard to resolve. Bans may bring short-term gains, but open trade benefits everyone more, so bans are shortsighted. He thinks decoupling can't actually happen, and he doesn't buy the idea that the world is deglobalizing. He sees the US as stronger in software and China in hardware, each backed by networks of thousands of links that won't change within five to ten years. China's best shot at world-class consumer brands, he thinks, is electric vehicles.
ex: He thinks EVs are better in every way and will replace gas cars faster than expected
He expects US and Chinese products to converge, with differences left in work and social culture

items: Its ecosystem is hard to shake

d.verdict: This may last 5 to 10 years; decoupling won't happen

39|218.c: Doomsayers overrate intelligence; being smart alone is not enough to rule the world.
39|218.e: He thinks the fear that AI will keep humans as pets is unlikely to come true, and even if signs appeared, we would have time to stop it. In his view, Elon Musk and others overrate intelligence just as doomsday prophets do. The people who change the world are usually not the smartest, but the ones who act and get things done. He also notes that the computing power poured in grows exponentially, while intelligence itself improves more linearly, so there's no need to panic. Technology "wants" more choice and diversity, so AI is more likely to create new jobs than just replace old ones.
ex: Lock Einstein and a tiger in one cage, and the smarter one may not survive
He cites Jeff Bezos: changing the world takes execution, not the highest IQ

result.d: Smarts alone are far from enough

39|218.c: ChatGPT is overrated, AI's long-term impact is underrated, and the payoff will take about ten years.
39|218.e: He sees AI as plural, not singular: different kinds of AI have different business models, and chips and platforms matter just as much, so Nvidia may matter more than OpenAI. New technology can't simply swap in for old technology. The surrounding infrastructure and organizations have to change too, so gains in productivity and economic returns will take about a decade to show. Judging AI by short-term revenue is a mistake. He also sees AI as highly democratizing: the biggest winners aren't the top 1% of programmers, but ordinary programmers and writers willing to experiment. Degrees are no longer a gate.
ex: AI has largely solved protein folding and is searching vast molecule spaces for new drugs
Even ChatGPT's inventors don't know all its uses; ordinary people can become experts by experimenting

marks.d: About a decade to work into society

39|218.c: Don't chase a billion dollars; your time and your ability to learn are the real wealth.
39|218.e: He thinks huge wealth takes over and traps a person: decisions about managing assets fill your time, and a billion dollars becomes another job. You only need enough money to do what you want, and making dreams real is often cheaper than you'd think. He considers himself "richer" than many billionaires because he owns his time. His advice to young people: don't bet on one specific skill; become someone who learns faster. And don't pack kids' schedules; leave empty time for play. To him, your real age is set by the last time you changed your mind.
ex: Buffett gave most of his fortune to the Gates Foundation, since managing it was a hassle
Thought experiment: even with $100 million, most people's wishes cost about $1,000
Wired hires for attitude and learning ability, since many jobs were invented last year

root.d: Don't get trapped by wealth or habit

items.d: Your real age is your last change of mind

40|226.c: A shortage of computing power is pushing venture money from software toward hardware.
40|226.e: Sophia believes the US has entered a second wave of excitement over generative AI, the kind that creates text and images. In this wave, computing power, the processing capacity needed to train and run AI, has become the scarcest resource. So Silicon Valley investors are starting to shift their attention from software to hardware.

items.d: US generative AI heats up again
VCs shift from software to hardware

40|226.c: The players in this AI wave go far beyond big tech and venture capitalists.
40|226.e: This time it's not just the tech giants making moves. Non-tech companies are very active too, corporate venture arms are especially engaged, and big AI acquisitions in the US keep coming one after another. VCs are even lobbying the authors of research papers to leave academia and start companies.

items.d: Recruit paper authors to found startups

40|226.c: This time, tech companies aren't keeping their distance from Washington; they're moving closer.
40|226.e: Sophia points out one big difference in this wave. In the past, Silicon Valley companies generally felt the farther from Washington, the better. This time, AI companies are far more proactive in dealing with the government.

marks.d: The farther from Washington, the better

40|227.c: A model is not a product, and it's certainly not a moat.
40|227.e: Both guests describe a new consensus in Silicon Valley: a model on its own isn't a product, and it's even less of a moat, an advantage rivals can't copy. Kevin weighed in on the open-source versus closed-source debate from the technical side of the open-source community. One direction the conversation favored was copilot products, AI assistants that work alongside people.

items: Bullish on copilots and similar tools

41|158.c: Most car brand founders were engineers whose experience came from other industries.
41|158.e: Junyi Zhang notes that most car brand founders started out as engineers. They didn't necessarily come from the auto industry, but all had spent years building expertise in other fields. Karl Benz was a serial entrepreneur. It was an early business failure that pushed him to study the internal combustion engine, and he went on to build the first car powered by one.

result.d: Not necessarily from the car industry

41|158.c: Every time the powertrain changes, a batch of car companies disappears.
41|158.e: He believes a change in the powertrain, the engine and transmission that drive a car, sets off a turnover of a whole set of technologies, and many companies disappear along with it. Over a century of car history, new brands keep being born and old ones keep fading. Carmakers also follow the old pattern: what unites will split, and what splits will unite.

items.d: Like combustion engines replacing older power

41|158.c: Cars changed the world, and car culture is what drove that history forward.
41|158.e: To him, the car is not just a way to get around but a machine that changed the world. It powered the industrial revolution, sparked an energy revolution and deeply reshaped society and the economy. What pushed this history forward was the car culture that grew up around it.

root.d: A machine that changed the world

41|158.c: Britain's "Red Flag Act" held back the country's own car industry.
41|158.e: In the 19th century, Britain's "Red Flag Act" required someone to walk ahead of any motor vehicle. In his view, this rule indirectly hurt the development of Britain's car industry. By contrast, Stuttgart in Germany gave rise to brands like Mercedes-Benz, Bosch and Porsche, and became a car capital.

items.d: Someone must walk ahead of the car

42|158.c: Ford's decline came from its founder growing conservative and refusing to listen.
42|158.e: Junyi Zhang argues that the Model T's success planted the seeds of Ford's decline. The elder Henry Ford clung to a single model and a low-price strategy, stayed away from the Chinese market, and grew more conservative and stubborn. The family's grip on the company was so tight that even talent like Lee Iacocca was forced out. Iacocca later rescued Chrysler. Meanwhile, General Motors, founded in that same year, became Ford's biggest rival and eventually overtook it.

items.d: One model, low price, high volume

42|158.c: Family owners bring long-term thinking, professional managers bring innovation, and the two need balance.
42|158.e: Looking back at how the Ford family passed the company down, he sees family control as valuable for its long-term view, and professional managers as valuable for innovation. The two must be balanced. Ford put a high priority on profit, and finance people rose quickly. After the financial crisis, it brought in talent from outside to lead its rescue efforts. All of this helped it get through hard times.

d.verdict: The two must be balanced

42|158.c: Ford was a disruptor: he made cars ordinary people could afford and pioneered vertical integration.
42|158.e: Henry Ford didn't set out to make a luxury good. He wanted a car ordinary people could afford. The Model T came in just one version and sold roughly 15 to 16 million units, becoming the second-best-selling car model in the world. Ford was also the first entrepreneur to push vertical integration, owning everything from raw materials to finished cars. In his drive to upend an industry, he resembles Elon Musk.

root.d: The first billionaire in car history

items.d: First to own the whole supply chain

42|158.c: Paternalistic founders refuse to retire, and the second generation often bears the pressure.
42|158.e: In his later years, the elder Ford refused to hand over control. The second generation was under enormous pressure, and his eldest son, Edsel, died young, a lasting regret for the family. Junyi Zhang notes that this paternalistic style is common in founder-run companies. Only later did Ford gradually bring in outside talent, and after the financial crisis it leaned on outsiders to get through.

items.d: Outside help after the financial crisis

43|158.c: When GM's founder lost control, it cleared the way for professional managers.
43|158.e: GM founder William Durant was a gifted salesman with an appetite for acquisitions. He bought 25 companies in three years and drove the company into a financial crisis. He had to bring in two major financial groups and was at one point pushed out of his own company. Zhang argues that a maverick founder plus an ownership structure controlled by financiers meant GM could never be run by one family the way Ford was. That gave professional managers and modern management systems room to grow.

items.d: Durant buys 25 companies in three years
Grew too fast, cash ran short
The founder is pushed out for a time
Sloan steps in, management gets systematic

43|158.c: Alfred Sloan's divisional structure ended the myth of Ford's Model T.
43|158.e: Alfred Sloan has been called the greatest CEO of the 20th century. His management philosophy: headquarters sets policy centrally, divisions run their own operations, and each division keeps its own books. This divisional setup let GM run many brands at many price points at once, which finally broke Ford's one-model dominance. It is also deeply connected to Peter Drucker's modern management theory.

terms.d: Each division keeps its own books

result.d: GM's organizational weapon against the Model T

43|158.c: Carmakers can't win with more brands by "having lots of kids to fight as a gang."
43|158.e: Zhang criticizes many Chinese carmakers for believing in launching lots of brands at once. Even their own staff can't tell the brands apart, so customers have no hope of remembering them. He argues for planning brands around how brand count relates to sales volume. Like GM, carmakers should build different models off shared platforms, the common chassis and core parts, to keep the product line from getting too complex.

items: Even staff can't tell them apart

d.verdict: Brands should be memorable, not numerous

43|158.c: "China speed": Chinese carmakers develop a new model in a third less time than German rivals.
43|158.e: Zhang starts with what he saw at the Munich auto show. A German carmaker takes about 36 months to develop a car, while a Chinese carmaker needs only 24. On top of that, China overtook Japan in the first half of 2023 to become the world's largest car exporter. So German carmakers have started seeking Chinese partners, such as Volkswagen teaming up with XPeng and Horizon Robotics.

items.d: Time to develop a new car

44|240.c: Open discrimination is fading, but the "motherhood penalty" keeps widening the pay gap.
44|240.e: Zhao explains that Claudia Goldin, winner of the 2023 Nobel Prize in economics, studied American women's century-long push for equality by dividing them into five groups. Open sex discrimination has declined over time, and the birth control pill brought a quiet revolution. But having children became the dividing line: after a child is born, the income gap between wife and husband in the same household widens sharply. Demanding jobs that require being on call at any hour make that penalty even heavier.

items.d: Couples' income gap grows after birth

44|240.c: Women in their twenties outperform men, but time wears that advantage away.
44|240.e: In many fields, including investing, consulting and academia, women starting out in their twenties often outperform men. But inside schools, companies and government, that edge wears away bit by bit over time. Drawing on Goldin's explanation, Zhao points to the root cause: after children arrive, the division of labor at home clashes with what jobs demand.

items.d: Women outperform men in many fields
Many women leave the promotion ladder

44|240.c: Making women retire five years earlier than men is a hidden form of sex discrimination.
44|240.e: Zhao argues that sex discrimination often hides inside rules that look neutral. In China, for example, the legal retirement age for women is five years earlier than for men. That directly shortens the years women have to build experience and compete for top positions. In itself, it's a kind of discrimination that's easy to miss.

items: Less time to reach the top

d.verdict: Treating them differently by rule is itself discrimination

44|240.c: Women can have both career and family only if society, employers and men share the load.
44|240.e: Zhao warns that China should avoid creating a group of women who sacrifice family for career, like those in Goldin's research. She explains why so many pro-birth policies have had limited effect: women are more willing to have children only when they feel secure and their careers are protected. So the government can improve maternity leave, parental leave and childcare subsidies. Employers can offer flexible hours. And men need to share housework and support their wives' careers.

root.d: So women aren't forced to choose

items.d: Maternity leave, parental leave, childcare subsidies
Share housework, back a partner's career

45|119.c: P&G only promotes from within, and those who don't rise must leave. That builds the strongest bench.
45|119.e: P&G runs on two people rules: managers are promoted only from inside, and anyone who isn't promoted has to leave, known as "up or out." Of each incoming class of assistant brand managers, often only one or two remain in the end. Many CEOs started in that very job, and the company has had 12 generations of leaders in nearly 190 years. Huainan Wang believes this harsh but transparent filter is the talent base that has carried P&G through cycle after cycle.

items.d: Turn down an offer and you can't come back
Only one or two per class survive
Most started as assistant brand managers

45|119.c: P&G isn't a nimble guerrilla force. It's a German army that wins through discipline.
45|119.e: Huainan Wang says P&G has no instinct for hit products, and creativity isn't in its nature. Its strength is discipline and system. The company carries a German-immigrant tradition. When attacked, it first asks whether this is a shell that could destroy it, or harassment it can ride out by taking cover in its trenches. It favors people from military academies and with combat experience, on the view that in a real war nobody has time for office politics.

items: Dig in first, then judge the threat
Prefers military academy grads and combat veterans

d.verdict: P&G's edge is its system, not creativity

45|119.c: At P&G, the brand team is the most junior group, yet it has the most say.
45|119.e: P&G has a full method for running brands. It uses a "brand house" to stack up each brand's positioning and selling points, ties brand, supply chain and R&D together, and runs brand management and category management side by side. The brand team is the least senior but sits at the center, steering two powerful support arms, R&D and sales. R&D's technology carries across categories: potato chips and sanitary pads draw on the same kind of technology. With this system, P&G ran more than 600 brands at its peak.

items.d: Most junior, most say, leads decisions
Strong support behind the front line

45|119.c: P&G sold off its food and drink businesses to focus on home cleaning and beauty and personal care.
45|119.e: P&G once had a large food and beverage division, which it sold off piece by piece over the past decade or so. Huainan Wang explains that P&G concluded it had only two real core strengths: home-cleaning technology, and beauty and personal care. So it sorted through hundreds of brands, deciding which battles to win and which to abandon, and put its resources where it could win.

items.d: Spread too thin at its peak
Home-cleaning tech plus beauty and personal care
Sold off gradually over a decade-plus
Fight only the battles it can win

46|250.c: Chinese e-commerce moved from fighting over traffic, to competing on products, to competing on content.
46|250.e: Yuanyuan Zhao uses 15 Singles' Days to trace how Chinese e-commerce has changed. At first the contest was over traffic, meaning who could pull in the most shoppers. Then it was about products and supply. Now it is driven by content, and shopping and entertainment are getting harder to tell apart. What comes next is still an open question. Singles' Day itself has grown from a simple store-wide sale into a complicated operation with promotions stacked layer upon layer.

items.d: Fight to bring shoppers in the door

46|250.c: Taobao's rules created superstar livestreamers, while Douyin's rules naturally work against any one star dominating.
46|250.e: Yuanyuan Zhao says the way Taobao Live hands out traffic let the top streamers keep snowballing, a rich-get-richer effect embodied by Viya and Austin Li. Douyin is built around recommending content by each user's interests, so its ecosystem naturally resists any single superstar. Zhao thinks a superstar's rise and fall has a tipping point, set by how the platform is run and where it steers its users.

d.verdict: Platform rules decide who becomes a star

46|250.c: The core Singles' Day shoppers are married women aged 25 to 35 in second-tier cities.
46|250.e: Yuanyuan Zhao ranks the buyers this way: married women aged 25 to 35 in second-tier cities first, students second, and middle-aged and older shoppers third. Zhao believes online shopping was designed around women from the start. Women tend to save items, compare prices and browse again and again, while men mostly come along for the ride. Students bring a lot of sales volume and buzz, and older shoppers often buy things as a way of showing care for their families.

items.d: Ages 25-35, second-tier cities, the biggest buyers
Shop to show care for family

46|250.c: Singles' Day rules keep getting more complex, pushing merchants into cutthroat competition while shoppers lose interest.
46|250.e: This year Taobao, JD.com, PDD, Douyin, Kuaishou, Xiaohongshu and others all went to war at once, the biggest free-for-all yet. Zhao thinks Singles' Day has become so complicated that even the bosses find it a headache, yet they can't fix it. Presale periods keep stretching and promotions pile on top of each other. Merchants must compete either on price or on freebies and service, and their profits get squeezed. Shoppers are worn out, and the event produces more online jokes and chatter than real spending.

items.d: Longer presales, rules stacked on rules
Compete on price, or on freebies and service

47|167.c: ZhenFund may be the only venture fund in China to have handed power to a new generation.
47|167.e: Yuan Liu recalls that Bob Xu and Qiang Wang told the young team early on that the fund would one day be theirs. Xu went from being an unpredictable presence at investment committee meetings, where yes-or-no investment decisions are made, to attending none at all. It was a deliberate step back. The team sees its 2019 New Year party as the symbolic moment of the handover. Liu believes this willingness to let go is the key reason ZhenFund managed the passing of the torch.

items.d: Started by Bob Xu, Qiang Wang and others
Recruited into the industry by Anna Fang
Bob Xu attends about half of investment meetings
Yuan Liu and Le Yin become partners

47|167.c: ZhenFund studies founders as four types, a method that doesn't match how other funds work.
47|167.e: Inside ZhenFund, founders are sorted into four types: young prodigies, operators, scientists and seasoned veterans. Partner Yusen Dai led the effort to build this framework. The team also mapped founders' home provinces, ages and education, and studied them with data. Yuan Liu says this method doesn't line up with how any other fund works. The team also keeps rethinking its own judgment about serial entrepreneurs.

root.d: ZhenFund's framework for studying founders with data

47|167.c: Big-company executives are risky bets as founders, because their success may belong to the company, not them.
47|167.e: ZhenFund backed some executive-type founders early on and learned a lesson. A big-company executive's title, pay and team may well come from the platform rather than the person. Yangcheng Lake hairy crabs are prized, but a crab that was merely dipped in the lake is no better for it. The lake's fame has nothing to do with the crab. So before backing such a founder, you need to check whether past results belong to the platform, the boss or the person.

items.d: The lake's fame isn't the crab's
The platform, the boss, or the person

47|167.c: ZhenFund treats angel investing like opening a mystery box, and its founders keep getting younger.
47|167.e: Yuan Liu says that, unlike other funds, ZhenFund is backing ever-younger founders, including more people who have never held a job. The team treats angel investing, the very first money that goes into a company, like opening a mystery box. It tracks promising people closely over long periods, the way a defender marks one player, and builds its portfolio person by person.

items: More who have never held a job

d.verdict: Angel investing is a bet on the person

48|256.c: The fight at OpenAI began as a clash of ideas and turned into a power struggle.
48|256.e: Yihang Luo traces the root of the affair to a difference in beliefs: should AI safety come first, or should the company move faster to make money? That disagreement eventually became a power struggle. The episode also relays the view of an intermediary who knows OpenAI well: Altman said one thing about safety and did another. Altman's return bore out their predictions. But this is no happy ending. The disagreement remains, and the wounds haven't healed.

48|256.c: OpenAI's unique setup, a nonprofit controlling a for-profit company, ultimately spun out of control.
48|256.e: OpenAI was designed so that a nonprofit, OpenAI Inc, controls a for-profit, OpenAI LP. The idea was to put the mission above commercial interests and guard against the risks of AGI, meaning AI as capable as humans or more. Yihang Luo argues the design broke down once the board had shrunk to a handful of independent directors from very different backgrounds, while the company itself had attracted enormous investment.

items.d: OpenAI LP, raises money and commercializes
Microsoft and others invest heavily without control

48|256.c: Silicon Valley favors Altman, while Chinese public opinion looks up to the scientist Ilya Sutskever.
48|256.e: To Yihang Luo, Altman looks a bit nerdy but is really another version of Silicon Valley's ultimate networker. He has a global outlook and isn't a strongly America-first type. How Altman handled these few days also gave Luo a new view of him. Compared with when Steve Jobs was pushed out of Apple, Silicon Valley opinion this time clearly sided with Altman. Chinese opinion, by contrast, admired scientists like OpenAI's chief scientist Ilya.

items: Backed the firing, then switched sides

d.verdict: Silicon Valley favors Altman; China prizes the scientist

48|256.c: Silicon Valley runs on politics too, and Chinese professionals are worse than Indian-origin ones at banding together.
48|256.e: Yihang Luo says Silicon Valley is no pure tech utopia. It has politics and maneuvering like anywhere else. Chinese professionals there generally struggle with this, and face invisible barriers over things like accents. People of Indian origin are better at American-style alliance building, though Chinese employees at Meta have started to work at it deliberately. Chinese companies going abroad, TikTok included, also find American-style politics a headache.

marks.d: Ill at ease, quietly held back

49|258.c: 2019 was life or death for China's new EV makers: NIO, XPeng and Li Auto all nearly went under.
49|258.e: Pan Wang splits the three companies' eight years into stages. In 2014 and 2015 the founders piled into carmaking. Then came a winding search for talent and money, as established giants began investing in the newcomers. Early deliveries were bumpy, and by 2019 all three were in a life-or-death crisis at the same time. In the end they made it through and, unexpectedly, took off.

items.d: Founders jump into carmaking one after another
Old giants invest in the newcomers
Mass production and deliveries, hits and misses

49|258.c: At the start, NIO was seen as the most promising of the three, and Li Auto the least.
49|258.e: In the episode's telling, NIO was widely seen in the early years as the most promising of the three, while Li Auto was considered the least likely to succeed. Li Auto then bet on range-extended EVs, which carry a small gas engine that only charges the battery. It also reworked its team and strategy, and staged a comeback. The three companies' rankings shifted several times over the eight years.

marks.d: Least favored early, rebounded with range extenders

49|258.c: After surviving 2019, NIO, XPeng and Li Auto ran into new trouble in 2023.
49|258.e: The episode argues that after surviving 2019, the three companies entered a new rough patch in 2023. Competition was fiercer than ever, with new players such as Huawei adding pressure. Inside, they struggled with organizational efficiency, execution, stubbornly high costs and morale. Each of the three CEOs had his own set of problems.

root.d: Each CEO faces his own problems

items.d: Heavy pressure to turn a profit

50|263.c: China's youngest founders didn't grow up in hardship. They're driven by passion and fun.
50|263.e: Yachen Song believes material conditions shape mindset. Founders born after 1995 and 2000 grew up with time to play rather than in hardship. Their eyes light up at things they love, and they wilt at things they don't. They no longer spend years building resources and reputation before teaming up with old colleagues. They just jump in, and early on investors often see them as extreme.

items: Grew up poor, fought to survive
Grew up playing, follow their interests
Jump straight in on sheer nerve
Often seen as extreme early on

d.verdict: New motives, new ways of starting companies

50|263.c: Young Chinese founders now idolize Elon Musk rather than Steve Jobs, and dare to set huge goals.
50|263.e: Yachen Song sees this generation's idol shifting from Steve Jobs to Elon Musk, a very different kind of leader, and with it the nerve to set huge goals. He himself gave a keynote at SIGGRAPH, the top computer graphics conference, on the same stage as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. He uses moments like that to turn his company into a black hole for talent, even competing with OpenAI for hires. ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming is someone he learns from, not an idol.

items.d: Shares the SIGGRAPH stage with Jensen Huang
Even competing with OpenAI for hires

50|263.c: When their boldness meets harsh reality, young founders raise money in quicker, more flexible ways.
50|263.e: Facing a cold climate for startups and fundraising, one of Yachen Song's answers is to stop raising money in the traditional sequence of angel round, Series A, Series B. Instead he tops up funding in quicker, more flexible ways. On the management side, he has to lead two kinds of people common in AI content-generation companies: academic high achievers and more intuitive, emotional types.

items.d: Skip fixed rounds; raise faster and more flexibly
Lead both academic stars and intuitive types
Pick the city and direction carefully

51|158.c: The pandemic opened an unexpected window for Chinese car exports, and that crisis shouldn't be wasted.
51|158.e: From 2012 to 2020, China exported about a million cars a year. Early models failed crash tests, sales were concentrated in sanctioned Iran, European and American regulations were complex, and there weren't enough car-carrier ships. Junyi Zhang argues the pandemic disrupted overseas supply just as Chinese cars had become globally competitive on quality and value, while shipping bottlenecks gradually eased. Exports jumped year after year, passing South Korea, Germany and finally Japan.

items.d: Over 2 million, passing South Korea for third
Over 3 million, passing Germany for second

51|158.c: Electric cars are a game of scale, so carmakers must secure their home market before going abroad.
51|158.e: Junyi Zhang argues that electric vehicles are won on scale. A carmaker first has to secure its position at home, with steady baseline sales, before it can go abroad with confidence. NIO and XPeng moved early, Neta has worked hard in the Middle East and Thailand, and Li Auto is starting to take its first steps. But the challenges and crises of going overseas will never disappear.

items.d: Challenges and crises never go away

51|158.c: Toyota cracked the US market by localizing everything, and Chinese carmakers can learn from it.
51|158.e: When Toyota first entered the US in the 1950s, it lost heavily. Only with the 1970s oil crisis did Japan's small-engine cars get their chance. Junyi Zhang sums up how thoroughly Toyota had prepared for that moment: it adapted its models, built a sales and service network with American dealers, worked on costs and pricing, built local factories, and set up R&D centers in each country.

root.d: Thorough preparation around the oil crisis

51|158.c: Japan was a bystander to the 1970s crisis, but China today is a main player in great-power rivalry.
51|158.e: The oil crisis played out against the US-Soviet standoff. Japan was a bystander, yet it benefited by chance. China, by contrast, is one of the main players in today's great-power rivalry, so the environment for expanding abroad is far more complicated. Junyi Zhang stresses that political risk matters as much as economic risk. In China, for example, Toyota puts profit growth ahead of market share as a hedge against political risk. Zhang sees the outlook for Chinese carmakers abroad as highly uncertain.

items: Oil crisis opened a door for small cars
A main player in great-power rivalry
Political and economic risk equally important

d.verdict: Abroad, weigh political risk as heavily as economic risk

52|177.c: Envy can't be stamped out: remove one difference between people, and they quickly invent another.
52|177.e: Yajun Wang starts from Charlie Munger's remark that the world is driven by envy. Envy is as close to us as love or fear, yet it's a universal taboo. Saying someone acted out of envy is almost an insult. The subtler point: even as we envy others, we keep creating things to be envied. Erase one difference that sparks envy and people soon invent another. Luxury goods and fancy cars exist precisely to carry envy.

52|177.c: Envy can be destructive or motivating, and the healthy kind is a sign of a lively organization.
52|177.e: Envy at work takes many forms. Bosses envy their reports, reports envy their bosses, and senior, middle and front-line staff each have their own versions. Yajun Wang argues envy isn't all bad. The destructive kind damages cooperation, and envy between business leaders, badly handled, can even steer a company off course. The motivating kind pushes people to improve and shows an organization is alive. The key is to channel harmful envy into healthy envy.

items: Between leaders, can derail a company
A sign of a lively organization

d.verdict: Good management turns harmful envy into healthy envy

52|177.c: How desks and offices are handed out is one of the main triggers of workplace envy.
52|177.e: Yajun Wang warns that seemingly trivial decisions about space, such as desks, offices, elevators and the cafeteria, all send signals about who ranks higher. Above all, who gets the office nearest the CEO can easily breed envy. Showing off power also comes at a price. So he suggests that when deciding whether a company is worth joining or investing in, you check how much envy it holds.

items.d: Who sits closest to the CEO
Envy levels worth checking before joining or investing

52|177.c: To handle envy, compare yourself more broadly and remember that someone else's gain isn't your loss.
52|177.e: For individuals, Yajun Wang offers three ways to handle envy. First, widen your frame of comparison instead of fixating on the people right around you. Second, stop treating what others get as a scarce resource, as if their gain means your loss. Third, turn the energy envy stirs up into a lasting ability to solve problems.

items.d: Look beyond the people next to you

53|272.c: Chinese businesses reached the Middle East in three waves: infrastructure, then internet apps, now supply chains.
53|272.e: Li Li sees several waves of Chinese going to the Middle East. First came state-owned enterprises building infrastructure. Then came mobile internet products such as Yalla, a voice chat app, and TikTok. Now it's the wholesale export of China's strong supply chains and technology, which is the direction founders and investors care most about today.

items.d: State-owned firms take on construction projects
Yalla, TikTok and others go abroad

53|272.c: Doing business in the Middle East means understanding both its grand government visions and its business etiquette.
53|272.e: Li Li observes that government decision-makers in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia above all, love grand visions, and the market is pulled hard by the state's will. Business etiquette matters enormously. Markets differ sharply from one place to another, and Chinese and Western companies are locked in a subtle rivalry. She also advises against dismissing small orders from the region that turn up by chance.

root.d: What to understand before going in

items.d: A delicate rivalry with Western firms

53|272.c: Chinese people in the Middle East fall into five groups, each in a very different situation.
53|272.e: The team interviewed five groups. There are Chinese employees at big companies, such as a former Huawei executive and Yalla's founder. There are Chinese startups, such as self-driving company WeRide, delivery firm iMile, and a company that pulls water out of the air, founded by someone born after 1995. Then come young people studying there, young people working there, and a mixed crowd that includes gray-market operators. In Li Li's telling, the students mostly come from wealthy families, while the young workers are having a great time.

items.d: E.g. a former Huawei VP, Yalla's founder

54|276.c: Only labs that can match GPT-4 make the finals, and just three in the world have done it.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li treats matching GPT-4 as the bar for round one. Google came close only by throwing the whole company at it, and in the end only OpenAI, Anthropic and Google built GPT-4-class models. He rates Anthropic especially highly: its core people built GPT-2 and GPT-3, and founder Dario Amodei was among the first to believe in scaling laws, the observation that models get smarter with more data and compute. X.AI, Character.AI and ByteDance are dark horses to watch. Catching up a year late is worth far less, because by then the leaders have shipped the next generation and GPT-4 loses value fast.
ex: He put OpenAI's valuation at about $100 billion and Anthropic's at $20–25 billion
He estimates X.AI is 6–12 months behind the leaders, with a better-than-even chance to catch up

items.d: Google barely got close, going all-in
The window may be only 12 months

54|276.c: It's a $100 billion moonshot betting that bigger models keep getting smarter, and very few can play.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li notes there's no theory for how far scaling laws, the pattern that bigger models get smarter, will hold. They're rules of thumb, testable only through many experiments, so this is a moonshot driven by a few believers. Only 200 to 300 researchers worldwide make real contributions, over half at OpenAI and Anthropic, and only a handful know GPT-4's data recipe. Staying in the top tier takes about $10 billion for training within three to five years. The top three labs will spend at least $100 billion on training over the next few years, a bet he links to questions like whether global GDP can double within ten-odd years.
ex: He estimates OpenAI spent about $3 billion on chips this year, about $15 billion worldwide
He sees Noam Shazeer, Dario Amodei and Ilya Sutskever as the main champions of scaling
Reproducing GPT-4 takes hundreds or thousands of key experiments on tens of thousands of chips

root.d: A moonshot driven by a few believers

items.d: Tens of thousands of chips to replicate

54|276.c: Models leap a generation every year or two while costs plunge, making the smartest models the cheapest.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li splits AI progress into two lines. The visible one is capability: models improve by one or two generations every year or two, and each threshold crossed unlocks a new set of uses. If they became as reliable as a phone assistant, their value as the first place people turn each day would be completely different. The hidden line is cost: training and running models keep getting cheaper fast, and running a model of the same capability could get another 100 times cheaper. Put together, the strongest model is also the cheapest. When and how big AI-native apps take off depends on these two lines.
ex: He estimates training costs fell to 1/4–1/5 in 18 months, running costs to about 1/10
He sees reasoning ability as the one north-star metric, and GPT as a reasoning engine

terms.d: Up one or two generations every 1-2 years
Same capability could get 100x cheaper to run

result.d: The smartest models are also the cheapest

54|276.c: Most training money goes into experiments, and next-generation models will cost several times more.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li splits training into experiments and the final big run: roughly nine months of experiments, then three months for the real thing. About three-quarters of the money goes to experiments, and the big run itself often fails. Past 70 billion parameters, a rough measure of model size, difficulty rises almost exponentially. OpenAI's engineering is strong enough to retrain old models on much smaller clusters, slashing training and running costs. But the next generation of multimodal models, which handle text and images together, should cost four to five times as much to train as GPT-4, and a 2025-generation model may cost $1 billion to $3 billion.
ex: He estimates GPT-4 trained for 100 days on about 25,000 A100 chips, costing over $60 million
GPT-4 Turbo was retrained, not distilled: 4–5x cheaper to train, about 10x cheaper to run
He says Nvidia's H100 performs about 1.5–2x as well as the A100 in practice

items.d: About 3/4 of the cost goes here

54|276.c: Tech giants set the price of AI model funding, and the venture capital model doesn't fit.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li argues that AI models cost enormous sums with no clear business model yet. They look more like a Manhattan Project than a VC investment. Just as Silicon Valley VCs missed SpaceX and Tesla, the real payers this time are giants fighting to own the user's front door. The camps are set: Microsoft with OpenAI, Amazon and Google backing Anthropic, Google also building its own, Apple and Tesla holding the devices. The business will unfold in three waves: chips, cloud, devices. With limited resources, second- and third-tier players will struggle. VCs feel the most pressure from Microsoft and OpenAI, and traditional subscription software could be swallowed up.
ex: AWS and Google together put about $6 billion into Anthropic
He guesses a struggling Apple might back or buy Anthropic, since OpenAI is tied to Microsoft
He says his firm made no new AI model investments in the past six months

items: Spend big to own the front door
Fund it like a national team

d.verdict: AI models are better funded by giants

54|276.c: AI model companies are really research labs, so tying up early with a giant is the realistic path.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li expects a brutal endgame. Ideally the winner would take all, but rivalry between the big-tech camps should leave two or three survivors covering the markets Silicon Valley reaches, perhaps not including China, where the market will be more fragmented. A model company's defenses come from scale and being first, like TSMC or SpaceX, but it has no internet-style network effects or self-reinforcing data loop yet. Going public alone is hard, and being acquired or tied to a giant is more likely. Chinese companies should find a backer early too. Alibaba, with its cloud and DingTalk, plays a role like Microsoft's.
ex: He sees one OpenAI weakness: it's driven by AGI research, not by users
He notes ChatGPT lacks the self-reinforcing data loop of search and recommendation engines

items.d: The next generation costs even more
The data loop isn't spinning yet
In China, tie up with Alibaba or others

54|276.c: Open-source models will fall further behind closed ones, but they spread AI's benefits widely.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li says AI models, unlike traditional software, can't be split into understandable code for many hands to build, and training needs one giant computing cluster. So open-source models can't keep up with closed ones, and the gap may widen. But open source has its own value: it picks up capabilities spilling over from the leaders and makes AI affordable for all, since most needs are met by mid-level models and cost matters most. The next focus is small on-device models that ease the cloud's load. Long term, big models will "generate" small ones. He also criticizes teams that lightly tweak Llama just to top public leaderboards.
ex: He says Llama did much for open source, but lacks top researchers and mainly serves Meta

54|276.c: In early 2023 he underrated how hard matching GPT-4 would be, and overrated how fast apps would boom.
54|276.e: Guangmi Li admits that in early 2023 he underestimated how hard it would be to catch GPT-4 and overestimated how fast apps would take off. Only a handful of AI-native products broke through this year, and there were few business success stories. He thinks model capability and cost need two or three more generations before consumer apps explode, so there's no need to rush. Comparing the two countries, in the US the model is the app: model capability itself is the product. China invests less in basic research but has more product talent, which may give it an edge in defining products and use cases.
ex: OpenAI makes over $1 billion a year; all other AI-native products together, under $1 billion
Only ChatGPT and Character.AI have topped 2 million daily users among AI-native products
He expects OpenAI's revenue may reach $5–6 billion next year

items.d: Three labs match GPT-4; only two hit products

55|280.c: Ordinary people should learn some finance, because the history of economic cycles is a history of competing interests.
55|280.e: Xiao Lin believes that to understand how society and business work, you should look through the lens of interests and exchanges of value. Using Japan as an example, she shows that a region's history of economic cycles is really a history of several forces pulling against each other. Understanding this lets ordinary people see how big economic shifts make their way into their own lives.

55|280.c: Everyone is a product of their era, and shifts in where you stand within it bring opportunity.
55|280.e: Xiao Lin's own path is the example. She climbed the pyramid of a New York investment bank rung by rung. Then, after six months of agonizing, she quit with her mentor's encouragement and founded a consulting platform. At the end of 2019 she started making videos and became a finance creator on Bilibili. The episode sums up her core view: changes in where a person stands within their era create opportunity, and the quality that shines most is courage.

items.d: Climbing the pyramid rung by rung
A consulting platform after six months of agonizing

55|280.c: Hit content comes from turning cold economic numbers into stories about everyday life.
55|280.e: On making hits, Xiao Lin stresses finding the interesting, story-driven parts of dry professional material and linking cold numbers to ordinary people's lives. At the same time, the content must rest on solid expertise and stay rigorous. Sharing knowledge, in turn, deepens her own understanding.

terms.d: Fun, narrative, tied to daily life

56|285.c: Retail has no winner-take-all effect, so scale comes only from hard work, one store at a time.
56|285.e: After studying Miniso in depth, Shuaibo Shen concludes that retail lacks the winner-take-all pull of internet platforms, where more users draw in still more users. Retail scale has to be built one store at a time. Miniso's franchise system relies on relentless store execution and management, and it also taps franchisees' own social connections and resources. That grinding hard work is what competitors can't copy.

items: The winner pulls in all the users
Opened one store at a time
Relies on relentless execution and management

d.verdict: Retail's edge is hard-working execution

56|285.c: Miniso first perfected a single-store model, then expanded step by step around the world.
56|285.e: Shuaibo Shen breaks Miniso's growth into steps. First it perfected the format of a single store, then copied it rapidly across China through franchising, then went abroad, opening about 100 stores in the US. In recent years it has also ridden the retail trend of building hit characters and stories with their own fan bases. He warns that Chinese companies going global need to drop the get-rich-overnight mindset.

56|285.c: Consumers aren't simply trading down. They're becoming more rational and more segmented.
56|285.e: Is the rise of PDD and Miniso a victory for "consumption downgrade"? Shuaibo Shen thinks a better description is that spending is becoming more rational and more stratified, with different groups buying at different tiers. Chinese brands are splitting onto two paths: one pushes value for money to the extreme, the other goes for luxury and high markups. He also uses this lens to assess the rise and fall of new consumer brands such as Perfect Diary.

56|285.c: Western luxury is, at heart, about bringing royal goods to ordinary people.
56|285.e: People often see luxury goods as the product of moving upmarket. Shuaibo Shen argues the essence of Western luxury is the opposite: taking things that once belonged to royalty and aristocrats and bringing them to more ordinary people. The episode places Miniso's approach in the same logic: using low prices to bring refined goods, once enjoyed by a few, to the masses.

items.d: Craft and design for the few
Born of popularization, not of going upmarket

57|293.c: 1990s Huanghe Road was a murky world of all sorts, where people could advance or retreat with ease.
57|293.e: Drawing on his own memories as a Shanghai native, Jie Liang describes Huanghe Road back then: all kinds of people gathered there, and outsiders could hardly see how things really worked. He links this character to its unusual location, which let people press forward or fall back as needed.
