Once the stock market heated up, it also became a landmark where investors gathered, the very backdrop of Blossoms Shanghai.

root.d: The main stage of Blossoms Shanghai

items.d: All kinds of people gathered here
Outsiders couldn't see how things worked
Its location let people advance or retreat
A gathering spot during the stock boom

57|293.c: China's early stock market started with just eight stocks, and everyone was feeling their way in the dark.
57|293.e: Jie Liang recalls that when the Shanghai Stock Exchange reopened, only eight stocks were listed, and the rules, the players and everyone's understanding were still being worked out. In such an immature market, one dramatic story followed another. Regulations were filled in gradually, only after each incident.

items.d: The Shanghai Stock Exchange opens again
Rules and understanding still being worked out

57|293.c: The show's big takeover battle is based on China's first stock market takeover fight, the Bao'an-Yanzhong affair.
57|293.e: Jie Liang unpacks the show's plot from an expert's angle: A Bao buying at the bottom, Boss Qiang's takeover attempt and the counterattack. He points out that the story is modeled on the Bao'an-Yanzhong affair, the first merger-and-acquisition battle in China's capital markets. This fight for corporate control, waged by buying shares on the open market, exposed gaps in the early rules and left important lessons for later regulators.

items.d: The acquirer secretly buys shares on the market
Announces its stake and bids for control
The first case pushes rules forward

58|295.c: Chinese entrepreneurs have come in waves since the economy opened up, and today's founders are the sixth.
58|295.e: Wu sorts Chinese entrepreneurs by generation. First came farmers and people on the margins of city life, starting from nothing. Then intellectuals left secure state jobs to go into business. After that, the PC internet and then the mobile internet carried Chinese entrepreneurs onto the world stage. He once called entrepreneurs a group that had long been overlooked. Today's founders, he says, are the sixth wave since reform began.

items.d: Founders who rose from village and township firms
City people outside the state system
Educated elites quit state jobs to trade
Fortunes made on PC and mobile internet

58|295.c: The sixth wave is the "strangest" generation of founders, because they start from a different place.
58|295.e: He gives three reasons. The era of rapid growth is over. Every market is already crowded. And many in this generation come from families that already own property and wealth. Their starting point, background, and surroundings all differ from those of the five earlier generations, who built everything from scratch. That is why their outlook and spirit differ most from those who came before.

root.d: Most unlike the five before it

items.d: No more rising tide for everyone

58|295.c: In a more conservative era, copying Moutai's slow craftsmanship is more realistic than copying Tencent.
58|295.e: Wu sees internet entrepreneurs as a revolutionary generation: they made money and got resources without relying on the government. But that needed a society in the middle of dramatic change. Now society is entering a more conservative period. Craftsman-style business leaders like Ji Keliang, the former chairman of the liquor maker Moutai, who won by honing one craft for decades, offer a path that is easier to copy. He also stresses that once the entrepreneurial spirit disappears, a country struggles to move forward.

items: Easier to copy in conservative times

d.verdict: In a conservative era, Moutai is easier to follow

58|295.c: AI favors big companies, so big opportunities will shrink, and young people should simply live as they like.
58|295.e: He sees AI as a platform-style, winner-take-all tool. Its benefits tend to pile up at big companies, instead of opening startup chances for everyone the way earlier waves did. From that he infers there may be fewer big businesses to build, and many people will settle for running small ones. His advice to his daughter's generation: stop fantasizing, stop trying to please others, and live the life you actually like.

items.d: A platform tool that favors big companies
Not everyone gets a shot at a startup

59|309.c: Building AGI takes a new kind of organization that fuses science, engineering, product, and business.
59|309.e: He believes technology shapes how things get made, and old organizations can't produce new things. Google Brain invented the Transformer, the design behind today's models, but not ChatGPT, because its research teams each chased their own ideas with no top-down, moonshot-style plan. AGI, AI that can handle almost any task a person can, needs frontier research plus refinement inside a big system with real users. So science, engineering, product, and business must merge. After ChatGPT, money and talent became available at once. He judged the window would be very short, so he started the company.
ex: Overnight in the US, he estimated compute costs: about $100 million needed within months
He thought the fundraising window was roughly February 2023 and had mostly closed by April
The company began with 30–40 people and grew to about 80, keeping the team elite

59|309.c: If a problem can be solved by scaling up, don't count on a new algorithm to solve it.
59|309.e: As early as 2017 he settled on language models. He sees them as modeling the world in probabilities. With enough tokens, the units a model reads, one can become a general model of the world. Later he saw it as the only problem that matters. Interning at Google taught him to stop endlessly tweaking architectures on small datasets and focus on the big direction. If a design is general and can scale, the scaling law (bigger models and more data mean better results) holds. He puts the odds of failure near zero. Even hallucinations, where models make things up, must be fixed by scale, just of something else.
ex: As a PhD student he led papers with Turing Award winners Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio

items.d: If scaling works, skip new algorithms

59|309.c: A model that reads very long text at once is like new computer memory: the moonshot's first step.
59|309.e: From day one he bet on long context: how much text a model can take in and remember at once. He sees it as the foundation of a new kind of computing. With lossless long context, images and audio no longer need separate tokenizers, and personalization needs no extra training: a user's full history with the AI is the best personalization. Quality isn't just length but faithfulness to the source, reasoning, and following instructions. Long context isn't catching up to GPT-4; it's a new dimension GPT-4 lacks. The next milestones, a world model that unifies all media and self-improvement without human data, are two or three years away, he guesses.
ex: Kimi, the company's only product, launched able to read about 200,000 Chinese characters
He likens year one to building and test-firing a rocket prototype, the moonshot's first step

items.d: Text, images, and sound in one model
Keeps getting better without human data

59|309.c: Make contrarian bets with real odds of being right, or you add nothing to humanity's ideals.
59|309.e: He argues that an ideal everyone can think of adds nothing to humanity's total stock of ideals. But contrarian doesn't mean different for its own sake: you must judge the odds of being right. Catching up to GPT-4 is a must for Chinese models, but not the finish line. You need unique abilities. From day one the company built only consumer products, and Kimi's north star isn't search. Being 10–20% better than search isn't worthy of AGI, and a product that gets only that share of its value from AI won't hold up. He sees little point in chasing leaderboards. The best ranking is how users vote.
ex: He thinks Chinese models have already begun to differ, but it will take time to show

items: Bet on your own read of direction
Early bets on long context and consumers

d.verdict: Contrarian bets must likely be right to add anything

59|309.c: Chasing near-term product-market fit gets you flattened by better models, so scale users and models together.
59|309.e: Investor Allen Zhu argues startups should find product-market fit first and that open-source models are enough. Yang sees "find fit in a year or two" and "change the world in 10 to 20 years" as two mindsets. The underlying technology caps what apps can do, and app-only companies keep getting run over by upgrades. Some uses jump from zero to one but have little room after, while stronger models open up exponentially more uses. So grow users and models together: you need users and revenue, and user input improves the model, but long-term investment can't stop. He also expects closed models to win by drawing talent and money.
ex: Customer-service, chatbot, and form-filling dialogue companies were all crushed by more general technology
He sees AI image tool Midjourney and copywriting apps as big leaps with limited room after

59|309.c: Sora is video generation's GPT-3.5 moment, and generating video is a byproduct of compressing the world well.
59|309.e: Sora, OpenAI's video model, did what he expected, just sooner, which shows the gains from scaling are far from used up. Its key breakthrough is keeping scenes consistent over longer stretches. The bottleneck is fitting data at scale. Its DiT architecture isn't general enough, and one architecture for all media is still unsolved. He rejects Meta AI chief scientist Yann LeCun's view that modeling the world by generating pixels is wasteful. Modeling video is also lossless compression, no different at root from predicting the next word. Video compresses the physical world and text compresses human behavior. The two will merge, linking the digital and physical worlds.
ex: He imagines Sora plus GPT handling more tasks end to end, like self-driving and housework
He admits Chinese models lag GPT-4 and Sora but could gain an edge within 2–3 years

items.d: Compressing world and behavior become one

60|312.c: Bubbles aren't scary: they leave behind infrastructure and a very few winners.
60|312.e: The view on the show is that a capital bubble isn't something to fear in itself. Money poured in during a bubble turns into infrastructure that future apps can build on. The cost is that most companies die, and only about 1% remain. So a bubble deserves respect, not fear.

items.d: Lots of capital and companies rush in
A few make it through the cycle

60|312.c: AI apps will take off later than mobile apps did, but will spread faster once they work.
60|312.e: AI apps have to wait until models cross a capability threshold, when they suddenly go from useless to useful. So they may show up later than mobile internet apps did. But once they are useful, they could spread far faster than mobile apps ever did. That means not being too optimistic about near-term adoption, and not underestimating the boom that comes after.

items: Need models to cross a threshold

d.verdict: AI apps arrive late but spread faster once useful

60|312.c: Investing in AI means mapping the talent, and young people are now leading major projects.
60|312.e: As an angel investor, someone who backs companies at the very start, Yusen Dai maps AI talent by tracing top North American AI schools, advisor lineages, and where people move. For example, Sora's two core authors came out of the same Berkeley lab. OpenAI's willingness to put a researcher born after 1995 in charge of Sora is seen as a sign of a young, energetic organization. Moves like Saining Xie and Kaiming He returning to academia, and Andrej Karpathy leaving OpenAI, are also signals on the map.

items.d: Four top North American AI schools
Someone born after 1995 can lead Sora

60|312.c: A true world simulator is still far off, and no one knows how to build one unified model.
60|312.e: Sora hints at a "world simulator," a model that can simulate the real world. But simulating the world means going from physical cause and effect to social cause and effect, and that road is long. The deeper obstacle is that no one has found a workable path to a single unified model that handles every kind of data, from text to images to video. That is a major hurdle on the way to AGI, AI that can do what people can.

60|313.c: The resources to catch Sora aren't out of reach, but catching up within a year is too optimistic.
60|313.e: The guests interviewed many people to piece together a rough picture of Sora's talent, computing power, data, and technical approach. This is a shared view the show gives in the voice of "we," and the episode page doesn't say who said what. The conclusion: the money and computing power needed aren't out of reach, and the leading AI model companies and big tech firms can all afford them. But Sora has raised the bar, and thinking anyone can catch up within a year is too optimistic.

61|317.c: Tech believers and market believers each see only half the picture. He wants to see both.
61|317.e: He compares Zhilin Yang's faith in technology and Xiaohu Zhu's faith in the market to blind men touching an elephant: one finds the trunk, the other a leg. That the two camps clash so hard shows each is incomplete. Each argument holds together, yet neither links technology all the way to a business. A cylinder looks square from the side and round from below, so arguing over its shape is really about viewpoint. He calls himself a third voice, working toward general AI and on specific uses. Technology is the engine, the market is the steering wheel, and a car needs both.
ex: Before his US trip: half a step slower, one step faster. After: one slower, three faster.
OpenAI wants ten million GPUs for training; Nvidia makes only about a million a year.

marks.d: Starts from tech, then finds uses
Ideals a step slower, use three faster
Backs only apps that earn money fast

61|317.c: His new company rests on one belief: once machines master language, strong AI will arrive.
61|317.e: For twenty years he has wanted to describe life with math, and he thinks Newton-style linear methods break down in tangled, nonlinear systems like living bodies. Using ChatGPT confirmed his earlier view: once machines master language, strong AI will follow. Language is the backbone of all concepts, so it can also become a new tool for modeling life. Sora, OpenAI's video model, is by contrast just a simulator. It doesn't understand physics, so it isn't a true world model. He decides by first settling vision, mission and technical route, unlike Meituan co-founder Huiwen Wang's heroic style of hiring first and thinking later.
ex: From 2021 he ran a sleep project to gather real-world health data from daily life
He brought a US phone home to use ChatGPT with his own account and IP
He chose to build large models in February 2023; by the April launch, about 50 staff

items.d: ChatGPT shows strong AI is coming
Vision, mission and tech route first

61|317.c: General AI isn't a hammer for every nail. He wants three model towers for three kinds of use.
61|317.e: He rejects the idea that general AI can simply do everything. Talking about a hammer that smashes anything, without asking where the nails are, doesn't explain why a model can solve a real problem. He sorts uses into three worlds. The virtual world is entertainment: novels, film and games all run on a story engine that can drive text, images, sound and interaction. The world of life is health and medicine. The real world is productivity and decision support. His goal is to "build people": human-like advisors such as doctors, lawyers, teachers, even scientists. A large model, he says, is at heart a decision engine.
ex: He calls the virtual world the Land of Illusion, borrowing from Dream of the Red Chamber
"General assistant" is too vague, he says; "advisor" describes the role better than "assistant"

root.d: Human-like advisors; the model makes decisions

items.d: Entertainment, driven by a story engine

61|317.c: Medicine demands the most from AI and offers real value, so it deserves a top model.
61|317.e: He says medicine reaches the sky and stands on the ground: it demands the most from a model and offers real value to people. Baidu and ByteDance stumbled in healthcare years ago because machines couldn't understand language, so they could only tweak processes like booking appointments. That has now changed. Building a top model turns model strength into a barrier others can't copy. Open-source and small models can't handle medicine, OpenAI could but chooses not to, and China's giants got burned and would need a true believer at the top to try again. That leaves an opening for Baichuan.
ex: If AI could "supply" a million doctors in China, he says, the value would be huge

terms.d: Real value for the people served

result.d: Turns model strength into a barrier

61|317.c: More important than product-market fit is technology-problem fit: new tech that solves an industry's old problems.
61|317.e: He broadly agrees with Xiaohu Zhu that a business must make money and needs real uses, but thinks Zhu sees only the fast-money market. Both markets exist. Saying a small open-source model trained for a few months is good enough is survivorship bias; small models can't handle big fields like medicine. Big fields need big technology, and nobody agrees on them yet, which is the opening. He values technology-problem fit: building the piano isn't the bottleneck, writing the score is. He agrees the US and China differ. The US has a hammer looking for nails, while China must open up uses faster so data keeps improving the model.
ex: Zhu said game characters were no edge; Wang asked: a corner shop or a skyscraper?
He shares Zhilin Yang's views on scaling and long text, not his "Moore's law of uses"

items: Find a product people pay for
New tech meets old industry problems
Model as a thinking, deciding engine

d.verdict: When tech fits real problems, real use runs three steps ahead

61|317.c: Fighting Sogou out of a dead end gave him the confidence to build large models.
61|317.e: Sogou entered search four years after Baidu and sat inside the web portal Sohu, with struggles outsiders never saw. Through its input method and browser, it still won about 18% of the market in Baidu's shadow. He sees the input method, the keyboard app that guesses what you type, as the product closest to a large model: it squeezes the internet into a language model that predicts the next word. His old "three-stage rocket" now becomes three layers: capability, use case, application. Being sidelined taught him respect and tolerance. He also thinks startups have shared interests and truer information, while big-company bosses get misled by distorted reports.
ex: He suspects Robin Li's "only two months behind" claim came from distorted team reports
Apple spent about $10 billion over ten years without a car, proving William Li right
The team has 240-plus people, about 70% on algorithms and 20-30% ex-Sogou

items.d: Led about 50; the group never agreed
Decided in February, announced in April

61|317.c: He stopped anxiously chasing GPT and started building what makes Baichuan different into the model itself.
61|317.e: Last year Baichuan sprinted after GPT, he says, starting late and scrambling for people and money until its first model shipped. After Chinese New Year he dropped two habits: treating catching up with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 as the main job, and putting capabilities in apps outside the model. Now model and app are built as one. Belittling technology and worshipping it are both unhealthy. If apps lag, the industry becomes a game of pitching investors. So when some on the team wanted to copy Sora, he stopped it within a week: it follows a different line from GPT and stands for neither AGI nor a real use.
ex: His bar for a super app: tens of millions of daily users
He could accept Baichuan being bought like Sogou, but won't live in anyone's shadow again

items.d: Build the edge into the model; drop Sora copy

62|324.c: Model-building startups lack real uses and data but carry high valuations, so he backs none of them.
62|324.e: He calls himself a market believer: he trusts apps that earn money right away, not pure technology stories. China has churned out more than 200 large models, which he sees as pointless. Startups have neither exclusive uses nor data, yet start at high valuations. GPT-4-level research costs at least $40-50 million and is wasted once someone open-sources a rival, so most startups don't really dare spend. He even thinks model companies may earn less than the old "AI Four Dragons," China's four star computer-vision startups. He believes many agree but stay quiet for fear of seeming not to believe in AGI.
ex: He dropped weekly calls with US colleagues after six months of arguing got nowhere
Chinese VCs, he stresses, have never made money by following the consensus

items.d: Over 200 models, hard to tell apart
Can't beat giants who own the data
One open-source release wipes out the spending

62|324.c: Tech founders won't merge and antitrust blocks sales to giants, so investors have few ways out.
62|324.e: He thinks founders with technical backgrounds never believe they're worse than rivals, so peers rarely merge. The natural exit is selling to a giant, but antitrust rules block that. Without them, he'd back Wang Xiaochuan, since the company could sell to Tencent or Alibaba. Some funds jumped in from fear of missing out, and Alibaba's big bet on Moonshot AI was a giant's FOMO too. A team that only matches open-source models isn't worth much to a buyer. He calls Huiwen Wang, a business talent, building models a techie's romance; Meituan buying his Light Year roughly returned investors' principal.
ex: Private model setups fell from about ¥10M early in the year to under ¥1M by year-end
Mobile internet's early "homegrown operating system" craze left few companies standing
He sees little appetite for deals at Tencent; Alibaba is the only giant showing interest

items.d: Price wars make solo survival hard
Tech founders won't defer to each other

62|324.c: The opportunity is in apps: sell to businesses first, replace human work with AI, and earn now.
62|324.e: He thinks China's first generative AI boom will be in services for businesses. Train an open-source model for two or three months and it reaches the top 30% of humans, enough to replace half a sales team. China's flood of short sales videos, plus clients' performance data, keeps improving the product, an edge the US lacks. US foundation models cost so much that the app layer is left with thin wrappers or grand projects that won't work soon. China's base models are weaker, so apps there can add value, often surprising foreign peers and Middle East investors. Sales management, which most model founders don't understand, is the scarce skill.
ex: An AI video-interview company doubled its interviews in 2023, to nearly a million
It raised a tenth of what its rival raised, and the rival has since folded

62|324.c: Consumer AI must wait for its "iPhone 3 moment"; apps people rarely use won't last.
62|324.e: He thinks large models are still at the iPhone 1 or 2 stage. A consumer boom needs an "iPhone 3 moment," like the multi-touch screen that set off the mobile internet. He sees personal assistants as fake demand. Consumer apps must be used often and truly needed; otherwise, once the technology curve flattens, they're easy to replace, which is why Midjourney, the AI image tool, can't hold its ground. He also tells Chinese founders not to build on someone else's foundation: make a great app on a Chinese model and the model company may simply copy it. Better to use open-source models.
ex: Half his team has switched to Gemini, at $10 a month, half ChatGPT's price

items.d: The experience matures and the masses arrive

62|324.c: Progress will slow after GPT-5, so the safest bet is letting the US experiment and China follow.
62|324.e: He thinks language models are nearing their peak. After GPT-5 progress will slow and breakthroughs will move to image and video models; Sora will also top out in a few versions. Open source trails closed models by about a generation, but catches up fast once the curve flattens, as Android did with iOS. True AGI is at least five to ten years off: more intelligence needs more energy, and before controlled fusion Earth lacks the compute. Cutting costs for 90% of jobs may take 3-5 years; the last 10% needs vast compute. So let the US experiment; China can follow at a tenth of the cost, with less risk.
ex: IBM and Lenovo in the 286-to-586 PC era: followers caught up as progress slowed

items.d: The gap shrinks as the curve flattens
At about a tenth of the cost

62|324.c: More people and money won't buy product-market fit. Don't burn cash; treat every round as the last.
62|324.e: He thinks AI startups can't find product-market fit by adding people and money; growing from ten staff to a hundred won't help. China's business software market faces three to five more years of winter, and survivors win, so the key is growing without burning cash. He has his companies budget to break even if revenue falls 20%, since money always goes out before revenue comes in. He likes number-driven software that runs on one GPU, not stories. On missing ByteDance, he admits he saw only personalized news, not Douyin. Zhang Yiming was reserved and hard to read; neither the man nor the numbers tipped him off. His biggest regret.
ex: Good founders explain the opportunity, its size and why them in under twenty minutes
He calls Ele.me, the food delivery app, his most idealistic investment

63|169.c: China's overseas buying spree peaked with the Syngenta deal, then came to an end.
63|169.e: Wei Wang sees this history as an era with a beginning, a climax and an end. Lenovo buying IBM's PC business and Geely buying Volvo were the pioneers: small fish swallowing bigger ones, in deals few expected to work. In 2016 a Chinese company paid $43 billion for Syngenta, known as the crown jewel of agriculture. That was the era's high point. Afterward, attitudes abroad toward Chinese buyers shifted, and the era slowly wound down.

items.d: A pioneer of small buying big
Chinese capital heads abroad to buy
Foreign attitudes toward Chinese buyers shift

63|169.c: A merger is like dating, marrying and living together. What matters most is knowing why you're buying.
63|169.e: He splits a merger into four stages: strategy, choosing a target, doing the deal, and integrating afterward. He likens them to finding a partner, getting married and living together. The first step matters most: be clear about why you're buying and what strategy the deal serves. Integration after the deal closes often drags on for years.

63|169.c: Chinese buyers tend to keep the staff and managers they acquire, the opposite of Western buyers.
63|169.e: In his view, Western buyers often cut jobs and replace management right after a deal, and the results are frequently brutal. Chinese buyers do the opposite and tend to keep the existing team. He puts the difference down to culture: East Asia's Confucian tradition makes buyers gentler toward the companies they acquire.

d.verdict: East Asian-style integration treats acquired firms better

63|169.c: Buying abroad is really buying time: you get a ready-made business instead of starting from scratch.
63|169.e: He explains why he pushed for buying companies abroad rather than only building businesses overseas. Buying a mature company skips the long years of building one from zero, and a proven business carries less operating risk. He calls this trading time for space. But he stresses that no deal is good or bad in itself; what matters is whether the price is right.

items.d: Get a working business at once
Only if the price is right

64|276.c: Physical hardware is now AGI's biggest bottleneck, turning the race from a sprint into a marathon.
64|276.e: He has revised last year's view that AGI was a 100-meter sprint where you could pile on chips and data without limit. Q1 brought Sora, Claude 3, an open-source free-for-all and Nvidia's big conference. Now he expects a longer, wider front: GPT-4.5 and GPT-5 will arrive later than hoped, and the top model changes hands within a month. Above all, data centers and energy now set the timeline. One data center can hold only so many chips, and America's grid, planned decades ago, can't handle the surge. In the short run, Nvidia's Jensen Huang matters more than OpenAI's Sam Altman.
ex: Past about 32,000 chips in one data center, many engineering problems must be solved
The top tier is OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini; xAI and others are second tier
Inflection dropped out: models grew alike too fast, and it had no big-tech partner

items.d: Data centers and power take years
The top model changes hands monthly

64|276.c: Climbing toward AGI has two faces: the south face is models, the north face is products.
64|276.e: He thinks there's no agreed definition of AGI. What matters is the intelligence itself, not its form, and it will eventually move from the digital world into the physical one. The south face is core capability: reasoning, coding, handling images and sound, and agents that act on their own. The north face is killer apps with hundreds of millions of users, such as information search. OpenAI climbs both; Anthropic climbs only the model side. AGI will unlock gradually, each year's model gains opening new uses, so far mostly faster coding and search. The economy tied directly to AGI is under 0.1% of the world's.
ex: In the rosiest story, AGI doubles world GDP from $100 trillion within 15-20 years
If AI took 10% of world GDP, that's $10 trillion, about 300 million white-collar salaries

items: AI that acts on its own

d.verdict: Abilities grow yearly, unlocking AGI step by step

64|276.c: Software will go from vending machine to bartender, and everyone will be able to build it.
64|276.e: He thinks AGI will first rewrite how software gets made. Old software was a vending machine: limited choices, with countless niche needs unmet. Once models understand plain language, use tools, and write and fix their own code, software becomes a bartender mixing to order, and developers grow from tens of millions of professionals to everyone. Microsoft plus OpenAI could swallow many single-purpose subscription business apps (SaaS); firms with complex workflows and unique data stand a better chance. SaaS companies must embrace young people because the methods have changed. Google's fact-finding search is the crown jewel challengers want.
ex: Startups like Cognition hit about $2 billion valuations with no revenue; AI coding is overheated
Coding's value mostly sits in base models, within reach of model labs and Microsoft

items.d: Made to order; everyone can build

64|276.c: Power plus chips equals intelligence. Without a big infrastructure build-out, there's no app boom.
64|276.e: He compares today to the Manhattan Project, the moon landing and the 1990s information superhighway: huge infrastructure comes first, then a golden age of apps. Money isn't the only bottleneck. Even with tens of thousands of H100 chips, you may not build a 10,000-chip cluster in three months. The hard parts are network layout, interconnects, stability, liquid cooling, land, and cheap, steady power. These are engineering problems, not research ones, so time will solve them. Near-term limits are TSMC's capacity, CoWoS packaging and high-bandwidth memory. Chips benefit first, then ad platforms, cloud and devices. The cycle runs 10-20 years, so long term it's no bubble.
ex: By his estimate, 8,000 H100s cost about $300 million; 100,000 need $3-5 billion
He expects about 4 million AI GPUs shipped this year, over 6 million next year
Training a GPT-5-level model uses about a fifth of Shanghai's daily electricity

64|276.c: Scaling hasn't slowed. Progress only looks slower because nobody has added enough compute and data yet.
64|276.e: GPT-4 used 20-30 times more compute than GPT-3.5, and no newer model has had such a jump yet, so it's too early to call a slowdown. Scaling laws, which say bigger models trained on more data get better, still hold. Good data beats extra parameters; there's roughly enough for GPT-5, but GPT-6 may need a breakthrough. Efficiency varies wildly: the same model can take hundreds of chips for one team and thousands for another. He rejects Xiaohu Zhu's views that AGI is five to ten years off and that progress slows after GPT-5, expecting a two-year plateau, then a jump. The real test: can agents finish long, valuable tasks?
ex: GPT-4: about 1.8 trillion parameters, 13 trillion tokens, 25,000 A100s for 100 days
Small commercial models can cost 10-100 times less and handle 60-70% of queries

64|276.c: OpenAI should target Google, the softest giant. Chipmakers will levy a compute tax, model labs an intelligence tax.
64|276.e: Chasing both AGI and a super app, OpenAI must make money. If AGI takes ten years, it needs billions to tens of billions a year, and relying on investors and Microsoft alone isn't healthy. Among the seven tech giants, it can't easily fight Microsoft for businesses, Nvidia for chips or Apple for devices; Google is the easiest target. Microsoft and OpenAI are stable, AWS backs Anthropic, and Nvidia will back three to five labs so OpenAI doesn't dominate. Short term, Jensen Huang has the upper hand. Long term, if chips escape Nvidia's grip, Sam Altman could be intelligence's new prophet: one collects a compute tax, the other an intelligence tax.
ex: ChatGPT must grow from about 50M to 300M daily users to shake Google, he says
Growing paid users from about 10 million to 30 million means roughly $6 billion a year
He estimates copying Sora takes 4,200-10,500 H100s training for a month

items.d: Collected by model makers like OpenAI
The physical limit at the bottom

65|28.c: The pass-the-parcel relay of rising valuations has broken, so most VCs now lie low.
65|28.e: She sees the chain that dollar funds relied on breaking. Each round bought in at a higher price, and an IPO paid everyone out at the end, like pass-the-parcel. Now fundraising and exits are both stuck. The earlier a shareholder came in, the harder it is to get out and the less bargaining power they have. Some have switched to living off dividends, and deals that look like equity but work like loans are hard to do too. So most firms have chosen to lie low.

items.d: Early backers stuck, with no leverage

65|28.c: The rules have changed: VCs used to profit from contrarian bets, and now they profit from consensus.
65|28.e: She believes the rules of the game have changed. Venture capital used to make money by backing what others doubted. Now it makes money on what everyone agrees on, so "venture" has come to mean avoiding risk. In practice that means investing in areas the state encourages: new energy, new materials and hard tech. Consumer companies are still worth a look, but only ones that make money.

items: Pass it on until the IPO

d.verdict: Venture capital has become investing that avoids risk

65|28.c: The industry has shrunk by at least a third, so she aims to survive like a Jurassic rodent.
65|28.e: She estimates the industry has shrunk by at least a third, and venture capital has become a game for fewer players. She hasn't left the table. Instead she casts herself as a rodent in the age of dinosaurs: when giants rule, the first job is to stay alive. Her position is already low enough that she doesn't fear it getting worse.

items.d: At least a third have left
Who should still put money into VC?

65|28.c: Big tech has closed the window for startups, so she has never touched general-purpose models.
65|28.e: She hasn't looked at large models since day one. Capability and resources sit with the big companies, and the "fool's window" that once let startups in has closed. Her AI bets avoid general models. She backed DP Technology, which uses AI for science, and aiXcoder, which does AI coding, and she sees opportunity in robot hardware itself.

items.d: Big companies dominate; the window is closed

66|140.c: Most frontier technologies get filtered out in a funnel; very few become real products.
66|140.e: Zhifei Li describes frontier tech as a funnel: many start, very few become standard products, and most eventually disappear. Early on, frontier technology usually reaches customers only through one-off custom projects, which are hard to standardize. In his view, a vision with no plan for the path and the pace is irresponsible.

66|140.c: A single model for every medium should be autoregressive, generating output one piece at a time.
66|140.e: He sees GPT-4o pointing the way: one model that moves freely between understanding and generating text, sound and images. He believes a unified model should be autoregressive, producing output one piece at a time, the way you write a sentence. GPT-4o can generate sound but not yet video, and Sora isn't autoregressive, so the two haven't been unified. Next, multimodal models must merge with embodied AI, AI with a body that acts in the real world. Only when reasoning improves will true agents, AI that does tasks for you, arrive.

d.verdict: A unified model should be autoregressive

66|140.c: As model prices collapse, companies that make money selling API access will struggle.
66|140.e: He saw ByteDance's steep model price cuts coming, and they're bad news for companies whose business is selling API access. Model companies, he says, must work out whether they'll still have a place after three to five years of all-out competition. He borrows a metaphor from Ming Zeng, Alibaba's former chief strategist: model companies stand on drifting ice floes. They must stay nimble and leap onto solid ice the moment it appears.

items.d: Pay-per-use sales get hard to sustain
What's left after 3-5 years of competition
Stay nimble, jump when the moment comes

66|140.c: Frontier tech startups often slide into a vicious cycle once they raise money.
66|140.e: He is broadly pessimistic about frontier tech startups and thinks they fail in similar ways. They focus on tactics and chase technical impulses, only thinking about strategy once fundraising goes wrong. Founders fall into illusions and ignore cash flow. In his view, the urge to expand after raising money can drag a frontier tech company into a vicious cycle.

items.d: Forced to shrink or limp on

66|140.c: Twelve years in, he has gone from arrogance and wasted effort back to pragmatism.
66|140.e: Looking back on 12 years, he admits early overconfidence in technology. He made strategic choices that left the company nowhere to stand when the giants rolled in, and worked hard in ways that achieved nothing. When he saw the company might die, he fell into depression for a while. At the bottom he saved it through layoffs, deliberately doing less, and careful attention to profit and loss. Later he channeled his tech urges into writing on his WeChat blog instead of shaking up the company. Ringing the IPO bell, he said the result didn't match 12 years of hardship.

items.d: Layoffs, doing less, counting every cost

67|177.c: Nvidia is organized like a GPU: decisions are spread out and handled in parallel.
67|177.e: Yajun Wang points to Conway's law: the way an organization communicates shapes the products it builds. At Nvidia about 60 senior executives report directly to Jensen Huang, information flows openly, and people "reason together." Decisions are spread across many nodes and handled at once, so the organization ends up looking like the GPU it makes, a chip that runs many tasks in parallel.

67|177.c: Each of Jensen Huang's management rules defies common sense, yet together they form a system.
67|177.e: He lists eight practices that seem to defy common sense. The 60 top executives are paid the same, down to the cent. There are no one-on-one meetings. Documents are discouraged; instead, employees email their five most important items. There are no layoffs. Nvidia builds only what others can't and ignores market share. And it doesn't make plans. Each rule goes against the norm on its own, but together they serve one distributed system.

items.d: 60 executives paid the same, to the cent
High standards push people to grow

67|177.c: To learn from Nvidia, give people context instead of tightening control.
67|177.e: Many companies copy Nvidia's surface rules, he warns, and the common mistake is to keep managing through control. The real point is to give employees full background and context so they can make their own calls. Strategy isn't words on paper; it's action.

d.verdict: Copy Nvidia by giving context, not adding control

67|177.c: Without love there's no innovation; fear is always innovation's enemy.
67|177.e: Nvidia lists love and care among its values. Yajun Wang argues that once fear rules an organization, people stop daring to experiment, and innovation dies. Trust is the foundation for spreading decisions out and working across teams. Only when an organization tolerates failure will talented people try what others can't do.

68|358.c: AI applications came in three waves over the past decade: computer vision, self-driving, and large models.
68|358.e: Yu Chen divides the past decade of AI investing into three waves. First came computer vision, which produced China's "AI Four Dragons." Then self-driving, where Level 4 autonomy, needing no human within set areas, proved extremely hard to deliver. Then large models. After investors went all in on large models at the end of 2022, the investment pace itself split into several phases.

items.d: Gave rise to the AI Four Dragons
Full autonomy proved hard to deliver

68|358.c: The large-model race is a poker game, and the giants hold the most chips.
68|358.e: He likens the model race to a poker table. The giants have the most chips, followed by the startups that lead in fundraising. For those further back, the first task is raising money, and this year there's a cutoff line for staying at the table. Club deals, where several investors buy in together, stand out in this wave. Even after watching the cards this long, he still won't say for sure that startups have a chance.

68|358.c: From the start, MiniMax was a top-secret project with its founder personally in charge.
68|358.e: As MiniMax's first investor, he recalls founder Junjie Yan leaving SenseTime to start the company. It was a highly secret project with the founder personally involved. Products began with digital humans, AI-generated virtual people, then evolved into Glow, Xingye and Hailuo AI. Hillhouse helped bring in Qianchuan Zhang, former head of product at Toutiao. Yunqi added money in nearly all five of MiniMax's funding rounds.

items.d: Digital humans to Glow, Xingye, Hailuo

69|276.c: Information search is where today's models best find product-market fit.
69|276.e: He thinks information search is the best fit for what today's models can do, and Perplexity, an AI search product, seized on that. Its CEO built the product first and the model later; users and revenue grew fast, and it's valued at about $3 billion. But it must face Google and OpenAI head on. In China, AI search is held back because content is split up among walled-off platforms.

69|276.c: AI-native apps haven't broken out at scale yet.
69|276.e: Surveying the AI startup landscape, he finds model companies valued far above app companies, and the app scene still looks "boring." Neither model ability nor product craft is good enough yet, and the cost and speed of using models aren't there either. He expects models to shrink quickly over the next 6 to 12 months and run on phones and laptops, setting the stage for an app boom.

root.d: The app scene still looks boring

69|276.c: GPT-5 is slow because research and infrastructure have to advance together.
69|276.e: He compares OpenAI to pioneers pushing west across America. Scientists drive the train at full speed while infrastructure engineers lay track just ahead of the engine, and the two must keep pace. So the rhythm of big model leaps depends on how fast the infrastructure gets built. GPT-4o is more like a step along the way.

result.d: Possible only when both keep pace

69|276.c: Startups and giants depend on each other; it's not a story of the small toppling the big.
69|276.e: He notes that nearly every AI startup today lives in the giants' orbit. They rely on big companies for models, computing power and money, and the giants are buying stakes, as Nvidia did in Perplexity. So the old story of small companies toppling big ones doesn't fit. The two depend on each other.

items: Rely on giants' models and compute

d.verdict: Startups and big companies depend on each other

70|372.c: Self-driving gives large models another way to make money.
70|372.e: He Xiaopeng notes that no general-purpose model company has made money yet, but large models can earn their keep through self-driving. So China needs both companies that build general models and companies that understand those models and engineer them into specific products. He puts XPeng in the second group.

items.d: Provide ability but rarely earn directly
Understand models and put them in cars, like XPeng

70|372.c: Putting large models in cars means rebuilding the data pipeline and adding a "brake" and a "goalkeeper."
70|372.e: After ChatGPT appeared, he read papers, went to the US and visited Jensen Huang, and realized large models follow a machine's reasoning, not a human's. Putting one in a car means rewriting the data pipeline around that logic, collecting more data and pre-training the model on it. The first results were completely unusable and took enormous amounts of training. On top of that, the system needs a "brake" and a "goalkeeper" as safety backstops.

70|372.c: Large models create a network effect that makes it ever harder for small carmakers to keep up.
70|372.e: He describes a self-reinforcing loop. Stronger AI needs more data. More data costs more money. Higher costs mean selling more cars to support the system, and selling more cars brings in more data. This network effect makes it harder and harder for smaller companies to keep up.

items.d: Need more car sales to cover

70|372.c: Making cars is like swimming in a sea of blood, and the industry is heading into chaos.
70|372.e: He says making cars is like swimming in a sea of blood, so hard that the surest way to hurt someone is to get them making cars. The industry has entered a knockout round that is also an all-star game, with alliances and mergers happening constantly. He thinks an era of chaos is coming soon, and his own goal is to finish first.

70|372.c: This overhaul goes beyond cutting off an arm to survive; even the head has to go.
70|372.e: Looking back, he says that with a proper car-brand mindset he would have positioned XPeng higher, and with a better grasp of the auto business he would have started with the P7. After the setback with the G9, he sees this overhaul as far more drastic than sacrificing an arm. In managing people, the worst thing is to keep switching between gas and brake. His own style has moved from democratic to centralized.

root.d: He Xiaopeng in the middle of change

items.d: Should have started with the P7
Don't flip between gas and brake

71|387.c: Robotaxis only catch on when nobody's at the wheel, and mass rollout is still 3-5 years away.
71|387.e: He thinks Apollo Go, Baidu's robotaxi, became a hot topic in Wuhan because there was no safety driver inside. Even 100,000 cars wouldn't create buzz if each carried one. Public awareness usually lags the technology by more than a year; Baidu and Pony.ai both went driverless at the end of 2022. He expects the next "Wuhan" in China's biggest cities, and more than one. Mass rollout will take three to five years, and costs fall through standardized mass production, not cheaper parts. Robotaxis will provide basic city transport, but private cars won't disappear.
ex: Firms committed to full autonomy fit on one hand, he says, but more than one will last
Cost per car must fall from well over ¥100,000 to about ¥100,000
In 2024 Pony.ai and Toyota formed a joint venture dedicated to mass production

items.d: About an hour without a takeover
Baidu and Pony.ai, both at year-end

71|387.c: Progress is measured in hours without a human taking over, and each tenfold step needs something different.
71|387.e: He breaks progress into steps of 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 hours without a human takeover, each taking years. The early steps come from machine learning models and large fleet data; end-to-end models, one model from sensors to steering, cut losses between modules and reach about 100 hours. From 100 to 1,000, noise like rain, roadwork and time of day makes it hard to tell whether a change helped or hurt. Without a reliable yardstick, teams go in circles, and many stall here. Pony.ai built scenario-by-scenario metrics. Past 1,000 hours, the focus becomes reducing risk to other cars and pedestrians.
ex: Pony.ai is now at 10,000 hours, about ten times a human driver, by his account

items.d: Beyond human; less risk to others

71|387.c: The better driver assistance gets, the further it drifts from driverless cars. They're like soccer and basketball.
71|387.e: He thinks the two have fundamentally different goals. L4, true driverless, must handle everything alone, with safety near 100% and at least 10,000 hours without incident. L2, driver assistance, helps only when confident and otherwise hands back to the driver. Users accept a problem every ten hours; what matters is cost, coverage and the human-car interface. The more L2 is tuned to please users, the further it evolves the other way, like a family doctor who knows a bit of everything versus a specialist who must be right. So he rejects He Xiaopeng's claim that Tesla's FSD will catch Waymo next year: they aren't comparable.
ex: Their L2 went from a takeover every 10 hours to every 8: friendlier, but further from L4

items: One error per 10 hours is fine

d.verdict: Like soccer and basketball: specializing makes them harder to bridge

71|387.sc: When data gets in the way
71|387.c: Once a system beats human drivers, more data stops helping and starts getting in the way.
71|387.e: Every human drives differently, and their choices in the same situation often contradict each other. Driving can't be averaged, and averaging will never beat humans. While a system is worse than people, imitating human data brings fast progress. Once it surpasses them, ordinary driving data drags it back down and makes the model harder to settle. Past 1,000 hours, data from 100 cars is enough; choosing what to keep is far harder than piling up volume. He thinks Tesla's FSD hasn't reached even 1 hour, so it's too early to say more data is always better.
ex: Adding 1,000 hours of data to a 6,000-hour model dropped it back to about 4,000
Musk too has said data from empty straight roads is useless: the model quickly stops learning

items.d: Choices clash in the same situation
Ordinary data pulls it back down

71|387.c: Your goal picks your path: lidar is like cheating on a test, and the car's own smarts come first.
71|387.e: He sees the camera-only versus lidar debate as a difference in goals. Cameras are the hardworking student who must learn to judge distance from data; lidar measures distance directly, like cheating on a test, and even a top student struggles to beat a cheater. Tesla isn't aiming for full autonomy, so camera-only's cost and looks suit it. Anyone going fully driverless won't rely on cameras alone, especially now that the cost gap has shrunk. Smart roads and onboard intelligence help each other, but a car must drive where roads have no sensors, so onboard intelligence comes first. Right now, it's actually helping smart roads.
ex: Lidar fell from about $80,000 a unit early on to a few thousand yuan today
The good-student-versus-cheater analogy, he says, comes from lidar maker Hesai

items.d: The good student; suits driver assistance
First priority; works without roadside gear

71|387.c: Contests reward only the final score, so you can hide your hand; companies must show progress.
71|387.e: After twenty years of programming contests, he thinks persistence depends on whether you want to, not whether you can; saying you don't want to because you don't qualify is an excuse. Contests are selective: you must rank near the top just to compete. Rivals can roughly see each other's progress, so there's an art to hiding your hand: at 90 points, show only 80 so rivals relax, then reveal your cards near the end. A company is different. Interim results matter, because publicity, hiring, partners and public support all depend on them. Only after standing at the top, he says, do you see what separates first from second.
ex: He came last in four finals, possibly a record, since just reaching one is hard
He took second place last year and jokes that runner-up is the biggest loser

marks.d: Hide your hand until the last moment

72|395.c: Driver assistance (L2) and driverless cars (L4) are completely different products and can't be judged on one scale.
72|395.e: Xing Meng argues that driver assistance sells car owners a better experience of sharing the driving with the machine, while driverless cars sell cheaper rides. The two have different safety red lines and different parties liable when something goes wrong. So when L4 companies see Tesla's FSD software as a "grade schooler," it isn't about who is more capable. They are aiming at different goals. Putting both on the same L1-to-L5 scale of driving automation has caused a lot of confusion.

items: Product still very early, like a Pre-A startup

d.verdict: One L1–L5 ruler can't compare these two paths

72|395.c: Tesla's end-to-end FSD V12 is driver assistance's "GPT-3 moment": the approach works, but no leap in experience yet.
72|395.e: He has driven every version from V11.3.6, the last one that wasn't end-to-end, to the end-to-end V12.3 and V12.4, and felt updates speeding up. End-to-end means one model handles everything from seeing the road to deciding how to drive, instead of hand-written rules. V12 reignited the industry's excitement about self-driving, and nearly every Chinese rival is following suit. But he compares it to GPT-3, not ChatGPT: the approach is proven, but the user experience hasn't taken a real leap yet.

items.d: Nearly all Chinese rivals go end-to-end

72|395.c: Until driver assistance is good enough, there is an ideal takeover rate, and lower isn't always better.
72|395.e: In driver assistance, a person and a machine drive together. The product aims for a good shared-driving experience, not for removing the human entirely. Xing Meng believes that until the system drives well enough, the takeover rate, meaning how often the driver has to grab the wheel, should be neither too high nor too low. There is an optimal range. That is completely different from L4, which aims for a car with no one on board to take over.

marks.d: No one on board to take over

72|395.c: Tesla's pure end-to-end approach, with no rule-based safety net, is very hard for Chinese companies to copy.
72|395.e: Tesla's end-to-end system has no hand-written rules as a fallback. It dares to hand driving decisions entirely to the model, which Chinese companies find hard to do. To really work, end-to-end must also clear several hurdles: a data loop where fleet data keeps flowing back to improve the model, heavy spending on computing power, and regulatory compliance. He has even roughly estimated what it would cost to replicate FSD. As for whether end-to-end is the ultimate weapon, he says L2 and L4 should be discussed separately.

root.d: Nearly all Chinese players are going end-to-end

items.d: Driving decisions left to the model

73|276.c: Pure language pretraining may hit a wall, and self-play reinforcement learning is the way onto a new path.
73|276.e: Guangmi Li's biggest worry is that the classic scaling law for language pretraining, where bigger models trained on more text get better, may stop working beyond about 2–3 trillion parameters. After GPT-4o, a big leap may not come soon. If there's a wall, there are three ways out: multimodality, especially vision, though there's no evidence yet that image training produces intelligence; 100,000-GPU clusters, which are extremely hard to wire together; and self-play RL, where a model trains against itself and learns from rewards. He sees the third as a fundamental shift, and says that as an AI CEO he'd put 200% of resources on RL.

root.d: May stop working past 2–3 trillion parameters

items.d: Especially vision; no sign of intelligence emerging
A mega-project that is very hard to connect

73|276.c: Language models and RL multiply each other, so a strong base model has to come first.
73|276.e: He compares it to genes and lifelong learning. Language pretraining is like a genome, compressing knowledge humanity built up over a long time. Reinforcement learning is like a person's trial and error on new tasks over a lifetime. In a line from OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever: the model tries different paths on a new task, and when a result beats expectations, it updates its weights to reinforce that path. Self-play RL needs a base model that is already strong. So the two don't replace each other; they multiply.

terms.d: Like a genome: compressed human knowledge
Like lifelong learning: improve by trial and error

73|276.c: Google absorbing Character.AI marks the end of the first half of the AGI race.
73|276.e: To him, Google absorbing the chatbot companion startup Character.AI signals the end of the first half, which was driven by scaling up pretraining. The second half will be driven by self-play reinforcement learning, where models improve through trial and error, and both Claude 3.5's progress and OpenAI's "Strawberry" (that is, Q*) point there. For now, though, only a few hundred of the most central researchers agree on this shift. It hasn't spread beyond them yet.

73|276.c: Silicon Valley bets on a shared robot "brain," while China bets on complete robot hardware.
73|276.e: General-purpose robots are a hot area in Silicon Valley, and investors are hunting for "the OpenAI of embodied AI," meaning AI that lives in a physical body. But the field is still stuck on basic science problems, and robots can't yet generalize across tasks. He sees the US and China taking different approaches. Silicon Valley invests in shared robot foundation models, an Android-like general brain. China bets more on complete hardware, the way phone makers do.

items: Hoping for the OpenAI of embodied AI

d.verdict: No general ability yet; both sides are early

73|276.c: Coding is the surest bet among AI applications right now.
73|276.e: Silicon Valley's AI startup hot spots are search, coding, video, and robots. In coding, several companies, including Devin, Augment, Magic, and Poolside, are already valued at $2–3 billion each, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet's jump in ability made the coding tool Cursor take off. Video is a tempting market, but the field is unsettled and the window of opportunity will stay open a long time. General-purpose robots still need breakthroughs in basic science.

74|395.c: Self-driving won't have a sudden ChatGPT-style moment. The real turning point is making the business pay.
74|395.e: After four months of riding driverless cars in the US, Xing Meng concluded that self-driving won't be set off by a single technical breakthrough, the way ChatGPT was. The race in Level 4 autonomy (cars that drive themselves with no human, within set areas) has shifted from research to running fleets. The real dividing line is whether each car, in everyday service, earns more than it costs to run.

items.d: Driverless cars already run in set areas
Build safety and efficiency through daily service
Daily operations earn more than they cost

74|395.c: Cruise chased speed and fell just as fast. For driverless cars, safety is life or death.
74|395.e: Kyle Vogt founded Cruise, and a team of about 40 sold it to General Motors for $1 billion within two years. It was once the industry's number two, but a single safety accident sent it tumbling. Waymo, also a self-driving unit inside a big company, put long-term commitment and steady operations first. Their different styles ended in very different fates. When driverless cars go commercial, one accident can be fatal.

items: A long-running project born at Google X
Steady operations that built a safety record
Already running driverless at scale in Phoenix
About 40 people, sold for $1B in two years
Fell fast after one safety accident

d.verdict: In commercial self-driving, one accident can be fatal

74|395.c: Frontier bets like fully driverless cars need a big company paying the bills for years.
74|395.e: Waymo started in 2009 as a project inside Google X, and the money kept flowing through several changes of leadership. Xing Meng argues that Level 4 self-driving (no human driver, within set areas) is more than an engineering problem. It needs deep pockets and a long-term commitment behind it. The episode also looks back at why Uber, once a serious contender, dropped out of this long race.

items.d: Mawakana and Dolgov take the helm

74|395.c: Self-driving is moving from rules engineers write by hand to one model that learns to drive.
74|395.e: Waymo's roots trace back to the people trained in DARPA's driverless-car challenges, run by the US defense research agency. Early systems relied heavily on rules written by engineers. As data grew and models improved, the industry shifted from writing rules to letting models learn from data. Waymo sees end-to-end design, where one model goes straight from what the car sees to how it drives, as the ideal: the cleanest, most elegant architecture.

items.d: Contests that trained the first talent
Models learn to drive from data
One model does it all, the cleanest design

75|402.c: Pre-training is running out of easy gold. Reinforcement learning on top of it is the second gold mine.
75|402.e: Yi Wu thinks pre-training, where a model first reads huge amounts of text, is yielding less and less. Post-training with reinforcement learning, where the model improves through trial and reward, is a second rich vein. o1 doesn't change the road to AGI (human-level general AI). It adds a new layer on top of pre-training, a few more rungs on the ladder. And data produced by reinforcement learning and search during post-training can be fed back into pre-training.

items.d: First gold mine, now thinning out

75|402.c: o1 is a GPT-3 moment that proves what's possible, not yet a ChatGPT moment everyone uses.
75|402.e: The first time he used o1-preview, he was surprised by how long it reasoned before answering, backtracking, searching and reflecting. That also puts different demands on the computing systems behind it. It proves reinforcement learning can raise the ceiling on what models can do, much as GPT-3 once did. Whether it becomes a hit product everyone uses, like ChatGPT, depends on the full release. o1 also lets ordinary users get strong reasoning without crafting careful prompts.

75|402.c: Reinforcement learning has three hard parts, and they all have to be solved together.
75|402.e: Reinforcement learning is far more complex than pre-training, where sheer scale works wonders. You need three things: prompts (what the model practices on), a reward model (how it learns it's wrong), and search and exploration (how to steer it from a wrong answer to a right one). Each is hard, and they're tightly linked, so a separate team is unlikely to train the reward model alone. Whether RL finds its own scaling law, where more compute reliably buys better results, looks promising but complicated.

terms.d: Tells the model when it's wrong
Moves from wrong answers to right ones

75|402.c: o1 doesn't point to specialized models. He still believes in one unified, do-everything model.
75|402.e: He believes reinforcement learning raises general ability, not just scores in specialist areas like math and code. On his roadmap to AGI, step one is long context, the ability to take in very long inputs, and step two is reasoning. So o1 doesn't mean the industry will splinter into a pile of single-field models. He still expects one unified model that is strong across the board.

items: Long context first, then reasoning on top

d.verdict: o1 is a step toward general reasoning, not specialization

75|402.c: In 2019, OpenAI was mining with its eyes closed: sure there was gold, unsure where.
75|402.e: Looking back on 2019 at OpenAI, Yi Wu says people were already discussing scaling laws, the pattern that bigger models trained on more data get better. But nobody knew exactly where the gold was. They just kept digging on faith. Management chased big news and blog posts, and blog attention was for a while a key performance metric. That faith in scale, plus strong technical taste, became the bedrock of the OpenAI that came later.

items.d: No clear direction, driven by belief

76|317.c: Large models learn and answer fast, reinforcement learning thinks slowly, and each lacks what the other has.
76|317.e: Wang Xiaochuan borrows from Confucius: learning without thinking, and thinking without learning, both fall short. Large models learn from huge amounts of data and answer instantly. That's fast thinking, but they don't really reason. Reinforcement learning, where a model improves through trial and reward, is good at reasoning and fixing mistakes against a score. That's slow thinking, but it builds up little knowledge. o1 combines the two, and he predicts the learning and thinking systems will eventually merge.

items: Can go beyond its training data

d.verdict: The two systems will eventually merge

76|317.c: o1 is a real upgrade: it found a path from fast thinking to slow thinking.
76|317.e: He sees o1 as an upgrade in approach. Models move from being centered on language to first writing out a chain of thought, their step-by-step reasoning, and only then answering. Early reinforcement learning experiments had no chain of thought. Now it's taken very seriously. Training in two stages has also made models better at generalizing, getting problems right that they haven't seen before.

items.d: Writes out its reasoning step by step

76|317.c: Reinforcement learning works best where right and wrong are clear, and Wang thinks medicine is next.
76|317.e: Reinforcement learning, where a model improves through trial and reward, relies on a score that says good or bad. That's why it paid off first in math and coding, where answers can be checked. Wang Xiaochuan thinks medicine also has fairly clear standards for judging answers, so it can benefit too. Baichuan is applying reinforcement learning to medicine to build medical reasoning, with the goal of a "digital doctor."

items.d: Run the code to check it

76|317.c: Startups must stay out of the giants' firing range and build apps that lift the whole field.
76|317.e: In his view, startups have almost no chance inside the big companies' firing range, the areas giants can cover with little effort. They have to find places the giants can't reach. For applications, he favors products that lift the whole ecosystem, a rising tide that raises all boats, rather than settling for small wins picked up along the way. He also expects the main approach to shift over the next few years from reinforcement learning toward solving problems with code.

77|411.c: Once the internet industry matures, buying and merging existing companies becomes the main way to grow.
77|411.e: Fubin Lu argues that once the internet's fast-expansion phase is over, there are fewer openings for new companies and more existing ones. Buying, combining and restructuring those companies then becomes an important way to grow. The backdrop for the conversation: in 2024, overseas buyout funds were active, and Chinese policy was encouraging mergers and restructuring.

77|411.c: Buying a company isn't a financial game. You have to step in and run it yourself.
77|411.e: Moving from venture capital to buying controlling stakes, he found the two are fundamentally different. A venture investor holds a minority stake and bets on growth. An acquirer takes control and answers directly for how the business performs. In his view, success depends on truly understanding what you've bought and being willing to run it yourself, not on financial leverage, the borrowed money that amplifies returns.

d.verdict: Value comes from knowing the business and running it, not leverage

77|411.c: He only buys internet businesses that are hard to copy, already profitable, and undervalued by the market.
77|411.e: He screens targets layer by layer. The business must have an edge competitors can't easily copy, it must make money on its own, and the market must be pricing it too low. After buying, he raises its value through hands-on operations, such as fine-tuning ad spending and reorganizing teams. He plans to hold for the long term.

77|411.c: Hands-on operating skills from China's internet industry can be used to remake companies overseas.
77|411.e: He points to deals such as Grindr, the dating app, and Investing.com, the financial news site. The idea: a global view, meaning the ability to find and close deals across borders, combined with the operating methods honed in China's internet industry, can reshape companies abroad. Along the way, you also have to handle very different geopolitical environments.

terms.d: Find and close deals across borders

78|395.c: Tech startups valued at over $100 million in their angel round are less likely to succeed later.
78|395.e: Xing Meng has noticed that frontier tech companies valued at more than $100 million in their angel round, the very first funding, actually succeed less often. None has succeeded so far. When the valuation gets too high too early, the company tends to spend its energy on polish and fundraising stories instead of real technical progress. Growth soon hits a wall.

78|395.c: Self-driving startups and their investors rode a full roller coaster over eight years.
78|395.e: In 2016, General Motors bought Cruise for $1 billion and set off a wave of self-driving investment. The industry then sank into a slump, before funding peaked again around 2021. Eight years on, roughly half of the self-driving companies founded around 2016 are still standing. Both L2 (driver assistance, with a human still watching) and L4 (fully driverless within set areas) are now dominated by a few leaders.

items.d: About half survive as the field consolidates

78|395.c: Real incubation means helping shape the product and the team, not just handing out resources.
78|395.e: Comparing incubators in China and the US, he finds most Chinese ones don't go deep enough. Real incubation means helping define the product and build the team, and sharing responsibility with the founders. Offering office space and services is the accelerator model. That's why he left Didi and went back to venture capital: he wants to help more early-stage companies get started.

d.verdict: Most Chinese incubators don't go deep enough

78|395.c: The self-driving boom and bust holds lessons today's AI model industry should take to heart.
78|395.e: He sees self-driving's arc, from technical breakthrough to investor frenzy to a shakeout that left a few leaders, as a mirror for today's AI model industry. In a downturn, companies must quickly build a business that sustains itself and keep a tight grip on cash burn to survive into the next cycle. He also expects driverless technology to spread over the next decade in long-haul freight between cities, ports and light passenger transport.

79|417.c: Tesla's event sold a vision but skipped technical details and never showed robotaxis can make money.
79|417.e: The discussion casts the event as more of a fan gathering. Tesla showed its Cybercab and Robovan driverless vehicles and the Optimus humanoid robot, and set aggressive timelines, but said almost nothing about progress on FSD, its self-driving software, or its technical approach. Optimus interacted smoothly with people, yet some movements hinted that humans may have been controlling it remotely. The core question, whether driverless rides can become a profitable business, went unanswered.

items: Operating costs and how to profit
Whether the business can work at all

d.verdict: Lots of vision, too few verifiable technical details

79|417.c: The two-seat Cybercab and fleets of owners' cars will struggle to beat existing ride-hailing networks.
79|417.e: The two-seat Cybercab looks futuristic, but it gives up passenger space and is less practical to operate. Having private owners put their cars into Tesla's network struggles to match today's ride-hailing networks on both financing costs and maintenance. Running driverless fleets also carries many visible costs that are hard to automate away. And Tesla's goal of unsupervised driving in 2025 was seen as far too aggressive.

items.d: Can't match ride-hailing on cost and upkeep

79|417.c: Tesla falling while Uber rose shows investors asking who will capture the robotaxi profits.
79|417.e: After the event, Tesla's stock fell while Uber's went up. The discussion reads this split as the market rethinking who will end up with the money from driverless ride-hailing. Until the operating problems are worked out, owning the cars and the self-driving software doesn't guarantee a slice of the pie.

items.d: Short on tech and operating details

80|426.c: People are the point of AI. It should help people talk to each other, not replace them.
80|426.e: When ChatGPT arrived, Zhou Yuan's first reaction was a strong sense of rupture. But he soon settled on a view: people are the purpose of AI. So Zhihu uses its AI search tool, Zhihu Zhida, to make finding information cheaper and easier, while keeping the value of in-depth discussion between people in the community. AI isn't there to replace that exchange.

items.d: AI search that makes finding information easier

80|426.c: At heart, Zhihu may be a newsroom run by society as a whole, able to grow without limit.
80|426.e: Early in his career, Zhou Yuan was a generalist reporter who wrote about everything. Starting from how a newsroom works, he imagined handing questions, writing and editing over to society at large. A newsroom like that could expand without limit. When ByteDance came at Zhihu head-on with its Q&A app Wukong Wenda, his answer was that Zhihu may not be just a product.

80|426.c: Zhihu must grow through a healthy community. Chasing scale alone bends the community out of shape.
80|426.e: After going public, Zhihu swung back and forth on strategy under market pressure to grow, and longtime users complained the content was being watered down. Zhou Yuan's conclusion is to return to growth driven by the community's ecosystem, the cycle linking writers, readers and content. A good experience for creators and real value for readers are the foundation. Chasing scale without them distorts the community itself.

80|426.c: Perplexity is more a content product than a search tool, and search has been upended several times before.
80|426.e: He sees Perplexity, the AI search startup, as a content product rather than just a search tool. He also points out that search has been "disrupted" several times already, with the shift from search engines to recommendation feeds as one example. So he sees AI search as one more change in how content reaches people. Zhihu has launched its own AI search product as well.

81|431.c: Whoever first builds AGI that crushes its rivals will become the biggest monopolist in history.
81|431.e: He sees AGI (human-level general AI) as a brain that can design products, set business strategy and even plot against competitors, so whoever controls it can keep entrenching their lead. The first company to build overwhelming AGI would hold an unprecedented monopoly, like Windows once did, but with a far more powerful tool. He says Sam Altman could become the biggest monopolist ever. He calls that a statement of fact, not an insult, but a worry for the industry. 01.AI, he stresses, isn't and shouldn't be racing to build AGI first and beat everyone.
ex: He says 01.AI often loses PhDs to big firms offering 5,000–10,000 GPUs versus its few thousand

81|431.c: Don't chase the priciest AGI. Design for cheap inference, the cost of running models, from day one.
81|431.e: He compares the big labs' approach to building the fanciest kitchen, then trying to squeeze it into a small apartment: train the most expensive model, then shrink it. 01.AI does the reverse, designing for cost-effective inference from the start. It builds the model, the serving infrastructure and the apps as one stack, and pairs model experts with leaders who understand product-market fit. He thinks inference costs can fall about 10x a year, or 20 to 50x with focused effort. Once costs cross a threshold, search, social, entertainment and shopping apps will spring up like mushrooms after rain.
ex: GPT-4o launched about five months earlier at $10 per million tokens, he notes
He says Yi-Lightning beats May's GPT-4o at a price dozens of times lower, still profitably

terms.d: Drives down the cost per call
Model experts paired with product leads

81|431.c: AI's profits are upside down. Chips take most of the money, which should flow back to apps.
81|431.e: He looks back at mobile internet and deep learning: the US invented most of the technology, but China deployed it faster and cheaper, with apps and unicorns just as strong. In a healthy industry, apps capture the most value, platforms sit in the middle and chips take the least, as with PCs, the internet, mobile and cloud. AI has flipped that, and chipmakers take the lion's share. China can build apps on models only about five months behind America's, drawing on deep product-market-fit talent and strong execution. He hopes models, AI infrastructure and apps together can steer chip profits back to apps.
ex: The US invented mobile internet, but China's apps later did better

items.d: Like ChatGPT, which should get the most

81|431.c: AGI is about seven years off. Use the window to build app ecosystems that rivals can't easily dislodge.
81|431.e: He reckons GPT-2 to GPT-4 took about four years, and the next jump that size, facing diminishing returns and higher costs, will take about seven. Citing Epoch AI's analysis, he sees AGI as more likely around 2030, limited by data, GPU and high-bandwidth memory supply, chip-to-chip transfer and global power. In that window, China should race to build apps in search, social, agents and hardware, gathering users early as WeChat, Douyin and Facebook did, so it has the strength to compete and coexist. App companies must make money first. Chasing AGI alone burns through resources.
ex: He questions the assumptions behind Situational Awareness and its roughly three-year path to AGI

items.d: A big leap in about four years
About seven years, with diminishing returns

81|431.c: Never underestimate OpenAI. The hard part has moved from pre-training to how models think while answering.
81|431.e: He thinks OpenAI times its releases: whenever rivals reach 80 or 90 percent of its level, it plays the next card it's sure of. He senses its gap with Google widening. GPT-5 reportedly hit training trouble and was delayed. o1 didn't greatly improve understanding. Its value is pairing fast and slow thinking: the longer it thinks, the better it answers. Pre-training was hard 18 months ago but is common now. Post-training and reinforcement learning are the new hard parts. He expects inference-time ideas to go far beyond o1.
