His team alone devised three designs, and dozens of companies will produce hundreds.
ex: He thinks Ilya Sutskever's exit didn't hurt OpenAI and may even help Altman move faster
His TC-PMF adds to product-market fit: when the tech is ready and costs fall enough

items.d: o1 opened it, more innovation will follow

81|431.c: Nvidia earns most, Microsoft sits safest, and Google, though strongest in research, is squeezed from both sides.
81|431.e: He sizes up Silicon Valley. Nvidia is the biggest winner, but its edge will be tested as GPU demand shifts from training to inference. Meta is the spoiler, open-sourcing what it can't win. Microsoft is best placed for now, but its own models are weak and its OpenAI ties may sour. Musk's xAI executes like a Chinese company and is a dark horse. Google has the deepest research and reinforcement learning record, yet results lag. ChatGPT and Amazon squeeze its search business, and adding AI is a dilemma: replacing search hurts ads, separate products split users, and merging muddies answers and revenue.
ex: Google earns about 1.6 cents per search, while Perplexity can lose money to win users
His team found Perplexity still hallucinates often, so he doubts it can replace Google

root.d: Each player in a different spot

items.d: Biggest winner, tested as inference takes over
Strongest research, stuck in a search dilemma

81|431.c: Consumer AI apps will boom in early 2025, ending with assistants that do tasks for you.
81|431.e: He thinks super apps grow gradually. AI-first apps first remake existing products, as Perplexity does with Google, then create new categories. The likely endgame is an assistant that completes tasks for people, as interfaces move from tapping screens to chatting to simply delegating. Shopping sites could become passive price-comparison warehouses, and app stores and standalone apps may vanish. With inference now affordable, VCs shifting to apps and his own willingness to invest, he predicts a global consumer app boom in the first half of next year. He also thinks China's app playbook and talent pool far exceed America's.
ex: He wants to cut tasks that take 40 to 50 seconds down to one second
He says China's six AI tigers differ: business clients at home, consumers abroad, entertainment, chatbots
Phones stay the main device, and always-listening glasses and earbuds will speed up delegation

items.d: Shops become price warehouses, apps may vanish

82|441.c: AI tends to concentrate power, while crypto is built to spread it out.
82|441.e: Vitalik sees the two technologies as philosophical opposites. AI depends on concentrating computing power and data, so it naturally creates centers of power, and OpenAI shows the risks of that centralization and monopoly. Blockchains, shared ledgers that no single party controls, aim for decentralization and equality. They try to fix a lack of trust and fairness.

items: Relies on concentrated compute and data

d.verdict: Crypto can act as a check on AI's power

82|441.c: AI can be an efficient participant inside crypto systems like exchanges and prediction markets.
82|441.e: The two don't have to be enemies. AI can work as a tool inside protocols such as decentralized exchanges, which match trades through code rather than a company, and prediction markets, where people bet on future events. That makes them run more efficiently. In turn, open and transparent crypto infrastructure can help people keep control of their own thoughts and data as they interact deeply with machines.

root.d: Where they meet beyond the rivalry

items.d: Keeps your thoughts and data your own

82|441.c: Crypto is shifting from financial speculation toward helping people cooperate and build trust.
82|441.e: Scaling technologies such as Layer 2 networks, built on top of Ethereum to make transactions faster and cheaper, are maturing. As a result, the crypto world's center of gravity is moving from financial speculation to social coordination and building trust. He also warns that blockchain applications still face risks around cost and privacy.

83|177.c: Nvidia grew up through repeated failures and quick changes of course.
83|177.e: Yajun Wang traces Nvidia's history back to the failure of its first two products, NV1 and NV2. After NV1, the company changed direction, survived thanks to the Riva 128, and then bet on gaming. The NV30 setback later pushed Jensen Huang to change how he managed. Big decisions sometimes worked and sometimes didn't. What mattered was correcting course quickly after each failure.

83|177.c: Nvidia's management turns strategy into action, not documents.
83|177.e: Yajun Wang boils Jensen Huang's management down to a few tools. Meetings use a whiteboard to work through problems on the spot. Employees regularly report their five most important tasks, the "Top 5," and every project has a "captain" who owns the result. Behind it all is Huang's belief that strategy is action, not words. It gets adjusted constantly during execution rather than written down on paper.

items.d: Work through problems on the spot
Report your five most important tasks
One person owns each project end to end

83|177.c: A stable chip architecture plus CUDA built a self-reinforcing network that makes Nvidia hard to replace.
83|177.e: On product strategy, Nvidia has kept its architecture stable for a long time, so developers can keep building on it. The GPU and CUDA, the software platform that lets programmers use Nvidia chips for general computing, turned that accumulated work into an ecosystem. The more people use it and the richer the software gets, the harder the hardware is to replace. That self-reinforcing network is the foundation of Nvidia's edge.

84|448.c: A model is not a product, and he thinks pure model companies won't exist in the future.
84|448.e: DeepLang AI was founded in 2021 as a bet on large models. By the second half of 2023, more and more players had piled in, it was getting harder to train a model that stood apart, and the company's early lead was being copied. Fanchao Qi changed strategy. He stopped treating the model as the product and started building from concrete user needs. He predicts there will be no pure model companies in the future.

items.d: Bets on large models and information access
Hard to train a distinctive model

84|448.c: Combining several models can offset how unpredictable any single model's output is.
84|448.e: He thinks models aren't robust or stable enough, and that is a major reason AI products struggle to work in practice. So their product has five models working together, managing the uncertainty of the output at the product level. That uncertainty also deeply shapes how AI companies organize themselves.

items: Uncertainty managed at the product level

d.verdict: Manage uncertainty at the product level

84|448.c: Information keeps exploding while human attention doesn't, so products should deal in information, not whole articles.
84|448.e: People's capacity to process information has barely changed, while the amount of information keeps growing, so the gap keeps widening. Fanchao Qi sees content as just a container for information. Products should go back to the information itself, finding and delivering it piece by piece rather than as whole articles, to help people close that gap.

items.d: There's a limit to what we can process

84|448.c: Power in the content world is shifting from creators to the people consuming it.
84|448.e: AI lowers the barrier to creating, so content will pile up and outstrip demand. That gives readers and viewers more say. He imagines creators will mostly supply firsthand information and raw material, while platforms may become a personal assistant for each user, reorganizing information to fit what that person needs.

85|227.c: A candidate is a product, and winning means achieving product-market fit with the national story.
85|227.e: The guest treats a presidential candidate as a product, and voters and the mood of the times as the market. A candidate's record, positions and personal story win broad support only when they match how Americans currently see the country's direction. So he borrows the startup idea of product-market fit to explain why a candidate wins.

terms.d: The product: record, positions, personal story
The market: voters' sense of where the country is headed

85|227.c: A campaign is an organization that scales at breakneck speed, reaching voters through field work and media.
85|227.e: A presidential campaign has to grow from a small team into a huge nationwide organization in a very short time, much like a fast-growing startup. There are two main ways to bring the candidate to voters. One is grassroots field work that mobilizes voters directly. The other is media strategy, which shapes how the public sees the candidate.

85|227.c: Voters' frustration with the economy is the main force that changes which party holds power.
85|227.e: Looking back at the 2024 election, the guest argues that voters' dissatisfaction with the overall economy swayed votes more than any single issue. The governing Democrats paid the price. The episode also discusses the limits of the Democrats' media strategy.

items.d: Inclined to punish the party in power

85|227.c: Tech leaders are moving from reacting to regulation to actively taking part in politics.
85|227.e: As the tech industry has grown in size and influence, Silicon Valley and Washington have become more closely entwined. The guest sees tech elites no longer just responding to regulation but actively shaping policy, most visibly in AI and cryptocurrency. Still, he thinks the future of tech regulation remains highly uncertain.

d.verdict: Silicon Valley's political stance has shifted, but regulation remains uncertain

86|276.c: Every AI model product is ultimately racing to become the next Google.
86|276.e: Guangmi Li reasons from how computing and the delivery of information have evolved. The way people reach information moved from portals to search to recommendation feeds, and next comes an engine that gets tasks done for you. ChatGPT's biggest card is its chance to beat Google. A product that merges search, recommendations, Q&A and getting things done will end up as a "task container." He also notes that Google itself grew out of a fringe market at Yahoo's edges.

86|276.c: AI models' biggest new contribution is a new kind of software, judged by how often tasks get done.
86|276.e: He compares two eras. Mobile internet's biggest addition was content, and e-commerce was measured by GMV, or total sales, and order conversion. In the AI model era, the biggest addition is a new kind of software, and products should be measured by task completion rate. So a chat box is probably not the most effective way to draw out a model's intelligence. Models need to be more proactive, and a personal or super assistant may be a better form.

d.verdict: Chatbots are probably not the best way to use model intelligence

86|276.c: In 2025, the most commercially valuable AI will be agents that handle long, multi-step tasks.
86|276.e: He sees long-horizon tasks, jobs that take many steps over a long stretch, as the next big focus, and heavyweights at the core of the field are all working on them. Devin was the first agent, AI that acts on its own, to truly take on long, complex tasks. The AI coding tool Cursor is also evolving fast, from completing the next line of code to completing the next action. Next year it may generate entire pieces of software end to end.

items.d: Cursor predicts the next line of code
Starts carrying out steps for you
Devin takes on long, complex tasks

86|276.c: A killer app that wants to stay ahead must integrate everything from product down to chips.
86|276.e: Discussing Anthropic, he notes that it won over developers and heavy API usage through coding, and could grow into an ecosystem or even an operating system. But he thinks building only the top-layer product isn't a lasting defense. A killer app that wants to stay ahead must optimize downward: cost, model architecture and size, the mix of training data, even inference chips. It needs end-to-end integration from the app to the bottom of the stack.

items.d: Decides what the model is good at

86|276.c: The key bottleneck to scaling AI is data, not compute or algorithms.
86|276.e: Going back to scaling laws, the pattern that models improve with more size, data and compute, he thinks what's really holding progress back is data, not compute or algorithms. The episode also covers the pre-training "data wall" Ilya Sutskever described, and the lack of a universal reward model for post-training that can judge everyone's work. So one key for 2025 is hiring top experts in specific industries to label thousands of task-plus-reward examples, in a way that scales.

items.d: The key bottleneck: expert-labeled tasks and rewards

87|458.c: Li Auto's endgame is an AI company. Cars are AI's biggest vehicle in the physical world.
87|458.e: Li Xiang believes the second half of smart cars is true artificial intelligence, and cars are AI's largest application in the physical world. So Li Auto should be seen as an AI company, with cars supplying the hardware and revenue. He insists this isn't chasing the ChatGPT hype. The direction was set long ago, and ChatGPT just let him go public with a hidden strategy. The motive is a regret from Autohome, the car website he founded: it won online but never changed manufacturing or logistics. He guarded one tree and missed the forest.
ex: The AI and self-driving direction was set at the Yanqi Lake strategy meeting in September 2022
He answers critics who call it storytelling with about 10 billion yuan of R&D a year
Early fundraising was hard, so serious in-house self-driving work began only after the IPO

items.d: Competition among car websites was over
Sets the AI and self-driving direction
ChatGPT lets the hidden plan be said

87|458.c: OpenAI leads because it has all five layers of capability and grabbed the top gateways to users.
87|458.e: He breaks OpenAI into five layers: setting industry standards, research, engineering, productizing and commercializing. He thinks it matters more to AI than Google did to the internet. Capability alone isn't enough. You also need the gateway users start from, as when Google won AOL's homepage and Baidu bought hao123. OpenAI tied up with Microsoft and Apple. So he thinks the personal-assistant race is still about grabbing a ticket. True mass adoption awaits agents that get things done on their own, the "iPhone 4 moment" for ordinary people.
ex: ChatGPT: about 80% share, 3.6 billion monthly visits. The runner-up: only 200–300 million, he says
ChatGPT Pro costs $200, a sign it isn't yet a mass-market product

items.d: Build products the public can use
Plus Microsoft and Apple as distribution

87|458.c: A foundation model is the AI era's operating system plus programming language. You must build your own.
87|458.e: In smartphones, most makers were wiped out. The survivors, Apple, Huawei and Xiaomi, did more than one kind of hardware, and the key was owning the operating system and software. By the same logic, the AI era's dividing line is whether you build your own foundation model, which can grow into one super gateway across car, phone and computer. Li Auto's assistant, Lixiang Tongxue, is that attempt. It starts with over a million owner families. Li Auto admits it follows in language models and aims to climb step by step, while defending first place in China in spatial intelligence, understanding the 3D world.
ex: Starting with 1 million-plus owner families, first serving about 3 to 5 million people
Kids already use Lixiang Tongxue to discuss homework, draw and make comic strips
In language models, go from outside the top 10 to fifth, then top three

items.d: Owners of OS and software win
Same experience in car, phone, computer

87|458.c: AI will go through three stages: boosting people, acting as an assistant, then becoming a silicon family member.
87|458.e: He divides AI's evolution by who decides and who takes responsibility. In stage one, AI only amplifies human ability, and decisions and responsibility stay with people. In stage two, AI takes on a task, completes it independently and owns the result. In stage three, with no instructions needed, AI proactively takes care of a household's affairs, and its memory carries on over time. He cautions against giving AI family-style names before it reaches that stage.
ex: Stage one: AI makes an image, but a person still has to fix it
Stage two: a driverless car fetches kids from school, or an agent writes your weekly report

items.d: Assists, while people decide and own it
Completes tasks independently and owns results
Cares for the family without being asked

87|458.c: AI delivers abilities that work with high probability, so research, engineering and productizing are all essential.
87|458.e: Traditional software delivers features, and an error is a bug. AI delivers abilities, which are inherently probabilistic. Demanding that AI succeed every time judges an ability by a feature's standard, so acceptance should shift from item-by-item tests to an overall exam. In the feature era you could buy a supplier's solution and learn as a guinea pig. In the ability era, building only the product is like carving flowers on stone. You must research first, then engineer, then productize. He agrees the model is the product, and apps are eggs the model lays along the way.
ex: Like hurdler Liu Xiang: anyone might win once in 10,000 races, but Liu wins far more often
Validation uses a scenario-generating world model plus trials with 1,000- and 10,000-person tester groups

terms.d: Understand how models relate to memory

result.d: Product alone is carving flowers on stone

87|458.c: Carmaking is moving from processes to software to data, and data makes expert know-how copyable.
87|458.e: He splits the auto industry into three eras. BT is repeatable process, Ford- and Toyota-style. IT is control through software. DT is an end-to-end data loop covering every customer and tied to financial data. Veteran experts can't write down what they know, but with complete data, what works can be captured as best practice. He also argues that best practices in specialized fields never appear on the public internet, so a company's own data is its edge in post-training, the extra training on top of a general model. That makes post-training's scaling law work in Li Auto's favor.
ex: Changzhou's second plant hit full output in about 15 days. He says legacy carmakers need 6–12 months
Self-driving trains only on the top 3% of driving clips: lawful, safe and efficient
A well-sited new company store can sell 100-plus cars a month within 3–6 months

items.d: Software control, people stuck in processes
End-to-end customer data tied to finances

87|458.c: End-to-end driving only gets you to L3. L4 needs the generalization a VLA model learns.
87|458.e: An end-to-end model, one model from seeing the road to steering, plus a vision-language model can stretch the gap between human takeovers to hundreds or thousands of kilometers. That's L3, but it can't generalize enough for unsupervised L4. With rule-based systems, each rare case you fix may spawn three new ones, and armies of engineers patching rules intersection by intersection can't replace learned ability. He thinks language and spatial intelligence will merge into VLA, a vision-language-action model. On sensors he goes vision-first, but keeps a front-facing lidar as a "seat belt" for family cars.
ex: After trying FSD V12 in the US, about 200 people trained a first end-to-end version in a month
The 2025 goal: 500 km between takeovers, about 10 times the level then
At night, cameras see about 100 meters and lidar about 200

marks.d: Roughly L3, a takeover every hundreds of km
Vision, language and action in one

87|458.c: Going electric just gets you into the final. L4 decides the winner, and robots come after.
87|458.e: He thinks electrification only gets carmakers into the final, much as Samsung entered phones through hardware and Apple and Google through software. What decides the winner is L4, full self-driving, and today's sales, cash flow and model spending all serve to win that ticket. He doesn't think robotaxis will kill private cars. L4 actually makes owning a family's own mobile space more worthwhile. He's 100 percent sure Li Auto will build humanoid robots, but a car is already the simplest no-contact robot, so without L4, robots are out of reach.
ex: Like renting versus buying a home: people still want stable, safe space of their own
Launching a steering-wheel-free L4 car within three years depends on technology, policy and trust

root.d: No L4, no entry to the trillion club

items.d: Top talent plus compute for training and inference

87|458.c: MEGA failed not on looks but because Li Auto misjudged the market's size and operations lagged.
87|458.e: He admits it was a mistake to treat the 5.3-meter MEGA as a cross-category product for sedan, SUV and minivan buyers. Its length made road trips and parking hard, and most buyers turned out to be existing luxury-minivan owners, a market with a low ceiling. More deeply, revenue passed 100 billion yuan in just over three years, but operations were still stuck in the Autohome era, and the strongest product leaders were pulled off to fix processes. The fix: put product chiefs willing to argue with him back in charge, and fill gaps in the city charging network.
ex: Charging satisfaction (NPS) rose from the 30s to nearly 90 via city stations, app fixes, certified chargers
Five seats or six? Boarding evidence persuaded him to split the design into two models, R7 and R8

items.d: Monthly sales of the whole segment
Even doubling gets only this far

87|458.c: A company should be a fair ranked ladder, a family runs on giving, and the two mustn't be swapped.
87|458.e: A gamer for decades, he thinks games hook people because they're the fairest system. Li Auto's sales rankings, incentives and job levels borrow from the ranked ladder: transparent rules, and you can move up or down. Family and close friends, though, run on giving and receiving, and many people get it backward, trading on sentiment at work and bargaining at home. At work, a CEO's first customers are employees. At home, the most important person is your spouse, then the kids. After nearly being pushed out in 2008, he learned to treat himself well and share his troubles with partners.
ex: He still plays Overwatch an hour or two a day and prefers team play
When funding collapsed in 2008, he shouldered it alone, though partners would have mortgaged homes to help

d.verdict: Keep each system in its place, or relationships suffer

88|402.c: Operator isn't o3 with hands attached. It's o1 stretched sideways to see and act on screens.
88|402.e: Yi Wu sees o1 and o3, OpenAI's reasoning models, as going deeper: given a question, the model thinks silently with no feedback from outside. Operator runs a loop instead: look, think, act, look again, and what it sees changes with the page. Its chains of thought are short, and it mostly fixes mistakes by undoing actions. So it's more like an o1 that sees and works in a loop, possibly on a new base model. It doesn't raise the ceiling on pure reasoning, but it widens what the model can do. And once it has eyes, it must handle every kind of website from day one.
ex: The model closes pop-up windows on its own
After failing to calculate a refund in the browser several times, it switched to a calculator

d.verdict: No higher reasoning ceiling, but far more it can do

88|402.c: No secret recipe: the barrier is excelling at base model, data and RL system all at once.
88|402.e: He doesn't think there's a magic formula. How much post-training can unlock depends on the potential of the base model, which must handle images and text natively. The data doesn't need pre-training scale, but it has to demonstrate exactly the behaviors the base model lacks. Hardest is the reinforcement learning (RL) system: on web tasks, every step must actually run on a computer and send the screen back. Chinese teams know the path and have half the infrastructure. The gap is doing all three superbly at once. Agents built by wrapping a general model in prompts fall far short of a purpose-trained computer-use agent (CUA).
ex: Math training just keeps writing; web training waits for the computer at every step
Scaling training to thousands or 10,000 GPUs makes environment waiting a major engineering headache

terms.d: Sets how far post-training can go
Demos like closing ads or backing out after errors
Runs each step, sends the screen back

88|402.c: OpenAI's 2016 failure shows that neither reinforcement learning alone nor a good base model alone is enough.
88|402.e: He looks back at OpenAI's early web agent project. It tried to train a large LSTM, an older kind of neural network, to use the internet purely through reinforcement learning, with no base model, no human labels and too little compute. It failed. Nine years later the recipe is complete: multimodal base models can understand what's on a screen, and o1 and o3 proved reinforcement learning works at scale. So he calls 2025 the breakthrough year for agents, but only if the two are combined. Either one alone won't get there.
ex: About 20 to 30 people were laid off after that project failed

items.d: Pure RL, no base model; it failed
RL for reasoning proven at scale
Multimodal base plus RL: agents break through

88|402.c: Going from L3 to L4 is a huge leap: from completing tasks to creating something new.
88|402.e: OpenAI ranks AI ability in five levels. He sees L1 through L3 as following instructions that can be checked: a person sets the task and a verifier judges whether it's done. L3 just adds observing the outside world and acting on its own. L4 gives the AI only a direction and expects results beyond existing knowledge, so it must judge good versus bad, not just right versus wrong. He doubts that arrives within two or three years. A crude L5 may appear first as agents passively working together, say when websites deploy their own agents. But truly self-organizing still needs L4-style creativity.
ex: He expects single agents operating human interfaces to dominate for the next year or two
If most requests come from agents, websites may open dedicated doors for them

items.d: Observes the world, acts on its own
Given a direction, goes beyond existing knowledge

88|402.c: Agents sell time. 2025 shows what they can do; real revenue waits for reliability.
88|402.e: He thinks an agent's value comes from needing people less. Filing taxes, returning goods and buying supplies all compete for the same attention, and a reliable agent runs them in parallel. You may not get three times the time, but double is already valuable. For businesses, it's a cheaper AI employee. But this year is mainly about benchmark scores jumping. People still complain about o1's quality, and running agents reliably and cheaply will take time. Agent tasks come with a clear success signal, so they suit reinforcement learning better than chat. Still, researchers must clean user data. There's no automatic flywheel: intelligence comes first, product follows.
ex: Operator scores 30-something on the OSWorld benchmark; he expects 70-80 this year
Pausing for a human before paying looks like a layer the safety team added

items.d: No one needs to watch it
Taxes, returns and purchasing at once
For companies, it's an AI employee

88|402.c: AI reasoning has just started tilting toward the physical world. Startups should take the less popular paths.
88|402.e: He splits intelligence into three layers: abstract reasoning over text, reasoning over images, and reasoning about the physical world. The web pages Operator handles are basically text turned into images, with none of the spatial reasoning needed to find socks or pack a suitcase. The needle has moved only from 90 degrees to 80. OpenAI will earn money in the digital world first and invest its way into physical intelligence. Multimodal models, reasoning and agents are consensus now. Giants drive tanks down the main road, so startups should seek long-tail niches or contrarian bets. Academics should tackle open problems like personalized memory and forms of human feedback.
ex: Even if general models cover 99%, the last 1% in support, logistics and taxes is huge
The US already has a dozen-plus industry-specific agent companies; China has fewer
After DeepSeek and Operator launched, his team dropped a paper planned for ICML

marks.d: Web pages are text rendered as images

89|473.c: R1 revealed the answer to o1's riddle, but it hasn't settled who wins the race to AGI.
89|473.e: Jiayi Pan likens o1 to a riddle from OpenAI, and DeepSeek was the first team to hand in a clean answer. R1 is what set the field on fire, because it showed researchers where to start. Even people doing vision-language pre-training switched to visual reasoning. But he holds back: DeepSeek hasn't shipped a run of game-changing products the way OpenAI has, and US labs have 10 to 100 times more compute. What R1 proves is that DeepSeek turns resources into results extremely efficiently, while post-training is still early.
ex: Kimi k1.5 took a similar path but lacked open-source track record and a one-line headline
OpenAI reportedly has hundreds of thousands of H100s; Stargate targets millions of new chips

items.d: Vision and agent teams pivot to reasoning

89|473.c: AI progress now walks on two legs: pre-training compute times compute spent thinking at answer time.
89|473.e: He thinks pre-training still improves, but each generation comes slower and costs far more. Nearly two years after GPT-4 there's no GPT-5, and DeepSeek V3 and Llama 405B haven't clearly beaten GPT-4. o1's charts show that both post-training compute and test-time compute give log-linear gains: steady improvement with each doubling. The gains come from longer chains of thought: break the problem down, try, then double-check. His rough analogy: ability is roughly the two kinds of compute multiplied. Until now the money went into pre-training while inference was cheap, so both legs will now move together.
ex: Estimates he cited: GPT-4 pre-training about $50 million, the next generation maybe over $200 million
In o1's published chart, AIME math accuracy rose from 20-30% to nearly 80%
o1 to o3 took three or four months; FrontierMath rose from about 1% to over 20%

89|473.c: Reinforcement learning doesn't teach answers; it rewards results, so reasoning is closer to a discovery.
89|473.e: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has a model imitate correct answers. Reinforcement learning (RL) only says whether the outcome was good and lets the model explore. When the ideal behavior is too complex for people to demonstrate step by step, defining only the goal can uncover paths no one imagined. He doesn't see this as dismissing human knowledge: pre-training supplies the knowledge, and RL organizes it into reasoning or agent behavior. Three companies reached similar recipes independently, which makes it look more like a discovery than anyone's invention. RL may also be the only known method that reaches superhuman performance.
ex: He quotes an OpenAI researcher's line: "Don't Teach, Incentivize"
He compares the model's spontaneous self-correction to the "divine move" in Go

d.verdict: When you can't demonstrate, defining the goal goes further

89|473.c: R1-Zero's gains come down to the model teaching itself to spend more thinking on each problem.
89|473.e: R1-Zero starts from the V3 base model, skips supervised fine-tuning and goes straight to large-scale reinforcement learning. The reward checks only whether the answer and format are correct, not the reasoning style. As training goes on, accuracy and response length rise almost in lockstep: the model discovers that thinking longer earns more reward. The so-called "aha moment" is a chain of behaviors, pausing, looking back, spotting an error, switching approach and re-checking, that no researcher wrote in. He leaves an open question: the curve was still rising, so why did DeepSeek stop?
ex: AIME accuracy is about 70% in one try, near o1 with 16-vote majority
Average responses grew from a few hundred tokens to nearly 10,000
TinyZero replication: 1 for correct, 0.1 for format; a 3B model learned self-correction overnight

89|473.c: Drop the value model, process rewards and tree search: the cleanest algorithm scales best.
89|473.e: Long chains of thought often contain a wrong step that gets fixed later. Was that step a mistake or useful exploration? A value model, which scores each step, can't judge well, so GRPO drops it. It samples several answers per question and scores each against the group, adding old-data reuse and a KL limit on drifting. Rule-based rewards cover fewer tasks but are hard for strong models to game. Process rewards stumble because a "step" is hard to define and labels are costly, so they only suit best-of-N filtering. MCTS has no clear moves in language, so the search tree explodes. He sees no plot behind OpenAI's early process-supervision paper.
ex: If a reward model learns "more emojis = friendlier," the model fills screens with emojis
In long multiplication, is one line a step, or the whole calculation?

items.d: Hard to score wrong steps in long chains
Steps hard to define, labels costly
Compare within a group: the minimum that works

89|473.c: R1 turns R1-Zero's scientific finding into a readable, general-purpose product.
89|473.e: R1-Zero is purer technically, but its output is hard to read, mixes languages and generalizes poorly. R1 takes four steps. A cold start on hand-picked long chains of thought gives exploration a good starting point. Reasoning-focused RL follows, with a penalty for mixing languages. Then supervised fine-tuning on reasoning plus general data turns the specialist back into a generalist. Finally comes RL across all domains. He notes R1-Zero isn't truly zero, since it was already pre-trained on internet text. k1.5 skipped a Zero stage and is still strong, so Zero's value is proving the path works with few human priors.
ex: About 600,000 reasoning samples plus 200,000 general ones, roughly 800,000 in total
Reasoning data gets rule-based rewards; general data gets a reward model

items.d: A few curated long chains of thought
Turn the specialist back into a generalist
Rule rewards plus a reward model

89|473.c: R1's extra training may have cost only six figures in dollars, but it rests on V3.
89|473.e: He did a deliberately high back-of-envelope estimate: about 10,000 steps, about 1,000 responses per step, up to about 10,000 tokens each. That's roughly 100 billion tokens. At the going price of $2.20 per million tokens, it comes to about $220,000. Optimized, maybe $100,000, and even a high estimate is $1 million. The host pointed out that R1 depends on V3, and he agreed only the extra step is cheap. So he thinks companies building industry reasoning or coding agents can simply post-train on V3, while labs chasing AGI still need the full stack, pre-training included.
ex: He guesses R1 trained on 100 to 200 GPUs, but the paper doesn't say
The V3 report puts context extension at about $200,000, post-training about $10,000

items.d: About $5.3 million, per the V3 report

89|473.c: Distilling from a strong teacher beats a weak student practicing alone, but students can't just copy answers.
89|473.e: DeepSeek used R1's outputs to distill Qwen and Llama, training smaller models to imitate the big one, and open-sourced versions from 1.5B to 70B parameters that run locally. In the paper, a 32B model distilled from R1 clearly beat the same model trained with R1-Zero-style RL directly, because big models find good strategies more easily. But RL after distillation still adds gains, so, as he puts it, even a slow student has to practice. Competition now extends beyond training the biggest base model to teacher data, distillation recipes and inference deployment.
ex: On leaderboards, distilled Qwen-1.5B beats GPT-4o on AIME by about 10 to 20 points

root.d: The big model discovers; small ones inherit

89|473.c: Having the reward model reason before scoring is k1.5's finding most likely to be widely adopted.
89|473.e: He sees k1.5 following the same main path as R1, with more reproducible detail in its report. Tasks like math proofs can't be judged by rules alone, so k1.5 still trains a reward model. Instead of having it output a label directly, it writes out reasoning first, compares solutions and checks for errors before judging, and accuracy jumps. Coding problems get auto-generated unit tests, and some vision problems come from synthesized spatial-relation questions. It also renders text as screenshots for training, so the product doesn't suddenly get worse when it meets screenshots.
ex: The new approach was fine-tuned on only about 80 labeled examples
Error rate fell from about 15% to about 1.5%

89|473.c: Thinking more must still be efficient; RL with a length penalty is the best way to shorten reasoning.
89|473.e: k1.5 adds a length penalty to its reward. Wrong answers should stop as soon as possible, and even right answers are nudged shorter, though correctness always dominates. Curriculum sampling picks problems the model could solve but hasn't mastered. Of four ways to shorten chains of thought, model merging, SFT and DPO all work, but RL with a length penalty does best at the same token count. On the systems side, partial rollouts cut off very long responses and resume them next round, so GPUs sit idle less. He accepts the host's counterpoint: chat users may prefer long answers, and cost matters more for API and on-device use.
ex: Learning only from good samples usually adds 3-4 points; k1.5-style algorithms add 10-20
He wouldn't be surprised if current RL frameworks became 50% to 100% more efficient

cells.d: Don't waste tokens on wrong answers

90|324.c: DeepSeek convinced him AGI is at least possible, and that machines may already have low-level consciousness.
90|324.e: Xiaohu Zhu says the shift came from using it himself. In his view, DeepSeek's writing, its depth and the reasoning it shows can no longer be explained as stitching words together by probability. He hedges: the path is proven in fields with clear rules, but fuzzy fields still need high-quality data to guide reinforcement learning, so he says only that AGI is at least possible. He accepts that consciousness is a spectrum, and thinks machines can easily cross the low threshold but remain far from human-level consciousness. He also says he'd invest in DeepSeek.
ex: Out-writes 99% of people; beats most at coding, science and medicine within 6-12 months, he predicts
He tests it daily with questions about existence, philosophy and quantum mechanics
He'd invest in DeepSeek, but less at a high valuation, sizing the check to the risk

marks.d: May have crossed the low threshold

90|324.c: Open source catching up is a curse for the leader. Closed models need a real leap to survive.
90|324.e: His math is simple. The leader spends ten times as much to get 10-20% better, and Chinese teams catch up within a year at a tenth of the cost, so users have no reason to pay. Closed models' only way out is a next generation, trained on 100,000-GPU clusters, that's two or three times better. Otherwise they survive only on proprietary data, hardware or industry niches. DeepSeek grew purely by word of mouth. Once developers build around its open architecture, it becomes the Android of AI, and OpenAI open-sourcing then will be too late.
ex: ~20M daily users in 20 days, no ads; possibly 100M+ in two or three months
His question: without hardware locked in like the iPhone, why would anyone need iOS?

items.d: Rivals spend a tenth as much

90|324.c: Piling on compute brings diminishing returns; the bottleneck is now expert-level, high-quality data.
90|324.e: He says he heard doubts in Silicon Valley last year about scaling laws, the idea that more compute reliably makes models smarter. As he understands it, two or three US companies trained on 100,000-GPU clusters for about six months with no clear gains. DeepSeek's key breakthrough was moving from human feedback to reinforcement learning: with a good batch of starting data, the machine can push forward by rules on its own, at far lower cost. Fuzzy fields need PhD-level experts to label data, and low-quality labels are worth less and less. So he sees the $500 billion Stargate as showmanship. Nvidia demand remains, but growth may disappoint.
ex: A chef analogy: the same core skills yield Sichuan or Cantonese food, depending on the data
Some Chinese companies already run DeepSeek on domestic chips

items: 100K GPUs for six months, no clear gain
10x the cost for a one-year lead

d.verdict: With scaling stalling, data quality is the key variable

90|324.c: Models are good enough now. Chinese AI apps will boom in 2025, and model startups must pivot fast.
90|324.e: He argues that with one of the best models now open source, app companies no longer need to worry about building on someone else's foundation. In China you can even treat the base model as free infrastructure, so apps will boom in 2025. The later a model startup pivots, the less room it has. Big tech firms can keep closed models for their own products, but most companies should rethink. He also openly questions why Li Auto needs its own large model and personal assistant, since existing open-source models are good enough.
ex: He credits Kai-Fu Lee for shifting toward applications early
If Baichuan sticks with healthcare, it can build proprietary data on open models
Qwen's inference price for AI hardware makers is as low as 10-20 yuan

root.d: The later you pivot, the less room

90|324.c: Most data flowing back from users is useless; the real edge is mindshare and owning workflows.
90|324.e: He calls this his biggest lesson in two years. People used to think the flywheel of more users, more data and a better product was the strongest defense in AI. It turns out chat data is repetitive and thin. What matters is a small amount of dense, expert data. So the value of a big user base shifts to mindshare, retention and distribution. DeepSeek's edge is mostly that it won users' minds first. App companies should take over customers' whole workflows rather than expect data to improve the product on its own.
ex: Best case: quote half the client's current cost and take over the entire call center
First movers like ChatGPT and Perplexity differ little and can't stop rivals with a better experience

90|324.c: What you call an agent doesn't matter; what matters is how much work it replaces without humans.
90|324.e: He sees OpenAI's five-level framework as just a definition. An agent, an AI that acts on its own, is still a program, and the test is whether it finishes half, 80% or 90% of a job with no human stepping in. Coding is going through this now. Fuzzy-rule fields like medicine must go through it too, and that will be the bigger breakthrough. He thinks chat models have already replaced search, while personal assistants remain unproven. DeepSeek could become a $100 billion-plus company; for other startups he'll only imagine $1-10 billion. Going overseas is low-hanging fruit for Chinese teams.
ex: ServiceNow rose 3-4x in a year on bets that AI replaces services and lifts margins
He calls DeepSeek an iPhone 3G moment and expects another hit app this year

items.d: Share early coding tools could replace
Half the work with no human help
Medicine and others must repeat this

91|475.c: RL for reasoning ended up with rule-based rewards; process supervision had led the community astray.
91|475.e: Junxian He's team started similar work about two months before R1 came out. They first tried reward models and process supervision, which scores each step, on math reasoning. After a long time tuning, results were poor, and the simplest rules worked best: for math, check only the final answer; for code, check whether it passes unit tests. He thinks Kimi, DeepSeek and others all converged on this path. The community had taken a detour following OpenAI's process-reward paper, and what OpenAI published may not be how it built o1. Open-ended questions with no standard answer may still need reward models.
ex: They released results five days after R1, calling it R1-like, not a replication
Process rewards with online PPO failed for 2-3 months; dropping the reward model worked

items: Generalization breaks down at larger scale
Higher ceiling in theory, hard to get right
Check math answers, run code tests

d.verdict: The simplest approach worked best

91|475.c: DeepSeek works like a university lab: low-key, honest and willing to bet on unproven approaches.
91|475.e: He wasn't impressed at first. High-Flyer came from quant trading, it started late, the scramble among Chinese model makers was already on, and he saw it as just another startup. Its first paper changed his mind: open about details and written like a university lab's work. While the industry rushed to claim it beat GPT-4, DeepSeek mostly stayed out, and it came late to consumer products. He guesses the team faced no pressure to beat rivals within months, so it dared to invest in unproven architectures. But he stresses this is his reading of the papers, not inside knowledge.
ex: In late 2022 High-Flyer touted about 5,000 A100s and opened the cluster to universities for free
He used that cluster himself and found it mature, not just PR

root.d: Keeps making different choices to cut costs

items.d: A small team runs a supercomputer
Lots of detail, unflattering results included

91|475.c: DeepSeek's first paper stood out for studying how training behaves and admitting how much benchmark gaming inflates scores.
91|475.e: DeepSeek LLM largely followed Meta's Llama 2 architecture, so beating Llama 2 70B was no surprise. What he values is that the team didn't copy settings but studied how training behaves. It switched to a step-wise learning-rate schedule, which performs close to the usual cosine schedule and makes adding data midway easier. It studied scaling laws for hyperparameters and found that data quality changes the best balance of model size and data. Using small runs, it fitted curves that predicted the 7B and 67B models' results quite accurately. Rarer still, the paper openly showed how far gaming a benchmark can push scores.
ex: C-Eval is a Chinese benchmark his team released in May 2023; gaming it soon became common
His team's later tests found no clear sign DeepSeek's base model gamed benchmarks

items.d: A comparison the paper chose to disclose

91|475.c: Mixture-of-experts separates total size from per-step compute; fine-grained plus shared experts is the key.
91|475.e: A dense model uses all its parameters every time. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model splits the feed-forward layers into many experts, and a router activates only a few, so it can hold more knowledge with less compute. DeepSeek wasn't first, Google was earlier, but it kept digging in the efficiency direction. He thinks the traditional 8 or 16 experts are too coarse. DeepSeek cut experts finer and added shared experts that handle general skills like language and common sense. He stresses that what works small may fail at scale, and betting on an unproven path is risky, which is why he calls it brave.
ex: 64 routed experts plus 2 shared ones nearly match a dense 7B at about 40% compute
The 145B model, trained on just 200B+ tokens with ~22B active, nears 67B

terms.d: Finer division of labor, activated by input
Handle language, common sense and other basics

result.d: Huge total size, little compute per step

91|475.c: MLA, DeepSeek's own invention, shrinks the KV cache and helped set off a price war.
91|475.e: Standard multi-head attention stores keys and values (K and V) for every head, and this KV cache takes up huge memory during generation. GQA and MQA save space by sharing K and V across heads, but may lose expressive power. MLA compresses K and V into a small latent vector and expands it when needed, so the cache holds only the compressed version. He sees it as DeepSeek's own invention: compressed to the equivalent of about 2.25 groups, it still beats simply cutting groups. He adds that balancing expert load, device load and communication is unglamorous but decides whether a sparse design becomes real cost savings.
ex: V2 vs. 67B: 42.5% less training compute, 90%+ smaller KV cache, 5.76x faster generation
It sparked an API price war in May 2024; he heard margins were thin, not negative

items.d: Every head stores K and V
Dubbed the PDD of AI models

91|475.c: V3's breakthrough is mainly engineering: training a 671B model stably and cheaply.
91|475.e: V3 keeps MLA and lots of routed experts. Training ran with no loss spikes and no rollbacks, which he says must reflect a very strong engineering and infrastructure team. It used few GPUs for its size, the main reason it drew attention. Three things are new. It balances expert load without an auxiliary loss, adjusting a bias based on how often each expert is picked. It's the first to validate multi-token prediction with ablations at this scale. And it trained successfully in FP8 mixed precision at scale. He sees post-training as fairly light and not chasing leaderboards, with reasoning data distilled from an internal R1.
ex: 2,048 H800s and 14.8 trillion tokens, at about $5.57 million
Serving costs are over 10x lower than the dense Llama 3.1 405B

items.d: No auxiliary loss; tune a bias term

91|475.c: DeepSeek's reasoning ability was built up step by step, from Coder to Math to Prover.
91|475.e: He traces a second line running alongside the base models. Coder was how overseas developers first discovered DeepSeek, and its small and mid sizes were easy to deploy. Coder V2 still used a reward model because unit tests didn't cover enough and wrong code could pass by luck; he thinks rules would work too with better test coverage. Math introduced GRPO, which drops PPO's value model and uses a group's average reward as the baseline, saving memory and compute. Prover checks formal proofs with Lean, and when rewards were too sparse it dropped unsolvable problems rather than retrain a reward model.
ex: Coder V1.5 continued training on about 2T tokens, roughly 70% code
Math 7B continued from the Coder base on about 120B math tokens

items.d: Practical coding, still a reward model
Introduces GRPO, drops the value model

91|475.c: RL may just push answers the model could already find to the top, and DeepSeek said so.
91|475.e: The Math paper compared offline, iterative and online reinforcement learning (RL). Online worked best but was costly, unstable and hard to tune, and the community lacked mature code. What he admires more is the Pass@K analysis. After RL, the share of problems solved on the first try rose clearly, but the gap narrowed when multiple attempts were allowed, and sometimes the model without RL did better. He concludes that RL may just rank correct answers the model could already produce higher, without strengthening its core ability. Putting such a self-deflating result in a paper is scientific honesty.
ex: Rule rewards are stable but sparse; process rewards aim higher but rarely work across domains

items.d: All the answers the model can produce
The correct answer is already there
Pushes right answers to the top

91|475.c: R1 combines lessons from earlier wins and failures; next up are RL and test-time scaling.
91|475.e: R1's reward has just two rules: is the answer right, and is the format right. R1-Zero ran RL straight from the base model, and its chains of thought grew longer, with "aha" moments. R1 added a cold start on long chains of thought and is the version people actually use. The paper is short because the V3 base, GRPO, rule-based rewards and earlier failures were all in place. He thinks the truly original algorithms are mainly GRPO and MLA, and the rest is engineering and smart combination. High-quality internet data may be nearly tapped out, so synthetic data, RL and test-time scaling come next.
ex: R1-Zero's AIME score rose from about 0.2-0.3 to about 0.7-0.8
R1 writes well; he guesses humanities data or transfer from long reasoning, but can't tell which

items.d: MoE plus MLA; sparked a price war

92|477.c: AGI will come in three steps, information, physical and biological intelligence, in about 5, 10 and 20 years.
92|477.e: Ya-Qin Zhang splits the new wave of AI into three layers. Information intelligence handles text, images and video. Physical intelligence goes into self-driving cars, robots and connected devices. Biological intelligence links the brain and body. He expects information intelligence to reach human level in about five years, high-level physical intelligence to beat people at most tasks in about ten, and biological intelligence to take about twenty. Being smart isn't the same as getting things done, he stresses: information intelligence is like reading ten thousand books, but physical intelligence must travel ten thousand miles and learn skills in the real world.
ex: Within half an hour of first using ChatGPT, he felt it had passed the Turing test
He thinks text is basically solved; reasoning, multimodality and video generation remain

items.d: About 5 years; like the brain's IQ

92|477.c: Companies should lead on foundation models; universities should bet on talent and specific industries.
92|477.e: He likens foundation models to a horizontal operating system for a whole ecosystem. They need massive compute, data and real-world use cases, and most of the work is engineering that takes ideas from one to a hundred and beyond, which universities can't do alone. So Tsinghua's AIR ranks talent first, research second and industry impact third, focusing on smart transportation, the Internet of Things and AI for life sciences. China has plenty of engineers, he says, but lacks architects with a global view who can run big systems. He disagrees that big companies have taken all the large-model opportunities; specific industries still have room.
ex: In Microsoft Research China's first two or three years, about 80% of time went to recruiting
He rates AIR's PhD students as absolutely world-class

items: Heavy capital: compute, data, use cases

d.verdict: The base layer will consolidate; industry niches still have room

92|477.c: Self-driving is past the proving stage; what's left is who scales fastest and the business model.
92|477.e: In a Waymo in San Francisco, he found the ride smoother than a human's, and locals no longer treat it as a novelty. Two years ago he believed it would happen but couldn't say when; now he thinks the timing is clear. He believes Tesla's approach could reach Level 4 in theory, but not yet, because a robotaxi basically can't rely on a human taking over. The industry will split into three layers, operations, vehicles, and chips and parts, which can stand alone or combine, with no single winner. Leaders have run for eight to ten years, so starting a general self-driving company from scratch is no longer realistic.
ex: He says today's FSD may need a human takeover every 45 minutes
He judges Baidu's Apollo Go to be at least 10 times safer than human drivers

items.d: Most carmakers still just sell cars

92|477.c: Large models have loosened the three locks on embodied AI, but haven't fully opened them.
92|477.e: Self-driving and robotics used to be stuck in three places: data couldn't cover dangerous situations, endless rare cases made generalization poor, and perception, planning and decision-making were separate modules stitched together by rules. Large models brought scene generation, common-sense reasoning and a single end-to-end framework. Architectures shifted from different algorithms for different inputs to one Transformer working on tokens. He proposes a loop from real to simulated and back to real, which he sees as a world model. He stressed twice that the problems are only greatly eased, which is why people see a glimmer of hope this year.
ex: A large model can split "do laundry, drop at cleaners, pick up" into steps
Driving a car isn't opening a door: grip, heat and dietary rules need a real body

items.d: Generate many scenes from real data
Unified end to end, rules as backup

92|477.c: Humanoid robots are roughly where self-driving was a decade ago, and homes are the hardest setting.
92|477.e: He sees driving as a relatively closed problem and general humanoid robots as an open one, so self-driving arrives first and general humanoid products are still eight to ten years away. Robots fall into home, industrial and social types, and their back ends can share a cloud model, industry-specific models and on-device models. A human shape makes interaction natural and lets robots use stairs and doors built for people, but not every robot needs one. He imagines robots may outnumber people within 10 years, with everyone having a double that can be more capable but must obey its owner.
ex: The three robot types share about 70-80% of their back end
Driving can't err for even a few hundred milliseconds; breakfast can be a bit slow

marks.d: Only drives, so it arrives first
Constant contact with people on the street

92|477.c: AI extends humans rather than replacing them; the conscious ones are still us carbon-based beings.
92|477.e: He favors non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, used first to treat disease, like restoring sight and hearing or slowing Alzheimer's, and later to boost memory and intelligence. Organ replacement and drugs will extend life, but he doesn't think people can live forever. He flatly rejects the idea that intelligence past some level produces consciousness. We don't yet understand where consciousness comes from, and compute and data have nothing to do with it. He accepts carbon-silicon fusion as how humans take part in superintelligence, but the new form is an extension of us. Education will shift from drilling test questions to learning to ask questions and think critically.
ex: In 30 years driving may feel like riding a horse cart; some may live to 120-150
Workweeks went from seven days to five and four; someday one day a week may suffice

items.d: Restore sight and hearing, treat brain disease
Carbon-silicon fusion, humans still in charge

93|479.c: Search's edge is ranking plus user feedback, but owning a gateway users pass through can overcome it.
93|479.e: Qianchuan Zhang thinks link analysis like PageRank turned web pages into rankable units, which is how search found product-market fit. Ranking decides where attention goes, and feedback such as clicks and time on page improves crawling, indexing and ranking in turn. The gains compound, traffic concentrates at the top, and latecomers struggle to catch up. But data from a gateway product lowers the barrier: 360 rebuilt search on its browser and security software, and Bing did the same with Internet Explorer. Companies without such a gateway find it very hard to catch up.
ex: The top three results get about 80-90% of clicks
At Baidu he led an 8-tier site rating; each lower tier had about 10x more sites
He joined 360 in 2012; a month later it decided to build its own search

93|479.c: From search to recommendation to large models, algorithms keep getting more general and iterate faster.
93|479.e: He sums up his career as algorithm-driven: first a more general algorithm appears, then a rough product, and then it grows by serving users. Recommendation puts users and content in the same high-dimensional space and links them by distance and behavior. That requires a phone that knows who is using it and builds long-term history, which PCs couldn't do. 94|480.c: The hard part of dynamic sparsity isn't the idea but matching how GPUs read memory.

The idea is easy; the hardware is hard. Reading scattered individual words clashes with GPUs, which like to move contiguous blocks of data. 94|480.c: NSA gives up some freedom for its attention heads in exchange for almost no wasted memory reads.
94|480.e: Attention has many "heads," like several readers. In GQA, heads in a group share one set of stored notes. If each picks different blocks, the GPU must load them all, diluting the benefit of sharing. NSA sums the group's block scores and picks one top set, forcing the heads onto the same blocks. It stacks the group's heads into a batch to form matrix multiplications that keep the GPU's Tensor Cores, its matrix-math units, fully busy. She says she'd never seen a training kernel written this way. The cost is less diversity, which DeepSeek offsets with more heads. Triton's minimum matrix size implies 64 heads. She calls it "brute-force elegance."

94|480.c: Linear attention compresses history into a fixed-size matrix, and chunked algorithms make it fast on GPUs.

The cost is that not all history is kept, so the state's size caps memory. Training it step by step is serial, while fully parallel training brings back squared cost. Chunked algorithms run in parallel within chunks and pass state between them. That is exactly equivalent, not an approximation, and like NSA it is about forming matrix multiplications. 96|501.c: A world model is an exam, not a rulebook, and forms a reinforcement-learning loop with real roads.

A world model, an AI that simulates the road, sets the exam: safety, legality, comfort, navigation and efficiency, each at three difficulty levels. Safety is a hard floor, and a new version can't score lower overall than the old one. Real cases are rebuilt with 3D Gaussian splatting and practice ones made by generative models, so the model can't memorize answers. Models pass before hitting the road, and new problems flow back as data and questions. In 2021 a supplier demanded a high price, refused to hand over code and told Li Auto to disband its own team. Li Xiang refused, and after Chinese New Year 100-plus people started building in-house. Li Auto then tried heavy-map, light-map and map-free designs, which he says is the only way to truly see why Tesla dropped each old generation. By 2024 driving tech was clearly moving car sales, and a March strategy meeting named end-to-end the only answer.
ex: The first model braked better than a long-tuned rule system, though engineers never tuned it
On the first test drive, with Li Xiang up front, one or two takeovers in over an hour
