Named the only path, team locked down
Real user data starts flowing back

97|276.c: His biggest contrarian call: pre-training is far from over, and it sets a model's ceiling.
97|276.e: Six months ago he also put the odds that pre-training had peaked at 50%. Now he says the next top base models can still clearly beat today's. His reason: post-training and reinforcement learning, where a model improves through trial and reward, only draw out and strengthen abilities that already exist. They can't create new ones. Doing RL on a weak base is like drilling a weak student on practice tests, and gains flatten fast. He also thinks high-quality reasoning traces from RL can be fed back into pre-training to ease the data shortage. The hard part is getting training and inference systems to share the same GPUs.
ex: He calls the o-series drilling; only pre-training moves a model from primary to middle school

items.d: Drilling that draws out existing skills

97|276.c: OpenAI and Anthropic are drifting apart, and at root that reflects what each organization is good at.
97|276.e: OpenAI is betting on its o-series reasoning models and a billion consumers, leaning toward product and traffic, with a bottom-up culture. Anthropic is betting on base-model pre-training, coding and agents, leaning toward businesses and developers, and is more top-down. CEO Dario Amodei himself came from pre-training. He thinks OpenAI's pre-training slowdown wasn't a deliberate choice. The fast-paying o-series and ChatGPT absorbed management's attention, key people left, and pre-training staff moved to post-training. He judges Anthropic's and xAI's pre-training teams stronger right now, and once a lab falls behind, switching back is hard.
ex: Cursor pays Claude about 4–5 times as much per month as it pays OpenAI
He estimates Anthropic could be worth $300–500 billion if it stays ahead

d.verdict: Strategy follows organization and key people

97|276.c: Coding is the most general training ground, because code lets a model act on the digital world.
97|276.e: A good training environment changes, lets you take actions and gives instant feedback. Coding, games and science all qualify, and coding is the most general. When a model writes and runs code, it can gather information, process data and take actions, as if it grew hands. Growth in the digital economy may far outstrip the physical one. He expects agents to go from using computers and phones like our parents to working like skilled programmers within two years, with coding hidden behind consumer products. He puts his personal odds of AGI within two years at 100%, landing between late 2026 and early 2027.
ex: Office has over a million features most people never touch, and agents could use them all
He calls Manus the "ChatGPT moment" for Claude's tool use

items.d: A live environment you can act in

97|276.c: Traffic alone can't keep users, and a 10x better experience breaks through old advantages.
97|276.e: Some veteran investors say OpenAI should become a platform because training models is too capital-inefficient. He firmly disagrees, calling it old business instinct applied to a new, research-driven game. What matters is the size of the lead. If a new model is only slightly better, brand and traffic still win. If it's ten times better, users move. Google has matched benchmarks several times without winning traffic because the gap wasn't big enough. So he worries that by putting a billion users ahead of AGI, OpenAI could miss AI's chance to spark a scientific renaissance. App companies should ride research breakthroughs, not drive research with growth targets.
ex: ChatGPT, AlphaGo, Claude 3.5 and Manus each had a magic moment
He thinks DeepSeek may be right to skip chasing traffic and keep building models

97|276.c: Intelligence itself is the biggest application: agents are the main course, and science is Everest.
97|276.e: He argues all investment and thinking should center on making models smarter. The climb goes like this: GPT-3.5 unlocked conversation, Claude 3.5 Sonnet unlocked coding, then come coding agents, general agents and AI for science, with robots further out. Chat is just the appetizer. Video and image generation are dazzling but don't necessarily make models smarter. He thinks AI for science is closer than robotics. Agents can run virtual labs, and foundation models for proteins, RNA and virtual cells may be nearing their own GPT-3 moments, with a possible boom in 2026–2027.
ex: Robot data is collected by hand, so 100 million hours may cost hundreds of millions
He sees smart glasses as a phone accessory at best, not a replacement

items.d: Unlocked by GPT-3.5, just the appetizer
From coding to general: the main course
Costly data, weak generalization, further out

97|276.c: Token use shows how much intelligence a product taps, and agents are stuck on long context and memory.
97|276.e: He gauges how fully a product uses intelligence by tokens consumed per task, tokens being the units of text a model reads and writes. More isn't smarter, but it means fuller use. Agents depend on long-context reasoning, tool use and instruction following, and Claude clearly leads. In a thousand-step task, tool outputs quickly fill the context, and the hard part is reasoning and reflecting well, not cramming in more text. Reasoning data at a million tokens barely exists, and costs grow roughly with the square of length. He thinks long-term memory may matter more than bigger windows, and standard access to personal data could be a huge opportunity.
ex: A chat uses thousands of tokens, AI search tens of thousands, Manus 700,000–800,000 per task
He likens intelligence to electricity: long context is wiring, MCP the socket, apps the appliances

root.d: Decide whether agents leave the lab

items.d: Hold the original goal through long tasks
May matter more than bigger windows

97|276.c: Inference will keep pushing up GPU demand, and profits will eventually shift to models and apps.
97|276.e: Two forces drive compute: pre-training is back, and agents reason continuously and work in teams, which he estimates can use a thousand times more than chat. But value is split wrong today. Traditional SaaS doesn't burn compute nonstop, yet an AI subscription is like a flat $20 monthly electricity bill, so heavy users cost more the more they use. If Deep Research can make one researcher as productive as three to five, a pro tier at $1,000–2,000 a month is reasonable. Training models is like paying upfront for humanity's future R&D, so long-run profits should move from chips to models and apps.
ex: He estimates Nvidia takes 80%+ of profits, Anthropic loses money, and Cursor has negative gross margins
He sees Nvidia aiming to be a cloud provider, and buying Lepton fills its software gap

result.d: Profits should shift toward models and apps

97|276.c: If the US reaches AGI along today's path, China reproducing it is almost certain.
97|276.e: The gap has narrowed fast over two years, with some capabilities matched in three to six months, and China's huge education system keeps supplying top talent. US labs must spend their vast GPU fleets on exploring and serving users, and exploring may cost 5 to 10 times as much as copying. If pure reproduction takes only tens of thousands of chips, China is very likely to reach AGI. DeepSeek showed that ample capital, risk-taking, strong infrastructure and a small team can make a real breakthrough, and open source helps get past geopolitical blockades. He ranks organization and culture just behind compute, and the key is what a lab dares to give up.
ex: He estimates pure reproduction needs roughly 30,000 to 100,000 GPUs
He most hopes ByteDance becomes China's DeepMind, a long-term AI research lab

items.d: Trial and error burns huge GPU budgets
A route to AGI is validated

98|508.c: Single-purpose robots couldn't scale, and ChatGPT made general-purpose robots look reachable.
98|508.e: The old approach was a hundred robot types for a hundred scenes and tasks. Neither the code nor the hardware could scale, so industrial robot shipments stay far below cars and phones. Deep learning first won in vision, and AlphaGo showed neural networks plus reinforcement learning could handle continuous control. But ChatGPT is what changed expectations: people saw for the first time that one AI method could be general enough. Humanoids are favored because they offer a fairly general-purpose body. He thinks approaches are converging, and the likely order is technology first, then use cases and business.
ex: He dates the full outbreak of this boom to the second half of 2023

items.d: A hundred robots for a hundred scenes
Shipments far below cars and phones
One method can be general enough

98|508.c: Humans are general-purpose VLAs, and in the end these models will merge into one embodied model.
98|508.e: He sees a person as an agent that fuses vision, language understanding and action, which is what a VLA, a vision-language-action model, aims to be. The letters matter less than the requirements: it must be end-to-end, scalable and able to generalize, and touch or sound can be added too. Eventually language, self-driving and robot models will merge into one embodied model, an AI with a body that acts in the real world. He thinks the biggest open problem is finding an architecture that scales. That's a scientific question (how do humans learn?) and an engineering one (data, compute, hardware), and progress will come in levels, as in self-driving.
ex: Robot foundation models aim to work like LLMs: pre-train first, then adapt via fine-tuning or prompts

98|508.c: Stitching off-the-shelf models together is a stopgap, since the model never learns to act physically.
98|508.e: The first phase swapped traditional modules for ready-made models. SayCan had a language model propose candidate actions and a value function judge whether each was feasible. Inner Monologue fed environment feedback back into the reasoning so the robot could correct course. VoxPoser had a model write code marking where to act and what to avoid, then passed that to a trajectory optimizer. He finds these useful short term, and his team built a closed-loop version too. But the model is only bolted onto robot tools and never learns embodied skills itself, so this path won't lead to a true robot foundation model.
ex: With a 10Hz VLM watching, his team's robot squats at once to grab a dropped box
PaLM-E has 562 billion parameters and can plan, but still calls RT-1 to act

items: Works short term, hard to generalize

d.verdict: Long term: pre-trained, end-to-end models

98|508.c: For robot data, diversity matters more than sheer volume.
98|508.e: Google's RT-1 collected data with a dozen-plus robots for over a year. It got nearly every seen task right but only about 75% of unseen ones. His takeaway: repeated demos of the same task, object and placement add little. Variety in tasks, objects, positions and states is what drives generalization. Self-driving is similar: most expert driving data is routine traffic, while the rare extreme cases decide safety. Architecture sets the ceiling, and data quality, quantity and mix set real performance. Pooled data from many labs is uneven, but training on it together still helps.
ex: RT-1: 13 robots, 17 months, about 130,000 episodes, 700 tasks
Open X-Embodiment pools data from about 60 labs, mostly robot arms with grippers

marks.d: Uneven quality, joint training still helps

98|508.c: Robots with different bodies should share one brain, with a small motor controller for each.
98|508.e: Octo let users swap the action format during fine-tuning. CrossFormer went further, training on data from single arms, dual arms, wheeled robots, quadrupeds and even drones together. Most parameters are shared, and each body type gets its own action head instead of forcing one output format. Joint training beat single-body training on some tasks, which suggests skills transfer across tasks and bodies. That's why he has doubts about a unified action space, one long vector with a section for each kind of action. Future robot bodies can't all be listed, so the vector would keep growing.
ex: RDT: about 1 billion parameters, pre-trained on ~1 million episodes, using a unified action space

98|508.c: A vision-language model isn't an action model, so pair it with a small, fast action model.
98|508.e: Google's RT-2 output actions as tokens, like words, so common sense from the web carried over to control. It's seen as the first VLA and shines mainly on unseen tasks. But he sees two bottlenecks. Emitting continuous control as tokens isn't real action modeling, and a large model runs only one to three times a second, too slow for moving targets or delicate contact. His team pairs a slow VLM that grasps meaning and passes on hidden signals with a fast action policy of tens of millions of parameters that reacts directly to vision. It's still trained end to end. Figure's Helix, Physical Intelligence's π0 and Nvidia's GR00T are similar.
ex: RT-2 can put a banana on the German flag, concepts learned from internet pre-training
When someone moves the target, the dual system keeps up while RT-2 often fails

items.d: Fast: tens of millions of parameters, direct actions

98|508.c: A model that can predict future frames understands physics, and that improves its decisions.
98|508.e: ByteDance's GR-1 first learned to predict future frames from video, then was fine-tuned on robot action data. The scaled-up GR-2 showed bigger models had lower loss and higher success rates. His team has one diffusion Transformer, a model that generates by gradually removing noise, produce actions together with future images, depth and even touch. The gains are biggest on unseen objects and harder tasks, and he sees this as a world model built into the VLA. Later work borrowed pre-trained video generators, which knew without task training to pick up a spoon before scooping. UP-VLA then unified understanding, prediction and action.
ex: It guessed a hidden banana was a pear, wrong object, but the gripper motion made sense
Opening a fridge, the model predicts how the door swings and roughly what's inside

98|508.c: Imitation has a ceiling RL can break, but you can't just train a whole VLA with PPO.
98|508.e: He compares it to ChatGPT, which kept improving through RLHF after supervised fine-tuning. Robots likewise need reinforcement learning to get past the limits of imitation. In experiments, pure imitation policies scored under 50 on some tasks, while purpose-built RL came close to perfect, with especially big gains on unseen tasks. But training a whole VLA directly with standard PPO can make it worse. The compromise has two steps. First freeze the VLM, train only the action head with RL and save successful runs. Then unfreeze the VLM and train it on those runs with supervised learning. He admits true end-to-end RL on the full model hasn't been done yet.

items.d: Trial and error in the environment
Pass gains back to the big model

98|508.c: Defining robots by use case is outdated, and general abilities can find paying uses along the way.
98|508.e: He did his PhD on self-driving, and in 2020 decided that field was settled and that robot models would eventually cover driving too, so he switched to robots and returned to China to found a company. It builds everything itself, from body and joints to dexterous hands and motion control, since the supply chain is immature and hardware and software must evolve together. It sells first to universities and researchers, then to manufacturing and service businesses, with homes last. A robot is useful once it matches humans on one narrow step, so real uses may arrive more smoothly than for language models. Scaling shows early signs, but no "aha" moment yet.
ex: Its dexterous hands already sell in volume, and he says the business loop has started turning
His five-year vision: robots seen everywhere, and in some homes too

99|517.c: Fusion goes commercial on cost per kilowatt-hour alone, and that takes a breakthrough, not gradual savings.
99|517.e: He thinks generating power from fusion, if cost is no object, is already basically feasible in science and engineering. The real issue is cost per kilowatt-hour. Matching coal-fired power counts as commercial, and going ten times cheaper would supply energy at massive scale. A traditional low-temperature superconducting machine used directly for power might cost over 100 times as much as coal. Trimming 10–20% a year can hardly close a gap of two orders of magnitude. It takes a one-time breakthrough in materials or technology, and he sees high-temperature superconductors as that breakthrough.
ex: He puts the first demo plant at 0.4–0.5 yuan/kWh: above coal, but near the tipping point

99|517.c: Magnetic-confinement tokamaks are the main road, and inertial confinement doesn't suit power plants.
99|517.e: Earth can't recreate a star's gravity, which leaves inertial confinement and magnetic confinement. He chose magnetic confinement because there are over a hundred such machines, the most evidence, and they're closest to breakeven. Inertial confinement reactions last only nanoseconds, making steady operation hard, so it suits research on extreme conditions and weapons physics. Tokamaks, ring-shaped chambers that hold hot fuel in place with strong magnets, became mainstream after the Soviets proposed them and got clearly better results, drawing money and talent. He treats that consensus as an asset that lowers scientific risk, not a final verdict.
ex: NIF's gain counts only laser energy hitting the target, ignoring under-3% electricity-to-laser efficiency
"Controlled" means steady output at design power, say 500 MW; all at once, it's a weapon

99|517.c: Stronger magnets are the fastest lever: double the field, and machine volume can shrink to about 2%.
99|517.e: Fusion gain depends on the product of fuel density, temperature and confinement time, and pushing one often drags down the others. There's no first-principles model, so scaling laws come from fitting data across a hundred-plus machines: the triple product rises roughly with the field to the 3.5th power and size to the 2.5th. Double the field, and linear size can drop to about 30%, volume to about 2%. Copper magnets overheat within seconds. Low-temperature superconductors need about 4 kelvin and cap the field, forcing big machines. High-temperature superconductors handle at least double the field, the key to going small.
ex: ITER has cost about €25 billion and taken about 30 years
SPARC aims to do similar work for about $1 billion; he thinks $400 million suffices

items.d: At least double the magnetic field
Triple product rises with field to the 3.5

99|517.c: HH70 is like the first steel ship: it proves the thing can be built, not that it's cheaper.
99|517.e: HH70, switched on in 2024, proved a fully high-temperature superconducting tokamak can be built, started and run. But he rejects claims that it proved smaller-and-cheaper. That only holds when comparing at equal performance, say Q≥10, meaning ten times more energy out than in, and that's HH170's job. HH70's discharges last under a second, and its key parameter is about 10^17, four orders of magnitude short of the 10^21 needed. The team went from design to assembly in about two years by machining mature systems before the full design was frozen. Doing it step by step would never have been fast enough.
ex: Over 96% of parts are Chinese-made; imports are mainly cryopumps, valve boxes and some sensors
About 150 staff, with roughly 20 doing physics and most of the rest engineers
It builds the machine, magnets and core systems itself, buying only replaceable parts

items: A full HTS machine can be built
Smaller and cheaper at equal performance

d.verdict: Equal-performance comparison awaits HH170

99|517.c: A three-step plan separates experiments from products, with each step raising money for the next.
99|517.e: Step one, HH70, proves the whole machine works. Step two, HH170, goes for Q≥10 at low cost. Only step three is a demo power plant that can be sold to plant owners. A team that has never built a tokamak can't raise 3 billion yuan and shouldn't bet on world-class performance at once. Proving the machine with HH70, then high performance with prototypes like the Jingtian magnet, makes a credible fundraising chain. Demo plants are built to order, targeting 40,000–50,000 yuan per kilowatt, about 20–25 billion yuan for 500 MW, close to China's fourth-generation high-temperature gas-cooled reactors.
ex: HH170 peaks near 23 tesla; the demo plant targets about 29 tesla at 10x the volume
He says the cost edge comes from HH70's detailed bill of materials, not cheap manufacturing
He admits commercial products are 2030–2035 away, which demands patient capital

items.d: Built and switched on, machine proven
About 3 billion yuan, aiming for Q≥10

99|517.c: The closer to real hardware, the more problems arise, so turn scientific risk into engineering risk.
99|517.e: Looking back on the build, he says problems grow bigger and costlier the closer you get to hardware, and the most expensive often hit at the final step. The worst part is not knowing why. Once you guess the cause and find a testable fix, the rest is just time. So HH170 keeps a conservative physics design similar to ITER's and doesn't gamble on new physics at the same time. It only asks the engineering to hit its numbers. Risk splits two ways: whether each subsystem reaches high performance, tested first with prototypes, and whether the whole machine assembles without losing performance, backed by HH70's experience.
ex: A full-size toroidal magnet lost performance at the last step, so they built another, shock-proofed throughout
Magnets, heating and power supplies are about 90% of hardware cost, so they get tested most
The Jingtian magnet hit 21.7 tesla, validating HH170's magnet design and process

root.d: Turn science risk into engineering risk

items.d: Test high performance one by one

99|517.c: Helion's extrapolation is too risky, and one approach rarely has room for a second-place player.
99|517.e: CFS shares their high-temperature superconducting tokamak approach, and its SPARC is the closest comparison to HH170. Helion uses a linear field-reversed configuration. Its published parameter is about 10^17, four orders of magnitude short of 10^21. He likens that to designing a plane for 10,000 meters using flight data from 0 to 10 meters, with room for new physics the equations don't cover. He doesn't predict failure but calls its 2028 power target very aggressive. He also sees a strong first-mover advantage in fusion, with talent and money flocking to the leader, so companies mostly pick different approaches.
ex: He thinks high-science-risk exploration suits research institutes better than companies
He expects a local winner in both China and the US; China has under 10 fusion startups

d.verdict: Companies should pick paths with manageable engineering risk

99|517.c: AI's ultimate bottleneck is energy, and any energy supply eventually gets used up.
99|517.e: He sees AI growing exponentially, held back first by chips and data and later by electricity. Growing energy supply tenfold requires a big drop in cost per kilowatt-hour. And there's never a glut: whatever is supplied gets used by new applications, just as compute has never been in surplus. In turn, AI can speed up fusion. It can compress complex physics into fast approximations for real-time plasma control, replace some costly diagnostic hardware, and calibrate simulations with a few real experiments. Energy Singularity plans to replace some control algorithms with AI but isn't working with outside AI companies yet.
ex: DeepMind controlled plasma purely with AI on a European tokamak, publishing two Nature papers
About 100 experiments might shrink to 2 physical runs plus lots of simulation

items.d: Soon used up by new applications

99|517.c: The first kilowatt-hour needs three hurdles cleared: high gain, long steady operation and deuterium-deuterium fuel.
99|517.e: The first hurdle is gain. Q=1 only breaks even inside the plasma. Counting generation and plant losses, it still consumes net power, so plants usually need Q between 5 and 30, with Q=10 a common engineering threshold, while keeping the plasma stable. The second is moving from 1,000-second pulses to tens or hundreds of thousands of seconds, even months of steady running, where any subsystem failure stops the machine. The third is fuel. Deuterium-tritium needs regulated tritium bred from lithium. Deuterium-deuterium is ten times harder, but seawater holds enough deuterium to last humanity for ages.
ex: He cites a magnetic-confinement record of about Q=1.25, and NIF's 1.5 excluding laser losses
A high-Q machine near coal-power cost would be fusion's "ChatGPT moment," he says

99|517.c: Science poses no fatal flaw, so success depends on quickly turning smart people into experts.
99|517.e: In 2021 he spent about six months breaking the problem into a checklist and found nothing clearly infeasible. If the company fails, he believes, it will be for lack of people, money or execution. There are no ready-made fusion engineers, so smart, driven, resilient people must be trained fast into specialists: start from first principles, simulate, calibrate with experiments, then deliver hardware. Hardware roles can't be split too finely, because one careless screw can force a rebuild. He compares a startup to climbing an ever-higher mountain. If you fall, you train more and climb again.
ex: The team studies ITER's final design report and SPARC papers for trade-offs, not to copy numbers
Days run 9 a.m. to about 8 p.m., often overnight in testing; he criticizes more than praises

items.d: Pin down physics and engineering limits

100|533.c: China is the toughest market, but Mercedes won't trade price cuts for volume and will protect resale value.
100|533.e: Pressed on three straight years of falling share in China, he admits competition has intensified but won't cut prices to chase sales. Protecting the resale value of cars already sold matters more than short-term volume. He likens a Mercedes to a Swiss watch you don't throw away after three years. The answer is to match China's speed and digital innovation, partnering with tech firms like Tencent to bring familiar phone features into the car. China R&D is also moving from local tweaks to serving the world. Beijing, Shanghai and German teams hand off work almost around the clock, and many initiatives now start in China.
ex: Mercedes still sells over 700,000 cars a year in China
It plans to invest 14 billion yuan in China; one-tap parking built there has gone global

items.d: Protect resale value of cars sold
Bring the phone experience into the car
China's work goes to other markets

100|533.c: He misjudged how regions differ, so the 2030 goal is an EV in every segment, not all-electric.
100|533.e: He admits he overestimated Europe five years ago. Back then he would have forecast at least a 25% battery-electric share there in 2024. It came in around 13%, with North America under 10%, while new-energy vehicles took about half of China's market. China's shift spread upward from entry-level city cars, and luxury competition works differently, so he doesn't think Mercedes has lost in China. The goal is now an electric option in every segment by 2030 at the latest, without locking into a single 100%-electric scenario worldwide. Electric cars and high-tech combustion engines will coexist for the foreseeable future.
ex: The host cites China's EV share rising from 4.7% in 2019 to 47.6% in 2024
The S-Class still leads the top-end sedan market, but he says that isn't enough

items.d: His estimate five years ago for 2024
Including plug-in hybrids and range extenders, about half

100|533.c: High luxury margins let Mercedes act as its own venture capitalist, betting steadily on new tech.
100|533.e: Some saw the 2020 shift toward high-margin models like the S-Class, G-Class, AMG and Maybach as luxury winning out over electrification. He says the two don't conflict. Luxury cars generate cash, so Mercedes can be its own venture investor, putting profits back into new technology and products. Electrification is also moving from the top down, and there's already an electric G-Class. Chasing technology without making money isn't sustainable, so core models like the C-Class, E-Class and GLC stay, with a major technology upgrade.
ex: The CLA: up to 866 km of range, about 11 kWh per 100 km, an 800-volt system
The CLA debuts two platforms, a new drivetrain and software stack, headed to 40-plus models

100|533.c: Carmakers should be the head chef and conductor, not write every line of code themselves.
100|533.e: When the host used Tesla to press him on doing everything in-house, he said there's no one-size-fits-all golden rule. Mercedes must own the overall architecture and core capabilities, such as its MB.OS operating system and battery-management software, which dates back to the 2007 electric smart. For other modules, integrating partners' work is more efficient. He also stresses that range comes from engineering the whole car, with aerodynamics and countless details mattering as much as the battery. Solid-state batteries and high-silicon anodes are in development, but he's in no rush to set a production date.
ex: Mercedes has hired thousands of software engineers and works with Tencent, Amap and Qualcomm
In a solid-state battery demo, an EQS drove over 1,000 km on one charge

d.verdict: No one-size-fits-all golden rule

100|533.c: Widespread technology just raises the bar, and luxury still comes from craftsmanship, personalization and design.
100|533.e: Asked whether luxury cars still matter once technology is available to all, he uses the decathlon: electrification and AI turn ten events into twelve, but those are just basics. Customers still crave distinctive craftsmanship, personalization and design, the difference between off-the-rack and an Italian bespoke suit, and Mercedes won't become a volume brand. Nor does he think Mercedes must become an AI company. It's still a maker of physical cars, and AI's value is reducing human error and giving people back time. DeepSeek showed him that clever methods can drive innovation cheaply and speed adoption.
ex: L3 driving launched in Germany then the US, its speed cap rising from 60 to 95 km/h
When he first saw DeepSeek news, he called his Beijing strategy chief to check it out

terms.d: EVs and AI become required events

result.d: The decathlon now has twelve events

100|533.c: On a 51–49 decision, back the 51, reverse fast if wrong, and never just play it safe.
100|533.e: Anyone can make an 80–20 call, he says. The hard ones are 51–49: bet on the 51, and if the facts prove you wrong, drop your pride and change at once. Professional managers are often called cautious, but he argues playing it safe doesn't work in a transition, and the company is investing money, engineers and partnerships at record levels. Cuts target layers and processes, not attacking strength. A team with only a goalkeeper can only keep retreating. He sees himself as the brand's custodian: technology, brand, customer experience and finances must improve together, and he must leave the company better than he found it.
ex: He took over in May 2019, the first Mercedes CEO not of German origin at appointment
Citing the founders' spirit, he says innovation isn't a faster horse but no horse at all

items.d: Don't cling on to save face

101|536.c: No view is always right, so find someone to argue the other side before any big decision.
101|536.e: He debated intensively in his first two years of college and came away assuming every view has a flip side. At his company, he wants reports to include both data and a clear opinion, and if no one objects to a big decision, that worries him. He admits final calls still come down to taste and intuition, but intuition must be grounded in users: have you actually talked to them, spent time in their communities, watched how they create? Many fights are about ego rather than facts, and going back to the facts settles them. Hence his rule: users over ego.
ex: At his college debating peak, he did 14 debates a week
He treats investors as a mirror that shows the team's hesitation and wavering

items.d: Data without an opinion isn't worth discussing
No objections is a warning sign
Talk, join communities, see their work

101|536.c: A product should win users like a closing debater wins judges: instantly clear, with few, precise features.
101|536.e: In debate, he says, you aren't really persuading a well-prepared opponent but judges and audiences hearing the topic for the first time. In product terms, that's the user. So a product should make sense the moment it opens, without pop-up explanations, as Apple shows. He won the most best-speaker awards and also lost the most rounds. Looking back, he talked over others and said too much, so audiences remembered nothing. Products work the same way: users need one or two key features, and piling on more dilutes the main point.
ex: Repeating every point in a farewell debate's last three minutes buried his main line
He cites a claim that about 90% of most software's features are never opened

items.d: Judges remember only one or two points

101|536.c: Data is a rearview mirror: it prevents mistakes but can't validate breakthrough innovation.
101|536.e: At OnePlus, data infrastructure was thin, so his mentor took him on the subway and to malls to watch real users. He found many people down to about 10% battery during the morning rush, and that people care most about battery when it's nearly full or nearly empty. At CapCut, with a release every two weeks, he built a habit: write down a hypothesis, ship the roughest MVP, check the data, review the gap. It helps new hires deliver solid work fast and blocks experiments that hurt metrics. But you can't A/B test an iPhone or a Tesla, so when intuition and data clash, he goes with intuition.
ex: He noticed many users down to about 10% battery at morning rush hour
OnePlus shipped one phone a year, while CapCut shipped a version every two weeks

items: New hires hit 80/100 in a week or two
The CEO carries the conviction risk

d.verdict: When they clash, he picks intuition

101|536.sc: The rise and end of Noisee
101|536.c: A model's weakness can pick your product category: if characters won't stay consistent, make music videos.
101|536.e: He noticed that users in the community around Suno, an AI music tool, loved sharing their work, while musicians on video platforms often had only a static cover image. Video models then couldn't keep characters consistent, so they couldn't tell a continuous story. But music videos and trailers are built on jump cuts and don't need consistency. Before launch, he hand-made music videos in CapCut for Discord users to test demand, and after Suno v3 came out, the product took off. Users weren't paying for a stronger model but for a finished one-minute video with transitions and music.
ex: The day after he sent out hand-made videos, about ten people asked for the link
Seeing users loved it, Discord admins posted the product link for him

items.d: Suno users love showing off songs
Make videos in CapCut for users
A full one-minute video, not clips

101|536.c: If each model upgrade doesn't make the product 5–10 times better, it isn't truly AI-native.
101|536.e: After Kimi took off, he proposed shutting down Noisee himself. Generating images and video doesn't create intelligence, Sora and Kling were already ahead, and his original contrarian bet no longer held. At his startup he still fell into the classic product manager trap of over-polishing, preparing about 50 sets of CSS and JavaScript templates until the product looked like an engineering system. He stopped it after Chinese New Year 2025. His test: every model generation should make the experience five to ten times better. Elegance, like MCP covering many sources with one framework, signals you're heading the right way.
ex: As templates piled up, AI's share of the product fell from about 80% to about 20%
Seeing people screen-record their Grok 3 games to share them, he built "HTML to website" overnight

101|536.c: Judge AI products less by how fast they burn tokens and more by the value each token creates.
101|536.e: He first treated token burn rate as the key metric, tokens being the units of text a model processes. He later switched to per-token valuation: how much value each token creates. If building a website takes a million tokens and most go to trial and error, using far fewer for the same result is better, much like how efficiently oil or electricity converts to useful work. He draws a line, though. If an agent could cure cancer or prove the Riemann hypothesis, cost wouldn't matter. Everyday user tasks must be efficient. The sequence is speed first, then raise the share of useful tokens.
ex: Devin-style rapid, high-volume output represents the speed-first stage

items.d: Waste fewer tokens on trial and error

101|536.c: A product's "shell" is the environment that shapes behavior, and offering only a text box is irresponsible.
101|536.e: Many dismiss products built on top of models as mere "wrappers." He rejects the put-down and calls the shell a container and environment: the same person behaves differently at a street food stall and at a French restaurant. Handing users just a chat box pushes the hard problem of using intelligence well onto people who don't know what to type. Midjourney is the good example. On Discord, users saw others' images and prompts in public, then copied, imitated and remixed them, so the community became the manual. That's why YouWare guides users with a feed of creations and easy ways to remix them.
ex: Midjourney users went from typing "a dog" to writing prompts hundreds of words long

items.d: See what the model can do

101|536.c: Coding will go from professional photography to everyday snapshots, and new creators will spawn new platforms.
101|536.e: He sees traditional programming as professional photography, while AI coding should be like a phone camera anyone can use. Phone cameras created phone photographers, which made Instagram and TikTok possible. Programming in plain language is likewise creating web coders who never existed before, and that matters more than making veteran programmers faster. He compares model companies to Sony supplying camera modules. YouWare is betting on becoming the content platform of the coding era and is hunting for a breakout format like Douyin's lip-sync videos, though he admits one may not exist.
ex: An English teacher's quiz or a math teacher's trig visualization shows users new ways to create
Hand someone a finished Lego set and most of the fun is gone

terms.d: Like phones making everyone a photographer

result.d: The Instagram of the coding era

101|536.c: Super agents and specialized agents will coexist, with specialists called on for their domain know-how.
101|536.e: He uses forms of government as an analogy. A centralized super agent has a higher efficiency ceiling but stifles diversity. Many specialized agents calling on each other are less efficient but protect the floor. He'd personally like to build an OS-like agent that orchestrates everything, but realistically expects each category to have its own orchestrator. An "Agent Rank" may emerge, ranking agents by results, cost, clicks, conversions and ads. Specialists must first get into the calling network, then hold a spot with top results, or 80% of the results at half the price. Their moat is know-how, data and accumulated user behavior.
ex: A designer with ten years' experience may deliver faster and cheaper than an elite graduate

marks.d: He'd like an OS-style orchestrator too
Each category gets its own orchestrator

101|536.c: Agents are a gorilla with its first fire stick: don't tune base models, trust them to improve.
101|536.e: He thinks today's agents have only just learned to use tools and are still very primitive. Startups won't be the ones making models smarter, so they needn't tune base models, just as MacBooks long ran on Intel chips. Model companies are like basic education, producing smarter minds. App companies are like vocational training, adding experience and an environment. Further out, new hardware must capture more of life's context, and an operating system must generate interfaces on the fly for each task, which he estimates is 10 to 20 years away. Agent networks also still lack identity, authorization and bidding systems.
ex: He estimates phones and computers capture only about 20% of life's context
The company assumes a 99.9% chance of dying and works daily to survive

items.d: Phones and PCs cover only about 20%

102|538.c: Progress comes from scalable size and data, not from clever architecture tricks.
102|538.e: He credits AlexNet's success to timing: ImageNet and Nvidia's CUDA were both ready, so it only had to scale up. Language AI's leap after 2019 also came mainly from dropping human labels so unlabeled text could scale without limit, not from the Transformer itself. Self-supervised computer vision couldn't follow that path. Contrastive learning only learns to ignore the image tweaks humans design, and masked image modeling (MIM) only learns to cope with hidden patches, so gains fade as it scales. To him, architecture always serves the algorithm, the data, and the systems.
ex: AlexNet grew models from a few megabytes to over 700
In early 2022 he argued MIM showed no clear scaling law, and was criticized for it

d.verdict: From 2022 he stopped still-image representation research

102|538.c: Training on mixed images and text brought understanding but not generation; the two never fused.
102|538.e: He admits he underestimated multimodal AI when starting the company, thinking that mapping images into language space and predicting the next token would recreate GPT. Step-1 mixed images and text from pretraining on and understood images well; answering questions about text in images worked as well as running OCR first. But generation was hard to control, and removing the generation branch midway barely hurt understanding. The team then had the two feed each other data and training signals for over six months. Each got stronger, but one plus one never beat two: the understanding model spotted perspective and anatomy errors but couldn't steer the generator.
ex: He thinks China's 2021 100-billion-parameter models got only a few hundred billion tokens: badly undertrained

102|538.c: Bigger models can get worse at math, because compressing data optimally rewards skipping steps.
102|538.e: Step-2 has over a trillion total parameters and writes very well, yet for a while its math trailed a 7-billion-parameter model. Retesting models from 1 billion to 70 billion parameters, he found knowledge and emotional intelligence rose with size, while math reasoning rose, plateaued, then fell. The cause is the data: online solutions often skip steps. Big models can learn to blurt out answers, while small ones must calculate step by step. However accurate each skipped step is, errors pile up over a long chain. So higher compression doesn't mean more accurate computation.
ex: Step-2 uses 200-plus billion active parameters and trained for over nine months
Thought experiment: big models blurt sums of a dozen two-digit numbers with 90%+ local accuracy

cells.d: Errors pile up; it gets worse

102|538.c: o1's key isn't its reinforcement learning algorithm but a way of thinking that can backtrack.
102|538.e: He thinks PPO, GRPO, or even the simplest policy gradient all work; what matters is how the chain of thought is organized. Pretraining already narrows the search a lot: in a solution thousands of tokens long, fewer than ten forks usually change the approach. But some forks can't be computed within a single token, and rewarding the same token can't add computation, so rewards plateau. Reflection adds a "backward edge": go to the end, find the mistake, try another path. Training data usually deletes the detours, so they must be fed in at the start of training. He calls this a chain of thought about the chain of thought.
ex: Multiplying big numbers needs more computation than one Transformer step allows
In early 2024, labs tried RL rewarding only correct answers, with limited overall gains

items.d: One token's computing has a ceiling

102|538.c: Reasoning models generalize a way of working, and the best seeds are in naturally occurring text.
102|538.e: He trained an o1-style model only on math, yet it could write classical Chinese poems with correct meter and rhyme, drafting, checking line by line, and rewriting. But it couldn't handle endgames in the card game Dou Dizhu, which need minimax thinking about an opponent's best play, until synthetic data was added. Data the team hand-designed, like circling, connecting dots, and mazes, taught only exactly what it showed. o3 can only crop and zoom yet generalizes better, because web pages are full of "look at the whole, zoom in, then explain."
ex: On electronics repair sites, people zoom in on parts to explain: natural visual reasoning data
MathOverflow answers keep "wait"-style restarts; Chinese solutions often skip steps with "note that"

102|538.c: Image generation lacks a chain of thought; limiting difficulty, its GPT-4 moment could come within a year.
102|538.e: Autoregressive generation can't take back a move, and diffusion's denoising isn't reasoning about meaning. So he thinks image generation lacks even a basic chain of thought and trails language by two generations. Forcing multimodal pretraining before then might even hurt text ability. Generation needs reasoning to be controllable, and reasoning needs generation to supply actions: a deadlock. His fix is to limit the domain and difficulty, training only one-step edits like connecting two points, removing a person, or drawing a chart to a structure. Then synthesize chains of thought mixing images and text to train one unified model.
ex: StepFun has trained an editing model; its data is messy but it follows instructions far better
Video has built-in steps, but segmenting, cleaning, and matching it to language is a hard bottleneck

items.d: Only edits doable in one step
Middle images can be checked and redrawn
Within a year at most, he guesses

102|538.c: Long context helps applications, but a memory that never forgets can get in the way of reasoning.
102|538.e: Companies need to load documents, and reference material reduces hallucination, so long context is a useful container. But human memory is layered: working memory lasts seconds, a middle layer filters and strengthens, and only then does long-term memory set. Transformers treat 100,000 to 10 million tokens as one kind of short-term memory, never compressing or forgetting. Doing math tests back to back, a model gets worse, yet needle-in-a-haystack tests still reward never forgetting. He imagines a planner holding the search tree's high-level state and an executor holding only the current path, cleared at will, with their teamwork learned end to end through RL.
ex: o3 was reportedly described as reasoning six straight days, producing tens of millions of tokens
If the search space is a binary tree, stored information can drop to roughly logarithmic

items.d: Long-sequence module finds the rough spot
Keeps the search tree's high-level state
Holds only the current path; cleared on switching

102|538.c: The next wall is environments and feedback; only autonomous online learning makes a true agent.
102|538.e: Reinforcement learning (RL) for coding means building an environment and writing tests for every project. Even with people hired to build them, it's far less efficient than a person reading docs, experimenting, and learning from feedback. A teacher grading an essay comments separately on the opening, style, flow, and typos, but today's RL squeezes all that into one score, so the model doesn't know what to fix. The next generation must turn plain-language feedback into its own rewards and keep updating itself in changing environments. He maps OpenAI's AI levels onto algorithms: chatbots to next-token prediction, reasoners to chain of thought plus RL, agents to autonomous online learning.
ex: He thinks a breakthrough in autonomous learning may not even take two years
Today's tool-using systems still belong to the reasoning era; LangChain-style chaining to the chat era

items.d: Strong chain of thought plus RL

103|542.c: The business model decides almost everything; scale and traffic can't substitute for making money.
103|542.e: Mobike drove orders with a nearly unlimited supply of bikes. Once it tried to break even, it had to raise prices and cut bikes, and orders would shrink sharply. It worked as a cost center in the mobile payment wars, but not as a business. Missfresh showed him that retail where you own the inventory has thin margins, and the internet adds only limited efficiency, so he rejects the idea of "internet plus retail." Since then he only picks areas that are purely online, high-margin, and gain from scale. ByteDance taught him to judge the end state with common sense first, then get the details right one by one.
ex: He built Gua Gua Long from scratch at ByteDance, among the youngest ever promoted, at 28
Judging the end state: how many players remain, monopoly or fragmented, supply- or demand-driven

items.d: Chasing hype at the peak is risky
Retail has little room to gain efficiency

103|542.c: AI is an information-revolution-scale change, so apps should come in sideways, through creative tools.
103|542.e: He sees the mobile internet as just computers and networks in a new setting, while AI is closer to the invention of the computer itself, so mobile-era playbooks don't apply. He isn't a top scientist, and 2023 was late to start building models. In PC history, productivity tools like Office and Adobe came first, then search and social. ChatGPT is closer to office tools plus search and sits too near the model's core, so he avoided the language mainline and went for multimodal creative work. Without your own model or traffic, an edge can only come from distinctive data and interaction design.
ex: The first product relied on assets and templates, which gather human creativity AI can't yet replace
He sees AI as a new camera and canvas, also changing how creative work is organized

103|542.c: The subsidy war had to be fought; what nearly killed them was cash flow and fundraising timing.
103|542.e: By June 2023 the first product had over a million monthly active users. Rivals quickly copied it, and he felt skipping subsidies meant being wiped out. In September it was taken down for lacking China's required registration for AI models, and cash fell to about 4,000 yuan. He cut staff and pay, launched memberships, and prepared to pay for servers himself. He thinks the strategy and business model were right. The mistakes were not understanding cash flow as a first-time founder and setting the first-round valuation too low. Lesson: when things go well, press the advantage and build reserves, or you can't weather headwinds.
ex: Subsidies burned about $3 million; the team shrank from 50–60 people to about 30
From September 2023 to January 2024 he met three or four investor groups daily; none invested

items.d: Rivals copy it; subsidy war begins
Three or four investor meetings a day
Over $20M raised in three rounds in 2–3 months

103|542.c: Once AI agents matured, Lovart let the AI plan the workflow for designers.
103|542.e: The first product was hard to use, so only the designers most eager to learn AI used it. The second version first asked designers to build workflow nodes on a canvas themselves, but designers think in feel, not logic, and the plan stalled. Around December 2024, Claude 3.5's agent abilities and tools like MCP, a standard way to plug AI into other software, arrived. He switched to having the AI break down and plan the workflow for designers, and the barrier dropped sharply. The product uses a canvas as the desk and a chat box for talking, plus a toolbox and an editor.
ex: Idea to product took three or four months, with all-nighters through the May Day holiday
Inspired by Manus, he wanted to build the Cursor of creative work

items.d: Designers think in feel; it stalled
AI breaks down tasks; barrier drops

103|542.c: Timing sets what it costs to win users; miss the window and ad spending becomes a bottomless pit.
103|542.e: Lovart's late-night launch post drew about 800,000 views overnight and a like from Elon Musk. About 120,000 people joined the waitlist, but only tens of thousands got in, because paid plans weren't ready and opening fully would have blown up costs. He notes the first product paid about 3–4 yuan per user, versus about 20 yuan now. The difference is the missed window. Getting both brand buzz and real signups comes from the timing that pioneering innovation creates. Subsidies work in China but not in North America. Once the window closes, big companies' advantage in ad spending takes over.
ex: After it went viral, people grabbed every unregistered domain ending for the name

103|542.c: General-purpose agents will consolidate, but general models won't swallow specialized agents.
103|542.e: He sees general agents as like search engines and app stores: the place users go first, which ends up in a few hands. Specialized agents will multiply. General agents will call on them, but they'll also have their own devoted users, and the big companies' own tools will coexist too. Each field's data, interaction, and use cases differ too much for general models to absorb, assuming AGI doesn't arrive within five years. Pricing depends on who pays: professionals who create constantly suit subscriptions, while a client's one-off job can be priced per deliverable, or even by compute and electricity used.
ex: Like Photoshop coexisting for years with CapCut and Final Cut
If AGI arrived right away, he says, you might as well quit

items: Like search engines and app stores
End up with a few players
Different data, interaction, and use cases
Called by others, with their own users

d.verdict: General models won't absorb niches, unless AGI comes within five years

103|542.c: AI has dismantled the product manager role; the core jobs are teaching AI and writing code.
103|542.e: He believes the traditional product manager role no longer exists, and AI coding has greatly simplified the split between front end, back end, and testing. Two kinds of core roles remain: people with industry knowledge who can teach their understanding to AI, and people who write code. His team of nearly 100 came mostly from operations on the first product. His advice to peers: specialize in one field, hand industry knowledge to AI, embrace AI fully, and position yourself before models get smarter. The best moment, he says, is when the future you predicted actually happens, and you're the one who made it.
ex: He identifies with Jin Yong's hero Yang Guo: cause a stir, then quietly leave

104|547.c: Every big tech shift changes how people interact with machines, and he has bet on that twice.
104|547.e: After the iPhone launched in 2007, he decided phones needed a software foundation that ran on any hardware, and his team of twenty-some built for MTK, Android and Windows Mobile at once. In 2009, with under 4,000 yuan in the bank, Alibaba invested and then bought the company for about $10 million. He insisted on being paid entirely in Alibaba stock. At Alibaba he set up M Lab, betting on cameras, microphones and connected devices; QR scanning and image search came out of it. His takeaway: from keyboards to graphical interfaces to touchscreens, each shift changed the interface between people and technology.
ex: Two weeks before payday, staff could stay for stock or take computers as wages. Nobody left.
He says Alibaba's closed mobile OS started well but ended up mediocre

items.d: After the iPhone, a system for any phone

104|547.c: A highly uncertain new bet can't be valued fairly inside a big company, so he had to leave.
104|547.e: In 2014 he figured AI plus AR glasses would take at least 1 billion yuan and five years; in hindsight, even that wasn't enough. Inside Alibaba there were two options. Do it quietly and you can't hire top people. Do it openly and you take resources from sister teams, which is unfair to everyone. Jack Ma flew back and talked with him for over three hours, then agreed, warning only that it would consume him. Alibaba co-founder Eddie Wu, very open to new things, first got Google Glass and handed it to the team. Much early money came from people who trusted him.
ex: He put in $2.3 million himself; Eddie Wu and IDG each matched it
He says Rokid raised money sitting down, never on its knees

104|547.c: Smart speakers can't be the device people live on; pivot to AR early, with the numbers worked out.
104|547.e: He thinks an everyday device needs rich input, rich output and many settings, and speakers have none. People are awake about ten hours a day but spend under two in the bedroom or living room, and Chinese users prefer earbuds. In 2019 Rokid moved fully from speakers to AR in about a week, with two hard rules: departing staff got statutory severance plus one month, and ten months of cash had to remain to prove out AR. About 60% of staff left. He talked with each one and promised to rehire them first. His biggest regret is moving six months to a year late, only because he hated losing people.
ex: Dealer launch Jan 15, 2020; COVID hit five days later. Any later, he says, was fatal
Infrared fever-check glasses sold in 80 countries and gave Rokid its first mass production

Speakers shut down, everything into AR
Severance plus a month; ten months of cash
Fever-check glasses led to mass production

104|547.c: AI must be available instantly, and glasses skip the hassle of pulling out a phone.
104|547.e: He believes AI is only valuable if it's always on, catching small needs as they come up. VR headsets (which wrap you in a virtual world) must be taken out, put on and switched on, so they stay single-purpose, like game consoles. AR glasses are more like phones. Scanning a code on a phone means unlocking, finding the app, opening the scanner and aiming; he calls these steps "system cost." With glasses you just speak. An AI phone could skip apps too, but pulling it out and unlocking still adds two or three seconds. So phones won't vanish soon; people will just reach for them less often.
ex: Comparing screen time with a friend at Tencent's investment arm: mostly bursts under five minutes
For heavy tasks over half an hour, glasses can't replace phones yet

marks.d: Take out, put on, boot up: a console
Pulling out and unlocking adds 2–3 seconds

104|547.c: Glasses wearers will adopt AI glasses first, and a display is what makes them feel instant.
104|547.e: He cites a nearsightedness rate of about 92–93% among Chinese high school graduates. Even if half refuse to wear frames, about half of people could become natural AI-glasses users. He expects glasses wearers to adopt in three to five years, five to ten to be safe; non-wearers will take five to ten more, and shouldn't be talked into it. The display is key. Without one, a translation is read aloud only once the model is sure, which can take five to ten seconds per turn. With one, a rough version shows first and then gets fixed. Ray-Ban Meta targets outdoor social shooting; Rokid is meant for all-day wear.
ex: He says Americans mostly wear them outdoors or while driving, more like sunglasses

104|547.c: AI is a full reservoir, and glasses are at a BlackBerry-to-iPhone turning point.
104|547.e: He compares AI to a full reservoir; the next step is letting the water out to irrigate fields and make power. DeepSeek cut costs and open-sourced its models, so the math now works for hardware built on top. AI hardware comes in two kinds: embodied devices like robots and cars, and things you carry, like phones and glasses. Rings and watches show too little to become platforms. He thinks glasses are at a turn like BlackBerry to the first iPhone, perhaps this year or next, but the field is still a "dark forest" of hidden rivals. Big companies mostly skip displays; he expects head-on full-display competition next spring.
ex: Rokid aimed for several hundred thousand units; the bottleneck was production capacity, not demand
After going viral, they pushed quality from 70 to nearly 90, delaying launch to Q2

items.d: Show too little to be a platform

104|547.c: Hardware always gets matched; the lasting edge is the OS and ecosystem, and leads last only 12–18 months.
104|547.e: He points to battery life: Meta's glasses last about three to four hours, Rokid's four to six, and the extra comes from power savings in the operating system. Real-time translation needs a response within about 0.5 seconds, and a stable Bluetooth link is also a system skill. Hardware plateaus at the industry's limits, and latecomers catch up through mature suppliers, so it's rational for giants to wait. Software, experience and ecosystem, by contrast, reward whoever leads. A longer lead would take spending on materials, basic research and upstream capacity, beyond Rokid's size. So every product generation must be won again.
ex: Giants already see and understand AR; startups get only two or three years before giants care

items.d: Giants understood it from the start
Goal: leave giants no time to respond

104|547.c: A CEO's value is deciding boldly and admitting mistakes fast; he thinks 70–80% of his calls are wrong.
104|547.e: He estimates 70 to 80% of his decisions are wrong and doesn't see himself as a visionary product genius. His job is to decide fast when no one else dares, and to admit errors at once, with no concern for saving face. He rejected AR Lite three times; the team built a prototype behind his back, and he approved it only after trying it. So he believes a product company's results come from many decisions piling up, not one founder's vision. He also wants users to love the product without knowing who he is. The brand should be far better known than him.
ex: AR Lite can travel to a hotel and run big-budget games like Black Myth: Wukong
Asked if he'd sell the company again, he said why not; what matters is the product

items.d: Make the call when others won't
Users and the team give feedback
Not one second spent saving face

105|551.c: Car tech moves in cycles; rule-based self-driving failed because rare road situations can't all be listed.
105|551.e: Around 2003, appliance and phone makers jumped into cars but only copied the look. Their cars were too weak to pass crash tests, and they left within two or three years. He splits the past twenty years into four phases, each with a hot topic that faded. The industry once expected Level 3 driving (the car drives itself in set conditions) by 2020, but rule-based systems couldn't cover every rare case, and Level 4 startups faded. In 2023 the consensus was lidar plus HD maps, but maps can't keep up with changing roads. So the industry turned to cameras without maps. Next comes a Level 3 race.
ex: Phone maker Bird and appliance maker Chunlan both once tried making cars

items.d: Stiffness and crash tests are the bar
Hand-written rules can't cover rare cases
Powerful chips plus fast model updates

105|551.c: When data drives progress, suppliers fall back to manufacturing and carmakers take back design.
105|551.e: A car starts generating data as soon as it hits the road, and self-driving improves only by learning from that data. Under "black box" delivery, suppliers hand over sealed systems, so carmakers can't get the data or change the software. Suppliers are now opening up as "white box" partners and retreating to manufacturing, while design returns to carmakers so updates can move fast. He cites history: Delphi and Visteon were once divisions of GM and Ford, spun off around 2000 because running them in-house didn't pay. Taking design back today isn't about profit. It's about responding to users quickly.
ex: He spent nearly 18 years at supplier Delphi before joining Mercedes three years ago

items: Suppliers open up and just manufacture

d.verdict: Taking back design is about speed, not profit

105|551.c: The China team earned influence at headquarters step by step, through promises, delivery and trust.
105|551.e: During COVID, contact with Germany broke down, so the Shanghai team pushed local R&D on its own, running simulations and demos at home on German code, in time for the new E-Class to enter production in December 2023. Shanghai started from zero in 2021 and now has several hundred people; Beijing and Shanghai together have over 2,000 engineers. The rule: features launched in China are led by China and road-tested there, while the overall architecture is shaped gradually through data. At the 2023 Shanghai auto show, executives saw the real cars and changed their tone. They used to give orders; now data persuades them.
ex: Going global, China-built features need retesting, retraining and approval in Germany and the US: 6–12 months
China now builds parking assist for the world; German-made cars use Chinese algorithms

items.d: Features start flowing out to the world

105|551.c: Chinese and German drivers differ so much that parking and screen design must be tailored for China.
105|551.e: Germans mostly park outdoors, while Chinese drivers use underground garages, where shiny floors confuse ultrasonic sensors. The China team fixed this with camera-based correction and also built its own 3D navigation engine. Screen design is what frustrates him most: Germans find Chinese designs too button-heavy, while German designs take several taps to find a feature. The answer may be a fully China-specific interface. Disagreements get settled only with data and facts. German rigor has value too: before adding in-car karaoke, they asked whether a handheld mic could hurt someone in a crash.
ex: If the driver looks at the passenger screen for over 1.9 seconds, it dims automatically

105|551.c: Mercedes' CLA drives end to end on cameras alone, but Level 3 still needs lidar as backup.
105|551.e: The CLA is Mercedes' first end-to-end car (one model handles everything from seeing the road to steering), with no HD maps and no lidar; he says only Tesla does anything similar. He thinks lidar adds little once training is good enough, while adding cost and noise, based on 20,000–30,000 km of comparison driving with and without it. Performance dropped at first. The team wrestled for seven or eight months, trying mixes like rules on highways and end to end in cities, and committed only after old and new test cars ran side by side and the new one kept improving. Level 3 still keeps lidar as backup.
ex: He asks whether spotting something 300 meters away really needs path planning yet

items.d: One model replaces the rule-based system
Tempted to keep rules on highways

105|551.c: The fourth most-used feature in cars will likely involve AI, and Level 3 will free up driving time.
105|551.e: Front cameras are going from about 2.5 to 8 megapixels. Paired with large models, the car can move from recognizing what something is to guessing what it intends: an e-bike rider glancing around while crossing may turn right, and spotting a child makes the car more careful. Usage data ranks navigation first, media second and driver assistance rising; he thinks the fourth should be AI-related. Once Level 3 spreads, the car becomes a "third space" for work and leisure, with interfaces tailored to each person. With human and self-driving cars sharing roads, car-to-car messaging must be redefined, and the state should set the rules.
ex: Today's car-to-car messaging lacks precise location, so it can't tell which car got the message

105|551.c: Users decide what counts as luxury: perfect the features that matter, and treat safety as the floor.
105|551.e: He believes a brand can't call itself luxury; users decide, based on what Mercedes has built over 138 years. Usage data shows navigation and music are used heavily, while memory parking (the car learns a route into a fixed spot) is rarely used because most people lack a fixed space. So he opposes over-engineering for show. His rule is that whatever rivals have, Mercedes has too, only done better, with needs split by buyer groups such as AMG and Maybach. Cutting-edge technology is itself a luxury. On safety, a 0.1% risk is just a number to a company but everything to a family.
ex: Before a new car ships: about 5 million test km, 150 real crashes, 15,000 simulated ones

terms.d: Perfect the ones people use most

result.d: Users decide; you can't claim it

105|551.c: Tech's center of gravity has moved to China and the US, a once-in-a-century turn for Mercedes.
105|551.e: He says plainly that for over 130 years Mercedes has made decisions starting from Germany, but technology's center has shifted to China and the US. The legacy is heavy too: G-Classes from over 40 years ago are still on the road, spare parts must be stocked for twenty years, and several platforms need dedicated upkeep. He rejects the idea that young buyers aren't loyal. People age, their idea of luxury changes, and Mercedes still makes money in China. He urges headquarters to study rivals' technology humbly and follow trends in moderation, without copying blindly.
ex: Goal: by 2026, the China team builds a smart-cockpit platform for the whole world

marks.d: China builds the global cockpit platform

106|553.c: Embodied AI differs from internet AI in where knowledge comes from: a body interacting with its surroundings.
106|553.e: Internet AI learns from data already online. Embodied AI, meaning AI with a body that acts in the world, gets its data from that body interacting with its environment, in a simulator or in reality. Computer vision researchers drove the idea as a rebellion against passive recognition: labeling "this is a cat" and stopping is a one-way street. Embodied AI closes the loop between seeing and acting; each step changes the view, which shapes the next move. Object navigation, like finding a chair, became the first task, using simulators such as Habitat. Only later did the field turn to hands-on manipulation and merge with large models.
ex: When he returned to China in 2021, "embodied AI" barely showed up in Chinese searches
Early four-legged robots run on joint angles and motion sensors weren't called embodied

106|553.c: Language isn't the essence of intelligence; it's one big leap within higher intelligence.
106|553.e: When the host argued that language is the core of intelligence, he disagreed firmly. Insects dodging attacks and animals finding food are intelligent too; not talking doesn't disqualify them. His definition: reacting to changes in the environment to reach a goal. Simple reactions are short-range, while advanced ones plan further ahead. Language is like a crutch. It compresses communication and helps with planning, a key leap but not the essence. Vision, too, is just one kind of sensor; some creatures sense their surroundings without eyes.

items.d: A leap, and a crutch, for higher intelligence

106|553.c: Research skill is defining the problem well; synthetic data has been his through-line for eight years.
106|553.e: He studied semiconductor physics as an undergrad and got used to building a model first, then fitting data. In Stanford's cleanroom, testing one idea took a month; he thought fast but built slowly, so he switched to AI. He admits coding isn't his strength. His gift is turning fuzzy ideas into problems a machine can learn. To estimate the position and orientation of a whole category of objects, he shot real IKEA tabletops with a depth camera, then rendered digital mugs onto them. The right answers came for free, across hundreds of thousands of mixed images. That synthetic data approach carried into Galbot.
ex: A 2016 project learned multi-step hand-object actions from human videos, hinting at world models
The IKEA-plus-digital-mug paper became an oral presentation at CVPR 2019

items.d: Smart cup: an early world model

106|553.c: Software needs a reliable body, so a wheeled, two-armed design keeps mass production simple.
106|553.e: In 2020 Kai-Fu Lee urged him to do self-driving, saying home robots were fifty years away; he still believed homes were the biggest opportunity. Yet he first declined to start a company, because robot platforms then couldn't even move reliably, and software on bad hardware is pointless. It came together once Zhou Teng, who had mass-production experience at ABB, joined. Galbot uses a wheeled base of about 60 cm, two arms with seven joints each, and proven harmonic gears, avoiding legs and parts never mass-produced, which hurt yield and reliability. He calls this pragmatic, not conservative.
ex: He describes body and intelligence as rising together in a spiral
Business customers care only whether the job gets done right

items: Customers only care about the work

106|553.c: General robot models lack data, so start with robots limited to a few actions.
106|553.e: He argues language models are strong because internet text covers most of human language. Public images cover only a sliver of what eyes see, and action data only started piling up in the last two years. The gap isn't model design. So a fully general VLA (a model that sees, understands instructions and outputs actions) is impossible within a year or two. The practical path limits behavior to moving, grasping and placing, while generalizing deeply across objects and settings, so the same skills work for drinks, coffee, different convenience stores and pharmacies.
ex: A robot can recognize a gummy bag but can't tear it, never trained to tear

cells.d: Not possible in a year or two
Humanoid stories propped up by staging

106|553.c: Robots must become real productivity tools, not endless demos or one-off custom projects.
106|553.e: He separates research platforms from productivity products: the latter must produce close to what a person does per hour and run for long stretches, or they're backward technology. He sees two dead ends. One is years of humanoid stories propped up by choreography, teleoperation and staged shots, with no everyday use. The other is rebuilding for each new customer; even hundreds of millions of yuan in revenue won't scale. Ten thousand units would already be a phenomenon; top commercial cleaning robots sell only 10,000–20,000 a year. A repeatable shelf-stocking product could absorb tens of thousands, and with moving and sorting, hundreds of thousands.
ex: An unmanned pharmacy needs 20-plus hours a day, unlike a five-minute remote-controlled demo
Generality is still the long-term goal, but earn money along the way

106|553.c: No one can afford real-world data from 10,000 robots, so synthetic data must do the heavy lifting.
106|553.e: Self-driving data is nearly free: cars are useful, so drivers generate data at no cost. A robot with no useful job won't sell 10,000 units. He estimates a humanoid costs at least about 100,000 yuan, so 10,000 of them means 1 billion yuan. Running two shifts, plus labeling and quality checks, could cost several hundred million to a billion yuan a month, which nobody on earth can afford. And robot designs change every few months, shifting how they move and what the data looks like. So real data is only about 1% of Galbot's training, or less; its in-house synthetic pipeline does the rest.
ex: He criticizes firms that dismiss synthetic data, then fall back on teleoperation after selling robots

items.d: Two shifts plus labeling and checks

106|553.c: Training in simulation and moving to reality works; the hard part is physics like soft materials and contact.
106|553.e: To those who say simulated physics isn't real enough, he notes that humanoid robots learned to walk, run and jump through large-scale reinforcement learning (trial and error guided by rewards) in simulation. To those who say visuals don't transfer, Galbot in 2023 trained grasping of transparent objects and broken glass purely on synthetic data and made it work in reality. Rendering isn't the real barrier. The hard part is soft, squeezable, multi-contact and breaking materials, which supermarket work doesn't need yet. The plan: synthetic data plus a little teleoperation reaches about 98%, and real-world feedback plus reinforcement learning fix the rest.
ex: Soft-material tasks like tying shoelaces are where simulation still does worst
Counting from NOCS in 2017, he has about eight years of synthetic data experience

marks.d: Learned in simulation, works in reality

106|553.c: Real progress means no teleoperation, and autonomous robots at 10,000 units a year within five years.
106|553.e: He says some overseas demos hide operators backstage, and some in China don't disclose teleoperation, where a person remotely controls the robot. That wrecks the whole industry's credibility. He proposes two tests: public demos with no teleoperation, and sustained workloads with ongoing reports, like Galbot's unmanned pharmacies handling hundreds of orders a day. Valuations should match. Robots working reliably on production lines could be worth trillions of dollars; with only a dozen or two deployed, a valuation in the tens of billions needs rethinking. If no leading US or Chinese player hits 10,000 units a year within five years, investors will pull out and an ice age follows.
ex: China's workforce may halve in 10–20 years; failure would hurt robots' chance to fill the gap

items.d: Ongoing reports, hundreds of orders daily

106|553.c: Robots needn't do everything to create value; machines that do one job well can pay off first.
106|553.e: He admits we understand little about how humans coordinate their whole bodies; the cerebellum has more neurons than the cerebrum. Embodied AI won't mature in a year or two. Still, at 200,000 yuan in annual pay per person, replacing 10,000 workers is worth about 2 billion yuan a year, and nearly 10 billion with multiple shifts. Home robots could start light on chores and heavy on companionship and fun, with small pilots in three to five years; do-everything robots are decades away. He's bullish on Nvidia too: GPUs both render simulations and train models, so if synthetic data works, Nvidia could carry half the load.
ex: Over dinner, he showed Jensen Huang results trained purely on synthetic data, on his phone

items.d: At 200,000 yuan pay each, per year

107|28.c: Ending the funding winter needs both money and good startups to recover, and neither has.
107|28.e: She splits the winter into two parts: whether money is willing to invest, and whether there are startups worth backing. This year some cautious investors started writing checks, but the increase is small next to state-backed funds, the main players. Since 2023, yuan-denominated startup investing in China has relied mostly on state capital, betting on hard tech, AI, robotics and some low-altitude aviation like drones. Deal quality hasn't improved over the past two years either. Almost no new funds are entering consumer brands, and a livelier Hong Kong market only helps profitable late-stage companies. She made just two investments last year and doesn't feel she missed anything.
ex: An old bet paying off: oral-care brand Canban, backed in 2019, leads online, top four offline

terms.d: No better than two years ago

107|28.c: DeepSeek put good AI in everyone's hands but didn't solve apps' real gap: compelling use cases.
