107|28.e: She doesn't think cheap models were the bottleneck for AI apps. What's missing are uses that excite people and make an existing need dramatically better. Open source narrows the gap between big and small companies but doesn't create demand by itself. She credits DeepSeek with resetting what compute and algorithms should cost, bringing AI to ordinary users and leveling access through open source, and she likes its down-to-earth Chinese voice. Manus, an AI product pitched as doing tasks on its own, was hyped before the product was ready: her team tested about 50 showcase cases on its site, and none clearly beat deep-research tools.
ex: Half-joking, she treats DeepSeek like a fortune-teller: maybe nonsense, but the answers feel nice

d.verdict: High hopes magnify disappointment after trying

107|28.c: Needs get rewritten during planning, so technology and demand must advance in turns.
107|28.e: She uses trip booking as an example. She meant to go to Indonesia, found the hotels too pricey, switched areas, changed the itinerary, even the destination. Planning itself rewrites the need, and AI agents (AI that acts on your behalf) struggle to keep up. She rejects waiting for technology to mature and expecting demand to appear. She also rejects shipping a clunky product and hoping better models will rescue it. Her test: can AI capabilities in the next 6 to 12 months fill a real gap and save lots of time or bring real delight? Small improvements can't sustain a standalone business.

107|28.c: An agent has to actually take actions; a general-purpose agent is still a big question mark.
107|28.e: Her bar for an AI agent: it must click, call other software and execute, really changing the digital or physical world. If it only researches and plans, it's still just deep research. Screenshot-and-click agents work in principle, but in practice some links open and some don't, and the business value depends on who pays. As for where users start: if they still open apps first, agents will be scattered across Xiaohongshu, WeChat and Meituan. If phones open straight into a general AI assistant, phone makers win, though talking aloud in public is awkward. General and specialized bots will coexist, like general and vertical search.
ex: Most agent startups she sees automate one workflow, selling to businesses, small merchants and professionals

marks.d: Works in principle, not yet reliable
Changes the digital or physical world

107|28.c: An AI inside WeChat feels like a contact, so users expect more warmth and more skill.
107|28.e: She sees the Yuanbao app, Tencent's AI assistant, as a tool, but Yuanbao appearing in WeChat contacts gets treated like a person. She asked it to gather scattered posts about someone on Xiaohongshu and forums for a background check, and the results fell far short. She understands the limits on scraping, accuracy and platform agreements, but users judge only results. Praising the user before showing an info card is flattery for its own sake, and over time it feels too agreeable. The ideal is knowledgeable and funny, pushes back on a wrong premise, and comforts only when needed.

root.d: Treated as a person in contacts

107|28.c: She doesn't invest by age; small teams may succeed more easily, but they aren't cheap.
107|28.e: She sees many founders born in the 1990s and 2000s, even dropouts, building agents, but she won't screen by age: funds that chased 1990s-born founders a decade ago didn't succeed more often. The last generation of app companies needed complex organizations to scale, which exposed young founders' gaps in management and experience. AI-native small teams might build big businesses with those gaps mattering less, so the odds may improve, but only the odds. Small teams aren't cheap either: ten AI people can cost more than thirty used to, and with computing costs, they actually need to raise more.
ex: Video editing is what Crystal Stream sees most, like adding visuals for educational creators

107|28.c: Robots are stuck moving from simulation to reality, and AI glasses lack a must-wear reason.
107|28.e: Crystal Stream backed robotics startup Robotera and is looking for simulator companies. Real-world data is scarce, so robots must train in simulation, then move to reality and close the gap; simulators are key but hard to build. The industry hasn't reached mass production, so supply-chain opportunities are still unclear. She wears Meta glasses on trips for photos and audio, but she isn't nearsighted and doesn't wear them daily; an extra device on the face feels unnatural. Pop-up facts about flowers or résumés of people you meet aren't real needs, and several devices pushing alerts at once is just a burden.
ex: GoPro and DJI won with clear uses like sports and first-person shots
Smart rings feel less intrusive; stylish with health tracking, they might partly replace watches

items.d: Makes up for scarce real data

107|28.c: A film must first answer why anyone should go to a cinema; feminism should treat people as individuals.
107|28.e: A ticket costs dozens of yuan, and you must head out and sit in a dark room at a set time, while short videos, short dramas, cafés and travel are cheaper and comfier. Two holiday-season films about deaf characters had no clear audience and quickly lost screens to Ne Zha, which won with a strong story, weak rivals and nothing to explain. She saw Her Story twice, liking its realism and wit, though the men felt thin and some lines sounded like slogans. She wants men and women judged as individuals. She opposes stretching "objectifying women" too far, and also the idea that women deserve things simply for being women.
ex: Her Story grossed over 400 million yuan, and smaller cities did as well as big ones

items.d: Short videos and dramas always at hand
A far higher bar than the phone
Needs a reason nothing else gives

108|565.c: Consensus is either wrong or worthless, so look for the narrow door others haven't seen.
108|565.e: His reasoning: the future isn't linear, so views most people share are likely wrong. Even when they're right, everyone acts on them, so nobody stands out. Founders should ask three things: what is your business secret, what do you see that others don't, and is there a narrow door to the future? He criticizes stampedes like China's thousand-company group-buying war and today's hundred-company rush to build AI models, calling it exam-taking thinking that spreads resources thin on the same track.
ex: In 2015 he made three "investments": Nvidia stock, Tesla stock, and going all in on Horizon
He says Nvidia was worth about $10.7 billion then, and he urged friends to buy

items.d: Everyone does it, so no edge

108|565.c: Baidu lost the auction for Hinton's team, but it opened Baidu's eyes to deep learning.
108|565.e: As winner of the first ImageNet image-recognition contest, he knew how hard it was for deep learning pioneer Geoffrey Hinton's team to lift accuracy from 75% to 85%, so he wrote asking to work together. In a secret auction in late 2012, he planned to bid high early to scare off rivals, but he and Google kept raising the price, and Hinton chose Google. He sees the loss as a win: Robin Li grasped how much deep learning mattered, Baidu opened its Institute of Deep Learning in early 2013, and the auction raised the price of AI talent worldwide.
ex: The fourth bidder was year-old DeepMind, bidding in stock; he already sensed a future champion
He wanted both of Hinton's students but rated Ilya lowest, a misjudgment he admits

items.d: Going higher needed approval from China

108|565.c: Chips and platforms drive each era, and software can't be separated from hardware.
108|565.e: Seeing how much more efficient GPUs were than CPUs, he concluded that software and hardware are inseparable, and self-driving cars and robots would need dedicated chips. Baidu's leaders thought software made more money and chips were boring, one reason he left. He points to Microsoft and Intel in the PC era, and ARM, Android and Qualcomm in mobile: underlying platforms, not device brands, change eras. He knows he's good at winning business customers, not at building consumer brands, so he makes chips rather than cars. Nvidia was hard to unseat in the cloud, so he went after the first robot to reach the market: the car.
ex: In 2012 Baidu was Nvidia's largest AI customer worldwide
He calls Li Auto founder Li Xiang the carmaker most likely to become an "Apple"

items.d: Carmakers, phone makers; not his strength

108|565.c: Get investors competing to come to you; change your tactics, not yourself.
108|565.e: His first round came through old friend Huai Wang, without a single page of business plan. For the second, he met 50 or 60 firms and none invested; they only asked why he wasn't doing facial recognition and security. That gave him his funnel theory: whoever knocks on doors sits at the wide top, spending huge effort persuading, while investors who come to you are closer to deciding. So he insisted first meetings happen in his own office, turned some down, talked others out of it, had the rest compete on terms at once, and refused exclusivity agreements.
ex: After buying Mobileye, Intel also invested in Horizon, which he sees as Intel hedging its bets
Most Chinese chip investors, he notes, didn't understand Horizon's model and missed out

items.d: First meetings only in his office

108|565.c: Scientist-founders chase everything; Horizon survived only by keeping just its car business in 2019.
108|565.e: For its first five years Horizon worked on cars and smart devices at once, even trying toys, home appliances and air conditioners. Spread thin, it broke through nowhere. He thinks scientists have vision and technology but stall on business's first questions: who is the customer, what's the pain, and why can't others copy you? After dozens of strategy meetings in 2019, he chose cars alone: better to drill one oil well than dig many small holes. He stresses Horizon still had over 3 billion in cash, so it was a choice; without it, the company would have died.
ex: Hiking in early 2019, Li Xiang urged him to focus on cars; agreeing took months
Planned in waves, the ~600 layoffs (nearly half) were done in a month, bonuses still paid

items.d: Back to: who is the customer?

108|565.c: Strategy means not gambling; he spends 70–80% of his effort spotting fatal risks and steering clear.
108|565.e: Most entrepreneurs focus on the path to winning; he spends most of his energy on how the company could die. During the 2020–2021 funding frenzy, he judged the business couldn't justify bubble prices, so he kept raising while the window was open but didn't push up the valuation. Through roughly three years of downturn that followed, Horizon had cash and focused on products, and its IPO wasn't weighed down by an inflated valuation. Today's biggest danger, he says, is products not yet good enough, while driver assistance is changing very fast, so they must sprint. Building chips and software together turns sequential work into parallel work.
ex: Two bubble-era rounds of about $800 million each, $1.6 billion total, at a flat valuation
He says only Tesla, Huawei and Horizon build both their own chips and software

d.verdict: Healthy cash flow is the floor; strategy means not gambling

108|565.c: Selling to businesses means taking the customer's view; rejection usually means the product isn't good enough.
108|565.e: Consumer products reward self-expression, he says, but selling to businesses means seeing through the customer's eyes; even Baidu's research institute was really delivering for internal teams. The Changan deal was help in hard times: Changan was at a low point and wanted more independence, and the two went from a joint lab to mass production. Li Auto first used Mobileye, but the foreign firm wouldn't adapt to Chinese roads, so Li Auto switched to Horizon's Journey 3 chip within eight months. With XPeng, which sees driver assistance as its core edge, he plays a slow game; BYD came when another supplier stumbled.
ex: Changan's UNI-T topped 10,000 sales in month one: luck, he says, plus Changan's will to change
He tells his team to "lose gracefully, on purpose" when playing soccer with clients

items.d: First production deal, 10,000 in month one

108|565.c: Carmakers won't build their own driving systems; these will become standard parts, like phone modem chips.
108|565.e: He compares it to phone makers not designing their own modem chips: self-driving will become a standard feature with little room to stand out, so carmakers should focus on emotional appeal, which can't be standardized. Li Auto is the exception, because its real goal is AI, and driver assistance pays its way there. His timeline: fully hands-off within three years, eyes-off in five, minds-off in ten, with Level 4 (no human needed in most conditions) arriving in five to ten years. He says he's happy to be checked on this in five years.
ex: He once called Horizon a would-be runner-up; now it's the final lap, decided within three years

108|565.c: Robots need an entirely new computing architecture; the von Neumann design behind today's computers falls short.
108|565.e: He thinks self-driving technology has mostly settled, and robots are next, but they still lack a software ecosystem like Nvidia's CUDA that developers build around. Horizon's plan: five years to become the world leader in driver assistance, then five to ten years opening up a robotics ecosystem. Technically, the human brain uses very little power yet computes enormously, while car chips already exceed 100 watts. That gap calls for compute-in-memory (processing where data is stored), new compilers, new operating systems and new instruction sets. He expects robots to be useful in narrow settings within five years, and some general form within ten.
ex: Brain: about 20 watts and 5,000 TOPS, he estimates; one Journey 6P chip tops 100 watts

terms.d: Storage and computing no longer split
Rewrite the software stack for robots
Break free of von Neumann limits

108|565.c: AI should take on hard labor for people, not keep them penned in by algorithms.
108|565.e: He worries people are being farmed by algorithms: delivery riders' bodies are driven by dispatch software, and endless content feeds control users' minds. Horizon chose AI for the physical world so machines can do heavy, dangerous work, and self-driving should give everyone back their daily commute. He also says China lacks idealistic companies, praises DeepSeek's generation of founders for pairing ideals with clear strategy, and believes deglobalization is only partial and temporary.
ex: Horizon's models are Microsoft, Intel, Nvidia and Apple; no Chinese firm yet drives tech for humanity

marks.d: Does dangerous heavy work for people

109|569.c: Before making synthetic data, set up a way to measure whether it actually improves the model.
109|569.e: When he took over simulation at Cruise, GM's self-driving unit, in 2018, game engineers had rebuilt San Francisco in Unreal Engine. It looked stunning but was a pretty toy: the game team chased visuals, while the algorithm team needed better models. He first set two yardsticks, realism against real data and usefulness in training, then used early GANs (AI that generates realistic images) to make synthetic images look real. Rare cases were the main battlefield: one unusual accident could be varied by age, clothing, weather and lighting into tens of thousands of tests, with failures fed back into the model.
ex: He compares information per sample to espresso versus watered-down coffee
About 30% of Cruise's data was synthetic; each rare scenario ideally needs 1,000 to 10,000 samples

109|569.c: Cars rely mostly on real data and robots mostly on synthetic data; the ratios are reversed.
109|569.e: Self-driving sits on a century-old car platform plus production fleets that constantly send data back, and carmakers pay only for computing and bandwidth, so advanced driver assistance still runs mainly on real data. Robots have no installed base of millions of machines, so they must start with lots of synthetic data plus a little real data, or the business doesn't work. For collecting data by teleoperation, he sees three hurdles: return on investment, location and organization. Chinese factories are already highly automated, and overseas, unions and state-by-state rules get in the way; only Tesla can do it in its own factories.
ex: He thinks an industry led by teleoperation data outpacing synthetic data is unlikely

marks.d: No installed base to collect from

109|569.c: Robot simulation faces three walls: many body types, real physical contact, and vision-based reinforcement learning.
109|569.e: Cars all have four wheels, and switching models doesn't change how they interact with the world. Robots vary wildly in joints, hands, dynamics and control interfaces, so simulation must supply accurate data for each body. Cars try not to touch anything; robots must open fridges, pick up cups and type, which takes real physical parameters, not just visual reconstruction. Moving to reinforcement learning (trial and error guided by rewards) also means running many vision-enabled environments in parallel on one GPU, or throughput falls short. The industry can produce water at scale, he says, but much of it gives you diarrhea.
ex: Simulated fridge doors often won't open, and when they do, hinges and weight may be wrong
Real robots lift 1–2 kg, simulated ones only 0.1 kg; a client spent 6+ months failing to match

items.d: Doors and grasping need real physics
One GPU must run many environments

109|569.c: The real-data and simulation camps are converging; good data equals scene diversity times demonstration quality.
109|569.e: He finds that clients who publicly call synthetic data toxic quietly use it too, and training on real and synthetic data together usually works better. Most leading teams follow a data pyramid: internet data at the broad base, synthetic and simulated data in the middle, and a small amount of real robot data on top. Good data is the product of two things: diverse enough scenes and high enough quality demonstrations. Synthetic scenes cost mainly computing power, and one scene can run massively in parallel, which broadens the data far more efficiently than renting real locations.
ex: He says PI rents San Francisco Airbnbs for home data, far too little and too narrow
Imitation learning is an ordinary teacher demonstrating; reinforcement learning is the best teacher setting problems

result.d: Train on real and synthetic together

109|569.c: The robotics industry will split into four layers; no single company can easily own them all.
109|569.e: He likens embodied AI to inventing a next-generation car platform and its Level 4 self-driving software at once. Both are hard, and one company doing both is unlikely, so the industry will form layers: hardware bodies, foundation models, vertical applications combining hardware and software, and simulation-centered infrastructure. The foundation-model layer needs 100,000-plus GPUs, huge data and top talent, favoring big companies. Payment habits matter too. American users pay for AI, which makes specialization easy, while Chinese customers resist paying for software, so companies prefer charging for hardware and doing everything.
ex: Unitree sold robots to universities worldwide; graduates later made them the de facto standard
He puts Figure in vertical applications and sees much of its home story as marketing

109|569.c: The gap between simulation and reality can only be measured and shrunk over time, so you must deploy yourself.
109|569.e: From first principles, synthetic and real data will always differ; the key is knowing how small the gap must be for the data to help. Companies that only deliver data and leave training to clients can't see where the gaps are. So Lightwheel trains and deploys on many robots itself, feeding real-world results back into simulation. He stresses that simulation is not just a simulator: physics solvers, rendering, usable assets and scenes, interfaces and toolchains are all essential. Citing Jensen Huang calling Nvidia a simulation company, he suggests simulation may become the "third computer."
ex: He expects MuJoCo and Isaac Sim to merge into the fully open-source Newton

items.d: Train and deploy on real robots

109|569.c: Meta bought Scale AI for its data capability, and he guesses Alexandr Wang may succeed Zuckerberg.
109|569.e: He sees the deal as buying key talent. A decade ago, a Microsoft that understood AI would have bought Nvidia; for the next decade, the raw material Meta lacks is data. Meta wasn't among the top three customers of Scale, which labels training data for AI companies, so it couldn't get Scale's best data teams, and its internal AI group needed an outside leader to rebuild it. He guesses founder Alexandr Wang accepted a price near the current valuation for influence rather than cash, so Wang will likely be Zuckerberg's successor in ten years. He admits this is a bold guess from personal observation.
ex: He says mastering AI data is the entry ticket to a future $10 trillion company

items.d: Not impossible in three to five years

109|569.c: Robotics is at its GPT-1 stage; the biggest risk is treating fundraising as the reward signal.
109|569.e: He thinks robotics doesn't yet have a stable scaling law (more data and compute reliably yielding better models), much as Tesla's FSD only turned more data into steady gains once its end-to-end approach clicked. But robotics needn't wait ten years: top teams are talent-dense and can borrow what large language models taught about Transformers, data and compute, so optimistically the recipe could appear within a year or two. Being early isn't the same as a bubble. The real danger is teams treating talks, demos and fundraising as their reward. So he argues for serving customers from day one and using payment as feedback.
ex: Lightwheel started in January 2023 and landed its first paying customer that September or October

items.d: Within a year or two, optimistically

110|573.c: What separates an agent from a plain model is an environment it can interact with.
110|573.e: He draws the line at interaction. A plain model takes one input and gives one output. An agent works in a loop: it observes its environment, picks an action based on the task and its history, acts, changes the environment, and goes again. He sorts agents into four kinds, coding, search, tool use, and computer use, which differ in what they can see and do. Coding agents are the most mature and feel like many interns working in parallel. Computer-use agents may threaten RPA, software that runs scripted clicks, because workflows engineers once hand-coded can be done in one go.
ex: He guesses ChatGPT Agent merged the action sets of Operator and Deep Research

110|573.c: Context engineering iterates fast, but training the model end to end wins when rewards are clear.
110|573.e: He sees two routes. The Manus route skips training and iterates quickly through prompts, context, and multiple agents. End-to-end training works better when the task is clear and rewards and data are plentiful, as in coding and browsing, though with many agents it's hard to tell which one deserves credit. He reads Manus's blog post as being about the KV cache, where the model reuses text it already processed: a cache hit costs about a tenth as much. Hence the rules: keep the prefix stable, only append, mask tools instead of deleting them, keep memory in files, and use a to-do list to refocus.
ex: Manus's author came from the BERT era of per-task fine-tuning, so favors skipping training

items: Needs a strong model and good prompts
Behavior baked into weights, more stable

d.verdict: With clear tasks and checkable rewards, training wins

110|573.c: One agent is harmless, but thousands acting at once become an intelligent DDoS attack.
110|573.e: His worry comes from experience. An early web-agent demo of his actually booked a Tesla test drive, and he still gets pickup emails. Scale that up: one agent is nothing, but thousands hitting one site at once is an intelligent DDoS attack, the kind that floods a site until it breaks. Everyday failures could mean placing a huge order by mistake or sending a rude email. Read-only deep research is low risk. Agents that act on the real world are high risk. His fix is to pause and ask the user before any high-impact action. That shifts responsibility to the user, which actually helps the business case.

marks.d: Acts directly on the real world

110|573.c: Agent data must above all be diverse, and K2 manufactures that diversity with tools and personas.
110|573.e: He sees diversity as the first principle of agent data. If a model just invents tasks on one website, everything comes from what it already knows, and variety tops out fast. K2 gathered over 3,000 MCP tools, a standard way for models to call outside functions, from GitHub, then expanded them by domain to over 20,000. Each time it samples about ten tools into a small environment, adds personas set by system prompts plus simulated users, and writes a scoring rubric with each task to filter the attempts. For pretraining, an older model rewrites data to add variety, in chunks checked for consistency so factual errors don't slip in.
ex: Same Wikipedia data, ten passes: about 23.76 on SimpleQA. Rewritten data scored clearly higher
He likens rewrite errors to tea by the fireplace turning into eating barbecue
Math data rewritten as study notes reminds him of the Feynman technique

items.d: Generated layer by layer by domain
Scoring rules written with each task
Keep successes; rewrite or drop failures

110|573.c: Interacting with environments is expensive, so building environments may become the next thing to scale.
110|573.e: He runs the numbers. One deep-research task takes roughly 100 to 150 searches, and reinforcement learning, where a model improves through trial and reward, needs huge numbers of rollouts, or full practice runs. Websites ban browser IPs, cloud browsers are pricey, and local sandboxes eat CPU and memory. Multi-turn rollouts also have long tails: a few slow runs hold up the batch while GPUs sit idle. K2 turned heavy environments into services, launched extra rollouts, and only partly ran the stragglers, though that lets runs from an older model leak into training. The recipe is in the paper, he says. The hard part is making every step reliable craftsmanship.
ex: In a batch of 256, 250 finish in about 3 minutes; the last 6 take 10
Need 64 results? Launch 640 at once and stop when you have enough

terms.d: Rewards come from repeated trial and error
Search calls, IP bans, sandbox compute

result.d: Environments become the new place to invest

110|573.c: In RL, reward design is the crux, and task difficulty must match the base model's ability.
110|573.e: To him, rewards are the crux. Math and code allow verifiable rewards, like checking answers or running unit tests. Open-ended tasks like creative writing are hard to judge, so the model grades itself against a rubric. K2 combines both. On difficulty: too easy, and the model always succeeds and learns nothing; too hard, and the whole batch fails with no direction. OpenAI stresses tasks easy to verify but hard to answer, Qwen stresses high difficulty, K2 aims for medium, and he sees no conflict. He also sees K2's code sandboxes, built from GitHub PRs and issues at set points in time, as possibly the core of its coding skill.
ex: He compares reward hacking to a student cheating: right answer, nonsense reasoning
K2 uses Google's Fact Grounding to check facts sentence by sentence inside its reward

items.d: Check math answers, run code tests
The model grades open-ended tasks itself

110|573.c: Making training data is shifting from labeling input-output pairs to building environments and rewards.
110|573.e: He sees labeling work moving from writing input-output pairs toward writing tasks, rubrics, and verifiable rewards. Going further, an agent picks up new information on every turn of a multi-turn interaction. If those results could be turned into knowledge, agents could in turn supply data to language models. He also imagines agents finding trainable environments on their own, building sandboxes and finding rewards to improve themselves, though he admits this is just brainstorming. The mass of unused data sitting in rollouts is also worth mining.
ex: His SkillWeaver turns a web agent's successful runs into APIs it can call later
When users edit a coding agent's code, that's a reward, so users are the labelers

110|573.c: Agents are an extension of your brain, and everyone will have an army of them behind them.
110|573.e: He thinks of agents as an extended brain: whatever he's doing, a team of specialists works behind him. A good agent should also ask questions when instructions are vague and pin down what you want before acting. Coding agents do this fairly well. On timing, coding has already taken off. He and his friends write less and less code themselves, letting agents draft and then editing. Tool-use agents will follow soon, while browser infrastructure is still hard. The field moves so fast that after two weeks off from papers, he felt the world had changed.
ex: He has Claude write code, ChatGPT polish text, and Gemini read long documents
For a coffee maker under 100 yuan, a good agent first asks brand and color

root.d: Set goals and clarify what I need

111|577.c: Lidar got 99.5% cheaper mainly through better design, not bigger volume.
111|577.e: He believes most hardware cost cuts come from design; scale and automation only amplify a good design. Early lidar, the laser sensor that measures distance so a car can see around it, was hand-assembled from many separate parts and couldn't be automated. When the first product came out in 2017, the team was already asking how to take a device costing hundreds of thousands of yuan down to about $1,000. Their answer: volume alone couldn't squeeze out that much, so they had to design their own core chips instead of being an assembly shop. Heavy R&D spending across the industry also pushed prices down faster than usual.
ex: In 2017 one unit cost 200,000 to 300,000 yuan; today it's about $200
Hesai ships its fourth-generation in-house chip; he sees Tesla's one-piece body casting as design savings too

items.d: Built by hand, impossible to automate
Laser send-and-receive circuits on in-house chips

111|577.c: Customers paying real money is the most trustworthy feedback a startup can get.
111|577.e: He sees fundraising, valuation and fame as indirect signals; only a paying customer is truly convincing. Teams that go a long time without revenue lose honest feedback and start fighting among themselves. He doesn't dismiss OpenAI-style long bets, but Hesai prefers to have a business at every stage. Early on he treated having no revenue as the original sin: even when the direction was off, real payments kept the team focused on customers. He also warns that in Eastern culture bad news arrives too slowly and investors back whatever you say, so teams fool themselves. Responsibility for the direction can't be outsourced.
ex: Self-driving startup Drive.ai tested samples, ordered about $2 million, and paid upfront when asked
The customer refused to go public about it because Hesai was the only supplier that worked

111|577.c: Hard-tech founders shouldn't be a hammer looking for nails. Pick big markets where you can stand out.
111|577.e: The company began with lasers that detect natural-gas leaks and won a big deal for drone-based inspection, but certification and sales cycles were so long that it stayed a one-off. Air-quality (PM2.5) monitors then brought in a few million yuan but exhausted the team and had a low ceiling. He took this hammer-looking-for-nails state as a sign something was wrong. In 2016 he filled a blackboard with every industry lasers might enter and screened them by market size, differentiation, opportunity and team fit. Lidar won because it gives robots and cars 3D vision, with a very high ceiling.
ex: The first gas-inspection deal was about 20 million yuan, but the product became a museum piece
In Berlin in April 2016, alumni at carmakers heard about lidar and urged him to hurry

items.d: Drop directions with a low ceiling
And a fit with the team's skills

111|577.c: Disagreements usually come from different information, so sharing context matters more than who has the final say.
111|577.e: He and co-founders Yaoxing Xiang and Kai Sun split equity almost equally, which nearly every investor opposed. His reply: listening to advice is not the same as following it. The roles are clear. He runs business and fundraising, Kai Sun handles frontier technology and zero-to-one work, and Yaoxing Xiang leads one-to-ten engineering and manufacturing. He rejects the idea that one person must settle disagreements. Most disputes stem from different backgrounds, values and information, which shares can't fix. What matters is that decision-makers see the same information, so the three have long shared one office.
ex: Kai Sun holds about one point more equity because his lab brought the technology
The shared office was inspired by open-plan offices at European carmakers

items.d: Engineering and manufacturing, one to ten

111|577.c: Win the pickiest high-end customers first; their high margins pay for R&D.
111|577.e: Robotaxi companies wanted the best product, not the cheapest, so Hesai didn't build a drop-in clone of Velodyne, the US incumbent. It launched the 40-channel Pandar40, accepting that switching would cost customers more, and won deals on a better product. Hesai's average price was at times higher than rivals'. He rejects the idea that it won on value for money: starting high-end gave it the profits to keep investing in R&D, and revenue grew about tenfold in three years. Early big customers were mostly American; Chinese customers trusted foreign brands more and switched later.
ex: Gross margins once ran around 70% to 80%
Coding the laser pulses stops cars interfering; reading echoes tells rain, fog and dust apart

111|577.c: Lidar isn't a backup for cameras. It's a safety part that works alongside them, like an airbag.
111|577.e: He argues lidar and cameras run on different physics and should work side by side. Lidar sends out its own light and measures distance directly; cameras passively take in light and infer distance with algorithms. In a pitch-dark cave, if you can't see but your hand touches an obstacle, you trust your hand. Driving with eyes alone is imitating biology, not reasoning from first principles, and Leonardo da Vinci's bird-like flying machines failed too. Whether camera-only works should be judged by crash data. With prices near $200, lidar is shifting from a nice-to-have feature to a safety part like an airbag.
ex: He sees choices, not route wars: the industry tried 1550nm lasers, then returned to 905nm
He asks whether anyone buying a car would skip the airbags to save money

terms.d: Sends out light, measures distance directly

result.d: Brakes at night and for odd-shaped obstacles

111|577.c: Carmakers and suppliers should act like two departments of one company, not pass the blame.
111|577.e: With complex new technology, he argues, the customer can't win while the supplier loses; old buyer-versus-vendor projects usually end with both losing. Li Auto asked Hesai to go from 64 to 128 channels with size, cost and price unchanged, but worked through the hard parts together instead of squeezing the supplier. During Shanghai's 2022 lockdown Hesai was the only lidar supplier for the L9. The factory ran sealed off, with staff living on site, while he went to the US to coordinate. His rule: everyone should be where they're most needed. Bosch led an investment after reviewing over 100 lidar companies and pushed Hesai toward automotive-grade standards.
ex: Bosch called Hesai the whole village's only hope, and later dropped its own lidar effort

items.d: 128 channels, same size, cost and price

111|577.c: Going global isn't just saying your product is better; you must show what you bring locally.
111|577.e: Hesai's early overseas pitch was roughly "our product is better, so buy it." But as a company grows it inevitably meets political and social pushback, from patents to trade to defense agencies, and he admits he hadn't thought enough about how to get along with the world. Communication also means reading the cultural grammar. American customers value efficiency, so you can say you're strong and they'll check. European customers may take a deck full of "world's number one" claims as a scam, so Hesai leads with patents and technical detail and lets local staff do the talking.
ex: A top European carmaker narrowed 10+ suppliers to two or three, repeatedly checking delivery and quality
After 100+ roadshow meetings, he learned public investors need to hear why others will back you

d.verdict: Learn their cultural grammar before pitching the product

111|577.c: Hard tech is a marathon won through scale, and even the leader can lose first place.
111|577.e: Internet businesses have network effects, where each new user makes the product better, so treating every battle as decisive makes sense. Cars and robots rely mainly on economies of scale, so leaders can be caught. He cites Ming Zeng's advice to look ten years ahead, plan three and execute one, and focuses on what capabilities a win leaves behind. Hesai keeps design and manufacturing in-house, treating manufacturing as part of R&D, and its automotive-grade skills now carry over to ports, factories, lawn mowers, humanoid robots and robot dogs. As long as humans live in the physical world, he believes, lidar won't disappear.
ex: At the time, about 40% of business came from outside cars, at better margins
He rated his IPO odds at about 20%; no party at the listing, just power-bank souvenirs

111|577.c: An industry's opportunity is, at bottom, the opportunity of a country and its people.
111|577.e: He doesn't think a startup's success belongs to the team alone. Chances like electric vehicles come from years of national investment, and China, the biggest and fastest-moving market, gives local suppliers a place to train. He compares the home market to a gym for building muscle, while overseas is where you earn money on your merits. He sets Chinese companies three tasks: first export engineering capability, then make the world remember Chinese brands, and finally export culture and soft power, so the world sees how cool Chinese people are.
ex: He points to the gap between China and India to show what national groundwork means
He sees US-China relations as a bigger open question that directly shapes hard tech going global

items.d: Make the world remember the names

112|276.c: Maybe only OpenAI and Google will keep building do-everything models; the rest will each pick a niche.
112|276.e: The top three labs are close in ability, so latecomers struggle to break in. Both main approaches, pre-training and reinforcement learning (training a model by trial and reward), came from OpenAI, and new model generations now arrive every two or three months instead of six, so falling behind is costly. He thinks only OpenAI and Google's Gemini will keep building all-purpose models long term. Anthropic is narrowing to coding and agents, and Mira Murati's Thinking Machines leans toward multimodal AI and new interfaces. xAI may spend 10 to 20 times more than others without a breakthrough, and Meta is unlikely to reach the top three soon.
ex: Anthropic's annualized revenue rose from under $100M at end-2023 to about $950M in 2024
Mira's team raised $2B at a $10B valuation, the priciest seed round ever

112|276.c: If the model isn't good, users don't stay. ChatGPT is having its Coca-Cola moment.
112|276.e: He compares training models to Netflix making shows: the money turns into product, mindshare and brand rather than vanishing like paid ads. When a model gets stronger, lapsed users come back, which is why ChatGPT's retention may be second only to WeChat's. Most people no longer compare options. It's simply their default AI tool, the way people still reach for Coke even when tastier drinks appear. OpenAI is unusual in both pushing the frontier of intelligence and quickly turning each leap into traffic and brand.
ex: His imaginary 100-unit portfolio: OpenAI and ByteDance 40 each, Anthropic and Google 10 each
OpenAI reports about $12B in annualized revenue; Anthropic about $5–6B

items.d: It becomes the default AI tool
Harder to catch than a tech lead

112|276.c: AI labs will move into apps themselves, so startups' exclusive head start keeps getting shorter.
112|276.e: Labs spend fortunes mining intelligence, but selling API access alone doesn't give them enough lock-in or retention. Seeing Cursor make money, they naturally build apps themselves; even partner-friendly Anthropic now pushes its own products. A product company's job is to be first with an experience that wows users and earns traffic and word of mouth, but that exclusive window has shrunk from nearly two years to a few months. Costs aren't fair either: startups subsidize every token (unit of model usage), while labs earn API margins and can optimize end to end. Still, he stresses, tougher competition doesn't mean startups can't win.
ex: Claude Code launched 8–9 months after Cursor and passed its annualized revenue within 3–4 months
Startups' token losses can run from 1:3 to 1:10

112|276.c: ChatGPT bundles everything into one app; Google owns the whole stack. Google may win back ground.
112|276.e: For $20 or $200 a month, ChatGPT users get chat, search, coding, agents and office tools in one place, squeezing single-industry agent startups. Google runs from its own TPU chips and Gemini models through Docs, Chrome, Android and YouTube, so trailing on models by a few months barely matters. He used to think ChatGPT would overtake Google but has changed his mind: ChatGPT will have to sell ads, and Google is still the best ad platform. The big unknown is user habit: people type a few words into a search box but write full descriptions in ChatGPT.
ex: He expects 3–5% of users to pay eventually, with heavy users paying $200–2,000 a month
Searches are often two or three words; ChatGPT prompts often run 30–50 Chinese characters

items: A few months behind is fine

d.verdict: Different roads to one place; Google's scale may win

112|276.c: Hands-off, L4-level AI experiences already exist in search and coding; office work is next.
112|276.e: His north star for products is delivering an L4-level experience at scale in some field, a term borrowed from self-driving that means you can mostly let go. Today's two strongest agents, deep research and Claude Code, convince users to upgrade from $20 to $200 a month. Language and code are highly abstract forms of human activity, programmers are well paid, and software results are easy to verify, so the digital world breaks through first while the physical world moves slowly. Next up: structured, checkable office work like slide decks and Excel analysis. Generating slides is the toughest test of coding and agent skills.
ex: The user base could grow from about 30 million programmers to 500–600 million office workers
He thinks a new breed of AI product managers may come from algorithm or model backgrounds

112|276.c: Spreading bets no longer works; only concentrated bets on a few big winners pay off.
112|276.e: Miss OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Cursor, he says, and you've wasted this wave. Many Silicon Valley VCs passed on Anthropic's and Mira's seed rounds because the upfront spending was huge and margins were thin. Fund returns come from a few big winners, as with PDD, Xiaomi, Kuaishou and ByteDance in the past. To spot a bubble, he watches whether the smartest people still use the product, and right now quant traders and top programmers almost all use Claude. His biggest worry is circular revenue from massive capital spending: it inflates Nvidia's and the labs' revenue without creating real value for end users.
ex: He puts big Silicon Valley firms' AI capital spending this year at about $300 billion
Bullish on Chinese founders, he cites the saying: Jewish finance, Chinese AGI

113|309.c: Reasoning models are brains in a vat; agents have to think while acting in the world.
113|309.e: Reasoning models like OpenAI's o1, trained with reinforcement learning (learning by trial and reward), learned to make a guess and quietly check it, compressing many attempts into one success. But a model that only thinks internally is like a brain in a vat, cut off from the world. Models trained as agents call search, use a browser and write code, and each next step depends on feedback from the environment. Both spend extra effort at answer time, one by thinking longer and the other by taking more turns, and both can power hours-long tasks that run start to finish without a human.
ex: His example: clone a repo, port it to a new language, debug and fix it, unattended

items: Driven by feedback from the world

d.verdict: Two ways to spend more effort; hard tasks need both

113|309.c: AI's five levels needn't unlock in order; a model becomes an innovator when it helps build itself.
113|309.e: OpenAI ranks AI ability in five levels: chatbots, reasoners, agents, innovators and organizations. He argues agent skills needn't sit on top of strong reasoning; you can build agents first and add long reasoning later. Claude isn't a standout reasoner but is a strong agent, so these are separate dimensions, though the hardest tasks need both. The innovator level arrives when a model joins its own research, proposing ideas, running experiments, analyzing results and improving infrastructure, such as K2 helping build K3. The organizer level means many AIs working together; the hard part is training them jointly without overfitting to a few agent types.

cells.d: Deep thinker stuck in the vat

113|309.c: High-quality data is nearly fixed, so K2's core goal is learning more from every token.
113|309.e: High-quality data grows slowly; the best of it may be only tens to hundreds of billions of tokens (the word pieces models read), and rereading it means memorizing. So the question shifts from training faster to learning more from the same data, since a faster training system can't raise the ceiling on intelligence. K2 relies first on the Muon optimizer, the rule for adjusting a model's parameters, which unlike the standard Adam considers how parameters in a matrix relate. Second, it uses existing models to rewrite training text so it's easier to absorb. Critics say rewriting adds nothing new; he agrees the key is whether it adds genuinely new information.
ex: One surprise: at scale an internal value (max logit) blew up, fixed with new clipping
He calls it the first public use of a non-Adam, matrix-orthogonalizing optimizer at this scale

items.d: About twice as efficient at optimal compute

113|309.c: The data wall is real, but adding compute still beats a user-data flywheel for now.
113|309.e: He sees hitting the data wall, running out of good training data, as a fact. The way through is learning more per token and pouring more compute into reinforcement learning tasks, and progress hasn't slowed; it may even be speeding up. A flywheel where more users bring more data and better models hasn't appeared because scaling compute works so well: reinforcement learning trains on the model's own current outputs and learns from its mistakes, making it even more efficient than pre-training. Big models are also sensitive to noise, and noisy user feedback is still unsolved. Users still matter, showing what people need so teams can turn it into evaluations.
ex: He agrees next-word prediction is fundamentally flawed: big models skip steps, so RL must unlock reasoning

items.d: Trains on own outputs, learns from mistakes
User-data flywheel matters less for now

113|309.c: An agent is just multiple turns plus tools, and general agents will make many specialized ones unnecessary.
113|309.e: He boils agents down to two features: multiple turns are how a model spends more effort, and tools are how the brain connects to the outside world. Search plugs the model into the internet, and code lets it automate the digital world, since nearly any digital automation can be written as code. When the host said agents imitate people, he corrected him: the design goal is generality, and resembling humans is a side effect, just as planes were built for transport, not to fly like birds. If a general agent can handle long-tail tools, many industry-specific agents become unnecessary.
ex: Long-tail tools include company databases, personal documents and custom APIs

terms.d: How the model spends more effort
Link the brain to the world

result.d: A universal builder, not a human imitation

113|309.c: Agents' biggest problem is generalizing beyond training, and the fix is using AI to train AI.
113|309.e: Today's reinforcement learning often trains toward a single benchmark, and a higher score doesn't mean the skill transfers. That's worse for agents than for chat models, and good agent evals are scarce. RL generalizes better than supervised fine-tuning, which copies model answers, but it's still bound by what it saw in training. He notes most tasks come from human data or human design, with too little that is AI-native. The way out is letting AI help generate task environments and alignment research, and a good world model could also simulate environments. In effect, AI trains AI. K2 uses medium-difficulty tasks as an implicit curriculum, since very hard ones teach little.
ex: A model drilled to ace one math contest may gain only a few points elsewhere

113|309.c: Kimi open-sourced because it isn't far ahead yet; once the model is trained, the product is mostly done.
113|309.e: Last year he said leaders don't open-source; this year K2 went open. His explanation: Kimi isn't far enough ahead yet. The community helps deploy and serve the model, and downstream companies can train K2 into specialized agents for their own tools, but only the original lab can improve the base model. He expects the world's model companies to shrink from hundreds to a handful. On product, he holds that the model is the product: tools, context and environment are built together during training, and the interface on top is just a bonus. Investing first in getting the technology right, he says, makes the business more predictable.
ex: He rejects framings like "China's OpenAI" or "China's Anthropic," preferring a global view

items.d: Only the original lab can do it

113|309.c: Manage a team like reinforcement learning: set goals and rewards, and hand out few model answers.
113|309.e: He sees research, model training and team leadership as alike: knowledge comes from guessing and checking. So management should mostly work like reinforcement learning, setting goals and rewards rather than telling people how to do things. A little supervised fine-tuning, showing worked answers, can serve as a starting point, like the PTX loss that keeps a model from drifting too far, but too much kills initiative. The biggest risk is reward hacking, where metrics look good but the real goal is missed; the fix is more ways to observe and a deep grasp of the rewards. Citing The Beginning of Infinity, he says problems are inevitable but solvable.
ex: He quotes Kimi's own answer: AI is an amplifier of human civilization
Each step up, someone quits; he says the odds of success beat last year's

114|593.c: A warm winter forced a second pillar, and Salomon bet on trail running about 20 years early.
114|593.e: Salomon's roots are in snow. After a warm winter around 1980, the brand realized relying on snow alone was too risky, so it moved from ski boots to hiking and mountaineering shoes and invested early in trail running. That groundwork went beyond selling gear: it gave athletes equipment, coaching, recovery support and training plans. The fashion line wasn't bolted on later either. The Sportstyle line from its years under Adidas was already in the archive, and models like the XT-6 later took off and reached Paris Fashion Week.
ex: Early trail races around Chamonix drew only about 40 runners each

items.d: Search for a pillar beyond snow

114|593.c: Trail running's problem is the high entry bar, so build steps that turn casual outdoor fans into racers.
114|593.e: The core trail-running crowd stayed at about 100,000 people for a decade; Yin says it was really the same people, ten years older. The problem isn't consumers but the entry bar. Road running starts at 3 to 5 km, while trail races often start at 26 km with 800 to 1,000 meters of climbing, which scares young people off. So the brand built entry points level by level. It also redefined winning as something for everyone, even running five minutes longer than yesterday, and told ordinary participants' stories instead of star highlights.
ex: By 2025 the audience grew about 7–8x in under four years, with over 8 million members
Employee Nana, formerly in finance, climbed from fifth to second in the women's 26 km race
The Golden League raised the winner's prize from 20,000–30,000 yuan to about a million

items.d: Entry point for casual outdoor fans
Going up a mountain for the first time

114|593.c: Fashion brings in new customers and performance keeps them; it's a division of labor, not a trade-off.
114|593.e: Fashion trends turn over roughly every three years, but ways of doing sport get passed down, so fashion is for reaching and converting people and performance is for keeping them. Yin isn't worried that fashion dilutes credibility: ski gear, athletes and races remain core investments, and expert advice in real settings converts extremely well. He splits marketing into fast and slow. Social media, influencers and brand campaigns are fast; races, athletes, community and word of mouth are slow. Many foreign brands use Xiaohongshu as a barometer, testing reactions before deciding to open stores.
ex: Expert runners recommend shoes by distance and suggest wool socks against blisters on long hikes

items: Changes every three years or so

d.verdict: A division of labor; performance is the foundation

114|593.c: The falling share of women isn't churn: women made the brand popular, then brought men back.
114|593.e: Yin estimates Salomon's users in China were perhaps 80% men before 2021; women reached nearly 70% in 2022–23 and are now under 60%. Women didn't leave. As their numbers grew, they influenced more men. The two groups differ. Men take longer to decide, care about specs and fitting, and often become die-hard fans once convinced. Women care about the experience and comfort, want style alongside performance, and buy again more often. The shoe last, the foot-shaped mold shoes are built on, is a hidden factor: Asian women's feet resemble European men's, so the original last suited women, and the brand reworked it for Asian men.
ex: A new China-specific last started in 2023 and was finished in 2024
Worldwide, users are roughly half men and half women

114|593.c: Growing an audience means more settings, more recognition and more touchpoints, so people keep coming back.
114|593.e: Yin breaks audience growth into three parts: more use settings, a bigger place in people's minds, and more touchpoints. The key metric is repeat traffic, the same people returning across many touchpoints. The Anfu Road store in Shanghai shows how. The street's architecture suits a French brand, so Salomon rented the whole building, deliberately kept it from feeling too commercial, and gave each of the three floors its own job. The store also partners with nearby cafés, a wonton shop and a bakery, and visitors post their photos online, so the same foot traffic builds value at several touchpoints.
ex: Ground-floor pop-ups rotate every ~3 months; the top fan-voted design is slated for Paris Fashion Week

items.d: Welcome area and pop-ups, changed every ~3 months

114|593.c: Both niche and mass-market paths work; what matters is a single-brand focus and detailed execution.
114|593.e: After Anta bought Amer Sports, Salomon's parent, in 2019, sharing back-office functions, supply chain, talent and management practices all helped. But Yin thinks the decisive change was perspective: allocating resources around one brand and its core audience rather than the group as a whole. Niche players are meticulous but lack reach; big brands reach widely but may miss what specialists need. Both paths work, and what matters is the solution, an expert team and fine-grained execution. Next comes a "China engine," with Chinese R&D working alongside French R&D.
ex: China-led apparel comes first, with footwear advances like midsole foam rolling out in 2026–27

114|594.c: Platforms can't manufacture trends; they must spot real demand and help a lifestyle grow.
114|594.e: Ou believes every trend rides on a mass need or mood that gets sparked and amplified, so no platform can create one from nothing. Xiaohongshu's two-column feed, where users choose what to tap, and its user-written posts let it capture real motivations, not just clicks. The path runs like this: the community grows a lifestyle, users start searching for guides and gear, and brands arrive with mature solutions, so everyone wins. The precondition is protecting the community's authenticity; only once the ecosystem matures is there room for commerce.
ex: Cyclists lacked parking, so the team mapped route-side cafés willing to rack and watch bikes
Xiaohongshu began with a few PDF guides to shopping overseas

items.d: The real motive behind a trend

114|594.c: To take a mature hit shoe mainstream, first find people where performance meets fashion.
114|594.e: When the deep partnership began in 2023, the XT-6 was already an established hit; the challenge was crossing from the performance crowd to lifestyle and fashion audiences. The team used the platform to identify two groups: novelty hunters chasing new brands and rare items, and color obsessives with a sharp eye for colorways. Both sat right where performance meets lifestyle and loved sharing outfits. A network of buyer accounts then recommended the shoes, and sales took off.
ex: Sales topped 10 million yuan in the first month on the platform
Details like pink laces on a black shoe are exactly what color obsessives notice

items.d: Chase new brands and rare items

114|594.c: Buying is the start of sharing, and buyers' posts bring in the next wave of customers.
114|594.e: Ou finds that ongoing, companion-style content converts better than a one-off livestream. Sida Jiang, a marathoner with a strong sense of style, is a super-user bridging performance and fashion. The team built about a month of sharing around his Paris Marathon, before, during and after the race, and opened a dedicated sale only once comments filled with requests to buy. After buying, users kept searching for outfits, down jackets and shell jackets, so the brand added apparel. Buyers' posts then drew in new users, completing the loop.
ex: Over 5,000 post-purchase notes drew about 200 million views
After apparel was added, repeat buyers made up about 25% of the loop

items.d: A steady stream of outfit posts

114|594.c: The Salomon girls trend reflects women dropping performative rituals for an unforced, relaxed style.
114|594.e: Ou argues women didn't suddenly fall for trail running. They grew tired of piling on rituals, like getting up early to do makeup just for a staged photo, which felt like trying too hard. They wanted shoes that could splash through puddles and still walk into a café, driven by their own urge to explore. Shoes like the XT-Whisper captured that unperformed ease. The audience was described as wild girls in the city, and online content plus offline events amplified it.
ex: A launch-night run at the Anfu Road store reached No. 2 on Xiaohongshu's organic trending list

terms.d: No dressing up for staged photos
That also work in a café

114|594.c: When supply far exceeds demand, brands must first say who they are and what problem they solve.
114|594.e: In China, consumer goods supply far outstrips demand and products already do their job, so purchases are increasingly driven by setting, mood, taste and life stage. Search queries increasingly read like full sentences describing someone's situation. A brand can't just claim to be number one in its category. It must explain across many settings who it is and what it solves, and a specialist brand should first be the expert in its field. Ou defines seeding, content that makes people want a product, as solutions for the lifestyle people aspire to, from R&D through after the sale. It needn't please everyone: start with core fans who share the brand's DNA.

items.d: Be the expert in one field first
People who share the brand's DNA
From R&D through after the sale

115|597.c: Language is the hub on the road to general AI, so agents should generate actions, not pick options.
115|597.e: He switched early from computer vision to language because language can express almost anything, tying together knowledge, reasoning and action. When he started, most people worked on BERT, which can only choose among given options, while an agent's actions must be freely generated, so he chose the GPT route. He also found that the environment sets the ceiling: reinforcement learning (learning by trial and reward) could beat text games yet transferred to nothing else. A poor task teaches nothing good.
ex: When he started, about 95% of people were working on BERT
In Zork-style text games, RL could grind through one game but failed on any new task

d.verdict: Agents must generate actions, so the GPT route wins

115|597.c: Reasoning is language agents' core advantage because it lets skills transfer to new environments.
115|597.e: He sees three waves of agents. Symbolic rules couldn't cover exceptions. Deep reinforcement learning needed custom engineering for every environment, and skills didn't transfer. With large language models, knowledge absorbed from language supports reasoning, and reasoning carries skills into unfamiliar environments. His ReAct method has models alternate between thinking a step and acting a step, and it remains the backbone of most agents. He cautions that generalization is a spectrum: math transfers easily to code, but social savvy may not.
ex: In a new game, people reason a dark room may be dangerous and back away
DeepSeek's RL on math and code also made its creative writing stronger

items.d: AlphaGo and others; skills don't transfer
Prior knowledge plus reasoning, works anywhere

115|597.c: Code is the digital agent's hands, and important work nobody is doing is often the opportunity.
115|597.e: Humans build tools with their hands; digital agents operate machines with code. Code is an interface designed for machines, so it suits agents better than web pages or graphical interfaces. He built InterCode on a simple insight: running code returns feedback, so it is naturally a multi-turn environment. That line of work led to SWE-bench and SWE-agent. As for whether agents will work through APIs or by clicking screens like people, he expects the two to meet in the middle, with systems using code, screenshots and front ends together.
ex: He once wondered why nobody was building coding agents
Adapt the car to the road, or the road to the car? They'll meet halfway

115|597.c: In AI's second half, the bottleneck shifts from inventing methods to defining tasks and rewards.
115|597.e: In his essay The Second Half, he argues the path from language to reasoning to agents now has a shared recipe, so the hard question is what to use it for. Good rewards judge outcomes and can be computed by clear, transparent rules; math and code succeeded because right is simply right. Rewarding the process invites reward hacking, where models game the score, and optimizing for human preference can yield code that looks nice but doesn't work. He also notes that methods for audio, robotics and similar areas remain unsolved.
ex: Before, every monster needed its own weapon; now we have a machine gun
Turning Amazon or Facebook into training environments is among the hardest kinds

terms.d: Not a test you can cram for
Solves a problem people care about
Outcome checkable by rules, low noise

result.d: The scarcest resource of the second half

115|597.c: Sort tasks by reliability, duration and breadth; business uses should optimize for pass^k, getting it right every time.
115|597.e: He splits agent tasks along three axes: reliability versus creativity, time span, and breadth. Longer tasks lean on long-term memory; broader ones need multiple agents. For evaluation, pass@k only asks whether one of k attempts succeeded, hiding the need to be right every time. The τ-bench benchmark he worked on uses pass^k instead, requiring all k attempts to succeed. He thinks people neglect reliability because they're still in leaderboard-chasing mode rather than setting metrics by business needs.
ex: Customer service needs under 1 error in 100; a hard proof needs 1 success in 100
Editing a file takes about 3 seconds; some jobs take 3 days

root.d: Each axis needs a different goal

items.d: From bug fixes to large codebases

115|597.c: Startups should fear models that stop gaining new abilities; their opportunity lies in new ways of interacting.
115|597.e: He disagrees that models will swallow apps. The best combination is a new interface plus model abilities that keep spilling over, and both are essential. Copy a ChatGPT-style interface and the app loses its reason to exist the moment the model upgrades; a novel interface can't deliver value if the model stalls. Super apps create path dependence, with resources revolving around their existing form, so super apps of different forms still have room. Model companies already own the human-like assistant, so he favors Canvas-style products that generate an interface on the fly for each task.
ex: Cursor built AI into the code editor, a kind of collaboration humans never had
In 2020 Google held the Transformer yet used it first to improve search

115|597.c: Most AI apps have no data flywheel; memory is what turns a model lead into stickiness.
115|597.e: A real data flywheel needs two things: you train your own model, and user interactions give clear rewards aligned with the product's value. Most AI companies' growth actually comes from base models getting better. Without memory, chat products compete on model strength, and leads rise and fall with each model release; with memory, the context users accumulate keeps them around. Borrowing from von Neumann, he treats the outside environment as the outermost layer of a memory hierarchy, so software connected via MCP, a standard for plugging AI into tools, is in a sense memory too.
ex: Midjourney lets users pick images, a reward aligned with product value
Notebooks, Google Docs and Notion are people's external memory

115|597.c: AI is very capable yet creates little economic value, because it lacks context, not intelligence.
115|597.e: Models ace exams, reasoning and games, but economic value hasn't kept pace. He traces this to missing context: the rules sit in documents, but the boss's habits, the team's unspoken understandings and past trade-offs live in people's heads. So he names long-term memory, intrinsic rewards and multi-agent systems as the three key research directions. He also argues evaluations should stop averaging day-one performance across a hundred parallel universes and instead measure growth after a day, a month or a year. Needle-in-a-haystack tests, finding one line in a long text, are only a minimum bar.
ex: o3 lacks the background an ordinary employee picks up in their first seven days
Creators are like Einstein; organizers are like Steve Jobs

items.d: Beats most people on exams and reasoning
Habits and understandings live in heads

115|597.c: Overtaking a leader takes a different bet; the world will become more centralized and diverse at once.
115|597.e: Early OpenAI centered on reinforcement learning, with DeepMind as its benchmark. Doing only RL would have made it a follower even if it pulled ahead in places; GPT was the different bet. He thinks an organization doesn't need everyone to agree. If enough people believe, contrarian experiments can keep going. Looking ahead, OpenAI may become the Google of a new era, but intelligence is defined by many kinds of interaction, so there's no single ranking of the strongest. Centralization and diversity can intensify together.
ex: His advisor Karthik, second author on GPT-1, once had doubts too
A companion AI doesn't need top math skills; being too perfect feels fake

marks.d: Could be the new era's Google
Still centralized, a few super apps

115|597.c: Token costs aren't the problem; what matters is whether the value created covers them.
115|597.e: Some founders worry that agents burn hundreds or thousands of times more tokens, the units of model usage, than chatbots. His answer: spending $500 to earn $1,000 works. Use small models for simple tasks and big ones for high-value work, and first find applications worth paying for. A team doesn't need researchers either; research backgrounds tempt people to be a hammer looking for nails. As for incumbents, he says that if he ran WeChat he wouldn't rush to make it fully agentic. The real threat is a replacement of an entirely different form.
ex: Agents may use 500 to 1,000 times as many tokens as chatbots
WeChat beat QQ without being a more QQ-like product

116|609.c: Personalized recommendation was the right idea, but too early: it can't work without stable user IDs.
116|609.e: As a master's student he used a language model to measure web-page similarity for personalized recommendations, hoping to tailor content to each person the way a good teacher tailors lessons. But the PC era had no stable user identity. Security software often wiped cookies, so personal behavior never accumulated, and recommendations only became practical once mobile devices provided stable IDs. The company later moved into ad data. He admits it lost sight of its original goal and regrets not returning to recommendations in 2011–2012, when Miaozhen's data might have given it a shot.
ex: His thesis used Peking University's Chinese concept dictionary to measure page similarity
The first real user was Bullog, the site run by Luo Yonghao

116|609.c: Third-party ad verification must be sold to advertisers, because media outlets won't expose their real traffic.
116|609.e: He first tried to sell traffic analytics to media companies and hit a wall: they didn't want outsiders seeing their real numbers. Advertisers were different. Anyone paying for ads needs to verify the traffic is real. The early barrier was big-data computing: catching fraud meant tracing every IP address's history, which sent computing loads soaring. During the financial crisis the company survived on outsourcing work and loans, and after 2010, as ad budgets shifted from TV to the internet, Miaozhen took off.
ex: On its first day running on MSN, it received tens of millions of data points
During the crisis it survived on outsourcing and a loan of about 1 million yuan

d.verdict: Find the side that both pays and truly hurts

116|609.c: Listening too closely to existing customers made him miss the mobile internet.
116|609.e: He openly regrets missing mobile. Advertisers then widely believed phone screens were too small for ads, and he followed his customers' view; he didn't even get an iPhone until the iPhone 4. He explains it with The Innovator's Dilemma: feedback from an entire network of customers and partners can be wrong all at once. As PC traffic growth slowed, he moved into ad buying, drew criticism for being both referee and player, and eventually split the company in two.
ex: His first iPhone was the iPhone 4
Buying ads drew criticism that he was both referee and player

items.d: Phones seen as unfit for ads

116|609.c: Government work is a big market, but feedback is too slow for the rapid iteration AI needs.
116|609.e: After studying lean startup methods at CEIBS in 2014, he concluded half the staff could sustain Miaozhen's existing business. The problem wasn't a lack of talent but too many people piled onto a mature product. So he spun off Mininglamp Data and Yunji Robotics, turning one company into three. Mininglamp Data modeled itself on Palantir, starting with government and then expanding into manufacturing and finance. His reflection: government work is large but its feedback is very slow, a poor match for AI's rapid iteration. During the pandemic, Mininglamp shut down or spun off all its government business.
ex: Guangmi Li, researching Palantir at Sequoia, approached Mininglamp himself
Its first hired CEO, a former Oracle executive, was soon poached by Alibaba Cloud

items.d: Shut or spun off during the pandemic

116|609.c: EIP failed because it came too early and aimed too wide: chasing L3 agents before L1 chat worked.
116|609.e: In 2019 Miaozhen, Mininglamp Data and AdMaster merged, and he wanted to pool all of a company's data to train AI. The 2020 EIP plan tackled three layers at once, applications, data integration and models, using BERT underneath to train specialized models for tasks like customer service. The concept resembled the later ChatGPT plus Copilot. In hindsight, he admits it needed L3 agent ability, AI that acts on its own, when even L1 conversation wasn't mature. Bringing in Huawei's IPD product-development process was also the wrong management approach.
ex: The team grew from about 100 people to about 1,000
He expected to crack it in two or three years; American companies made the breakthrough

116|609.c: With only a month of cash left, he learned to run the company by the numbers.
116|609.e: A cooling funding market plus Shanghai's lockdown meant about half of revenue couldn't be invoiced or collected, while a thousand-person team kept burning cash, forcing big layoffs. At the worst point the company had about 100 million yuan and spent about as much each month. He rejects the idea that a big cash pile means safety: even 2 billion yuan is dangerous at 100 million a month. What counts is how many months you can last. He accepted a down round and borrowed personally to invest, and admits even another $500 million might not have won a three-front war. Now profitable, the company is safe with modest cash.
ex: Severance topped 200 million yuan, about a third of the new funding
He personally put in more than $10 million

items.d: Mininglamp Data and Yunji spun off

116|609.c: As models converge, the edge comes from x in y=f(x): continuous private data nobody can copy.
116|609.e: He explains it with y = f(x), where f is the model and x is a company's own context and data. As models become alike, ten companies using the same model still differ in competitiveness, and the difference is x. Code written by a thousand people over three years used to be a barrier; now AI generates code quickly, so the new barriers are industry-specific data, real environments and continuous feedback. Data also has a time dimension. Daily ad behavior or shifts in influencers' followers, if not stored at the time, can never be recovered.
ex: Ad data from the 2008 Olympics wasn't stored then and can't be rebuilt now
In-store data on shoppers, products and space suits training industry-specific agents

116|609.c: Selling tokens alone shrinks margins to utility levels, so Mininglamp trains small models and charges by value.
116|609.e: Public data can't be owned exclusively, and rivals can catch up fast through distillation, training on a bigger model's outputs. So companies that only sell tokens, units of model usage, end up with margins as thin as an electric utility's. Mininglamp therefore trains only small specialized models of 7 to 8 billion parameters, mainly for its own agents, and charges by the value delivered, not usage. He also opposes endless scaling: if a general multimodal model misreads text at the first OCR step, all later research is wasted, and with perhaps tens of thousands of expert tasks, scale may not cover them all.
ex: He cites OSWorld scores: about 44 for its 7B model versus about 34 for Kimi
He values pass@1, a single submission, to avoid accusations of gaming leaderboards

d.verdict: Vertical players win on data and use cases, not size

116|609.c: Tool-using agents can bypass platforms, so middlemen with no supply of their own are most exposed.
116|609.e: Many legacy systems, and outside ones like tax systems, have no APIs, so we need agents that operate web pages and computers the way people do. Once an agent can work several recruiting sites at once, users trust that cross-platform agent, and a platform that only connects parties without owning supply can be bypassed. He also separates workflows from true agents. Most so-called agents just follow preset steps; a real agent breaks down goals and picks tools itself. Both have their uses.
ex: One agent works Zhaopin, Boss Zhipin and 51job at the same time
Without irreplaceable supply, even Didi could be swapped out

items.d: Users come to trust the agent

116|609.c: AI amplifies top performers; the future company may be an owner plus a team of AI agent partners.
116|609.e: He doesn't see AI as a layoff tool but as a way to multiply his best people's abilities, and he hopes ordinary engineers and analysts become AI engineers or data product managers. In an 1,800-person company the CEO can't hold all the context, so each team must build its own evaluations and optimize end to end. He likens this to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models and calls it a mixture of agents (MOA). The end state may be just business owners and agent partners: owners hold the memory, evaluations and final responsibility, while agents share in business results and need identity and credit.
ex: Salespeople spend about 40% of their time filling out forms
Mininglamp has about 300 data analysts

117|618.c: Product work means optimizing within limits, and reading papers is how you see those limits.
117|618.e: He sees product work as finding the best solution under given constraints. When the technical limits shift, the best solution shifts too, so papers aren't just for engineers. He brushed up on linear algebra and probability, used Immersive Translate, a side-by-side translation tool, to get past the language barrier, and cross-checked answers across several models to catch hallucinations. The hardest part, he says, isn't the math but not knowing why something was done. So he places each paper on three threads: the history, the people, and the old approach it replaced.
ex: Read 200-plus papers, kept 100-plus, and picked 36 for the guide
After a week of raw English, he switched to Immersive Translate

result.d: Knowing why it was done that way

117|618.c: The Transformer won the hardware lottery: its design happened to fit GPUs perfectly.
117|618.e: In his view the Transformer, the backbone of today's models, won by fitting the hardware. RNNs process words one at a time and can't run in parallel, and CNNs struggle with distant relationships. Self-attention lets any two tokens relate directly through pure matrix math, exactly what GPUs do best, so it could scale with data and compute. He traces this back to Brook, which turned GPUs from graphics cards into general computing platforms, and to AlexNet, which scaled data, compute, and model size together. He admits theory still lags practice: many design choices were found by trial and error.
