ex: AlexNet had about 62.5 million parameters; ImageNet held about 14 million images
Brook's creator Ian Buck later helped build Nvidia's CUDA

items: RNNs compute in sequence, hard to parallelize

d.verdict: Parallel means scalable, setting up the brute-force era

117|618.c: From ResNet to LoRA to DDPM, learning only the change keeps proving a winning design idea.
117|618.e: Several breakthroughs share one idea: don't make the model learn everything, only the change on top of what exists. Networks deeper than about 100 layers got worse with training. ResNet had layers learn only an increment on their input, which made training far easier, enabled hundreds or thousands of layers, and still underpins Transformers and diffusion models. LoRA, a cheap way to fine-tune big models, freezes the original and trains two small low-rank matrices that merge back in at deployment, adding almost no delay. DDPM likewise just predicts the noise added at each step, reviving diffusion models after about five quiet years.
ex: The ResNet paper has nearly 300,000 citations
Later work cut diffusion steps from about 1,000 to about 10

items.d: Freeze the model, train small matrices

117|618.c: Chain-of-thought and InstructGPT showed post-training can deliver more than piling on parameters.
117|618.e: The chain-of-thought paper is about as simple as a blog post: have the model write out intermediate steps, or tell it to think step by step, and performance jumps. He sees it as the start of post-training, the extra training after pretraining, and the point where research focus shifted there. InstructGPT used supervised fine-tuning, a reward model, and RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, so a far smaller model beat GPT-3 at following instructions. He also notes ReAct linked thinking, acting, and observing into a loop before ChatGPT existed, proof that finding good problems is rarer than solving them.
ex: ReAct came out in October 2022, before ChatGPT
He counts Jason Wei among researchers good at spotting the right problems

117|618.c: Hand-designed rules work for now but get replaced once compute grows another order of magnitude.
117|618.e: He buys Rich Sutton's essay "The Bitter Lesson": general methods that can absorb more compute win in the long run. Stuffing human knowledge into a system helps short term but blocks scaling later. What should be built in are methods that find patterns themselves. He counts today's agent workflows, RAG rules (retrieve documents, then answer), and the rules in Claude Code's system prompt as injected human knowledge, and expects them to be replaced after another tenfold jump in compute. AlphaGo Zero learned from the rules and self-play alone, with no game records, showing closed domains with clear rules suit pure reinforcement learning.
ex: AlphaGo Zero beat AlphaGo Lee after 36 hours of training
About 1,600 searches per move inspired spending more compute at answer time

117|618.c: More GPUs doesn't mean faster training; stability and hardware-software fit decide real output.
117|618.e: Parameters grew about a thousandfold while per-GPU memory couldn't keep up. ZeRO, a way to spread a model across GPUs, removed duplicated memory so trainable model size grows with the cluster's total memory. At 10,000-GPU scale, bad cards and bit flips corrupt the whole computation, and when the loss blows up you roll back to a checkpoint. So the nominal GPU count isn't real capacity, and the system must find and swap failing cards automatically. He praises DeepSeek for designing its parallelism around the bandwidth limits of H800 chips, and thinks China's GPU shortage forced a focus on efficiency.
ex: GPT-1 had about 120 million parameters, GPT-3 about 175 billion; memory went 16GB to 80GB
About 50% MFU, the share of compute actually used, counts as good

117|618.c: Scaling laws are a tool for reducing the risk of blind bets, not just bigger-is-better.
117|618.e: Loss falls log-linearly as compute, data, and parameters grow, so teams can experiment with small models before committing months to a big training run. Chinchilla added that parameters and data should scale in proportion. Small models can also be deliberately overtrained, trading a one-time training cost for permanently cheaper inference. On data, he values what LAION-5B and RefinedWeb showed: cleaning rules can be hard-coded into computing pipelines, so data production can scale too.
ex: LAION-5B has about 5 billion image-text pairs, far beyond ImageNet
NSFW content was tagged, not deleted, to keep knowledge of human anatomy

117|618.c: OpenAI stuck with next-token prediction, then bet everything on GPT-3 once it saw the signs.
117|618.e: Back then, BERT's two-way fill-in-the-blank approach beat GPT-1 on many benchmarks and suited well-defined tasks. He sees GPT as open-ended, implicit multitask learning whose generality only shows at scale. Instead of switching to BERT-style masked language modeling, OpenAI decided GPT-1's problem was data. It built WebText from highly upvoted Reddit links, trained GPT-2, saw zero-shot ability, meaning it could do tasks with no examples, and went all in. GPT-3 set the interface of putting the task in the prompt, which we still use.
ex: GPT-1: about 0.1B parameters, 12 layers, about 5GB of text
Microsoft invested $1 billion; the team grew from 6-8 people to 30-plus

117|618.c: Multimodal AI turned when it moved toward Transformers and compressed images into latent space.
117|618.e: GANs framed generation as a contest between a generator and a discriminator and ruled image generation for five or six years, but trained unstably. ViT cut images into 16×16 patches treated like words. It trailed CNNs on small data but overtook them after large-scale pretraining, thanks to a higher ceiling. CLIP used the captions that come with web images for contrastive learning, becoming the basis for text-controlled images. Stable Diffusion moved generation into a compressed latent space, which he likens to reading a thick book down to a thin one. DiT swapped the backbone for a Transformer, and he expects Transformers to keep taking over image generation.
ex: CLIP used about 400 million image-text pairs with no human labeling
Latent diffusion cuts compute by at least two orders of magnitude

117|618.c: Once you see the limits, waiting can be a strategy, and people must own end-to-end results.
117|618.e: He sees deep learning history as a chain of dependencies that takes at least thirty-some papers to connect. Ilya Sutskever's years of sticking with unsupervised pretraining were a wait for architecture and compute to meet. For products: in a customer-service project, GPT-4o was capable but slow, and Chinese models were about 20% worse, so the team waited two or three months until Qwen3 met the need. For careers, he advises using AI heavily, building engineering skills, and reading principles that won't go stale. He also senses OpenAI is using GPT and MCP to connect apps, aiming to become the next operating system.
ex: Proofreading meeting transcripts with Gemini went from a day to about 30 seconds
He expects sparse attention may expand context 10 to 100 times

118|458.c: By what people will pay for, AI tools come in three tiers; only production tools change results.
118|458.e: He starts from a puzzle: AI is improving fast, yet he and his colleagues aren't working fewer hours or producing clearly better work. Most people use AI as an information tool, but the sources it finds may themselves be wrong, so even careful reasoning goes wrong at the root. Assistive tools, like in-car voice control and navigation, are seen as features a product should simply have. Only production tools, which replace skilled labor and change what an eight-hour day produces, get people to pay separately.
ex: Around him, only Cursor and Deep Research, which people pay for themselves, qualify
The craze for sharing AI reasoning screenshots turned repetitive within months

items.d: Replace skilled work; people pay extra

118|458.c: Building capability takes four steps: research, development, expression, business results. None can be skipped.
118|458.e: He drew four steps from DeepSeek V3: research builds understanding and a direction, development turns that into capability, expression makes the capability visible, and business results are the final test. R1's reasoning maps onto analyzing a problem, setting goals, working through strategies and reviewing gaps. Organizations make two common mistakes: jumping straight into development without research, and, when business goes wrong, changing tactics without reviewing or resetting goals. He says following best practice goes against human nature, so you have to keep fighting laziness and shortcuts.
ex: He spoke with DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng only once, days before OpenAI's o1 launch
He said R1 lacks an action step; it's just a very good "brain"

items.d: The final test; gaps go back to research

118|458.c: Self-driving has to evolve from insect to mammal to human driver, with no stage skipped.
118|458.e: Early systems ran on hand-written rules plus perception, like insects following fixed tracks laid by high-definition maps. End-to-end models, which go straight from camera input to driving actions, are like mammals: they learn by imitation and generalize better, but don't understand the physical world and often stop in unfamiliar scenes. VLA (vision-language-action) models come closer to a human driver: they understand 3D space and navigation and reason in language before acting. End-to-end wasn't discarded; it became VLA's action layer. The earlier work can't be skipped, and hoping to leap straight to the end is, in his words, like chasing a forbidden kung-fu shortcut.
ex: Li Auto began building its own driving system in 2021 and studying end-to-end in 2023
At messy roadwork, rules may crash, end-to-end stops, and VLA drives around

items.d: Like an insect; relies on HD maps
Like a mammal; learns by imitation
Like a human driver; understands, then acts

118|458.c: Li Auto's driver model goes through pretraining, driving-school post-training, and two rounds of reinforcement learning.
118|458.e: The language part borrows DeepSeek's open-source work, saving about nine months and several hundred million yuan, but 3D vision, high-res 2D images and traffic data must be trained in-house. A 32-billion-parameter cloud model is distilled into a 3.2B mixture-of-experts model for the car, since the full model runs too slowly onboard. Post-training is like driving school: driving actions are added for imitation learning, and reasoning is cut to two or three steps for speed. Reinforcement learning first uses human-takeover data so it drives like a law-abiding Chinese driver, then pure trial and error in a world model aims to beat humans.
ex: Onboard: 3.2B parameters and 8 experts, about 4B once actions are added
Long-range recognition in high-res 2D is 3–5x better than common open-source vision-language models

items.d: Cloud pretraining; language borrowed from open source
Learn from humans, then practice in simulation

118|458.c: World models serve as exam hall and data factory, cutting testing to about 4,000 yuan per 10,000 km.
118|458.e: Li Auto rebuilds real scenes and generates new ones to create a full virtual traffic world, a "world model." Its driving model can go on real roads or take exams inside it. The world model serves first as a test system, then as a training-data factory, and eventually as the operating system for large driverless (L4) fleets, which traditional IT software can't manage. Real cars can hardly recreate several road users at the same speeds and positions, but a world model replays a scene exactly, showing whether a fix really works. Real-car testing costs about 170,000–180,000 yuan per 10,000 km, versus about 4,000 here, mostly compute.
ex: A new unsolved scenario can be fixed after three days of training on generated data
He counts "predicting what happens next" as a driver skill, not the world model's job

118|458.c: The more capable a driving model gets, the more professional it must be, and hand-written rules still matter.
118|458.e: After its cars had driven 10 million km, Li Auto set up a superalignment team of over 100 people to keep the model's behavior in line with human values. He separates ability from values: how often it crashes is ability, while constantly cutting in during jams is efficient but unsettles passengers, so it's a values problem. He also pushes back on "models can solve everything." Facing a dozen-plus ETC toll lanes, the vision-language model got confused, and three or four months of extra data didn't help. Rules describing up to about 15 lanes fixed it in under a week. It's like memorizing multiplication tables: brains and tools don't conflict.
ex: The alignment team has more than 100 people
ETC lanes: months of extra data failed; rules fixed it within a week

118|458.c: Today's in-car chips only support L3; L4 must wait until a 32B model runs in the car.
118|458.e: Two Orin X chips or one Thor-U offer about 64GB of memory, enough in theory to hold a roughly 30B model, but not at the frame rate driving needs, so cars run only 3B to 4B models. He therefore sees this generation as essentially L3 (the car drives itself in set conditions, with a human taking over when needed). If regulations allow, true L3 products could appear in the third or fourth quarter of that year. L4 needs a 32B model running onboard, by which time cloud models may reach 320B. He thinks VLA can deliver full self-driving, though maybe not as the most efficient final design.
ex: At the same 10Hz, a 30B model performs 10x better than a 3B one
Orin didn't support language models; the team rewrote low-level code to run them in INT4

118|458.c: Li Auto plans backward from scale, aiming to be the world's leading AI device company by 2030.
118|458.e: He treats scale as a clearly measurable center, with user needs, technology and products, and organizational ability around it, each checking the others. To grow from about 145 billion yuan in revenue to 300–500 billion, family SUVs alone would hit a ceiling, so Li Auto is adding family sedans and MPVs while limiting the number of versions it sells. An AI device must sense, decide, act and reflect, and the car may be one of the AI era's highest-revenue devices. He doesn't want the market to price in AI early: either be first to L4, or reach $100 billion revenue with under 100,000 people.
ex: Revenue last year was about 145 billion yuan
Building its own operating system cost ~1B yuan over four years; he estimates it saved 5–6B

root.d: The car is the first choice

items.d: Operate software or the machine itself

118|458.c: Debate with energy is collective intelligence; without energy it becomes infighting. Three to seven people works best.
118|458.e: He believes disagreement has value. What separates healthy debate from infighting isn't how loud people get but whether the connection between them still has energy. In the hardest days at Autohome, which he founded, he, Zhi Qin and Zheng Fan stayed united in public while arguing hard in private, covering each other's gaps. Li Auto kept this setup: a core of 3 to 7 people combines several minds without falling apart, which he likens to a mixture-of-experts model. It rests on two kinds of caring: about users, and about the people sharing responsibility. So get the people right first, then the work.
ex: He spends about 60% of his time on people and organization
Li Auto's end-to-end team is about 200; rivals' rule-based teams may number thousands

118|458.c: People are meant to be unleashed, not remade. AI handles intelligence; humans must cultivate wisdom.
118|458.e: Becoming a father convinced him that every child is completely different. An organization should likewise combine people's different strengths into one whole brain rather than force everyone into one template. Daring to say "I need them" turns a relationship from control into mutual support. He defines wisdom as one's relationship with all things, and being smart is not the same as being wise. He thinks today's AI architectures have no self-awareness, but expects AI to surpass human ability within 5 to 10 years. Then people's real work shifts to their relationships with themselves, others and the world.
ex: If you've never lived in a forest, wood is just chopsticks and paper
He has sales outreach calls handed to AI agents, saving 20–30% of the time

d.verdict: AI solves intelligence; humans must cultivate wisdom

119|480.c: Once data runs short, algorithms matter again, and scarce chips push Chinese labs to rethink architecture.
119|480.e: When data could grow without limit, buying more GPUs and adding data was enough, and efficiency hardly mattered. Now that data and compute are both constrained, the only path is better algorithms that squeeze more intelligence out of limited data. Her gut feeling is that Chinese labs innovate more on architecture: with fewer chips and a sharper need for efficiency, they're keener to try efficient variants, while some GPU-rich Silicon Valley companies don't bother. The US does invest clearly more in optimizers, the methods that steer how a model updates during training. She adds a limit: in data-poor fields like robotics, gathering data pays off more than refining architecture.
ex: Kimi was one of the first Chinese teams to try the Muon optimizer

items.d: More data and GPUs no longer scale
Squeeze more intelligence from limited data
Chinese labs try efficient variants more
The US invests more in optimizers

119|480.c: The knowledge-storing half of the model has been reworked; the next architecture breakthrough is attention.
119|480.e: A Transformer, the design behind today's models, has two main parts. The feed-forward network (FFN), which stores knowledge, has largely been turned into fine-grained mixture-of-experts, now standard practice. Attention, the other part, deserves the same rethinking. The two save compute for different goals: a cheaper FFN lets you add more parameters, while cheaper attention lets the model handle longer context, which directly helps long outputs and agent workflows. She sees global attention as the main bottleneck to longer context. Solve it, and add-ons like RAG (retrieving documents to feed the model) may no longer be needed.
ex: She likens attention to working memory and the FFN to a network that stores knowledge

d.verdict: Cheaper attention buys longer context

119|480.c: Linear attention keeps returning when context gets too long; selective forgetting and rewriting finally made it work.
119|480.e: Remove the softmax step and attention can be rewritten as a step-by-step recurrence, like an RNN: each step costs the same, so total cost grows linearly with length. The 2020 wave faded because Flash Attention made exact attention fast. She thinks approximating softmax with kernel functions was the wrong direction anyway. Two changes made it usable. First came dynamic decay, which lets the input decide whether to keep or wipe memory. Then came the Delta Rule: read the old value, then correct it, so adding stores information and subtracting deletes it precisely.
ex: A fixed decay like 0.99 forgets uniformly; dynamic decay can keep (1) or wipe (0)
DeltaNet was proposed in 2021, but almost nobody followed up for years

items.d: Flash Attention made exact attention fast

119|480.c: Kimi Linear's KDA lets each memory dimension forget at its own pace, making better use of limited memory.
119|480.e: After DeepSeek R1 and Kimi 1.5, models routinely write reasoning chains tens of thousands of tokens long, and generating them with full attention gets expensive as the cache and compute balloon with length. Hybrid architectures can speed this up several times without losing quality. KDA builds on her Gated DeltaNet from last year, replacing one decay rate per attention head with a separate forgetting rhythm for each dimension. She says she only used the coarse version back then because the algorithms and GPU kernels weren't mature. She calls her own contribution modest: mainly deriving a parallel algorithm that skips one matrix inversion.
ex: Kimi dropped RoPE position encoding entirely; Qwen3-Next kept 25%
Yu Zhang ran most of the experiments testing each component's effect

119|480.c: Pure linear attention can't be enough; hybrids are settling on three linear layers per full-attention layer.
119|480.e: A linear-attention memory has a fixed size, so as context grows it inevitably overflows. That's why she says pure linear models can't work in theory. In a hybrid, the remaining global attention layers act as a safety net, and Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next show no clear drop on long-text tests. After training, it also turns out most attention layers do little; only a few key ones really matter. She calls 3:1 a provisional consensus in an immature field. The weak spot is multi-hop reasoning over long text, linking several facts to answer, and she thinks finer-grained decay may narrow that gap.
ex: ByteDance's from-scratch pretraining tests and Qwen3-Next both point to 3:1
MiniMax's early 7:1 mix had too few global layers

items.d: Too few global layers for long text

119|480.c: MiniMax M2 returned to full attention because its earlier tests never checked multi-hop reasoning.
119|480.e: MiniMax M1 used Lightning Attention, scored well and ran efficiently on benchmarks like MMLU, and shipped. But the evaluations didn't cover multi-hop reasoning, where the model must connect several pieces of information. Performance dropped sharply on agent and coding tasks, so M2 went back to full attention. She calls Lightning Attention essentially a weaker form of linear attention, stuck two years behind. Still, she sees progress as a spiral: retreating after too little validation is normal, and M3 may return to a hybrid.
ex: She says she wouldn't have picked this design if she'd been involved

119|480.c: Linear and sparse attention aren't rivals; the ideal is linear layers plus sparse global layers.
119|480.e: DeepSeek-style sparse attention makes every layer sparse, but it doesn't shrink the KV cache (the model's stored memory of past text) and needs a distilled indexer to pick key tokens. Hybrid linear layers cut that cache sharply, so decoding can serve bigger batches. She thinks linear attention's real rival is sliding-window attention, which only looks at recent text, and a fair comparison must hold memory size equal. The ideal design swaps the hybrid's global layers for sparse attention. The hard part is picking accurately: training from scratch gives sparse learning signals, which is why DeepSeek used distillation.
ex: She says GPT-3 and OpenAI's open-source model both mix global and sliding-window attention
Limited GPUs kept Kimi Linear from comparing against sparse approaches

119|480.c: Hardware is the final judge of an algorithm, and DeepSeek clearly leads at designing for it.
119|480.e: Transformers beat LSTMs, which need less computation in theory, because their main work is large matrix multiplication, exactly what GPUs do best. New GPUs lean even harder toward matrix math; by FlashAttention-4, even the exponentials inside softmax became a bottleneck. Her rule: an algorithm must be mathematically sound and also follow general principles, like respecting the memory hierarchy and favoring matrix multiplication. Don't expect chipmakers to bend to you. She judges DeepSeek clearly better at hardware fit. Kimi Linear still "makes do" with Triton kernels, and once open-source inference engines add support, a virtuous cycle should follow.
ex: DeepSeek's sparse-attention indexer computes in FP8 and skips softmax
Her one tip for young researchers: intern at a lab with compute

marks.d: FP8 matrix math, co-designed with hardware

120|625.c: Data is the gold mine of physical AI, and only carmakers control the whole data pipeline.
120|625.e: At Facebook he worked on satellite image analysis; after the Haiti earthquake, his team delivered before-and-after maps of population and buildings in under two days. Driver-monitoring footage of drowsy truck drivers pulled him toward self-driving, and he chose Cruise because the underdog story appealed to him. Cruise taught him three things: radical simplicity, large-scale infrastructure, and a continuous-learning machine that improves through data. He believes physical AI hinges on data, fast iteration and a closed feedback loop, and only carmakers can offer a data pipeline they fully control.
ex: The project once used more than 16% of Facebook's computing resources
In January 2024, about an hour's talk with He Xiaopeng convinced him to join

terms.d: Train in the cloud, pull data back

result.d: His core reason for joining XPeng

120|625.c: Language is an inefficient middle layer; removing it lets the model go straight from vision to action.
120|625.e: Building on an open-source large language model is the easy route, but it creates ever-deeper dependence: the capability isn't yours and has a ceiling. That's the "poison" he means. He gives three technical reasons. Language labels must be generated in the middle and checked by people, which hurts data efficiency. The physical world's inputs and outputs are continuous, so converting them into discrete words and back is a wasted step. And producing hundreds of tokens for a few control values makes deployment costly. The turning point came when adding more data hit a bottleneck.
ex: Hundreds of extra tokens just to output a few control signals
He cites DeepSeek-OCR: images needn't be mapped into text to be understood

items: Relies on an outside language model

d.verdict: Language in the middle hurts data and deployment efficiency

120|625.c: Progress means constantly removing things, and the hardest to remove are hand-written rules and extra losses.
120|625.e: Last year XPeng removed lidar and the hand-coded planning and control rules; in the first half of this year it removed language. Now the model directly outputs control signals on real cars, and even rules for scenarios like entering ETC toll lanes are gone. The biggest resistance, he says, comes from cutting rules and losses: when the model struggles, the team's instinct is to add a special loss term or rule. He has to hold the line on simplicity and scaling, and has pounded the table over it. He believes in his advisor's "simple is beautiful" and in "The Bitter Lesson," and doesn't think this is the end state.
ex: Testers applauded the moment the model outperformed the rules
He thinks Li Auto removed its rules only after "a big fire"

items.d: Even ETC lane rules are gone

120|625.c: Train a world model to understand the world, then cut its video-generating part, and you get VLA 2.0.
120|625.e: He sees Li Auto's approach, training language first, then vision, then both together, as just a better starting point that can't fundamentally solve self-driving. XPeng feeds in only paired vision-and-language data and outputs actions directly. Squeezing huge visual input down to a few dozen control values runs into the curse of dimensionality, so the team first trains a world model to learn how the world works. It reasons internally instead of in written chains of thought, and generating video checks whether it truly understands. Cut the costly decoding part and you have VLA 2.0, which XPeng's robots also reuse.
ex: The in-house base model is code-named "Turing," and he says it's not necessarily a language model

items.d: Reasons internally to understand the world
Skip the cost of generating video

120|625.c: Without language, performance held up and scaled fast, generalizing well enough to use one model worldwide.
120|625.e: The team feared that removing language would break traffic lights and turn-waiting zones. Instead there was almost no regression, scaling gains came quickly, and the model confused different inputs far less. In Guangzhou's crowded urban villages, the car waits for an oncoming car to clear a narrow lane, then smoothly adjusts to the other driver's subtle moves. He sees that as real thinking, not just imitation. The biggest surprise was strong performance overseas, so using one model for every global market became next year's KPI. He adds that Tesla's recent talk showed both teams had independently landed on the same path.
ex: Trained on roughly 270,000–300,000 hours of video alone
Real-world data grows 30–40% every quarter

120|625.c: Carmakers can't hand self-driving to suppliers; only strong in-house ability lets them define their products.
120|625.e: Kai Yu, founder of Horizon Robotics, says carmakers won't build their own driving systems. Liu first jokes "check back in five years," then explains. Third parties struggle to get the data they need at scale, while a carmaker can automatically spot data gaps and have its fleet bring that data back the next day. He agrees self-driving will eventually standardize, but one takeover a month and one every 20 km are very different experiences. He groups XPeng's cars, robots, flying cars and chips into two things: chip brains, and devices that act in the physical world. The AI race among carmakers is white-hot, and laggards may not survive.
ex: About 4.5 billion yuan for AI and self-driving in 2025 is "almost all spent"
When he asked for budget, He Xiaopeng replied with one word: "OK"

items: Hard to get data at scale
Missing data back the next day

d.verdict: An order-of-magnitude gap in takeovers changes the whole experience

120|625.c: AI R&D needs a system: a north star set from the top, breakthroughs coming from the bottom.
120|625.e: He criticizes Meta for reorganizing every six months on top of its performance-review cycle, which leaves little time for real work; the internet habit of rapid trial and error doesn't suit AI. Breakthroughs need small, focused teams, ample resources, and invisible engineering such as data, training infrastructure and fault tolerance. Direction needs a top-down north star and realistic timelines. In his first three weeks he subtracted: merging duplicate work, pausing nonessential projects, flattening the org, and skipping layered reports to look straight at frontline experiment results.
ex: Team leads write code and debug themselves
He often sleeps at 2 or 3 a.m. and wakes at 7 or 8

120|625.c: XPeng will launch driverless L4 in Guangzhou next year with the same architecture, more compute and thinking time.
120|625.e: XPeng keeps the same architecture but adds onboard compute, giving a bigger model more time to reason through hard situations. Running a commercial service comes down to making fewer mistakes, which cuts the number and cost of remote takeovers. He admits nobody knows how far scaling will go or how to guarantee a safety floor; safety alignment work is underway. Long context is also unfriendly for mass production, since the car must react instantly when an e-bike darts out. His first Waymo ride with his kids left him frustrated, but he doesn't see a generational gap, and expects the next tech stack to look completely different.
ex: Waymo does about 250,000 rides a week in San Francisco
His long-term goal: his kids riding to school on their own

121|632.c: Robotics saw two shifts in a decade: reinforcement learning as the cerebellum, large models as the brain.
121|632.e: Trained in computer graphics, he sees robotics as graphics in the real world. Back then, simulated robots could do backflips while real ones still fell over, and that gap was the opportunity. His first Google paper used PPO, a reinforcement learning method, plus sim-to-real transfer to teach a four-legged robot to walk, kicking off RL in robotics. Later, large models brought natural-language commands and common-sense task breakdown, acting as the brain, while RL handles walking and balance, the cerebellum's job. He thinks robot foundation models aren't yet a separate discipline; the mainstream still fine-tunes multimodal large models.
ex: Boston Dynamics relies on model predictive control; Unitree uses RL plus sim-to-real
A large model can break "make a cup of coffee" into steps

items.d: Understanding and reasoning; like the brain

121|632.c: Fine manipulation isn't usable yet; robotics' GPT moment is 2–3 years off, real deployment 5–10 more.
121|632.e: Simple pick-and-place succeeds over 90% of the time, but fine tasks like zipping a zipper manage only 30–40%, which is useless in practice. Progress has sped up over the past 18 months for three reasons: vision-language models learned to "think," company backing brought resources, and competition has even Silicon Valley working 9-to-9, six days a week. Still, he keeps pouring cold water: demo videos are often the best of ten tries, investors overestimate easily, and humanoids that can do real work barely exist. He expects deployment in factories, logistics and supermarkets within five years, and in homes within ten.
ex: Simple pick-and-place: over 90%; zipping a zipper: about 30–40%
On unfamiliar tasks at the CoRL robotics conference, it completed 10 of 25

121|632.c: Data is robotics' biggest bottleneck, and today's data hasn't even saturated the models.
121|632.e: Language data is nearly free, but robot data is scarce, and the real world is unstructured: anything can happen. He describes sources as a data pyramid: the closer to the top, the better the data matches the robot and the higher its quality, but the less of it there is. He thinks current data hasn't even saturated model capacity, so robotics hasn't hit its next bottleneck. Pretraining a robot model from scratch would take tens of thousands of GPUs, months of time, and more data than exists, so everyone fine-tunes large models. Gemini's vision encoder has seen vast internet data, so visual generalization comes free.
ex: The host guessed startups lacking big models push standalone robot models; he thought that likely

items.d: A gap from the real world
Easy to collect, but different bodies

121|632.c: Gemini Robotics 1.5 makes robots think before acting; splitting fast and slow models is a stopgap.
121|632.e: When the model outputs its reasoning, the robot first works out "this one is red, so it goes in the red pile" and then moves. That makes its behavior explainable, which helps safety and trust, and he says switching between text and action caused no confusion. Each decision allows only about 0.5 seconds of thought, so the system splits into a slow-thinking ER model that can call search, calendar and weather tools, and a fast VLA model that acts. He thinks passing messages between modules in language loses information, so one unified model is better. The blocker is compute: a big model can't yet make 5–10 decisions per second.
ex: Before sorting trash, it checks a map, sees it's in San Francisco, and follows local rules
A common problem after adding reasoning is overfitting: narrow labels produce absurd reasoning

result.d: Should end up as one unified model

121|632.c: Transferring skills between robot bodies was overhyped before; now there's hard evidence, but limits remain.
121|632.e: Earlier claims about cross-embodiment transfer, sharing what one robot body learns with another, were overstated, he says, and the gains from mixing data across robots were hard to measure. This time the evidence is harder. The tabletop two-armed Aloha, after mixing in data from an industrial two-armed robot at a standing workstation, learned to take books from a high shelf, like a driver handling a new car. But that's task-level transfer, not zero-shot use of a new body. The more different the bodies, the harder it gets, and the more data the target robot has, the less outside data helps. So humanoids, whose data is hardest to collect, benefit most.
ex: The experiment used three robot types; he calls the method a "secret sauce"
Single arm to two arms, or gripper to dexterous hand, transfers less easily

cells.d: E.g., robots whose data is hard to collect

121|632.c: Generalization depends on how much data covers, not whether it's real; generative simulation will replace physics simulation.
121|632.e: He largely accepts estimates that teleoperation is very expensive and thinks reaching the end goal on teleoperation alone is unlikely, so the next priority is "data, data, data." Generalization depends on how many situations the data covers, not whether it's real or synthetic. Simulation's meaning is shifting too: it used to mean physics engines, but now physically plausible generated video counts. The test of a world model is predicting the next frame from the previous frame plus an action, which most video models can't do yet. He admits he underestimated video generation; he once thought it wouldn't be usable until 2030.
ex: 500 home scenes went from hand-built models to writing 500 prompts
Genie-style models let you fly a dragon and see different worlds

d.verdict: The choice is mostly faith; he bets on scalable data

121|632.c: Dexterous hands need touch; on form he bets on humanoids, on architecture on end-to-end models.
121|632.e: His view of touch changed three times. At first he assumed it mattered. Then, seeing vision-only teleoperation pull out a credit card, he thought vision could cover 95%. Finally, teleoperating scissors with a dexterous hand himself, he found them uncontrollable without touch. He agrees with Elon Musk that robots can learn from video, but not that vision alone solves everything. On architecture, layered control worked fast early on, but the field is moving to end-to-end models, so dual fast-slow models only suit short-term validation. He bets humanoids become mainstream but not the only form, and that real-world data alone can't solve robotics.
ex: He rejects calling "VLA plus RL" a dumb architecture; it's just the field converging
Big companies can aim at the endgame; startups must ship first and get the flywheel going

root.d: Goal: AGI for the physical world

items.d: Humanoids mainstream, not the only form

121|632.c: Scale is necessary but not sufficient; China has the hardware, Silicon Valley has the patience.
121|632.e: The team grew from about 10 people nine years ago to about 150, showing the work needs big teams and lots of compute, but scale alone isn't enough. Goals come from the top, while paths often emerge from the bottom: the cross-embodiment result was pieced together by three or four small teams. He owns research speed and negotiated fast tracks for data approvals and equipment purchases. China supplies cheap, good robot hardware; Silicon Valley will fund a belief for ten years. He disagrees that China is following a Tesla-style path: Tesla's cars are useful on their own, which gets the data flywheel spinning, and robots haven't crossed that threshold.
ex: Buying a new robot can take more than 30 working days
Keeping people isn't about money but mission, and whether they get the driver's seat

122|324.c: There'll be no AI bubble for at least three years; today's pullback is building energy for next year.
122|324.e: He reads bubble signals in reverse: a real top comes when nobody questions anything and everyone piles in. Today the whole world is talking about a bubble, and some of the gloom is stirred up on purpose by stock market players. More important, compute and data centers are still in short supply, unlike in 2000, when vast amounts of fiber sat unused. He also rejects the idea that GPUs are written off in two or three years: old chips are still working, and the real bottlenecks are server rooms and power. In his view, today's AI has real revenue growing alongside valuations.
ex: In the 2000 fiber bubble, over 90% of the fiber went unused
GPUs five, six, even seven or eight years old are still running
US AI valuations are about 100x China's; he thinks one side must be wrong

d.verdict: No real bubble within three years

122|324.c: Consumer AI now competes on daily use and time spent; OpenAI is pivoting from weekly use to social.
122|324.e: He notes that Sam Altman barely talked about AGI this year. Instead OpenAI launched Pulse, a browser and group chats, all aimed at turning a weekly-use product into a daily one. Occasional-use products are easy for big companies to attack, while daily habits build defenses that deepen over time. If group chats create real social networks, Meta will face a genuine threat, and that's the condition under which he'd consider betting on OpenAI. China looks similar: Doubao leads in traffic and experience. Rather than bleeding alongside Meituan in instant retail, he thinks Alibaba should shift resources to consumer AI.
ex: He describes Pulse as an AI version of Toutiao, the news-feed app
He expects only two or three daily-use products like ChatGPT to survive

items.d: Q&A; easy for big firms to attack
Pulse and the browser raise frequency
Group chats build ties, aimed at Meta

122|324.c: The Transformer has basically peaked, but today's technology is already good enough for applications.
122|324.e: Citing Elon Musk's point that pretraining data is running out, he thinks language models have peaked, with a little room left in multimodal models. But stalled technology doesn't stop an app boom: industry-wide token usage grew more than tenfold in a year, a sign that models are capable enough for mass deployment. The costs work too. Simple monetization like ads can recover half, and big companies will discount tokens or even give them away to win strategic position. He warns, though, that 70–80% of token usage is padding with little technical substance.
ex: A startup he backs burns tens of billions of tokens daily with a million daily users

items.d: About 0.2 yuan per daily user in China

122|324.c: DeepSeek is an underrated turning point, and open source will put China's AI ahead in the long run.
122|324.e: Looking back in ten years, he thinks DeepSeek will be a key moment in AI: without it, China's open-source camp wouldn't be so committed, and AI controlled by a few private companies is risky in itself. He expects selling model access through APIs to become infrastructure, like water and electricity, and stop being a good business. The US–China gap is holding at three to six months. Catching up on algorithms and models is far easier than building data centers and power plants, and nuclear power is especially hard to build in the US. So within five to ten years, he believes, China's open-source AI will be far ahead.
ex: He thinks China's push into nuclear and solar power is absolutely right
When closed models slow down, he expects a boom in privately hosted 30B open models

items.d: Data centers and energy become bottlenecks
Open source far ahead in 5–10 years

122|324.c: A consensus that can't monetize is a bubble; model makers face worse odds than China's earlier AI stars.
122|324.e: Fund investors complain that venture firms crowd together: a dozen-plus funds pile into one deal, each owns a sliver, and rounds get inflated into "Series A-plus-plus-plus." In the internet era, every consensus eventually became a business, from the attention economy to bike sharing and power-bank rentals. Some of today's consensus bets are far from making money. With big companies' tokens nearly free and models bundled into cloud services, he can't say what independent model companies will compete on, and whether they go public doesn't really matter. He was five years early on electric cars and lost plenty, so on humanoid robots he'll only say time will tell.

cells.d: Bike sharing and others paid off
He was five years early on EVs
Model companies' path to profit is unclear

122|324.c: Startups should sit 15 degrees off consensus, three streets from big tech, and avoid building tools.
122|324.e: He deliberately avoids crowded bets, skipping foundation models and humanoid robots as too expensive and too hard to understand. His dozen-plus deals this year were mostly AI applications and robots that do real work. In this round, he says, big tech and second- and third-tier players are all in, so they're far less likely to keep making mistakes. Big-company blunders won't leave openings the way they did for Douyin and Kuaishou. Tool needs like flashlights and calendars are real but indefensible. So build what big companies won't: industry-specific tuning, on-premise deployment, your own sales team. And grow quietly for three years.
ex: Underwater hull-cleaning robots: murky, corrosive seawater makes it hard to enter
AI companion toys already have clear leaders after less than six months
There's almost no $100 billion opportunity left, but $10 billion ones remain

items.d: Easy for operating systems or models to copy
On-premise, own sales, far from big tech

123|637.c: Building apps on foundations you don't understand means the next model keeps wiping you out.
123|637.e: Before ChatGPT, three of his ideas in a row sat right on OpenAI's path: a writing assistant built on GPT-3, automatic spreadsheet charts built on Codex, and a workflow middle layer built on LangChain. Each time, the next official capability simply absorbed it. He concluded he'd been building a house on a foundation he didn't understand, so he joined Moonshot AI. After about a year there, he had worked out where model capability comes from, where it's heading, and how applications can keep their distance from general models. Only then did he start his own company.
ex: ChatGPT absorbed writing help; GPT-4's coding ability absorbed spreadsheet charts
Xingyu Zhou spent three hours on formulas in Wudaokou explaining "compression is intelligence"

123|637.c: Data sets the limits of intelligence, compute sets how fast you reach them, and algorithms bring emergence.
123|637.e: He uses a big circle and a small one. Data draws the boundary of what intelligence can reach, compute decides how fast you approach it, and algorithms are a moving small circle whose part outside the boundary is emergence, abilities nobody planned for. So data is the more fundamental ingredient, and the industry joke "as much human labor, as much intelligence" still holds. Open-domain data carries industry understanding, so defining and getting it is product work in itself. In closed domains like math and code, where rules can check answers, reinforcement learning can trade compute for data.
ex: Trained only on Chinese-to-English translation and Chinese summaries, a model learned English summaries

terms.d: Sets how fast you reach it
What crosses the boundary is emergence

123|637.c: An app company's opening lies in data its own product creates, not public or industry data.
123|637.e: He splits data into three kinds. Public data is available to everyone, so the race is who cleans and trains fastest. That favors foundation-model companies, and Chinese and US base models are now level on it. Domain data belongs to whoever has it, favoring big companies with real-world usage and industries that are already well digitized. Neither stage is an opening for app startups. An app company should design, from day one, data that didn't exist before its product, and make sure that data can train its own system. ChatGPT's conversation data is the precedent: the defensibility is in the data, not the interface.

items.d: Everyone has it; race to clean and train
Only some have it; favors incumbents
Didn't exist before the product; the app opening

123|637.c: A data flywheel needs filtering; feeding back unfiltered user data just makes the model mediocre.
123|637.e: He doesn't fully buy the "data flywheel" idea. Train on user data without filtering and the model drifts toward the average user, so useful data has to be better than the model already is. That's why early on ONE2X didn't learn from all user behavior; instead, video professionals labeled data, so production know-how stays in the system. Once that know-how is absorbed, users feel the product got smarter even if the interface didn't change. His north-star metric is "system intelligence": higher quality from the same input, or the same quality with fewer tokens.
ex: He notes perhaps under 0.1% of Tesla FSD data is still usable for training
Judging video means telling a 60 from a 70, like Midjourney's in-house artists do

items.d: Useful only if beyond current ability

123|637.c: First design a language for video, then derive the architecture, agents and interface from it.
123|637.e: Most teams start from a business problem and add features. ONE2X first defined how videos are structured and made, creating a domain-specific language, somewhere between natural language and code, that breaks a video into objects, attributes, values and grammar. Only then did it work out data storage, agents, workflows and the front end. The software interface is treated as an environment where people and AI agents both act, and shot order and editing steps are recorded in structured form. What matters isn't whether logs exist but whether the records can be learned from to improve the next output.

items.d: People and agents act together there
Just ways to produce useful context
Structured records that can be learned

123|637.c: Video is where AI-era content starts, so build production tools first, not a content platform.
123|637.e: He gives three reasons. Commercially, video has high unit value: besides CapCut, two or three dozen US video-processing software companies earn tens of millions of dollars a year, an "ant tools market" of small, profitable tools that's good for starting out. Technically, video breaks down into a limited set of basic skills, so like Go it can be made a closed domain. As for trends, the internet moved from text to video because production got harder; once AI levels that barrier, richer formats will win a bigger share. Generation is production, and tools sit closest to shifts in model ability, while content companies can be rewritten by the next model leap.
ex: A creator borrowed friends' accounts to buy maximum credits; he saw that as a payment signal
Using an early version, his own WeChat video channel topped two million views in a month-plus

items.d: Small tools that each make money
A closed domain of limited basic skills
Richer formats win once barriers fall

123|637.c: Multimodal AI is at its GPT-2 moment, so now isn't the time to build a super app.
123|637.e: He sees Sora 2 and Veo 3 as the first to fold single tasks like audio-video sync and shot planning into one model. That's the GPT-2 stage of language models, not a ChatGPT moment. To make a new video based on an existing one, you still use Gemini to break it down shot by shot into a text script first; nothing is end-to-end. An iPhone moment needs two things: multimodal System 1, the fast intuitive layer, must stabilize, and inference speed and cost must improve by several orders of magnitude. Until then, it's better to build production tools that keep adapting to new models while building up data and System 2, the slower reasoning layer.

marks.d: GPT-2 moment; single tasks just unified

123|637.c: App companies just haven't trained their own models yet, and being a "wrapper" is no shame.
123|637.e: Every model company is building products; app companies just haven't trained their own models yet. A general model has limited parameters, so its abilities crowd each other out, and an industry-focused team will eventually hit the base model's limits, left to tweak prompts or give up. At enough scale, owning a model also lets a company control costs, as Cursor shows. He sees System 2 as a wrapper built around System 1 anyway, thin or thick: with the same base model, results depend on the context supplied from outside. For now he treats Chinese model makers as his model department, trading scenario evaluations and seed data for training.
ex: Free-running ReAct loops burn tokens; fixed, deterministic steps generate fewer new ones
He likens industry systems with their own data to "a moon in every river"

items: At the limit, only prompt tweaks
Train on your own scenario data

d.verdict: At enough scale, app companies end up with their own models

123|637.c: Generative systems will squeeze out platform middlemen, shifting power from distributors to consumers.
123|637.e: In the software era, which he likens to a state supply store, power sat with producers. The internet handed power to distribution platforms through search, recommendations and e-commerce: platforms produce no information or goods, yet they control who gets seen. Generative systems can create content on the spot to fit a user's profile, surroundings and even current state, folding matching into production itself. Demand flows straight into production with no inventory needed, so power moves toward consumers. He admits this is logical extrapolation, and the endgame is a long way off.
ex: Recommendation algorithms forced tricks like the "golden first three seconds" and delaying the payoff

items.d: Software era, like a supply store
Search, feeds and e-commerce control exposure
Content made on the spot for each person

123|637.c: Creators' edge shifts to taste and recipes, and their currency moves from attention to trust.
123|637.e: Once generation becomes a public utility, the difference lies in how you use it. A recipe is a production method that can be copied and passed on, but the same recipe turns out differently in different hands. He sees two kinds of creators: "artists" who keep adding something above the system's baseline, and "prosumers" who create for their own consumption. When steady-quality content is no longer scarce, scarcity shifts to long-term trust in authors, IP and channels. Host Xiaojun Zhang asks whether original creators become unnecessary once machines learn their recipes; he concedes that disruption will be long and hard to avoid.
ex: He sees Substack and WeChat accounts feeding paid Zhishi Xingqiu groups as early trust economies
He hopes wedding videos and love-letter videos become as everyday as sending a message

root.d: Once generation is a public utility

items.d: Add value above the system baseline
Scarcity moves from attention to trust

124|312.c: AI in 2025 mostly went as expected; the surprises were China's open-source models and a funding rebound.
124|312.e: At the start of the year he expected the chain of technical progress, real products, then revenue to hold up, and it largely did. Reasoning, coding, and computer use stacked together to produce products that do work on their own, like Claude Code, Codex, and Manus, making 2025 the year of the agent. The real surprise was China: a stock market rebound reopened exits for investors, DeepSeek arrived, and its robotics and optical-module supply chains became globally competitive. He admits his call last year on humanoid robots' manipulation skills was wrong.
ex: GPQA scores rose from the 20s to the 80s and 90s, beating human PhDs
SWE-bench went from under 5 to nearly 80
By year end several general models reached IMO gold-medal level

result.d: Products that work on their own start earning

124|312.c: Models hold no lasting secrets, and Chinese open source can shrink the gap to 6-12 months.
124|312.e: Silicon Valley has no noncompete agreements, so talent and information move fast, and labs have similar data and compute. That's why rankings keep shifting and huge spending hasn't built an uncatchable lead. Chinese open source also broke three stories: that you need 100,000 GPUs for a good model, that all the talent is in Silicon Valley, and that China just distills others' models. Tight resources forced efficiency inventions like MLA, and DSA and Kimi's optimizer work are original too. His calibration: fully overtaking is hard in the short term, but a 6-to-12-month gap is realistic.
ex: Months after each top US model, a Chinese open model follows at 1/5-1/10 the cost
Manus first ran entirely on Claude 3.7, then quickly switched to cheaper models

124|312.c: An AI app is a factory that processes tokens, and deeper processing means stronger defenses.
124|312.e: He sees an app as a factory that buys tokens, the units models charge by, and turns them into results. In coding apps the model outputs code and users mostly receive code, so there's little processing and a thin defense. That's why Cursor competes with Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity all at once. First-generation apps were just an interface over the model, like plain sashimi. Advanced apps add live context, industry data, user preferences, and memory, plus a tools-and-environment layer, turning it into a full imperial banquet. He admits such calls could be proven wrong anytime.
ex: Manus beat several frontier models on the Remote Labor Index
ChatGPT's retention has been credited to its memory feature

items.d: Live info, industry data, preferences, memory
Can act and run tasks in parallel

124|312.c: Agents are a decade-long story, and vertical opportunities lie in data models have never seen.
124|312.e: He agrees with Andrej Karpathy's "decade of agents": self-driving took over ten years to go from demos to robotaxis, and agents will be similar. For now they're stuck in the prosumer market, because big companies' data, privacy, and permission barriers haven't opened. Coding is an open bet for every model lab, so startups' chance lies in data and workflows models haven't seen. He also sees a contrarian opening for general agents: when everyone thinks general-purpose is hopeless, infrastructure advantages can make the whole greater than its parts.
ex: White-collar workers use under 100 apps, so computer-use AI could improve fast
Manus's wide research can run over 100 agent tasks in parallel

items: Methods aren't in the training data

d.verdict: Vertical defenses come from data models lack

124|312.c: 2026 is when returns get counted, and subscriptions, ads, and usage pricing all have ceilings.
124|312.e: Capital needs faster payback: about half of data-center spending goes to chips that are obsolete in four to six years, model gains are slowing, and open source is cutting prices. Subscriptions already reach many payers, and prices fall even as models improve, much as Netflix struggled to raise prices for years. Ads and e-commerce mostly redistribute existing spending, and new ad formats take years to figure out. Replacing programmers doesn't mean earning their salaries: usage rises tenfold while unit prices drop tenfold. Enterprises adopt slowly. He thinks the era of buying growth with negative gross margins is over.
ex: OpenAI's annualized revenue is near $18 billion, with almost 600 million daily users
Office Copilot's adoption and revenue have kept missing expectations
He thinks app companies should target SaaS-like gross margins above 50%

items.d: Already widespread, hard to raise prices
Splitting an existing pie, slow to grow

124|312.c: The next returns will come from research and memory, and real memory must live in the weights.
124|312.e: He borrows Ilya Sutskever's framing: AI history alternates between scaling and research. The current approach shows diminishing returns, so finding the next one that can scale matters again. Researcher-led labs like Thinking Machines and SSI started at billion-dollar valuations precisely on that bet. Most benchmarks are maxed out, so the ability to design good tests is itself an edge. As for memory, today's version is mostly retrieval, like flipping through a notebook. Real memory should be online learning in the weights, which is also a prerequisite for proactive agents.
ex: He cites Demis Hassabis: AGI needs one or two more research breakthroughs
He thinks 2026's app race hinges on capturing more user context

124|312.c: The biggest revolution brings the biggest bubble; it hasn't peaked, but 2026 may bring a pullback.
124|312.e: Every technological revolution comes with a bubble, and AI may be the biggest revolution yet. But the sign of a top is bad companies and frauds also getting rich valuations, and we're not there. The risk is a mismatch of time horizons: public markets price mainly on long-term expectations, so if sentiment on AGI's payoff sours, strong near-term results won't hold prices up. He expects a significant US stock pullback in 2026, possibly in the second half, triggered by a softening job market and OpenAI growth falling short. He calls this strong opinions, weakly held.
ex: He borrows the book Boom to separate good bubbles from bad
He holds almost no public stocks but won't short, on principle
To GSR's Xiaohu Zhu: token usage will explode, but unit prices are falling too

items.d: Possibly in the second half of 2026

124|312.c: US and Chinese valuations are far apart, so he runs a barbell: the safest bets plus Chinese upside.
124|312.e: He runs the math. Thinking Machines is valued at $50 billion with almost no product, possibly more than all Chinese AI startups combined. Fast-growing US apps often get 30 to 100 times ARR, Chinese ones about 10 times. So he favors a barbell: on one end the safest assets like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, on the other cheap, high-upside Chinese companies, where an AI-era ByteDance would return 100x. He expects the gap to narrow over time. ZhenFund doesn't time the market and keeps backing the best people in the first round.
ex: ZhenFund made about twenty investments in 2025
Its best AI companies were mostly backed in 2022-23, like Manus and Kimi

items.d: Thinking Machines, second round, almost no product

124|312.c: Back obsessed founders who lead the way, and beware deals priced like favorites with long-shot odds.
124|312.e: Missing out on Xingxing Wang made him revise his framework and add obsession to his criteria. In a tech revolution, the big money usually goes to first-wave leaders who define a new form, while followers struggle; humanoid robotics already has about 150 companies. Successful teams are often roommates or classmates, while hastily assembled teams crack. He's wary of the gray horse: priced like a favorite, with the odds of a dark horse. He also admits that reverse-engineering early traits from today's winners risks drawing the wrong lesson.
ex: He once urged Manus to make its three-panel layout more chatbot-like, folding the workspace by default
He thinks Moonshot AI's Zhilin Yang was undervalued: a favorite at a dark-horse price

cells.d: Priced like a favorite, odds of an underdog

124|312.c: Once intelligence is cheap, agency, taste, and going out of distribution become the scarcest things.
124|312.e: Intelligence used to be a luxury and is now cheap, so agency, deciding what to do, and taste, choosing among options, matter most. Work should shift from linear to parallel: treat yourself as AI's boss, write throwaway code for one-off problems, and adopt the most advanced tools early. The deepest layer is going out of distribution. Models excel at things like their training data, and Picasso and Mozart became masters precisely because they produced very different data. For 2026 he's betting on agents, video and images, memory, and voice.
ex: For founders: anticipate the state of the art 6-12 months out; go global on day one
He notes Manus was the team's third attempt, so staying in the game matters

125|640.c: Model companies are a snowball of losses, and cash flow only comes once the burn stops.
125|640.e: Under scaling laws, training costs rise about tenfold a year. Call the last model's cost 1: it brings in about 2 in revenue, but the next model needs 10, so the net is minus 8, and the burn grows every year. There are only two ways to turn positive: revenue multiples jump sharply, or labs stop training models ten times bigger. So slower scaling is actually good news for investors, because the income statement suddenly looks great. When host Xiaojun Zhang objected that content companies can't stop investing, she conceded training needn't stop, as long as its cost stops multiplying.
ex: Netflix went from about -$3B cash flow in 2019 to +$2B when filming paused in 2020
She thinks Anthropic isn't spending less; it assumes a higher return on investment

items.d: Costs rise about tenfold a year
The only two ways to turn positive

125|640.c: OpenAI is a product company, and the market vastly underestimates its enterprise business.
125|640.e: She bet on OpenAI early because it's a product company first, not just a model company. ChatGPT has no social network effects. Its stickiness comes from being first and from the experience, and people want one assistant that remembers everything about them, so the market should concentrate like search. One non-consensus view is enterprise: consumer and business revenue are close to half and half, and companies hook it into email and internal systems easily. Another is that ads are a natural fit. Cloud is like early AWS, renting out spare compute.
ex: ChatGPT, including enterprise plans, is over 70% of revenue
Valuation rose from $30B to $500B, but per share only about 6x, after heavy dilution

root.d: A product company, not just a model lab

items.d: Underrated; plugs into office systems easily
Free users see ads; paid stays neutral
Rent out spare compute, like AWS

125|640.c: Google is perfectly positioned, but the threat OpenAI poses to it is just as real.
125|640.e: Google has breadth in search, YouTube, and office apps, plus depth in cloud and its own TPU chips. It can use its cost edge in price wars and bundle subscriptions to win users, and will likely take the low-to-mid $20 tier. But she doesn't pick sides. Search ads haven't dropped because people use ChatGPT like an encyclopedia, asking things Google never monetized anyway. Yet the questions behind the biggest advertisers, like insurers and law firms, are exactly the ones best suited to AI. Once OpenAI sells ads, it must grab share from Google and Meta's limited ad pool.
ex: She cites Gemini at about 650 million monthly users, ChatGPT over 1 billion
Models skim dozens of pages a second, weakening search's edge from top results

items: Ads mean fighting for the existing pool

d.verdict: Both threats are real; the market shouldn't pick one side

125|640.c: Robinhood turned a bad, cyclical hand into alpha over both bitcoin and the Nasdaq.
125|640.e: Brokerage is a deeply cyclical business: it booms in bull markets and stalls in bear markets. Robinhood did four things: expanded into a dozen-plus business lines to smooth the cycle, kept taking share, raised its pricing power, and held operating costs flat since 2022. She stresses being honest about beta versus alpha, returns that ride the market versus returns a company earns itself. Coinbase has almost no alpha over bitcoin, so you might as well buy the coin. Robinhood's users average 34 and are entering their prime wealth-building years, so she sees it as the next Charles Schwab.
ex: Crypto take rates rose from 10 to 60 points within three years
She added repeatedly near a $30 billion market cap early in the year; it nearly tripled
In 2022 it moved to single-GM units, each with its own product, engineering, and finance

terms.d: A dozen-plus lines smooth the cycle
Keep gaining share, raise take rates

125|640.c: Big funds almost can't deliver high multiples, so VCs should stay small and concentrate their bets.
125|640.e: Of the 2,000-plus VC funds she tracks, only about 80 returned more than 5x, and the largest of those was just $500 million. For a $20 billion fund to return 5x net to its LPs at 10% ownership, it would need about $1 trillion in total exits, roughly all US IPO value of the past five or six years. So funds should be small and focused. She believes in putting your eggs in one basket: deep research earns the conviction to go big, which lowers risk. Public markets have unlimited capacity, so in 2023, rather than guess which model company would win, the move was to load up on Nvidia.
ex: Ribbit put in $500 million within 24 hours of Robinhood's crisis and made over 7x
Greenoaks caps partners at five meetings a week

125|640.c: Taking a share of $400 billion in digital revenue won't pay off; AI must tap the labor market.
125|640.e: Her first ledger is the roughly $400 billion US digital revenue pool: online ads, e-commerce commissions, and subscriptions. She doesn't think AI can grow the ad pool, since corporate ad budgets have long held at about 3% of revenue. If OpenAI only grabs existing share, spending this much to build a mini Google makes little sense. The real prize is about $15 trillion in labor costs, with customer service alone around $300 billion. She judges this isn't a bubble today. Whether it becomes one depends on models continuing to improve and AI revenue continuing to grow.
ex: She estimates about $70 billion of visible AI revenue within 12-18 months
Walmart's AI supply-chain forecasting cut stockouts by 30%
She expects 2026 to favor hedge funds: long AI winners, short AI losers

126|641.c: Economic history is the story of how people and attention move, and each shift creates new hubs.
126|641.e: He sees human history as people, information and attention constantly finding new ways to move. Before electricity, information traveled by road, canal and port, so cities grew where those routes met. The telegraph, radio, TV, PCs and phones then stripped away physical distance. Every technological revolution changed these flows, and business boomed wherever they converged. For a long time the city was the biggest social product, and today's best consumer platforms are like cities too. So investors should look for where new technology creates the next hub. He is sure the winning AI model will become the new front door people open first.
ex: Steel let cities grow upward, packing ten million people into limited space
He once guessed glasses would be the next hub, but AI got there first

items.d: Roads, canals and railways built cities
Telegraph, radio and TV erased distance
Models become the new gathering point

126|641.c: Short video isn't a trimmed-down long video. What it really competes with is written text.
126|641.e: He sees writing as a high-barrier knowledge product: people spend years learning abstract symbols, which is why countries run literacy campaigns. Pictures are more intuitive, and long video carries on the tradition of theater and film. He first saw short video as a simplified long video, but now thinks it is a basic way people understand the world. It puts you right at the scene, with almost as much information as being there. So going a year without reading a book is nothing to be ashamed of, as long as you got the same density and amount of information elsewhere and weren't just killing time.
ex: Instead of describing "the moon is big and round tonight," just say "look."
Podcasts can run three or four hours because listening is company you can multitask with

marks.d: Highest barrier; you must learn to read
More intuitive, takes some readers from text
Nearly as rich as being there

126|641.c: How a product gets used is invented jointly by its makers and users, so new habits are unpredictable.
126|641.e: Early on he used Twitter only to log books he'd read. He found it boring and didn't get the 140-character limit. Then users started posting opinions and tagging each other, and the product took shape. On Musical.ly, TikTok's predecessor, he filmed scenery set to music and never guessed dancing would drive growth. So stories that a founder saw it all coming need a survivorship-bias check: the winners' convictions were necessary but predicted nothing. Investors should reconstruct the options on the table at the time. What they can do is judge, like a literary critic, whether a new work could become a classic.
ex: Douyin wins on content itself, Xiaohongshu on single-post quality, Bilibili on its core community's character

126|641.c: The most dangerous mistake is treating your own social circle as the whole market.
126|641.e: In the Web 2.0 era, when users created the content, he built a rule: back the advanced lifestyles of advanced people. Win over knowledge workers in top-tier cities first, then spread to everyone. Douban, Dianping and Xiaohongshu roughly fit. Missing Didi and PDD made him rethink. User-generated content needs creative users, so it skews toward knowledge workers. He didn't understand the offline world or the broadest population well enough, and some basic models spread straight to the masses without passing through early adopters. With AI, he doesn't predict specific forms. He keeps trying lots of products and sharpening his judgment.

items: Then it spreads from top-tier cities

d.verdict: Watching only your own circle misses the biggest market

126|641.c: AI differs from the internet in cost, responsibility, explainability and network effects.
126|641.e: On the internet an extra user costs almost nothing, but every AI call burns compute, so subscription and free-tier math must be redone. When a traditional app underperforms, you can blame the user. Productivity AI delivers the result itself, so the provider owns the outcome, which could upend process-based SaaS. We can explain steam engines and electricity, but AI's emergent abilities are still a black box. Models get a hidden network effect from usage data, but today everyone talks separately to the same model. A visible two-sided network hasn't formed, so social-leaning AI companies have weak defenses.
ex: Prompt guides suggest adding "magic words," so people don't use AI fully rationally
Tools deliver results, entertainment delivers experience; AI will cut steps with no experiential value

items.d: The provider answers for the outcome
Why new abilities emerge is still unclear
Many users, one model; no two-sided network yet

126|641.c: AI turns fleeting information into an asset, and dedicated devices matter because they're always there.
126|641.e: Old-style digitization moved neatly structured data from paper onto computers. Deep digitization handles messy information that used to be useless even when captured. AI can turn this raw material into meaningful content, multiplying the information a person owns by hundreds to tens of thousands of times. Phones can record, but they aren't built for nonstop capture, and users can't be sure they're still recording. A dedicated wearable makes people confident it's always there, and the data and habits it gathers become its defense. The cost is that privacy lines must be redrawn, and he admits law and social norms have no answer yet.
ex: A hundred hours of audio or a month of chest-camera photos used to be unsortable

items.d: Conversations and scenes can't be organized
Laws and habits both must change

126|641.c: AI is early in an app boom. Bubbles are normal; what matters is getting paid and delivering.
126|641.e: He thinks AI is earning money faster than the early internet. SaaS already taught the market to pay subscriptions, products usually earn revenue early, and teams compete directly on revenue per user. Bubbles are like foam on the sea: every cycle has them early, they give early projects funding, and what matters is whether you deliver. AI is no fake concept but a huge technological revolution. He likens 2025 to mobile internet's 2010 and 2026 to its 2011. Agents, AI that acts for you, don't need localizing country by country like apps, so they're naturally global. He calls it the start of a great age of exploration for Chinese founders.
ex: Over half of HongShan's deals are early-stage; being first institutional investor is a key internal metric
He thinks the model-versus-app fight hinges on how much tech offsets non-tech advantages

items.d: HongShan starts systematically scanning large models
Agent apps take off, global from day one
Apps flourish further and hardware catches up

126|641.c: Past a certain size, a company's CEO must become the living symbol of the whole organization.
126|641.e: From 1 to 10, understanding needs and building product matter most. Beyond 10, a leader's job shifts to building the organization, and product instinct no longer explains why some companies grow bigger. He compares it to a general: before modern communications, the general embodied the rules, discipline and morale of an army of a hundred thousand. A big-company CEO plays a similar role. Even if that isn't your nature, you have to play the part. Product talent and commander talent rarely come together. A team can fill gaps, but the bigger the organization, the less you can avoid it.

127|276.c: AI isn't a bubble. It's a war that none of the tech giants can afford to lose.
127|276.e: He thinks the giants are threatened on two fronts, so they have to fight. On the business side, developers now pick a model, GPT, Claude or Gemini, while cloud providers fade into anonymous back-end suppliers, as HP and Dell once did. On the consumer side, AI agents that act for you could bypass today's super apps. Platforms profit when users can't compare prices; once agents make everything transparent, the markup that ride-hailing and travel middlemen take will shrink. So the giants must defend and attack at once. He also faults Sam Altman's answer on how OpenAI will pay for $1.4 trillion in commitments: offering to find the questioner a buyer.

127|276.e: Looking out to 2030, he adds up three revenue streams. Subscriptions: 4 billion monthly users, 10% paying $200 a year, about $80 billion. Ads and shopping: $50–100 billion. The API, selling model access to developers: another $50–100 billion, because models will become the new cloud, the way Amazon built AWS after e-commerce. That totals $200–300 billion, close to Meta or ByteDance today. The unknown part is agents replacing office work: about 1 billion white-collar workers, each agent worth $1,000–10,000, a $1–10 trillion market. 127|276.c: When one lab pulls ahead, the other giants team up, so no model stays on top for long.
127|276.e: Under today's recipe, pre-training on huge amounts of text plus reinforcement learning (improving by trial and reward), know-how and people move fast, so no one pulls far ahead without a new approach. Model companies have little lasting edge, but the money and talent needed to compete are enormous. The stronger Google gets, the more it sparks an anti-Google alliance: OpenAI was founded to challenge Google, and Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon won't let one player dominate. Google's TPU, built in-house top to bottom, is the Apple of AI; Nvidia's open GPU ecosystem is Android. Demand far exceeds supply, so he'd own both and buy whichever dips.

127|276.c: Pre-training is nearly maxed out; next is online learning, models learning from use. Crack it and you're unbeatable.
127|276.e: Responding to Ilya Sutskever's view that scaling has stalled, he agrees that pre-training, learning from huge piles of text, is near its end, but online learning has barely begun. Today's models are frozen after training and can't learn from daily use, so there's no data flywheel. Mobile internet grew ten times bigger than the PC era precisely because usage generated data. Online learning means models that learn while they answer and interact, which needs longer context windows and infrastructure like LoRA, a cheap way to fine-tune. Front-line researchers told him signs of a breakthrough could appear in 2026. OpenAI leads, with SSI and Thinking Machines next.
