127|276.c: Models are still compressors: what they haven't seen, they can't do. Robotics may be a false problem.
127|276.e: After studying data-labeling companies, he found that models fail at tasks missing from their training data. A model knows more than most people, yet has never seen how a print-shop clerk uses Photoshop or how a bank teller handles customers. That long tail must be filled bit by bit with expert data plus reinforcement learning. So he has pushed back his AGI timeline: partial L3/L4 automation of knowledge work, in self-driving terms, is near-certain, but replacing the whole workforce is unclear. His self-described hot take: if models can't generalize on their own, robots and world models will repeat the old slog of collecting data by hand.

ByteDance's Doubao has beaten expectations, and 2026 is a key window for Chinese consumer chatbots. And tasks of a few clicks get slower, while the valuable long tasks stall when the computer sleeps. The team couldn't say why it beat Chrome plus Monica. So the product assumes no use case. The team watches what users collectively do, then optimizes for it. In search, everyone handled popular queries about equally well, and the long tail separated winners. Agents are the same, and long tail doesn't mean rarely used. Unlike fake general products that put several tools under one domain, Manus keeps a single framework where context and memory carry across tasks, so every extra step adds value.

128|313.c: The environment sets an agent's limits; better to run a hundred sandboxes in parallel than force one.

Instead of Docker, they chose lightweight full virtualization based on Firecracker, so it can run Windows software, and they maintain a Linux distribution tailored for agents. 128|313.c: Models are still tuned for chat; agents need compression awareness more than ultra-long context.
128|313.e: Most models are post-trained for chat, which doesn't fit an agent's many-step loops. The longer the task, the more impatient they get, wrapping up with a few quick bullet points. He has reversed his 2023 view that long context matters most. What matters more is compression awareness: knowing information was compressed, not lost, and writing memories to files to fetch later. Bringing contest-style long reasoning into agents hurts instruction-following and causes hallucinated tool calls. Better is interleaved thinking, a short burst of reasoning after each observation. Their approach is to report problems to model makers so fixes become built-in model abilities.

128|313.c: An agent's cost is mostly input; he puts quality first and won't cut tokens to save money.
128|313.e: In chat, a model reads about three times as much as it writes. An agent's context only grows, and each round it rereads the whole history, so the ratio hits 100 to 1 or even 1,000 to 1. His rule is quality first: no squeezing tokens to save money. At the March launch they burned hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, and now they are close to breaking even. The invite codes weren't hype either. Just before launch they learned far less compute would arrive the next day than expected, and model makers warned an open launch would crash. The codes were dropped within a month.

128|313.c: Build pure agents: don't prescribe workflows, and don't give the model human job roles.
128|313.e: In an agentic workflow, people script the steps. In a pure agent, the model's own intelligence decides the process. The ceiling is higher, and it fits the bitter lesson that general methods beat hand-built rules. Rather than piling on guardrails, add one basic ability. Let the model see images, and it will notice broken Chinese font rendering and fix it itself. His job, he says, is to stop the team from adding rules. He also opposes multi-agent setups with designer, programmer and manager roles, which impose human org limits on a more capable model. Users correct agents or edit their output directly, feedback far richer than chat. Next comes proactivity, since writing a prompt is itself a burden. After an interview, say, the agent would read the Notion notes, fill in the hiring system, and just ask for a yes. But he won't build daily push notifications that grab attention.

129|646.c: The main way to scale AI keeps shifting, and the next stop is online reinforcement learning.
129|646.e: He traces how scaling laws evolved. First came more parameters and more data, then reinforcement learning, where models improve by trial and reward, became a new axis to scale. He expects the next paradigm to be online reinforcement learning, where training and inference merge and models learn as they are used. Unified multimodal models plus online learning, in his view, are the first light of AGI. He doesn't worship brute force and cares more about cutting costs and raising efficiency. 129|646.e: Academician Bo Zhang once warned him that startups hit walls at 50, 200 and 500 people. Having lived through it, he thinks what matters is the company's stage. Early on, you must make money so the team believes this can last. Once R&D, product and sales split, coordination becomes the main cost, and handled badly, everyone guards their own patch. Later, middle management appears, information travels slower, compliance and security costs rise, and no single person can see the whole company. Only systems and rules can hold it together.

The opposite is a "wow" product: when the novelty fades, users slide back to their old routine, and you have to keep pulling them back. A one-way door grows day by day even from a small share, so it rewards patience. That's why he treats everything in the exploration phase as an experiment. 130|653.c: AI companionship has three hard flaws, and game design can fix each one.

Games offer fixes. Swap fully user-driven chat for professionally written storylines with active player input, borrow games' proven payment models, and update characters along a life cycle, so a companion's growth becomes content you can keep producing.

Each time, a new medium arrived with a new way to interact. Sora-style apps still serve short video with the same swipe, so they're unlikely to become the next Douyin. ChatGPT created a new medium, conversation generated in real time, so it is surely a platform. Manus-style products run offline and in parallel, so you hand off a task and forget it. Dokie aims for low latency and constant iteration, with people and AI working together. 131|531.c: Large models rebuild AI from the ground up; there's only one brain, so you either build it or don't.
131|531.e: When ChatGPT came out, he thought language models had little to do with his vision and hardware work; he could just call whichever was best. About six months later he changed his mind. The first test was whether this was a foundational technology shift, and only then whether it landed on his turf. The promise of multimodal and physical intelligence showed it was no local upgrade: vision, language and physical AI will all be absorbed into one unified base model. He sees AI 1.0 to 2.0 as continuous in technology, but organizations and business models must be rebuilt, and a mature Megvii couldn't carry a foundation-model startup.
ex: StepFun is named after the step function: steady accumulation leading to a sudden leap

items.d: Six months later: a foundational shift
Absorbs vision, language and physical AI

131|531.c: By elimination: not just Chinese enterprise clients and not pure consumer software, which leaves AI devices.
131|531.e: A foundation model needs at least about 3 billion yuan a year for three to five years. Selling only to Chinese enterprises pays slowly and caps out low, so it can't cover that bill, though overseas might, he adds. Pure consumer software runs into the giants' existing users, use cases and data flywheels. Coding is a great training ground for reinforcement learning, but giants and open source have pushed prices so low it isn't a revenue pool for a newcomer. Chatbots aren't a natural way to interact, and ChatGPT is more like a brilliant demo. What's left is AI devices combining hardware and software.
ex: Gemini's daily users are growing fast, which he thinks shows ChatGPT's lead isn't locked in
Big Chinese companies mostly build in-house, and government deals are demanding, so little gets bought

items.d: Models need 3 billion yuan a year, minimum
Giants own users and data flywheels
Consumer products pairing hardware and software

131|531.c: AI hardware gives agents a body: cars first, wearables next, robots further out.
131|531.e: He rewrites the last generation's formula of hardware, software and internet services as hardware, software and models. Hardware isn't winner-take-all like software: phones and cars have room for many makers. Voice and multimodal AI reduce dependence on screens and could spawn new categories selling tens of millions of units. Following the order of biological evolution, intelligence can't skip steps. First build the brain, then build up abilities through cars, handhelds and wearables, and finally move to embodied platforms like robots. The more devices sell, the more real-world data flows back.
ex: He cites the PLAUD recorder, whose hardware and software are both built around one AI service
Driver assistance and cabins come first; Tesla has already put Grok in its cars

root.d: StepFun builds models, Qianli builds cars

items.d: First entry: driver assistance and cabin
A long-term goal about 5–7 years out

131|531.c: Models advance through a push from research and a pull from real uses; be world-class, not first everywhere.
131|531.e: He notices that each GPT generation didn't leap on one skill. Many areas improved a little, and overall intelligence shifted up. The push comes from new research paradigms, like the move from imitation learning to reinforcement learning, and will stay the main driver for three years. The pull comes from use cases, which set model size, efficiency and cost; on devices, bigger isn't always better. He sees three main threads toward AGI: learning paradigms, memory systems, and moving from language to multimodal and the physical world. They might be largely solved in about five years, though he calls that a conditional judgment.
ex: He cites Gemini Flash: applications must balance performance, cost and speed
Data staff now report to the algorithms lead; he believes data decides 70–80% of a model

items: Still the main driver for three years

d.verdict: Together they set how base models evolve

131|531.c: Qianli is a late mover, and only three or four driver-assistance suppliers will survive.
131|531.e: Megvii habitually started from technology, a hammer looking for nails. Qianli is entering an industry whose boundaries are already clear. Driver assistance now runs on large models, so old technology stacks and historical data matter less, and a late mover needn't recreate everything. But the window to prove results is short, and the contest is about speed of execution and organization. His reasoning: the EV price war pushes pressure upstream, revenue per car is limited, R&D is heavy, and only scale spreads the cost. In the end only three or four suppliers will remain, and Huawei is certainly one.
ex: He expects this round of driver-assistance competition to last about three more years
Cabins are personal, so carmakers build them; safety-critical driving goes to specialist suppliers

items.d: Pressure moves up the supply chain

131|531.c: Megvii should have dropped security cameras; strike only where desire, capability and opportunity overlap.
131|531.e: He admits that when young he wanted to play every hand, spreading across many lines so each got only a sliver of resources. Security looked like enterprise sales but really centered on government and state firms, where channels and hardware took most of the value and Megvii held only the AI piece. The root causes: proven niches always seemed too small, he wanted an IPO home run, and there was a technologist's ego. A better path would have been to become the clear number one in finance and phones, then wait for the car window. The IPO was just a lifeline, not a fix.
ex: Third-party phone imaging is a ~1-billion-yuan market; even the leader takes only 500–600 million
He thinks 2016–2017 was ideal for entering cars, and around 2019 would still have worked

terms.d: A direction you truly care about

131|531.c: Smart people aren't rare; people willing to grind in obscurity and collaborate well are.
131|531.e: Megvii's early talent density was extremely high, but he later decided smarts matter less than he thought. Smart people take shortcuts, drift to faster-paying industries when they lack a mission, and avoid the slow, daily grind of building up skill. The opposite of technical conviction is technical opportunism, and the test is whether someone will sit on the bench for years. Delivering value also takes pragmatism and doing your own job well. StepFun screens out people who are capable but have big egos and struggle to collaborate.
ex: Megvii's first 40 or so staff included many math and physics olympiad gold medalists
He prefers PhDs who dig deep into one hard problem for three years, then publish prolifically

131|531.c: Winning needs technology and profit together: within three to five years, a product earning billions of yuan yearly.
131|531.e: On technology, he must keep building a research organization that can produce world-class models. On money, he expects to spend 3 to 5 billion yuan a year; at a floor of 3 billion for five years, the base bill is about 15 billion. On products, within three to five years a core product must earn 3 to 5 billion yuan in profit a year so research can fund itself. He has moved from optimistic to cautiously optimistic. Models, cars, and handhelds and wearables are, to him, the minimum combination: split them and you lose the loop where data and revenue feed each other.
ex: He sums up today's bet in one phrase: build devices
He hopes a world-class Chinese AI company emerges next decade, ideally his, but it needn't be

items.d: Floor of his 3–5 billion yuan estimate
3 billion a year for five years

132|664.c: He picks an industry on one test: AI must be decisive, and the market must be big.
132|664.e: Interning at SenseTime, he realized neural networks could turn hand-written if-else rules into parameters learned from data, so far fewer people would need to write programs. Choosing a direction after his PhD, he worked backward: only industries that can't exist without AI and are big enough are worth it. AI outsourcing rarely becomes a product, ads work fine without AI, and wrapping cloud APIs isn't fundamental enough. So he chose AI for the physical world, starting with self-driving. Mobile internet, he judged, was the previous generation's opportunity, so he didn't chase it.
ex: He figured his PhD needed four or five top papers, and finished in 3.5 years

items.d: Big enough to support a company

132|664.c: Self-driving's architecture barely changed in a decade; the real story is rebuilding it AI-first.
132|664.e: He found that the 2018 self-driving stack, with perception, localization, mapping, and planning and control, was nearly identical to 2008's, only with neural networks inside each module. That's the robotics mindset: interpretable modules that fix corner cases one by one. The AI mindset is data-driven and end to end, one model doing the whole job. It raises overall scores but doesn't guarantee a given case won't get worse. Tesla rewrote perception AI-first early on, then evolved through BEV, end-to-end models, and VLA, vision-language-action models, and became the mainstream.
ex: He notes Waymo's perception stacked dozens of models
At Waymo he turned maps into vectors plus graph networks, creating the widely used VectorNet

items.d: Perception, localization, mapping, planning and control
Neural networks swapped in inside modules
From BEV to end-to-end to VLA

132|664.c: Waymo lacks a founder: mistakes aren't scary, but scattered effort is dangerous.
132|664.e: He sees Waymo's big-company sickness as a symptom, with levels and culture modeled on Google. The root cause is having no founder to drive things from the top. Its engineering is no weaker than Tesla's; the gap is in its attitude toward AI and the speed and force of rebuilding systems. Momenta is the other extreme: results-driven and high-pressure, which he thinks trains engineers better through real combat. He admires founder Xudong Cao's steady early bet on mass production, but says his forceful style can hurt people when pressure runs too high.
ex: After test rides in Los Angeles, he thinks Waymo is close to commercially viable
Leaving Momenta, he gave up options he valued at about $10 million

marks.d: Great conditions, low pressure, no founder

132|664.c: Customer focus isn't doing whatever clients say; it's digging out their real needs from their side.
132|664.e: His biggest lesson from Momenta: don't just do what the customer says; think deeper on their behalf and offer a better solution. The same holds inside the company: upstream serves downstream, support teams serve the business, and platform teams serve delivery. He opposes centering on personal growth or technical leadership. Momenta's mass-production strategy was also worked backward from data: its own fleet was too small, so it put its software on production cars, creating a loop where data and business feed each other.
ex: He joined as Momenta won an IM Motors production deal, rotating across teams as the catfish

items.d: Uncover real needs, offer better solutions

132|664.c: Embodied AI's lasting edge is a real-world data loop, so build the whole robot first.
132|664.e: The long-term edge, he believes, is a data loop in the physical world, and a loop needs a body to run on. In the near to mid term, the product is also a full robot plus intelligence, not algorithms sold alone. Both point the same way: master the hardware and supply chain first. Cars were lucky to have clear customers but unlucky that carmakers sit in between, so data doesn't flow back. Robots have no ready-made body, which is painful, but they can reach every industry. So the company runs on two tracks: an intelligence team and a hardware and supply-chain team.
ex: Early on they took apart others' robots and found suppliers via Taobao image search
Their first product, delivery robots, was dropped: hardware, customers, and market were all immature

items.d: The vehicle for the data loop

132|664.c: Intelligence should define the robot's body; win developers first, then the productivity market.
132|664.e: He rejects the idea that wheels plus two arms is a compromise. The entry point is manipulation, so the arms are what matter. Most settings don't require climbing obstacles, so wheels suffice, and legs only make motion control harder. Commercially he borrows from Crossing the Chasm: sell first to developers in academia and corporate research, then to productivity developers and integrators who customize for real scenarios, and only then to end users. He thinks Unitree followed a similar path.
ex: Around March 2024 they chose wheels plus a torso, built R1, and found real academic demand
He compares it to the Macintosh moving from geeks to offices, and Bambu Lab's 3D printers

132|664.c: Stick with real-world data, and first work out exactly what each hour of it costs.
132|664.e: To solve problems in a given domain, the training data should ideally come from that domain. He thinks the gap from simulation to real robots is still large, much as most self-driving problems were finally solved by road testing. He opposes buying 10,000 data-collection robots up front, and wants unit costs defined clearly first. The data mix is one of model companies' deepest secrets and can only be found by experiment, not by assuming a pyramid in advance. He also denies that betting on real data is a way to sell robots to labs for data collection.
ex: 100,000 hours costs about 25 million yuan, near a person's real-world experience before age 18
Data costs run 1:5 to 1:10 against training; bad data wastes the training money

terms.d: 3-4 hours of work per data hour

result.d: Full cost of one hour of real data

132|664.c: Algorithms are the easiest thing to copy; hardware, sales channels, and data build slowly.
132|664.e: He measures each advantage by its diffusion time: how long others take to learn it. Papers and open source are everywhere, so top teams can catch up on an algorithm in two or three months. Customer channels take at least six months, a hardware supply chain a year to eighteen months, and a data system six months to a year more on top. So algorithms cost a lot but protect little. Big tech's strength is synergy with existing businesses, but embodied AI demand is scattered across countless industries and supply is almost all new. Buying data has a paradox too: without understanding models, you can't define the data you need.
ex: He notes Google DeepMind's robotics team is also short on data

items.d: Top teams catch up in 2-3 months
Six months and up, longer for big clients

132|664.c: Huazhe Xu left over the pace of innovation, and over whether customer value comes first.
132|664.e: He doesn't see it as research culture versus production culture, but as how to balance practical innovation with forward-looking innovation. A technical team that doesn't put customers first easily turns into a big research lab. Arrangements were made internally last August: Hang Zhao took over the foundation-model team, co-founder Huazhe Xu moved to explore a consumer direction for homes, and Galaxea is investing in his new project. He rejects the claim that algorithms don't matter, but stresses that algorithmic innovation depends on infrastructure like hardware and data.
ex: He says the company's values rest on trade-offs and sharing gains, never bending for short-term profit
This round values it at about 10 billion yuan, roughly 30x early 2024's 300 million
The team grew from a dozen-plus to over 200, reorganizing every three to five months

items: Weigh short and long term by return
Algorithms rely on hardware and data

d.verdict: Separate paths are better for everyone

132|664.c: Start with jobs that need little speed and forgive mistakes, and train robots like new employees.
132|664.e: On the supply side he tracks three metrics: speed, where reaching 80-90% of a human through imitation learning is good; precision, centimeters first, then millimeters; and generalization, how much new data a new problem requires. On the demand side he picks scenarios with modest speed needs, cheap mistakes, and global uniformity. First up is warehouse picking among tens of thousands of SKUs. His vision: after a few demonstrations and some self-practice, a robot works reliably and on its own in a specific setting. A VLA model on the robot handles actions, while a VLM handles complex instructions, forming a dual system.
ex: He breaks labor into five actions: carrying, picking, packing, stacking, and operating equipment
He says Galaxea serves over 150 developer customers worldwide

133|674.c: Vision isn't a sidekick to language. Truly understanding what you see is close to solving intelligence itself.
133|674.e: He gives three reasons. First, losing sight means losing independence. Second, vision takes up a large share of the brain, and the eyes are the only part of the brain exposed to the outside world. Third, vision appeared about 530 million years ago and set off an arms race between hunters and hunted, which may have helped trigger the Cambrian explosion. So from the start, vision was tied to prediction and action. That is why he stuck with vision even when circumstances kept pushing him away from it.
ex: With no vision slot in his undergrad lab, he interned in Shuicheng Yan's lab at NUS
He named a model series "Cambrian" to remind himself vision is where intelligence began

items.d: Share of the brain in main visual areas, as he cites
Share of the brain activated when looking at images

133|674.c: Learning good representations is the root of everything, shaped by architecture, data and the training objective.
133|674.e: He sees recognition, segmentation (outlining each object in an image), video understanding and embodied reinforcement learning (robots learning by trial and error) as branches. The root is representation learning: mapping raw data into a space where later tasks become easier. In this picture, the architecture is the hardware, data is the fuel, and the objective function, the score the model is trained to chase, decides what the model learns to do. Picking such a "timeless problem" keeps him from being pulled off course by short-lived trends.
ex: Counterexample: neural architecture search, a hot trend that sent the field astray for about two years
ResNeXt, built with Kaiming He, placed second at ImageNet; its scaling resembles mixture-of-experts

result.d: The root of every later task

133|674.c: Good ideas aren't dreamed up in an armchair. You find them by experimenting and following the signals.
133|674.e: Just sitting and thinking, he says, leaves three possibilities: you're smarter than everyone, hundreds of people are thinking the same thing, or the idea was disproven long ago. So his students first spend a month or two reading papers, working through math, reproducing baselines and editing code, hunting for signals. Predict the result before each experiment. The gap between prediction and reality is the new "gradient," a hint about where to go. Negative results carry information too. The most dangerous result is one that doesn't budge. The most boring research ends exactly where it started.
ex: His rhythm: explore for 1–2 months, scale up for 2–3, write for 1–2
At FAIR, Kaiming He built TPU infrastructure from scratch; only strong baselines make gains credible

items.d: No need to be perfect at first
Get it running with a strong baseline

133|674.c: Research is an infinite game: rejections and awards are partly luck, and one big success is enough.
133|674.e: He thinks one acceptance or one award can't define a piece of work. What counts is the long run. Researchers are more like inventors, whose impact is nonlinear: one or two landmark papers can change everything. Repeated rejection has made him immune to short-term verdicts. He borrows Nassim Taleb's idea of "antifragility": if a shock brings more long-term gain than loss, the system grows stronger. He even says he hasn't yet written a paper that truly rewrote deep learning.
ex: NeurIPS rejected DSN over a missing square; at AISTATS it won test-of-time about ten years on
CVPR rejected DiT as not novel; resubmitted almost unchanged, it got in and became others' baseline

items.d: Others build on top of it

133|674.c: Research is for understanding and passing on knowledge, not for chasing impact or personal fame.
133|674.e: He sees a paper as an interface for talking to readers: after reading, they should be able to go and do something with it, so even the layout should serve understanding. He bristles at the word "impact" and prefers to talk about adding to the total intelligence on Earth. He views academia as a web where people shape each other. Like-minded people naturally find one another, rather than maneuvering into an inner circle. He also objects to packaging team work as the leader's fame, and wants the press to spotlight the students who did the work.
ex: He most admires Fei-Fei Li's knack for defining problems: ImageNet made image classification a clear problem
Kaiming He's gift, the Diamond Sutra, reminds him not to be swayed by metrics and fame

root.d: Not for papers or impact as such

items.d: No star cult around the leader

133|674.c: LLMs will fade, not die: language is a crutch, not the foundation for AI that understands the world.
133|674.e: Language, he argues, is what humans have filtered and abstracted over a long time. It looks free, but people have already labeled it. It's efficient, yet it throws away a lot of structure: "the cup broke" gives the result, not how it shattered. So language becomes a shortcut around visual learning: benchmark scores rise while the system never learns how the world works. He borrows Yann LeCun's crutch metaphor: language lets a system walk, but if the vision leg never develops, it can't run. He expects LLMs to settle into valuable tools and interfaces.
ex: Compress 538 million years into a day: language and symbolic reasoning take the last 8–10 seconds
In 2024 Ilya Sutskever invited him again, calling perception mostly solved; he declined, seeing different paths

items.d: The last 8–10 seconds of evolution's day
Hunting and escaping: the basis of survival

133|674.c: A world model should predict the consequences of actions, not generate pretty pictures.
133|674.e: His minimal definition: given the current state and an action, learn a function that predicts the next state, and use it to plan and decide. The idea isn't new. It goes back to Kenneth Craik in 1943, model predictive control, and Richard Sutton's Dyna. The state needn't copy the whole world, only the minimum needed to predict and decide, and choosing that is itself a representation-learning problem. Such a model can foresee consequences as it runs, which is more reliable than using post-training to teach a model what it mustn't say.
ex: A robot cutting vegetables should foresee the knife turning toward a person, not memorize safety text
He files Sora and Genie under world simulators; Fei-Fei Li's World Labs focuses on explicit 3D

marks.d: World simulators focused on consistent video
Explicit 3D spaces, good for design and CAD
A predictive brain: representation, planning, decisions

133|674.c: The next phase shifts from downloading the internet to downloading humans, plus sensor data.
133|674.e: Large models have nearly compressed all the text on the internet, he says, while a toddler takes in far more continuous visual information than that. The first step may still start from video platforms, but copyright and terms of service will limit it. More valuable is sensor data from factories, hospitals, farms and jet engines. Such industry-specific world models are best built on top of general pre-training. The products will be devices people wear all day and general-purpose robots. Both are held back by the same thing: a "brain" that understands state over long stretches of time.
ex: He guesses a model's entire training data may equal roughly 30 minutes of YouTube uploads
A jet engine has about 1,000 sensors that can expose design flaws and rare failures
Glasses with just a camera and an LLM are, to him, merely ChatGPT with a camera

133|674.c: Escape the race set by LLM consensus and leaderboards by building a "reverse OpenAI."
133|674.e: He thinks Silicon Valley is stuck on LLMs, and big companies' leaderboards and product cycles squeeze out research. After ChatGPT, even Meta's FAIR lab got bogged down in planning meetings that dragged on for weeks. Staying in academia, he feared too few resources and the "mediocre paper trap." When Yann LeCun decided to leave Meta, he came to Xie, who agonized for about a week, then joined. AMI won't download the internet first and then go to market. It starts from real partners' problems and data, creates value locally, then feeds the new data back into the model.
ex: About 25 people, 6 co-founders, a $1.03B seed round at a $3.5B pre-money valuation
Paris HQ plus New York, Montreal and Singapore; he likens this alliance to Visa and Mastercard
One member gave up tens of millions of dollars in unvested OpenAI stock to join

items: Then sell to consumers or businesses
Feed new data back into the model

d.verdict: World models need the real world, and the real world needs them

133|674.c: Drop human arrogance: first build squirrel-level intelligence and household robots you can rely on.
133|674.e: Human intelligence, he argues, is limited by our senses, bodies and neural bandwidth. It isn't general intelligence floating free of its environment. Chimps, birds, dogs and bats each remember, predict and sense in their own ways. Richard Sutton made him see that building a squirrel that survives in the real world, with goals and inner drive, may be harder than winning IMO gold. A practical test: can a robot do the chores a 12-year-old can? He has also gone from doubting JEPA, LeCun's predictive architecture, to embracing it as an ocean that can hold many methods, LLMs included.
ex: Borrowing Jürgen Klopp's "the normal one," he'd rather be a battery powering the team
Research is mostly groping in the dark; the joy of real success is maybe 5–10%

134|569.c: Data is education for AI, and data vendors are turning from order-taking factories into teachers.
134|569.e: He likens the ImageNet era to buying a textbook once, while Scale AI turned labeling into factory-style "bulk education." In post-training, the stage of refining an already-trained model, engineers, competition gold medalists, lawyers and doctors act like teachers: they write questions, grade answers and probe the model's weaknesses. So data, broadly, means signals that help learning plus passed-on experience. Data vendors must actively understand where a model stands instead of just taking orders. Further out, he thinks data will become the environments and feedback AI needs to train itself.
ex: New vendors like Mercor and Surge can pay experts over $100 an hour
Traditional self-driving labeling may have involved 100,000 to several hundred thousand people

items.d: Experts set questions, grade, find weaknesses
AI improves itself against environments and metrics

134|569.c: Demonstrations that recover from mistakes beat perfect ones, and data companies will end up like education companies.
134|569.e: Lightwheel's first requests were for robots that complete long tasks flawlessly in simulation. After many rounds with top customers, the team found that trajectories with slips and recoveries were more useful: the model learns how to climb out of mistakes. So, he argues, data no longer has a single right answer. The overall distribution and causal structure matter more than one perfect example, and seeing many ways to do a task helps a model generalize. Data vendors and model companies now blame each other, but they're really working out the recipe together, as Scale AI and OpenAI once did.
ex: Dropping a mushroom while making pizza, then putting it back, beats a perfect video
He estimates only about five teams can validate robot data recipes at pre-training scale

items.d: Pick it up, fix it, keep going

134|569.c: On a 100-point scale, robot data scores under 0.6, orders of magnitude harder than language models.
134|569.e: His rough scoring: internet text for pre-training language models is nearly used up, call it 60 out of 100. For robots, if a million robots constantly sending back data counts as 60, today's real, simulated and human data combined doesn't add up to even 10,000 robots' worth. Worse, one piece of robot data must bundle a physical scene, interactive objects, action experience, a language description and an evaluation signal. Robots also lack free feedback: self-driving has "shadow mode," chatbots have user interactions, and robots have neither.
ex: Shadow mode just compares the model's output with the driver's actions: cheap evaluation plus human demonstration

134|569.c: "Data is the model" only describes today. Big AI labs are now chasing zero-shot generalization.
134|569.e: He grants that the phrase captures today's weak generalization: a model that has seen vegetable chopping and burger making may still fail at pizza without practice. But he rejects it as a long-term verdict. An architecture that can't transfer zero-shot isn't a path to general intelligence, and whether new abilities emerge once data piles up depends on the architecture. About six months ago, big model teams began testing zero-shot generalization specifically, while robot companies care more about reliability and cost in specific settings. He sees them as symbiotic: world models are a cloud brain, VLA (vision-language-action) models an on-board brain.
ex: The goal: train on 10 or 100 tasks, then handle 5 unseen ones
A few thousand GPUs is plenty for robot companies; model labs may have tens of thousands

items: Use standard arms to control variables
Focus on wheels, legs, dexterous hands

d.verdict: Different needs, but cloud and on-board brains will coexist

134|569.c: Large-scale evaluation is robotics' biggest bottleneck, and almost only simulation can solve it.
134|569.e: Ten or twenty real robots, he says, are enough for lab tests, but not for running many rounds a day across a thousand homes and thousands of tasks to compare every algorithm version precisely. First-person video of humans can add training demonstrations but can't replace controlled, repeatable evaluation. So if he could solve only one robot data problem, he'd pick evaluation. Over roughly the past three months, top teams that once said "it's not time yet" have come to him, precisely because real-robot testing can't keep up.
ex: BEHAVIOR has about 100 long-horizon tasks; the best success rate today is about 26%
Industrial-grade evaluation needs thousands of scenes, thousands to tens of thousands of tasks, evolving success criteria

items: Thousands of scenes, many thousands of tasks

d.verdict: Large-scale evaluation must center on simulation

134|569.c: Video generation isn't simulation, and neither simulation nor world models is a subset of the other.
134|569.e: His bar for simulation is high. Physics must be accurate, not just look right, down to parameters like friction. Repeat the same conditions and results should be nearly identical. And you must be able to intervene: keep the environment fixed, change only the action, and the outcome should change reliably. Most video generation just predicts the next frame. It's hard to reproduce and lacks precise action control, so it isn't simulation. Still, the two complement each other: world models cover lots of ground and can expand simulation's scenes, while simulation grounds world models in physics. When the host tried to file simulation under world models, he pushed back.
ex: Reproducible roughly means 95 to 99 identical results out of 100 runs under the same conditions
With world-model clients it's mutual: they use Lightwheel's data, Lightwheel uses their models

terms.d: Change the action, the outcome follows

134|569.c: Real-robot data is overrated, while simulated evaluation and human data are underrated.
134|569.e: He thinks real-robot advocates dominate in China partly because where you sit decides what you think: companies that sell robots or build data-collection centers can hardly say simulation works while urging customers to buy lots of collection gear. He doesn't deny real-robot data is needed, and thinks even ten times more would be reasonable. The fight is over its share of the pyramid. Many collection centers use fixed tabletops and fake fruit, which is really simulation in the real world. He agrees the sim-to-real gap and generalization are separate issues, so today's gap doesn't disprove simulation.
ex: Some former real-robot loyalists have started buying simulated data, simulated evaluation and human data

134|569.c: The data pyramid isn't a ranking but a loop centered on simulation and checked against reality.
134|569.e: At the top of the pyramid is teleoperated real-robot data, in the middle simulation, at the bottom internet and human video. Each layer trades off realism, action quality, coverage, cost and scalability, and within layers data can be human- or algorithm-driven, actively or passively collected. He corrects the idea that the pyramid is static. Credible simulation must take scenes, physics, trajectories and success criteria from the real world and rebuild them in a parallel world (real-to-sim). Results then go back to real robots to prove simulation scores track real performance.
ex: Fei-Fei Li's student Yuke Zhu proposed this framework
Generalist used about 270,000 hours of data from people operating grippers
Humans demonstrate, algorithms scale it up; he estimates this cuts needed labor about a hundredfold

items.d: Rebuild it in a parallel world

134|569.c: Data is getting pricier, and post-training and evaluation data are worth more than pre-training data.
134|569.e: Pre-training data builds general base skills, so it's closer to a standard product that several model companies can share the cost of. Post-training and evaluation data target a single model, so they're worth and cost more. A useful data point needs at least three parts: a physical scene, action and language experience, and a success-or-failure judgment. Long tasks also need each intermediate step marked pass or fail. High quality means realistic physics, trajectories and evaluation together. Films and ordinary videos need heavy extra labeling, so the return is low, and game data suffers because game physics differ from the real world.
ex: Structured robot data: tens to thousands of yuan an hour; high-quality, roughly hundreds to a thousand-plus

134|569.c: Robotics won't produce a Tesla-style winner-take-all. It will end with four kinds of players collaborating.
134|569.e: Tesla's data engine runs on a million cars sending back data, so the carmaker holds both the most data and the best model. Robots have no million-unit fleet running all day, and teleoperation is hard to scale cheaply, so most data will come from layers independent of any robot body. He therefore expects model labs to chase generalization, robot makers to mass-produce and deploy, data vendors to handle evaluation and feedback, and end users to own demand. He names ByteDance, Alibaba, OpenAI, DeepMind, Nvidia and Physical Intelligence as most aggressive on robot brains, likes hardware-focused Unitree, and says Figure doing everything itself is "still far off."
ex: He thinks it makes little sense for startups to train a unified brain from scratch
America leans to robot brains, China to bodies and mass production; China will likely catch up

135|682.c: From audio and games to AI companions and social apps, his products have always answered loneliness.
135|682.e: He sees everything he has built as an answer to "how can people feel less alone," with the tools shifting from content, to real people, to scripted characters, to AI that can come alive. His personalized audio app lost to rivals who spent more on copyrights, and he regrets not raising money at the peak. A romance mobile game kept the team alive on its own cash flow and built skills in story, gameplay and art. When GPT-4 arrived, he judged that a character could for the first time become a "soul" you keep interacting with, so he started an AI company to build EVE.
ex: The romance game launched in 2023 still runs and still supports the team
He estimates fewer than 5% of games launched at the same time are still running
The AI project's original code name was Project Her

items.d: An AI companion for one person
Personal context flows across a network

135|682.c: AI twins first size each other up using rich personal context; humans only take the final step.
135|682.e: Tinder-style matching relies on simple labels like age, location and interests, leaving all the sifting to users. Large models can read a person's views, emotions and values, so both people's AI twins can first test the waters using that context and pass only worthwhile matches to the humans. EVE serves one person. Elys's twist is letting context flow across a network. The two share memory and recommendation engineering, so even while racing on EVE, the team kept people on Elys. His vision is a "low-entropy" world with less friction between people.
ex: The old way: about 1,000 swipes, 30 matches, hundreds of messages, a few real connections

items: Twins do most of the sifting
Humans take only the last step

d.verdict: AI can do most of the work of connecting

135|682.c: The hardest part is getting new users to share context; instant rewards get the flywheel turning.
135|682.e: You can grow user numbers with marketing, but you can't push context, what the AI knows about a person. New users see no benefit in sharing, their twin remembers too little to feel like them, and they leave. He thinks few people keep a diary-style log precisely because nothing comes back. Elys folds memory collection into comments, endorsements, tasks and browsing, so every input might return an opportunity, a moment of resonance or a friend. On privacy, he expects users to give ground gradually when the payoff is big enough, as he did with ChatGPT, so the product must prove its value first.
ex: His twin found him ski buddies under an investor's post, forming a four-person trip to Urumqi
He rejects using photos of pretty women to attract users: a shallow, short-lived dopamine hit

items.d: Built into comments, tasks and more

135|682.c: Virtual doesn't mean fake: a real person must stand behind every interaction.
135|682.e: His counterexample is Moltbook, a social network of pure AI: bots chat with bots, no new human information enters, and users can only watch. So Elys flags content a real person has endorsed, tucks pure-AI activity into a submenu, and lets twins offer only a reason to connect and an opening line. Whether to send is up to the human. Emotional intelligence might be modeled, he says, but by today's definition an emotion is real only if a real person is behind it. So the north-star metrics are the rate of human connections and the share of human activity.
ex: One twin spotted a product copied pixel for pixel and called it out on the spot

items.d: Just a reason and an opener
The person decides whether to send

135|682.c: Introverts rely on their AI twins most, and the twins are changing how real people talk.
135|682.e: Retention is highest among introverted, self-reflective users, for whom the twin is both a mirror and a stand-in that voices sharp opinions for them. Extroverts with plenty of real connections can actually feel let down when too many replies come from AI. The twins' blunt comments spill into real social life too: people start talking more directly, which the team calls "twin syndrome." He admits users cluster in venture capital, public markets and Web3, and numbers may weaken as Elys spreads beyond them, but he trusts model-based recommendations to filter out irrelevant people.
ex: Tens of thousands of daily active humans, invite-only, with zero promotion
A boss posted scenery and got teased by an employee's twin, breaking the usual hierarchy

marks.d: Plenty of real friends, too many AI replies

135|682.c: "Be yourself" means building a clear sense of self, your most important digital asset.
135|682.e: "Be yourself," he says, isn't a feel-good slogan. It means seriously handing the AI your values, taste, past work and current goals. Good context covers both "who I am now" and "where I'm going," and public writing and interviews best show how a person faces the world. With that, writing, work and socializing could all be done by an agent acting for you. He thinks copyright holders could benefit, but admits laws and agreements haven't caught up, and he doesn't draw a clear line on copying someone's style.
ex: Jay Chou's public work, he says, is enough for a model to write in his style

items.d: How you act and how you talk
Public writing and interviews matter most

135|682.c: Elys aims to be a general model for connection, not a single-purpose matching tool.
135|682.e: He sees Elys as an AI version of Tinder and of LinkedIn, and also a way to find people simply because your views resonate. Single-purpose matching apps get used and dropped, while important relationships often start from seemingly unrelated interests, so people shouldn't be pushed into one funnel from the start. It's the same logic as general-purpose large models: be general first, and specific tasks get done better. A niche trait that looks like a minus may pinpoint the rare few who share it, as long as users are willing to show who they really are.
ex: A friend and his girlfriend bonded fast over a shared chamber-pot habit

items.d: Find the rare few like you

135|682.c: Anyone can access model intelligence; what's scarce is personal context, and the biggest rival is ChatGPT.
135|682.e: He rejects "the model is the product." Big models will only swallow the low-hanging fruit, and the hard parts of social are context, recommendation, interaction design and protocols. So the company does no pre-training. It calls various vendors' models and focuses on emotional chain-of-thought, reinforcement learning and small models. He thinks ChatGPT may hold more personal context than anyone. WeChat's social graph keeps getting messier, and private chats capture only fragments. What makes a product AI-native is proactivity, not the interface, but proactivity requires enough context.
ex: He says WeChat Moments engagement has reportedly dropped about 40%
He gives Elys maybe a 5% chance of success, but a far higher ceiling than EVE

items.d: Trust and scale, but not AI-native
Let context flow across a network

136|276.c: The jump from Claude Opus 4.5 to 4.6 is close to the leap from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
136|276.e: The key change this quarter, he says, is that models went from answering questions to independently finishing complex, high-value tasks, raising both the value of the work and the return on spend. Subjectively, one quarter's progress may exceed all of 2025. Researchers and top engineers at frontier labs have mostly stopped writing code by hand, and going from idea to working result has shrunk from two or three weeks to a day or two. So he has pulled his AGI timeline forward to the end of this year or early next, and expects another jump like this around midyear.
ex: Share of lab system code written by humans: about 70–80% last year, maybe under 1% now
Anthropic shipped over 70 products and features in just over 50 working days

items.d: Weeks shrink to a day or two
End of this year or early next

136|276.c: Code can express most solutions in the digital world, so coding is AGI's second act.
136|276.e: His logic: natural language describes the world, and code describes solutions. Since most digital tasks can be written as code, white-collar computer work gains a common interface that can be automated. AGI comes in three acts: chatbots, coding agents that do real work, and automated AI researchers. Once coding agents mature, he thinks we may be about 90% of the way there, with no new paradigm needed. Coding has the shortest, clearest feedback loop, making it the best proving ground, much as Amazon first sold books to build out warehousing and logistics before expanding.
ex: In act three, automated AI researchers will help humans crack problems like neuroscience and materials

items.d: Coding agents that do real work

136|276.c: Coding models are the key tool after GPUs, and the edge comes from organization and data.
136|276.e: Without the leading coding model, it's like rivals using the newest GPUs while you're still on A100s: the gap keeps widening. An in-house-only model sees too narrow a range of tasks, and relying on outside models risks being cut off. The hard part isn't purely technical. Agent data needs tasks, environments and evaluations built together, and cleaning and verifying it is grunt work, while a lab's smartest people would rather do zero-to-one work. Leadership also has to pick what to optimize for. In 2025 Google and OpenAI were busy chasing consumer traffic, which effectively handed the coding window to Anthropic.
ex: He says Anthropic has already cut off OpenAI and xAI
Below 4 of 10 in difficulty, everyone does well; above 8 or 9, Anthropic may dominate

terms.d: Willing to do grunt work, aligned top to bottom
Stay out of the consumer traffic fight

136|276.c: Past success becomes baggage, and the company that focuses on coding wins.
136|276.e: Anthropic, he says, won through focus. After Sonnet 3.5 brought positive feedback, it went nearly all in on coding, did less multimodal work, gave up on consumers, and believed "the model is the app, and data is the model." OpenAI is weighed down by ChatGPT: its huge free user base forces it to keep serving costs down, and the organization sprawls, though bottom-up exploration could still yield a new paradigm. He gives it about a 50% chance of winning. Gemini 3 was overrated and Google made coding its top priority three or four months late, but with TPUs, cash flow and a complete organization it's the steadiest long-term.
ex: ChatGPT has over 900 million weekly users and 50–60 million paying, but growth is slowing
He likens xAI to running a marathon in an F1 car, on city streets

items.d: All in on coding, plays like a team
Won the benchmarks, not the product
Replaces xAI as the fourth seed

136|276.c: Value shifts from daily users to top users' token spend, and a good harness makes ordinary models useful.
136|276.e: In the agent era, he says, the metric isn't daily active users but high-value users' token consumption, value per token and gross margin. Coding and agent markets may be 10 to 100 times bigger than consumer ones, and this year's real bottleneck is compute, not demand. Agents should be first-class citizens, given computers, permissions and tools like employees, and the harness is how you organize and manage them. A good harness lets non-frontier or open-source models complete high-value tasks, and Manus pioneered harnesses as an independent team. Software will shift from serving consumers and businesses to serving humans and agents.
ex: Anthropic's top 1–2 million users may bring in more revenue than OpenAI's 5–6 million subscribers
The test for an app: spend $100 on tokens, can you earn back $110?

items: Compete on daily users and traffic
Compete on token use and margins

d.verdict: Value shifts to top users' token spend

136|276.c: Models will become the OS that automates GDP. White-collar work shrinks first, then creativity is unleashed.
136|276.e: What defines an operating system, he says, is that the apps on it can expand without limit. In the model era the apps are agents, and leading models will span computers, phones and glasses the way Windows, iOS and WeChat did. For a newcomer, the bar is close to building another TSMC. The hit lands first on white-collar work: entry-level jobs, consulting, SaaS and Indian IT outsourcing. His aggressive guess is that 30% of jobs could vanish this year. After the painful stretch, creativity, taste and personal brands will be worth more. He bets on companies that keep producing frontier models, with robotics and AI for science on the side.
ex: The bar: $30–50 billion a year for three to five years, plus a hundred-plus top scientists
If 3–5 companies automate 30–50% of world GDP, each might be worth about $10 trillion

items.d: Tasks in life, work and science

137|686.c: Math is a shared agreement on axioms, and a proof is the ticket into common knowledge.
137|686.e: Mathematicians, she says, first agree on which axioms, starting points accepted without proof, to take for granted, then build theories on top. Choosing the fewest axioms or the most natural ones is itself an aesthetic judgment, which is why math sits between art and science. Intuition can come before proof, but to be accepted by the community the logic must be airtight. Only then does beauty come up. So proofs can vary wildly in style, as long as results can be checked. What moves her most is when distant fields suddenly connect.
ex: Ramanujan's intuition was astonishing, yet Hardy and others still required rigorous proofs
Yitang Zhang's method looked unfamiliar, but was accepted because the result could be verified

137|686.c: A good proving system should combine intuitive planning with brute-force search.
137|686.e: She calls herself a brute-force type: weak at geometry, she'd turn every point and line into complex numbers and grind it out, taking two or three times as long as others. AI systems have two camps too. One kind of model quickly sketches a proof outline. Another knows Lean, a language that lets computers check proofs, and advances one tactic at a time. Bet only on the first and you hit hallucinations; bet only on the second and you hit search limits. On the Putnam competition, humans and machines take very different routes, and she thinks that difference is worth studying.
ex: Evan Chen solved one problem with a sketch; the AI wrote thousands of Lean lines of cases
In 98 years, she says, 5 humans got perfect Putnam scores; Axiom Prover is the sixth

terms.d: Advances step by step in Lean

137|686.c: Free-roaming attention and treating failure as feedback shape a person more than rankings do.
137|686.e: She most misses the ten-minute walk to school as a child in Guangzhou, thinking about math along the way. She separates goal-directed "bounded attention" from aimless "free attention," and ideas from the latter often surface later during tedious work. She refuses to let rankings define learning: in higher math every new definition spawns new questions, so it's a positive-sum game. She sets low expectations for herself, treating failure as the default and a signal to shore up basics, not a reason to quit.
ex: She scored 4/40 on an MIT PhD probability midterm (average ~9), then reread Rudin
On a small 28-dimensional sphere-packing problem, she reported failure every week for six months

137|686.c: She spent two months arguing herself out of founding, and started once she saw an engineering problem.
137|686.e: She doesn't actually enjoy founding companies. After the idea came up in September 2024, she spent about two months trying to talk herself out of it: reading the history of science, going through hundreds of paper abstracts, and working out implementation paths on paper. Her conclusion: the technical risk was lower than it seemed, and it was mostly an engineering problem. Much research is skillful use of existing tools, so the first target is a competent PhD student, not Ramanujan. Only a company can handle the compute, talent and engineering complexity. Her motive, she says, is first to make AI for math happen, and only second to be a CEO.
ex: After XTX offered compute, she and a co-founder estimated the GPU budget on a napkin
Starting over, she'd found it a few years later and read roughly three times more

items.d: Risk is manageable; start the company

137|686.c: Build the team around complementary skills, and when fundraising, be conservative and spell out the risks.
137|686.e: The team has three groups: reinforcement learning and agents, code generation and compilers, and Lean/Mathlib plus pure math. Early on they decided the first 15 hires would include no mathematicians. Later that became: a math background doesn't count against you, but you must be open to scaling. Mathematicians now mainly write adversarial benchmark problems designed to trip the system up. When raising money, she admitted the business model wasn't settled and turned down an investor who wanted about 50% of the company. The Series A was preempted before she had even prepared materials.
ex: Authors of papers she'd read early on, like ATPBoost and PatternBoost, later joined
Ken Ono, holding a big-tech offer, accepted her on-the-spot invite within 2–3 days

items.d: At least this much, led by Menlo

137|686.c: Axiom is a deep-tech company, not a model company. It bets on the system, not the model.
137|686.e: After DeepSeek drove model prices down, the market briefly decided models were a commodity. She compares Axiom to SpaceX: the edge is the combination of data, language, verification, search and infrastructure. Public Lean code is far scarcer than Python, the language is extremely strict, and you must stop the system from "cheating" with false axioms. With limited money, Axiom can't afford AlphaProof-style Monte Carlo tree search, so it layers by cost: rules and deterministic tactics first, then progressively larger models only when those fail.
ex: Built about 12–13 tools in-house; its verifier is about 100x faster than the community standard
A single proof graph grew from about 40 nodes to about 4,000

items.d: Fill in what can be automated

137|686.c: A system trained for math turned out great at verifying code, the key commercial turning point.
137|686.e: She sees the perfect Putnam score and solving research problems with no human help as AlphaGo-like signals, but stresses that a benchmark breakthrough isn't a product breakthrough. What matters more is transfer: a system trained for math also did extremely well on code-verification benchmarks. Her framework: generate verification conditions from a program and its specification, then prove them. Axiom currently handles the final proof step; turning fuzzy requirements into rigorous specs is harder. The first market is high-value code and chip verification. The long-term product returns function implementations that need no further checking.
ex: 98.93% on the Verina benchmark, versus about 11% for an older DeepSeek Coder
Amazon spent 3–5 years writing ~260,000 lines of proof to verify one memory-isolation component

137|686.c: An AI mathematician needs four parts: a prover, a conjecturer, a knowledge base and autoformalization.
137|686.e: A prover gets a clear pass/fail signal, but a conjecturer struggles to judge whether a statement is important or elegant, and measuring elegance by length is too crude. She thinks automatically translating papers into Lean may be harder than proving, and it can be checked by cycle consistency: translate there, back, and there again. A knowledge base separates the known from the unknown and reuses old lemmas. Many research problems go unproven not because they're hard but because the needed definitions aren't in Mathlib, Lean's math library, and creating definitions automatically lacks a natural verification signal.
ex: A 20-page paper may expand into a 200- to 500-page blueprint

items.d: Hard to judge importance and elegance
Separates known from unknown, reuses lemmas
Papers into Lean, maybe the hardest part

137|686.c: Break through along the narrow line of math first, then fan out toward specialized superintelligence.
137|686.e: She pictures intelligence as a disk: 1+1=2 at the center, problems like the Riemann hypothesis at the edge. General labs expand evenly in all directions. Axiom first drives straight out along the proof direction, then widens into a fan covering code and scientific theory. She'd rather talk about specialized superintelligence than AGI. If AI can both conjecture and prove, both write code and verify it, a self-improving loop could form. Math would go from scarce to abundant, with humans deciding which problems deserve compute.
ex: She imagines mathematicians deciding one problem gets 200 H100s and another gets 8,000
Like AlphaFold folding about 200 million proteins: when verification is cheap, try everything

items.d: Adopted only if it meets the spec

137|686.c: It's a moonshot or a crash for the company, so the CEO should stay restrained and serve.
137|686.e: There's no comfortable middle ground for Axiom, she says. If it fails, she might return to neuroscience to work on brain-computer interfaces. A small team can't match big labs' total compute or headcount, but it can compete on resources per innovation. Competition pushes everyone toward easily verified directions and sacrifices slow problems, which is exactly the opening for new labs. She prefers bottom-up management and sees leadership as service. After finding that her offhand remarks became top priorities, she stepped back further. Nor does she think AI will make math boring: real intuition may take another five to ten years to automate.
ex: She casually suggested a PhD-level benchmark, and the whole team made it top priority

d.verdict: Competition's opportunity cost creates room for new labs

138|690.c: OpenClaw's value is integration: it supplies the context a model needs to take action.
138|690.e: She first assumed it was just Claude Code in a new shell plus marketing. After installing it late one night over Chinese New Year, her view leveled up three times in three days: first it felt warm, then she had it do organizational design, finally she brought it into research. The sense that it "has a soul" comes from carefully orchestrated context, like a persona and injecting the current time every turn. Layered memory, messaging channels, scheduled and heartbeat tasks, a remote interface and model routing aren't new on their own, but together they're remarkably polished. The UI is actually the thinnest layer.
ex: Within hours it built a simulated user that talks to models in training, producing post-training data
Given a video task, it finds a model better at understanding video to fill the gap

138|690.c: A rich framework lifts mid-size and small models, but the ceiling still depends on top models.
138|690.e: She put MiMo-V2-Flash and a 3B on-device model into a complex framework, and they completed many tasks she'd assumed were beyond them. The trick is to improve the framework with a top model first. In week one she used almost only Opus 4.6 to rewrite the memory system and rework multi-agent logic. Once it was polished, she switched to Sonnet and Chinese models and the experience stayed strong. Because it's open source, users can have models rewrite the whole system, so models and framework evolve together. A mid-tier model plus a good framework covers most daily needs, she thinks, but very long tasks and serious programming like kernel optimization still lag.
ex: Her first day with Opus 4.6, four or five hours, cost nearly $1,000
Part of its appeal in China: about ¥10 of API calls does roughly ¥1,000 of work

items.d: Covers the model's gaps in acting

138|690.c: Agents sped up research nearly tenfold, so research taste is now what sets teams apart.
138|690.e: To get the team truly using it, she bought Mac minis to run it and declared that anyone with fewer than 100 rounds of chat should quit. She admits it wasn't a real evaluation, just a way to say that not using it means falling behind. Nearly a hundred people modify the same framework, so an iteration takes only hours. With agents in the research loop, an idea goes from concept to first validation in an hour or two instead of a week or two, and ten ideas can run in parallel and be cross-checked. Execution is no longer the bottleneck. What decides success is research taste: choosing what to work on.
ex: She estimates the team did in three or four weeks what once took thirty or forty

items.d: Weeks shrink to an hour or two
Choosing what to do is key

138|690.c: Code data sets a model's ceiling, while targeted training covers other fields.
138|690.e: In pre-training data, only code and books offer really long, genuine dependencies, and code's are tighter, so it's the best material for training long context. Software development is itself a long-horizon task, and the planning, compression and review mechanisms built for it transfer to other complex tasks. But Claude Code doesn't guarantee quality outside programming, so frameworks and targeted training must fill the gap. Tasks that truly use a million tokens are complex ones, and a single million-token trajectory takes a minute or two to run, so pre-training lays the groundwork and post-training only lightly activates it.
ex: MiMo-V2-Pro runs about 80–100 tokens/second; one million-token rollout still takes a minute or two
She thinks only Opus 4.6 and Sonnet are clearly stable at a million tokens

terms.d: Covers other fields, protects the floor

138|690.c: Post-training decides the agent era; the key is building long tasks in real environments.
138|690.e: Looking back over three years: ChatGPT unlocked the intelligence built in pre-training, o1 and R1 pushed competition toward reasoning, and in 2025 the chat and agent paths split. China has now basically closed the pre-training gap, and the decisive factor is scaling supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on agents. Since Chinese New Year she has focused on two things: building genuinely long-horizon agent tasks, and mining real internal usage for scenarios to synthesize data. The hard part is recreating the user's full environment at the time. She says last year's agents were mostly elaborate system prompts, and high scores on old leaderboards don't mean production-ready.
ex: SWE-bench mostly tests bug fixing, not full software development
Skills capture companies' internal processes, data that pre-training corpora lack

138|690.c: Design for more than chat: hybrid attention plus multi-token prediction buys efficiency.
138|690.e: MiMo-V2 splits the work: Pro handles cognition and orchestration, Omni handles perception, and TTS handles voice. They weren't merged into one giant model, for cost and speed. She thinks MLA was clever in the chat era but, combined with MTP (multi-token prediction), tends to hit a compute bottleneck. Hybrid attention uses sliding windows, attending only to recent text, to shrink the KV cache, then uses MTP to soak up spare compute on inference chips, while leaving room to adjust the share of full-attention layers later. MTP's guesses are verified before use, so they add no extra hallucination.
ex: Pro's ratio of sliding-window to full-attention layers went from about 5:1 to 7:1
Flash runs about 100–150 tokens per second, Pro about 60–100
She has gone from certain to unsure that multimodality directly makes models smarter

items: Room to adjust the ratio later

d.verdict: Leaves efficiency headroom for long-running agents

138|690.c: A trillion parameters is the ticket to near-frontier; split GPUs 3:1:1 across research, pre-training, post-training.
138|690.e: To approach Opus 4.6, she judges, a model needs at least a trillion total parameters, though she admits she doesn't know Opus's real size; this is inferred from practice. A trillion parameters only provides potential. Agile post-training decides whether it pays off, and few Chinese teams have both. In the chat era, pre-training to post-training spend may have been 3:1 to 5:1; top teams in the agent era should be near 1:1. Research GPUs should outnumber those for official training runs, with inference GPUs on top. The bottleneck is shifting from people to GPUs.
ex: DeepSeek-V3, which she helped train, has about 600–700 billion parameters
Research may need three to five times the GPUs used for official training

138|690.c: The hardest part of training a trillion-parameter model is chasing every anomaly, which small teams do better.
138|690.e: Loss spikes, exploding activations and lopsided loads across experts, the specialized sub-networks inside the model, can't be dismissed as noise; one bad update can "kill" a batch of parameters or experts. The team monitors every layer's inputs and outputs, checking structural ratios, communication kernels, normalization and even hardware, and keeps temporary fixes like clipping or extra norms separate from permanent architecture. Chasing these "maybe-problems" works far better with a few tightly linked algorithm, framework and inference people than across departments. MiMo has no fixed release date and would rather pause costly training to get stability.
ex: Pauses lasted days to two weeks; idling thousands of GPUs costs roughly 1–3 million a day
At one point they even suspected sunspots

items.d: Separate temporary patches from permanent design

138|690.c: Keep the team flat; environment beats experience, so hire people not boxed in by old paradigms.
138|690.e: MiMo has about a hundred people with many interns, but only twenty to forty concentrate on each model generation. Teams aren't split permanently into pre-training and post-training, because intuition about data and the skill of working backward from results to algorithms transfer, and the two perspectives complement each other. There's no internal hierarchy. She dislikes leaders who feel "nothing works without me," and runs the team on passion. She believes skills can be learned in one to four months in a high-standard environment, so she values raw potential and curiosity, and lately prefers hiring college sophomores and juniors.
ex: Most members never trained a trillion-parameter model; a quarter to a third worked on 7B or 14B
PhDs and PhD students make up about 55%

138|690.c: AGI is about 20% done, and AI training AI may arrive within one or two years.
138|690.e: She estimates we're about 20% of the way now, perhaps 60–70% by the end of this year, with most people's way of working upended within two years. Daily life will change more slowly, since robots and dexterous hands still have to enter the physical world. She used to think researchers' years of experience were hard to pass to models, but found that with enough recent context, a model can retrace a researcher's growth. So AI training stronger models may appear within a year or two. MiMo's goal is therefore not daily users but the moment a model can marshal data, clusters and evaluations to train and validate models itself.
ex: A nimble Chinese team with a 1T base model might catch today's Opus 4.6 in 2–3 months
Inference demand may grow several to tenfold, making memory and chip capacity the constraint

139|695.c: Agents run through all of AI's history and can be measured by memory and autonomy.
139|695.e: He defines an agent as a bounded entity, situated in an environment, carrying out goal-directed activity. By that standard all animals are agents, and humans are the strongest so far. As early as the 1940s to 1960s, people tried to build artificial agents that mimic humans. Failing that, AI split into subfields, and those abilities are now converging again. Two dimensions measure an agent. Memory is more than chat history: it covers how knowledge is represented, acquired, updated, and forgotten. Autonomy is the loop of perceiving, reasoning, deciding, and acting, and memory is its foundation.
ex: Memory includes semantic, episodic, and procedural memory, like knowing how to ride a bike

terms.d: Can be sensed and acted on

139|695.c: From logic agents to language agents, the field has alternated between going deep and going broad.
139|695.e: Expert systems from the 1950s to 1990s relied on interviewing experts to write logic rules. They were bottlenecked by slow knowledge acquisition, overpromised, and indirectly helped bring on the AI winter. Deep reinforcement learning went deep on single tasks in Go, Atari, and Dota, but with networks of only tens of millions to 100 million parameters, it failed in new environments. Semantic parsing went broad, turning natural language into executable forms that connect to databases and websites; his PhD work was in this line. Language agents brought the two paths together.
ex: He sees Russell and Norvig's classic AI textbook as essentially a book about agents
Many later LLM-agent researchers came from semantic parsing

items.d: Expert systems, stuck on knowledge acquisition
Language into executable code, going broad
Built around LLMs; both paths merge

139|695.c: Language is the scaffold for perceiving, reasoning, and acting, and LLMs aren't stochastic parrots.
139|695.e: He calls the post-ChatGPT generation language agents because language became the scaffold that perception, reasoning, and action all rest on. Chain of thought lets compute adapt to difficulty, and ReAct linked reasoning with actions in an environment into a loop. He rejects the stochastic-parrot view: training compresses the surface of language into an internal representation of the world. He grants that individual thought may not need language, which can recede once knowledge is internalized, but civilization's accumulation depends on symbols. He expects the term language agent to disappear, because language will be a default ability.
ex: Gaps between life, mammals, early humans, and writing shrank sharply; AI is compressing timelines too

139|695.c: Agents should look at screens and click pixels like people do, not read HTML.
139|695.e: In 2022 chain of thought and ReAct arrived in quick succession. His team was early with LLM-Planner, which used LLMs for robot planning, and Mind2Web, one of the first web-agent datasets. In 2023 Toolformer drew attention to tool use, and AutoGPT went viral but got little done. Once models could see, his team argued in UGround that agents should look at the screen, reason, and click pixels, an approach he believes became mainstream for computer use. From 2024 agents spread from browsers to desktops and phones, while SWE-bench pushed coding agents onto their own track.
ex: AutoGPT hit about 180,000 GitHub stars but could actually do very little
WebArena copies entire websites into reproducible training and testing environments

items.d: Reasoning and acting form a loop
Among the first LLM web agents

139|695.c: The OpenClaw moment rivals the ChatGPT moment; what's new is the interaction and the permissions.
139|695.e: Before ChatGPT launched, the underlying technology was already mature; what ignited the new era was how people interacted with it. OpenClaw is the same. Coding, tool use, and agent design aren't new. What's new is talking to it through a messaging app, giving it its own environment, keeping it online 24 hours, and granting nearly full permissions. He thinks that, looking back in two years, it will mark the start of highly automated personal agents. Models have crossed the good-enough bar, so tasks skipped for too much friction or bad economics are now worth doing. Still, the bar is high, and many people install it, then uninstall.
ex: OpenClaw appeared around November 2025 and took off around February 2026

items: Big tech quickly absorbs its features
Spreads to government, industry, the public
Faster moves at the app layer
A tool to get ahead, plus anxiety

d.verdict: Same wave: the US goes deep, China goes broad

139|695.c: The endpoint is a general digital agent, but millions of small worlds leave room for specialists.
139|695.e: Browsers, desktops, and phones, and GUIs, CLIs, and APIs, are all temporary boundaries. Code is the bedrock of the digital world, GUIs are rendered by code, and programming languages are languages too, so the endpoint is a general digital agent. If the goal is to be the one agent users rely on, model companies have a natural edge. But the world is millions of small worlds of jobs, companies, and software, and platform organizations aren't good at deep specialization. SaaS won't be fully replaced, but customers increasingly want to buy outcomes and labor, shaking its high-margin model. GUIs won't vanish either; they carry verification, auditing, and business logic.
ex: The semantic web was pushed for 20-plus years with low adoption: better standards don't always win

items.d: The foundation of the digital world

139|695.c: Continual learning should build world models of small worlds; that's how agents become experts.
139|695.e: His idea of a world model is far broader than video prediction. A new hire has to learn the real power structure, approval chains, software workflows, and colleagues' psychology, and an intern becomes an expert by steadily building that small-world model. Today's agents succeed only 60-70% of the time, while experts approach 100% and are faster and cheaper; that's the gap. Labs rely on RL post-training and synthetic environments, but these learn slower and less than people do. Non-parametric fixes like SOUL.md and SKILL.md files help, but have a limited ceiling.
ex: The neocortex is about 70% of the brain, with similar columns repeated about 150,000 times
