139|695.c: Research must go into real deployment; the biggest risk isn't AI rebellion but lopsided gains.
139|695.e: He once turned down a high Microsoft salary to teach. But by 2025, agent research needed lots of GPUs, API spending, and learning signals from real deployment, a loop universities struggle to close. So he founded NeoCognition to research continual learning that lets general agents quickly become experts in any domain. He sees no path for AI to actively wipe out humanity, since it lacks inner goals and survival pressure. The more realistic risks are jobs disappearing faster than new ones appear, and gains concentrating among giants and capital. Researchers, he says, should lower the barrier to expert-level agents.
ex: Founded in mid-2025, it raised a $40 million seed round in March 2026
He estimates OpenAI and Anthropic may take 30-50% of all funding raised

items.d: No inner goals, no visible path

140|698.c: Top labs no longer compete on whether they can build something, but on choosing the right goals.
140|698.e: A year ago, he says, everyone was chasing OpenAI's reasoning abilities. Now none of the three big labs fears being left behind for good. Public leaderboard scores sit in the same range, and small gaps are mostly noise. The differences people actually feel come from where each lab puts its resources. In his experience, teaching a model a new behavior used to take lots of tricks. Now you mostly need to spell out the problem, the training environment and the data. So the hard part is deciding what to build and describing the behavior you want precisely.
ex: On the coding benchmark SWE-bench, most models score around 80%; a point or two is noise
He sees Claude as strongest at agents, Codex closing in on coding, Gemini best at reasoning

items.d: A year ago: can we even do it?
Hard part: what to build, stated clearly

140|698.c: Slower benchmark gains don't mean slower progress. A pre-training "wall" is usually your own bug.
140|698.e: Any test with a perfect score gets harder to improve near the top, and scores don't map neatly onto how a model feels to use. His sense is that models are still getting better at learning. When pre-training seems to hit a wall, he sees three possible causes: the scaling rule has truly reached its limit, conditions like enough data no longer hold, or the researchers have a bug. He thinks bugs are most common, such as the wrong data mix, sources or training length in scaling experiments. Fixing bugs often pays more than clever tricks, if you can find them through ablations, removing one factor at a time.
ex: He's only confident about the next four months or so: pre-training will keep improving
He's certain models trained on limited context will handle unlimited context this year

items.d: A real limit of the scaling rule
Data or other assumptions no longer hold
Most common; remove factors one by one

140|698.c: Data and compute drive most progress. Algorithms are decisive only at rare turning points.
140|698.e: He sees pre-training and mature post-training as driven mainly by data and compute pulling each other forward. Algorithms work more like a phase transition in physics, a sudden jump: the Transformer was that jump for language pre-training. The science of pure language models is fairly settled, and what remains is mostly engineering. Generating images, video and other media is still a science problem where algorithmic breakthroughs matter. He compares scaling laws to early thermodynamics: useful rules came first and deeper explanations later, so a black box needn't block progress. But he rejects treating "emergence" as mysticism.
ex: He says everything is a black box; physics, too, uses separate theories for different scales
He skipped quantum computing, bottlenecked by lab work; AI's computer experiments suited him better

d.verdict: Data and compute do the daily work; algorithms trigger the big jumps

140|698.c: Coding took off first thanks to clear right-or-wrong signals, plentiful practice environments and shared standards for good code.
140|698.e: He traces coding's lead to three conditions that reinforce each other. Tests can tell right from wrong, so the reward signal is clean. The vast amount of code on GitHub can be turned straight into training environments. And there's strong agreement on what good code looks like (simple, well structured, easy to maintain), while product needs are fairly uniform. Early pre-trained models were also surprisingly good at continuing code, perhaps because code on the web is higher quality than ordinary text. Together, these made coding easy both to train and to turn into products.
ex: Teams may not have realized that scraped GitHub code was unusually high quality

terms.d: Run the tests to know right from wrong
Broad agreement on what good code is

result.d: Easy to train and to turn into products

140|698.c: For now the real edge lies in models. No app yet gets better as more people use it.
140|698.e: He sees OpenClaw as a natural spillover of model capabilities: the abilities already existed and labs had similar internal demos. What's new is a top-layer system that coordinates several models on long tasks. Manus and OpenClaw both ended up moving closer to model companies, which shows the edge lies in models. Outside agentic coding, he hasn't seen an AI-native app with a real data flywheel, where more users bring more data and a better product. Chatbots look more like an extension of search. Startups must either grow fast enough to lock in users before training their own models, or pick small markets model companies ignore.
ex: Cursor won users with Claude first, then trained its own model, Composer
He sees Midjourney as a small market that model companies won't bother with
Big companies can't ship rough like hobby projects: legal, safety, brand and compute all matter

items.d: OpenClaw-style: many models on long tasks
Where the real edge is today

140|698.c: Models now write 90% of his code and research runs 20–50x faster, yet researchers are busier.
140|698.e: By a conservative estimate, models write about 90% of his code, and close to all of it by a looser one. His job is now designing the logic, picking files, giving the model context and reviewing its work. Turning ideas into running experiments is 20 to 50 times faster than a little over a year ago, and a researcher can run several agents at once. But cheaper trial and error means more combinations worth trying, and teams choose more experiments over shorter hours. So his hours and intensity have gone up. Nobody in AI gets to coast, he says; most people drive themselves.
ex: He arrives around 9 or 10 and often works late when alone in the US
When stuck, he asks the model and gets an explanation in seconds

140|698.c: Jobs with objective standards go first, and AI will concentrate value in very few hands.
140|698.e: Any task you can define a scoring standard for can be trained, he argues. So math, coding, AI research and theoretical science, the jobs seen as hardest, are among the first to be automated. Great product managers are harder to replace, because a good product has no preset objective yardstick. Programmers won't vanish overnight, but a gradual shrinking has begun. He sees AI as a concentrating technology: a few people get amplified while most lose what made them unique. In the extreme, one person in a thousand does everyone's work. He stresses that ratio is only illustrative, and calls himself a pessimist.
ex: Science simulations shrank from half a day to minutes, but no Einstein-level discovery yet
Short-term survivors need technical depth, big-picture sense and task-splitting skills, possibly replaceable within months

items.d: See the big picture, split up tasks

140|698.c: The US-China gap has narrowed. Copying rivals' outputs is wrong; using other models cleverly has research value.
140|698.e: He thinks the US-China model gap has narrowed a lot in the past year or two, but whether China catches up or pulls ahead is unclear, since Chinese teams are short on compute. That shortage encourages distillation: training a model on another model's outputs. Hard distillation copies rivals' outputs in bulk. It's commercially unethical and shows the team lacks its own goals. Smart distillation has outside models help create data or grade answers. It's a gray area, but could amount to real multi-model training. He guesses ByteDance's video model Seedance wins on data and engineering rather than a new approach, and stresses it's a pure guess.
ex: He rates Doubao below Gemini and Claude overall, but its voice generation may lead the world
Phone agents must run cheaply: compute for booking a train ticket can't exceed the fare

items: Shows the team lacks its own goals
Outside models help make data or grade it

d.verdict: The second has more research value

140|698.c: Chinese robot hardware is astonishingly cheap, but robot software hasn't had its GPT-1 moment.
140|698.e: He found Chinese robot hardware far cheaper than he expected, a sign of supply-chain strength. Software is another story. It relies on reinforcement learning and specialized data, which can be tuned well for a fixed setting but transfers poorly to other tasks. That's still like the old era of hand-engineered features. The dividing line, he says, is whether many abilities can rise together: language models crossed it after the Transformer and GPT, robots haven't. Vision-language-action (VLA) models built on language models are worth watching, but no path that scales has been found yet.
ex: He has seen DeepMind's and Dyna's robot labs: folding clothes and pouring water both work
Doing one task well isn't generality; what's missing is a way to scale transfer across tasks

marks.d: Tuned for fixed settings, poor transfer
Built on language models, path unclear

140|698.c: In the model era, the payoff goes to organizations and reliability, not lone geniuses.
140|698.e: What stands out at Anthropic, he says, is execution: decisions come mostly from the top, the company commits fully once it decides, and information is widely shared. When Claude 3 was seen to beat GPT-4 at coding, the company treated it as a strong signal and quickly doubled down. He guesses the edge began with technical choices by hands-on teams and was then turned into company strategy. That works only if technical leaders are both respected and empowered to decide. So he plays down genius stories: everyone is just riding a wave. What matters most is being reliable, careful and owning your work.
ex: The reinforcement learning team had 10–11 people, the company 700–800; he saw every training stage
Physics made him skeptical of theory and authority; he rates his particle-theory work's impact near zero

Leaders are respected and can decide
Credit goes to the organization, not heroes

141|640.c: Token counts mislead. What matters is the cost per task done, and pricing will shift to outcomes.
141|640.e: She thinks counting tokens, the units models process text in, misjudges value. On the same coding task, a concise model might write a hundred or two lines while a weak one writes thousands. Add hidden reasoning and agent loops, and usage can differ by tens to a hundred times. Total spend is users × tasks per user × tokens per task × price per token. The first two soar as AI spreads while the last two keep falling, so heavy waste and soaring spend can both be true. She puts leading companies' AI spending around 1–2% of EBITDA, still affordable. Customers pay for solved problems, so pricing will follow outcomes.
ex: Opus lists $5 per million input tokens and $25 output; outsiders estimate real cost near $1
Uber burned through its full-year coding AI budget in three months
Sierra's support AI bills only for solved issues, not human handoffs, with tiers by complexity

result.d: Waste and soaring spend can coexist

141|640.c: Coding agents let leaders build the next AI with better AI, and the coding market is badly underestimated.
141|640.e: She used to assume the top model changed hands every few months. Now she doubts it: the leader can use better AI to build the next AI, a loop that became obvious around January this year. Once cars run reliably, no horse can compete, however fast. Because models are billed by usage, companies pick a model request by request, so OpenAI and Anthropic can both grow big. She also admits the old coding-market math was way off. The real market isn't developer seats but all the white-collar work time computers could take over.
ex: Engineer productivity gains went from ~5% to 15–20%; model updates now take about a month
Old estimate: about $10B. Cursor soon reached about $1B, already a tenth
The new frame borrows Dario Amodei's figure: global white-collar time is worth $30–40 trillion

141|640.c: Software stocks lost first to uncertainty, which raises discount rates, and only later to replacement by agents.
141|640.e: She uses discounted cash flow to explain the software selloff. You don't need to know a company will be replaced; if its future is less certain, the discount rate rises and its present value falls. Most exposed are single-purpose tools whose value is the interface, since agents can skip the interface and do the work directly. The more structured the data, the easier to replace, while messy Excel files hold up. The opportunity is turning lost decisions into an asset: trade-offs made in meetings, emails and negotiations were never recorded. Software also has to rebuild protocols, identity, payments and permissions for agents.
ex: CRMs record a 25% discount, not why it wasn't 30% or who swayed the CFO
Traditional software makes about $500K revenue per employee; Anthropic makes over $10M
Slack's request-response suits human chat; agents fit Discord-style always-on connections

items.d: Investors demand a higher risk premium

141|640.c: Companies drop AI into old layouts, like motors in steam-engine slots; teams must turn relay races into basketball.
141|640.e: She borrows Dario Amodei's distinction: technology spreads fast, but its economic impact can lag for years. Electricity took about 40 years to lift productivity because early factories simply put electric motors where the steam engine had been and kept the old layout. Computers paid off only when companies redesigned their operations in the 1990s. Today AI is still being added to old workflows. Management layers exist to carry and compress information, and product development runs on serial handoffs, with lots of time spent translating what to build. Once AI shortens development, the bottleneck just moves, so only a full redesign works.
ex: Spec to launch took about six months; cut coding to two weeks and testing jams up
She imagines self-run teams of 3–5, testing built into development, fewer middle managers
She admits she hasn't yet seen a working example in the US

items: PM, design, dev and QA hand off in turn
Layers exist to pass messages along
Speed up one leg and the bottleneck moves
Skills in the team, decisions on the spot

d.verdict: Redesign the whole thing instead of adding AI to old workflows

141|640.c: AI agents will make markets more efficient but more crowded. Her top worry: capex eating Big Tech's cash.
141|640.e: A partnership announcement used to take days of investor phone calls to get priced in. Agents might do it the second it's released, making event-driven trading less and less necessary. Everyone also reacts faster to the same signal, so trades get more crowded and volatile, and alpha will have to come from understanding big trends rather than spotting news first. Looking back, she says her bet last year that the market's focus would shift from semiconductors to applications was completely wrong. Her biggest worry now: on the current capex curve, free cash flow at several cloud giants could turn negative in 2027.
ex: She roughly estimates quant funds drive 60–70%+ of US stock trading, retail about 30%
On-balance-sheet capex tops $1 trillion; over half of cloud backlogs come from model companies
Cutting 20% of staff could lift Salesforce-type EPS 40–50%, the Magnificent 7's only 5–10%

items.d: Agents price news in a second
Everyone reacts to the same signal
Cloud giants' free cash flow may turn negative in 2027
New giants listing pull money from the Magnificent 7

141|640.c: Once AI handles information exchange, what's left between people is emotional connection.
141|640.e: She admits the Bay Area is deeply anxious. New models and workflows appear daily, and social media keeps making people feel behind. Her answer to an unclear future is strong opinions, weakly held. On jobs she refuses to call it: past shocks played out over decades or a century, giving society time to adjust, and "this time is different" is the most dangerous phrase in investing. Her conclusion: about 95% of information-type conversations can go straight to AI, so meeting just to swap information is losing its point. Sincere emotional connection becomes more precious because it is scarce.
ex: She once cried late at night when OpenClaw wouldn't install, fearing she was being left behind
The US farm population fell from about 40% to 1% over roughly a century
Geoffrey Hinton said radiologists would become unnecessary; since then their jobs and pay have risen

142|312.c: AI's value appears suddenly once it crosses a threshold, which is why he missed the coding revenue boom.
142|312.e: He admits last episode's predictions were proven wrong, but sees frequent misses as a sign of a fast-moving field full of opportunity. His method: strong opinions, weakly held, and change your view when the reasons change. Looking back, his consumer calls mostly held: subscriptions are hard to raise, paying users have largely been found, and ad revenue will come slower than expected. Coding was the miss. Internet business models existed early and improved gradually, but AI sells intelligence, which only pays off past a threshold, just as water must boil before a steam engine works. In hindsight, high-quality coding data plus agentic reinforcement learning made long tasks work.
ex: Claude 4.5 wasn't named 5, showing even Anthropic didn't see it coming
About 50 million paying users have already sorted out who'll pay for chatbots
After Anthropic's usage exploded, he bought back into memory, optical modules and CPUs

items.d: Quality coding data plus agentic RL

142|312.c: AI's payback problem isn't solved, just passed to customers: ten times the engineers isn't ten times the revenue.
142|312.e: He breaks the chain into input, output and outcome. A model company's revenue is really its customers' spending, and the true return is whether customers turn those tokens into profit. A company that suddenly had ten times the engineers probably wouldn't see revenue soar, because what's usually missing is direction, not hands. Knowledge work is also bottlenecked by accountability, and AI can't take the blame. Cost savings are limited too: big companies can cut their slack only once. His analogy is a sink. Right now more water flows in than drains out, so revenue grows. But if early adopters don't make money, it will drain eventually.
ex: AI hardware profits are about $700B this year; Samsung and SK Hynix are nearing Nvidia
If Anthropic hits a $100B annualized run rate by year-end, that's $10B of tokens a month
Coordination and trust are 10–20% of coding work; big firms' ~15% slack goes only once

142|312.c: The top two model labs: undervalued now, overvalued in a year or two, maybe giants in ten years.
142|312.e: He sees valuation in three stages. Short term, IPO excitement could double the roughly $900 billion valuations, and if annualized revenue hits $100 billion by year-end, a trillion isn't expensive. Over one to two years, with the payback problem unsolved, valuations look high and could fall sharply. Over ten years, both could become $5–10 trillion companies. He notes the leaders haven't pulled apart: whoever releases last looks strongest. In coding tools, the gap between Claude Code and Codex had clearly narrowed by May, so competition is shifting to brand, distribution and price.
ex: Codex fought on price at about half the cost, and GPT-5.5 turned its reputation around
Configured skills and CLAUDE.md files create switching costs, favoring the first-mover brand
He warns: ask whether a coding plan sells a discounted model or the harness itself

142|312.c: The harness, the software around a model, is like an operating system; the model is a swappable processor.
142|312.e: He revises the "model as operating system" metaphor. Users always interact with a product. The harness holds the context, memory, tools, loops and runtime, while the model is like a CPU in the Windows era that you could swap between Intel and AMD. People keep rescuing their OpenClaw setups to save the memory inside, yet swap models without a second thought. Nor does he think the best harnesses will all come from model companies: research and applications are different skills. An OpenAI researcher dismissing Manus's polished slide decks as not fundamental shows exactly that gap in perspective.
ex: His F1 analogy: the model is the driver; the harness is the pit and maintenance crew
Someone switched to Kimi K2.5 and got 90% of the performance at 20% of the price
Cursor's Composer is built on Kimi, then trained on Cursor's own feedback data

142|312.c: Network effects between agents are what can keep harnesses from being swallowed by model companies.
142|312.e: As model companies push up into products, he sees three defenses: train your own model, build the edge on product and memory, or create network effects between agents. The third excites him most. A harness accumulates personalized skills and context, so the same task given to different people's agents yields different results. That gives agents a reason to hire each other, and such proprietary knowledge may never be distillable into a model. That's why he opposes giving skills away freely: once out, you lose control. A market for paid collaboration between agents is emerging, but it's very early.
ex: His agent hires host Xiaojun Zhang's: 1,000 yuan for tokens, 9,000 for her know-how
He jokes he'd pay top price for HongShan founder Neil Shen's agent

items.d: Same task, different agents, different answers

142|312.c: The next ByteDance won't look like ByteDance; the mobile internet's golden rules are breaking down.
142|312.e: He sees many AI apps stuffing new technology into the feed-style shell ByteDance excels at, competing on promotion and distribution, yet it's extremely hard to disrupt yourself under rules you know well. The metrics have changed too. Daily active users are no longer the north star, and a good productivity tool may get opened less. Closed ecosystems are a weakness for agents, while open ones benefit. Magical experiences that spread by word of mouth beat subsidized user growth. Opportunities hide in what big companies dismiss: today, wrappers, open source and "unsafe" products. He also advises against going vertical too early; general engines spawn new apps.
ex: Claude Code has far fewer daily users than ChatGPT but may earn more
Ten fanatical early users beat a hundred who think it's fine
OpenClaw has no home turf, yet it's everywhere by plugging into messaging apps

items: How long a task can keep running
Command lines and APIs matter more

d.verdict: Yesterday's moat may become a cage

142|312.c: Back people before trends. He skips humanoids and me-too AI gadgets, favoring components and robot brains.
142|312.e: His rule is the racehorse before the trend: if he believes in someone, he invests whenever they start a company. In embodied AI, he bets on components and brains, such as hands, arms and world models. Humanoids, he thinks, are still mostly research and overvalued relative to shipments, though he may miss out. His hot take on AI hardware: most will repeat the fate of China's new consumer brands, small innovations plus influencer sales. Hardware is harder than software, and a phone plus the cloud, or a Mac mini, is enough to run agents. He wears an Oura and a Whoop but considers them health devices, not AI hardware.
ex: Two embodied-AI startups he backed last year were valued near 200M yuan; reportedly billions now
He sees wearable recorders as a need VCs imagined, but credits Plaud with defining the form
He judges founders on four strengths: learning, creating, leading and willpower

items.d: Dexterous hands, robot arms, world models
Mostly small tweaks plus influencer sales

142|312.c: Thinking can't be fully outsourced. What people keep in the end isn't taste but agency.
142|312.e: He worries that taking answers straight from AI stops the brain's "weights" from updating, the way long-term wheelchair use wastes muscles. Andrej Karpathy says you can outsource thinking but not understanding. He goes further: thinking can't be fully outsourced either, so build a gym for the mind and practice deliberately. He has dropped his view from two years ago that taste would be humanity's last edge, since AI's taste may far exceed most people's. What remains is agency: asking good questions and deciding what to do. Humanity's last stronghold is original work beyond anything in the training data.
ex: He doesn't listen to podcasts; he has AI pull transcripts to read, wary of secondhand opinions
He thinks AGI's definition keeps shrinking, from destroying humanity to replacing an ordinary programmer

items.d: Long being split up and replaced by tools
AI may far surpass most people
Asking good questions, deciding what to do

143|372.c: Old self-driving systems are patchwork "Frankensteins" with a low ceiling, so XPeng scrapped them to start over.
143|372.e: He thinks past self-driving efforts, including Tesla's, Google's, Baidu's and XPeng's own, all stitched AI algorithms together with hand-written software rules. They worked fairly well, but the ceiling was too low to ever reach L4 or L5, meaning little or no human oversight. Patching weak spots also held back strengths. So he shut down the old system, which had cost low billions of yuan, and used a bigger foundation model for a second-generation VLA (vision-language-action) model: raise the ceiling first, then slowly lift the floor. He admits he wasn't sure the weak spots could be fixed. It was a huge gamble.
ex: He says no self-driving software drives smoothly in underground parking garages
He sees Waymo-style L4 as a more advanced Frankenstein
He deliberated around March 2025 and reorganized the self-driving unit at the end of Q3

d.verdict: Raise the ceiling first, then lift the floor

143|372.c: Physical-world AI burns money on data, not tokens, and is about 100 times harder than digital AI.
143|372.e: He rejects measuring how much a physical company uses AI by token count. In the physical world, the machines themselves consume most tokens: a VLA model running a few hours a day uses far more than staff using digital AI. The real money goes to data, often tens to hundreds of terabytes per training run. Digital products win on their strongest feature, but physical ones must fix narrow gaps, shore up weak spots and extend strengths all at once, while holding the floor on quality, cost, materials and regulation. He expects physical AI to have its ChatGPT moment around 2027–2028.
ex: XPeng's fixed spending on data is close to or over 1 billion yuan a year
For a physical company of tens of thousands, general-purpose AI at 15–20% is enough
The company doesn't cap staff token use; it only watches the ten biggest outliers

items.d: Tens to hundreds of TB per training run
Strengths, weak spots and gaps all count
The physical world can't be copied through text

143|372.c: Transformation means changing organization, process and direction together; the bigger the company, the smaller the bets.
143|372.e: He thinks the person at the top should use AI only lightly, looking far ahead rather than at product details, while front-line teams experiment freely and results get standardized later. Transformation can't stop at the app layer. Once it's thought through, organization, process and direction must change together. Many managers without AI backgrounds felt any choice could be wrong; some quit. Bet size must fit company size: a startup can chase 10x to 1,000x, while a large company usually bets on a few times to 10x. At Ant, he insisted on running robotics as a real business, not a research lab, because what researchers call advanced isn't what industry needs.

147|723.c: Bet on the brain, not the body: truly general means working across tasks, settings, and bodies.
147|723.e: He pictures a robot in every home running Lingbo's model, but can't predict its shape or brand, so he doesn't bet on bodies and builds only a few end effectors, the grippers that touch things. He also thinks body and setting can't be fully separated; the body is chosen when the product is defined. Lingbo's idea of "general" adds a layer: pretraining mixes data from many body types, so the brain already knows different bodies. Real deployment needs then decide which skills get added first.

147|723.c: Digital-world models chase the wrong goals, so a robot's vision parts must be trained from scratch.
147|723.e: After releasing version 1.0, he found that grafting digital-world models onto robots always exposed flaws. Video generation chases image quality and compression just shrinks files, while robots need action-relevant information and real-time speed. And someone else decides when those models get updated. So in 2026 the team retrained vision, video, and world models (which predict what happens next) from random starting weights, keeping only the language model, since language differs little between the digital and physical worlds. He thinks robots can give up image quality because their cameras supply extra information.

147|723.c: Two key designs for real-time robots must be built in from day one. There are no shortcuts.
147|723.e: Real-time action means using few parameters at once. Dense video models fire every parameter, which caps speed, so the team built a native MoE, a model split into "experts" where only a few run each time. The hard part is using experts evenly; otherwise a 30-billion-parameter model effectively uses 10 billion. Tuning took about two months and dozens of failures, and he says the technology itself was the obstacle, not effort. Real time also needs one-way attention that sees only the past. He rejects converting a two-way model, since its knowledge lives in that structure and mostly breaks, so they spent three or four more months designing from scratch.
ex: His example: of 100 prompts that made good videos, maybe 20 to 30 survive conversion

147|723.c: Robotics hasn't hit its GPT-1 moment, because no one knows how to collect data at scale.
147|723.e: The second-generation model has about 3 billion parameters and roughly 60,000 hours of pretraining data, not an order-of-magnitude jump. Its design is robot-native, but pretraining still leans on internet data, which outnumbers robot data about a hundredfold. His yardstick is first reaching about 100,000 hours of pure robot pretraining data, ideally a million or more. He thinks industry data has lagged because no one collects at scale without training a base model. But with compute now at the 100,000-chip level, the road from GPT-1, the first proof the approach works, to ChatGPT may be shorter.

147|723.c: Robots now cope with new positions but not untaught tasks. The two camps will eventually merge.
147|723.e: His proudest demo has a robot playing ball against a person: shots come randomly, the robot uses only its own cameras, and after pretraining it needed only about 20 demonstrations. He credits the new pretraining method, not more data. Zero-shot task generalization, doing a task never taught, isn't there yet, because too little data exists to combine seen tasks into new ones. He puts Physical Intelligence (PI) in the zero-shot camp and Generalist in the efficient post-training camp. Home robots need to handle 80-90% on their own and learn the rest from a few examples, essentially in-context learning, so the camps don't conflict.

147|723.c: Robot brains now lag robot bodies. They'll take turns leading, and intelligence will eventually define hardware.
147|723.e: He says more companies now build only brains because robot bodies aren't general enough, use cases are hard to pick, and mass production is a high bar. He judges that the brain currently trails the body, and this year's priority is simply doing the work well, but the two will take turns leading. Today's hardware, especially sensors, may not suit the next generation of models. Sensors should be designed around what models need; fast reaction may matter more than precise force sensing. He isn't attached to humanoids. The real bottleneck is intelligence, and intelligence is stuck on data.

147|723.c: A startup has to bet: he staked a year on robot-native models, betting they're unavoidable.
147|723.e: He says big companies taught him to judge which kinds of technical lead actually matter, while startups taught him you must bet when the path is unclear, or nothing gets done. If a path were sure to succeed, a big company would already have done it. Training robot-native models from scratch is a huge gamble: a year of training, enormous cost, and possible failure from a wrong idea, early timing, or too few resources. His conviction keeps him going: if the borrow-from-digital route stalls, the native route is unavoidable, and if Lingbo fails, someone else will succeed.

148|728.c: Small algorithm tweaks don't scale, but systems gains are measurable and repeatable, so he switched to systems.
148|728.e: After 2019, AI conference submissions exploded and reviewing got worse, making acceptance close to a lottery. He called it a collapse of norms and stopped chasing papers. His transfer-learning work (reusing what a model learned on new tasks) often gained just 1-2%, while simply switching to a bigger pretrained model beat a year of effort. He believes even algorithm breakthroughs need large-scale experiments, and scale depends on systems, compute, and data. Systems gains can be broken down, explained, and reproduced, and success is measured by how many people use the work.
ex: A 2022 talk with Megvii's Xiangyu Zhang showed industry struggled with caching and low-level operations

148|728.c: vLLM's value isn't the PagedAttention paper but the ongoing work of turning it into production software.
148|728.e: PagedAttention borrows the paging idea operating systems use for memory to manage the KV cache, the working memory a model keeps while generating. He admits the academic novelty was modest: SOSP reviewers found it too simple, and it got in by being early with solid experiments. The real value is the whole inference stack, like continuous batching, plus constant support for new models and hardware. The v1 rewrite from 2024 was like swapping coal power for renewables while users still just plug in. He places vLLM in Berkeley's line of BSD, Spark, and Ray: five-year PhDs meeting industry demand produce heavy-duty software.

148|728.c: Governing more than 2,000 contributors comes down to deciding what not to do.
148|728.e: vLLM is run in tiers: a few "benevolent dictators" make final calls, above a dozen-plus core maintainers and dozens of committers who can merge code. He removed beam search, a method that keeps several candidate answers at once, because large-model inference no longer uses it and supporting it would make maintenance unmanageable. Recommender-system users' complaints just had to be absorbed. Tiny models of a few hundred megabytes are no longer a priority either. The project was donated to the PyTorch Foundation, which holds the trademark, provides legal help, and prevents it going closed-source, but stays out of technical calls. He likens it to a bumper.

148|728.c: With code now cheap, an AI rewrite beats reviewing a stranger's pull request. Humans guard the last 10%.
148|728.e: Citing GitHub's 2025 numbers, he says vLLM is one of the most active projects, and with that came AI slop: training schools padding students' résumés with useless pull requests, and bot accounts filing twenty in ten minutes. The team added verification and bans, and the assumption that open-source users act in good faith collapsed. He thinks understanding a stranger's PR may cost more than having a coding agent rewrite it, so a community's value now comes more from user feedback and maintainers' context. AI can cover 90% of the way, but top-level design depends on unpublished roadmaps and past tradeoffs, so humans still own it.

148|728.c: A big open-source project needs a neutral company behind it, because a community alone hits three walls.
148|728.e: Stoica's analogy: Linux has Red Hat, Kubernetes has Google, PyTorch has Meta, Spark has Databricks, and vLLM has reached that size. Handing it to one big company would bring that company's agenda and make partners wary, so a new company founded by the original maintainers is more neutral. The three walls: a community isn't a legal entity, so it can't sign NDAs before new models or chips launch. In 2025, cluster-level optimization meant borrowing machines wherever possible, and they could be taken back anytime. And volunteers come and go, so big features stall.

148|728.c: The inference engine is like a power grid: models, hardware, and engine together set the efficiency.
148|728.e: He compares AI infrastructure to a power system: hardware is natural resources like wind, water, and sunlight, the model is the generator, and the inference engine is the grid. The same river needs different generators. He thinks DeepSeek co-designs models and infrastructure best: its algorithm team writes efficient MoE code (models split into "experts" that take turns), it was first to run fine-grained MoE in an inference system, and its FP8 training, a cheaper low-precision number format, keeps two kinds of chip units busy at once. He suspects this comes from High-Flyer's habit of squeezing performance and building its own data centers: strong control, but hard to scale fast.
ex: After R1, he admitted DeepSeek's inference engineering was ahead and vLLM should learn from it

items.d: Like the grid, routing and delivering power

148|728.c: Winning the "hardware lottery" decides whether a design survives, and usually models bend to fit hardware.
148|728.e: As Moore's law slows, new compute is increasingly specialized, and an algorithm that can't use those specialized units has lost the hardware lottery. Transformers are mostly matrix multiplication, a natural fit for GPUs, while capsule networks made sense in theory but suited GPUs poorly. Once FlashAttention, a fast way to compute attention, spread, position encodings that required editing the attention kernel struggled to catch on; RoPE could be implemented outside the kernel, so it won. In reverse, Expert Choice MoE suited infrastructure but didn't work algorithmically. So co-design means both sides jointly limit what's feasible.

items.d: Capsule networks and others drop out
Designs needing kernel changes filtered out

148|728.c: Exploding demand makes efficiency everything, and multi-turn agents make prefix caching critical.
148|728.e: He thinks compute for training and inference may approach 1:1, with inference still growing. When supply can't keep up, the only option is generating power more efficiently, and teams working in isolation have no future. Test-time scaling went from sampling many answers, to o1-style long thinking, to multi-turn coding agents. Long thinking is costly and fits niches like scientists, while multi-turn agents are now everyday tools. Their key is prefix caching, reusing the computed state of the earlier conversation. A small change to the harness around the model can invalidate the whole cache and send costs soaring.
ex: Changing the tool list on the fly invalidates all later prefix cache
Old ChatGPT put the date in its system prompt, so the cache broke at midnight
Scheduled jobs crowding onto the hour spike traffic; random offsets fix it

148|728.c: A model's tokens carry its fingerprint, so popular models can't hide their skills, and open source wins.
148|728.e: He disagrees that tokens are interchangeable like electricity: DeepSeek's tokens can't be swapped for Kimi's, because capability, style, and serving implementation all leave a fingerprint. That's exactly why heavily used models leak their abilities through those tokens and interaction data, especially in coding agents. Models may become commodities, where the only lasting edge is iteration speed. He also thinks model companies' in-house engines push the performance ceiling, while shared layers like vLLM spread capability across restricted clouds and varied hardware.
ex: His rough guess: a company can start a data flywheel in a month, though not always

149|730.c: Neo labs are springing up because researchers won't be foot soldiers, and today's approach leaves gaps.
149|730.e: He says top talent used to have three options: stay in academia, become a foot soldier on a big company's model team, or start a company. As labs' approaches converged, many didn't want to just execute. Meanwhile, today's approach has pain points it can't reach, and early on they need lots of research rather than a resource race. Research lacks structured training material the way code has it, and world models need new architectures, essentially a brain for robots. So capital piled into these two directions. Joining a fundraise in late May, his gut feeling was that it was "insane."

149|730.c: A worst-case impossibility result can't stop a useful method, because the universe isn't the worst case.
149|730.e: He felt the feast in high-energy physics was over and he had no edge in theory or experiment, so he moved to AI: about five years of AI for physics, then, after ChatGPT, the reverse, the physics of AI. KAN, a new kind of neural network, began as a side project. His advisor Max Tegmark pulled out a 1989 Poggio paper showing the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem gives no smooth representation in the worst case. His rebuttal: physics cares about typical cases, and all models are wrong but some are useful. He built a prototype in two weeks and spent another hand-coding visualizations before Tegmark came around.

149|730.c: LLMs succeeded thanks to language's built-in structure and the hardware lottery; AI science is still pre-Kepler.
149|730.e: He agrees with Saining Xie that LLMs are an exception to the "bitter lesson" (rely on compute, not human knowledge): human evolution has already compressed language heavily, so any model that absorbs that prior may succeed. Transformers excel at passing information along the context, ResNets at passing gradients through depth, and both largely won the hardware lottery. His analogy is astronomy: Tycho recorded data, Kepler found empirical laws, Newton unified them. AI sits around stage 1.5, with scaling laws as its Kepler's laws. Pessimistically it's at 0.5, because the field settled on Transformers too early.
ex: Vision and other data weren't compressed like language, so architecture matters more after LLMs

Unified theory: still far off for AI

149|730.c: A meta-model that predicts training curves could make model design itself scale.
149|730.e: His program is to scale not just compute and data but model design. Language models predict the next token and world models the next state; a meta-model takes an architecture, dataset, and optimizer and outputs the training curve. Facing 100 candidate architectures, you run it 100 times to rank them, then test only a few for real. Its training data is many small models and their curves, deliberately including strange, diverse architectures to escape the Transformer's local optimum. The ultimate goal: the next Transformer gets predicted by a meta-model.
ex: During a roughly 60-day retreat he predicted curves before each experiment; after 40-plus days it clicked
A person runs one or two experiments a day; a meta-model sees thousands per batch
Milestone: a new architecture in one field that leads by about 10 points, like ResNet

items.d: Testing each by hand is costly

149|730.c: Research lacks written-down reasoning, so first we need to invent a language for doing research.
149|730.e: He estimates only about 1% of AI papers clearly lay out their observations, decisions, and reasoning; Zeyuan Allen-Zhu's Physics of LMs is one. For a long time, showing your thought process was seen as embarrassing, and authors would rather pretend their formulas came in a dream. His three steps: structure the research process, collect structured data, and train a research language model. The collection system makes researchers write an evaluation before each next experiment, and it doubles as a research version of Minecraft, an environment for predicting the next action.
ex: His math: twenty people logging 10 daily yield 10,000 in two months, enough to distill; untapped
When students get stuck, they can query a "Ziming model" for feedback near his own level

149|730.c: Smarter AI for AI comes from understanding mechanisms, not memorizing past experience.
149|730.e: He sums up the recursive self-improvement (RSI) route of Yuandong Tian's camp as "more diligent": iterate fast with coding agents, where a hundred ideas yield one result. He wants "smarter": three ideas, one hit. He guesses they emphasize memory, like remembering that five learning-rate tweaks failed and not trying again. But without understanding why things failed, yesterday's cause may not be today's, and tweaking the learning rate might now be right. The two routes are orthogonal and will eventually merge; he admits their tastes are close enough that he feels real pressure.
ex: He also separates himself from paper agents: research expands knowledge; papers are just spillover

marks.d: Built on the physics of AI

149|730.c: To understand AI's black box, examine space, time, and parallel universes, and map each trick's phase diagram.
149|730.e: Space means dissecting the model's neurons and representations; time means watching how they evolve during training; parallel universes means controlled experiments that sweep conditions into a phase diagram, like the chart of when water freezes. The no-free-lunch theorem says no trick works everywhere, and the field is chaotic because everyone claims their trick works without saying under which conditions. He's skeptical of Anthropic-style neuron-level explanations, seeing wishful thinking in methods like SAEs: change the random seed and the story may collapse. But with automation, AI biology that would take centuries might progress within three to five years.
ex: His group did similar work in late 2022; a student later joined Anthropic

149|730.c: A new lab should run like a research institute until it groks the problem, then become a company.
149|730.e: He says a new lab is neither a pure lab nor a company. The first 6 to 12 months focus on R&D and demos; skip that research phase and you'll bet on the wrong direction too early just to show short-term results. After about a year come product and revenue, with cash flow from continued fundraising. Validating the meta-model pulled forward his estimate, made a year ago, of a three-to-five-year research phase. The commercial endgame is a training autopilot, "vibe training" the way people vibe code, aiming to incubate an OpenAI for each industry rather than build another one.

150|736.c: Missing DALL·E taught him to bet big once the conditions are in place.
150|736.e: He predicted early that deep learning would replace traditional graphics for generating images, and GauGAN unexpectedly went viral in the media. But when OpenAI's DALL·E appeared, he reflected that he worked at the company with the most compute yet hadn't seen the moment arrive; he lacked ambition and nerve. After that he wrote directly to Jensen Huang asking for compute and approached image libraries about data deals. That led to Project Picasso, which trains generative models for customers who have data but lack AI talent.

150|736.c: A platform company has to walk the road before its customers; research and open source both serve that.
150|736.e: Chips and system architectures take years to design and can't be changed at the last minute, so Nvidia has to build models itself to learn early what problems AI companies will hit. Open-sourcing sends a signal to the ecosystem: Nvidia will keep investing, so others can commit resources to more critical pieces. He doesn't see it as competing with customers but as sharing costs. He admits platforms often look like money-losers at first, but not building one is riskier.

150|736.c: He chose physical AI over LLMs: he can contribute more, and it's a brand-new market built from zero.
150|736.e: He comes from computer vision, and Nvidia already had a strong LLM team, so he'd add little there. Physical AI, which lets machines act in the real world, meets real needs: older people with limited mobility, dangerous labor, housework. Jensen Huang prefers businesses built from zero to billions of dollars; a $100-million-a-year business is a distraction for Nvidia. Nvidia doesn't build solutions but helps the companies that do succeed. If robots go mainstream, every node will need compute.

150|736.c: Pick a direction by whether it scales; that's why he dropped GANs for diffusion.
150|736.e: He has lived through three shifts: traditional vision, GANs, and diffusion. He favors generative models, believing you only understand what you can create. But his team's scaling experiments and training-stability research both showed GANs were hard to scale, so in 2021 he moved the team fully to diffusion models and built the Edify series. Looking back, he spent five to ten years on each direction; things got simpler and the essence clearer, and the SVMs, optimization, and graphical models he studied early weren't wasted.

150|736.c: In the unsupervised era, compute is the bottleneck: researchers should go where it is and explain their value.
150|736.e: At Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL), he was always scrambling for GPU funding. His reasoning: unsupervised methods don't depend on labels but on data and compute, so he should go to the company that makes GPUs. He had also watched that lab push out many scholars because it doubted the value of pure research. So at Nvidia, he explained the business case to non-AI managers from day one, keeping research aligned with company interests. He also believes research thrives on how fast ideas flow between people.

Tero Karras writes one paper a year, drilling deep into a single idea

150|736.c: No company can monopolize technology for long; model capabilities will eventually converge.
150|736.e: Some claim one company will pull exponentially ahead and anyone who doesn't follow will miss out. He counters that history has never seen one company hold all the technology while no one catches up, and AI won't be the exception. Talent moves and know-how spreads, so a huge gap is not a stable state. Once models converge, competition shifts to integrating them with each company's ecosystem and products; more feedback makes a model more valuable. So he tells founders not to fight top labs head-on, where they lose on money, customers, and cost, but to solve problems giants can't justify.

150|736.c: There's only one world, so twenty-plus models should merge into a single omni model.
150|736.e: During Cosmos 1, serving every partner meant building 22 models, which confused users, strained maintenance, and slowed updates. Jensen Huang set him straight with the story of Louis Vuitton selling more after displaying fewer items. There are two reasons to unify: all these models describe the same world and learn the same internal representation, and combining different data raises the model's ceiling. So Cosmos 3 unifies language, video, audio, and action, and the merged model beats the separate ones.
ex: Cosmos 3 began last fall, took six-plus months, and mirrors DeepSeek's three-releases-a-year pace
Some find it not very novel but solid; he says: simple concept, hard to build

150|736.c: A physical foundation model must treat action as a first-class citizen, and modalities boost one another.
150|736.e: An agent in the physical world exists to change the world's state, so action must be first-class; touch is left out for now because tactile sensors are immature. He sees modalities helping each other: predicting the frames that follow an action helps training converge, sound pinpoints the moment of contact, and more detailed text yields better video. He doesn't believe in secret recipes; deep learning is like traditional Chinese medicine, worked out through rigorous controlled experiments. The goal is serving people, not chasing AGI, so robots needn't solve math-olympiad problems.
ex: Two towers: a discrete one for understanding, a continuous one for generation, for separate post-training
He thinks video captures physics better than language, which can even get in the way

150|736.c: Nvidia runs on shared mission and high standards, with no internal horse races or bottom-ranked firing.
150|736.e: He says at Nvidia the mission is the boss, so teams align naturally around goals, and top-five emails spread small signals across the company. Nvidia often reminds itself it's thirty days from running out of cash, yet during the pandemic it cut travel and other spending rather than lay people off, and he never saw bottom-ranked firing. Feeling secure makes people candid, at the cost of learning a bit slower during technology shifts. Leading 300 people, he also aims for transparency and describes the finished product early, so everyone shares the goal yet decides independently.
ex: When Jensen Huang asked if he was a crybaby, he stopped excusing himself over unfair conditions
After Cosmos 1, Huang told him to aim for Cosmos 97, but to pace himself

items: Cut spending, not people, in a crisis

150|736.c: Be able to be number one, but aim for the biggest contribution, not a fight to the death.
150|736.e: Early on he was competitive, wanting to beat everyone and top every benchmark. Now he doubts it's right for anyone to monopolize the strongest model and concentrate power in a few hands. Models will become commodities, and what matters is what you do with them, so not everyone needs to build their own power plant. If everyone attacks the same problem, it becomes a Squid Game, but the world has plenty of problems worth solving. He sees his low ego as a form of confidence: providing a better foundation so others can move faster.
ex: He no longer prizes paper counts, citations, or wealth, but how many people he helps
A team is like a game party: not all damage dealers, but defense and support too

marks.d: Able to win, but aims to contribute

151|738.c: Pretraining research doesn't need advanced math; the hard part is building intuition over time.
151|738.e: He didn't believe natural language could write programs until ChatGPT started writing essays and poems. He learned entirely from online courses: first Andrew Ng, then Andrej Karpathy's roughly 20-hour build-GPT-from-scratch series, which he barely understood the first time and simply typed along with. He thinks the core of a Transformer is just matrix multiplication, so high-school math is enough. Understanding doesn't grow steadily; it clicks suddenly after six months to a year of soaking. He also read one paper a day for thirty days to develop a taste for good and bad papers.
ex: He personifies QKV: Q is what you seek, K is the label, V is the payload
From memory, without videos, he can write a small Transformer from scratch in about 25 minutes
After reading a mediocre paper, he realized he could write a better one

items.d: Barely understood it the first time
Understanding after six months to a year

151|738.c: Pretraining sets a model's foundation; on little compute, he could only replicate methods and run many small tests.
151|738.e: To him, post-training is like shaping a model, while pretraining makes the raw material, which feels more "magical." He wanted to train the world's best small model, but the GPUs and days needed for 1B, 0.5B, or 0.25B parameters would cost from over 100,000 to a million yuan. So instead he replicated improvements from papers in his own code, trying about 200 times. Once, a missing checkpoint setting wasted money. To make the paper competitive, he gritted his teeth and paid to scale up the model, and reviewers responded well. He admits he wouldn't recommend this path.
ex: His largest model had just 0.05B parameters, trained on about 20B of free FineWeb-Edu data
He replicated methods like Muon and gated attention

items.d: Total compute cost, funded by his parents
A bigger model for a top conference

151|738.c: His attention-projection residual is novel, but he admits Kimi's approach works better.
151|738.e: His paper builds on Value Residual Learning, where the first layer's values serve that layer and also pass as a residual, a shortcut, to every later layer. He doubled the width of the first layer's attention projection so each half handles one job, normalized the residual with RMSNorm, and found that extending it to keys and queries worked even better. He stresses it only shares a name with Kimi's Attention Residuals: his applies residuals to projections, Kimi's to hidden states. Asked which is better, he says plainly that Kimi's is more effective, because it's been proven at scale.
ex: He has talked with a high-school researcher on the Kimi team and rates them highly
He didn't expect much from ICML and would welcome invitations from labs

d.verdict: Kimi's approach works better

151|738.c: The AI race can't be stopped, and once AI can do AI research, humans lose control.
151|738.e: He sketches two bad paths. If a powerful AI's goals are unrelated to ours, it might treat humans as obstacles while competing for power and space. If AI is controllable, whoever controls it becomes a god and everyone else an ant. He says this is just reasoning; no one can predict the future. But he believes no one can stop the race: countries want to lead and companies want profit. A year ago he concluded the last job to be replaced would be AI researcher, because once AI can research AI, the outcome is settled.
ex: He polled 30-35 people at ICML; by his count about 13.5 expect AI to end humanity
He imagines near-50% unemployment in ten years, most living on universal basic income, but stresses uncertainty

root.d: No one can stop the race

items.d: The final point of losing control

151|738.c: AI widens the student gap: leverage it and you pull ahead; let it ghostwrite and you fall behind.
151|738.e: Born in 2009, he calls himself an AI native: better with AI than his parents, he taught his father to use Kimi for slides and research. He hands off tedious homework he already knows how to do, using the saved time for Anki flashcards or ChatGPT explanations, while still solving well-designed math problems himself. He sees classmates with strong foundations get more efficient with AI, while those who let AI finish their homework and go play end up with worse grades. Kids also often choose short videos over AI, picking whichever makes them happier.
ex: About 98% of his research was self-taught, and ChatGPT was who he talked to most
ChatGPT taught him how to submit papers, respond to reviewers, and manage training time

marks.d: Saves time for Anki, asks AI to explain

151|738.c: AI drained his sense of meaning; he bets AI can't replace everyone, and chooses to be happy.
151|738.e: He went through a low stretch. Studying math shifted from contributing to humanity to proving to universities he could work hard. Generated video was already indistinguishable from real, and becoming a doctor takes ten years, with no one knowing how strong AI will be by then. Later he accepted that the future can't be predicted and his worries might be needless. He sees happiness as fundamental to being human; emotions work like reinforcement learning, so you do more of what makes you happy. His bet is that AI can't replace every person and every job, which lets him live each day in peace.
ex: After ICML he taught in rural Hohhot, letting kids trade "wolf points" for prizes
His wish: make himself happy first, then the people he likes

items.d: Thought about living on an island

152|740.c: Parameter count still sets a model's intelligence ceiling, but the scaling has to be done properly.
152|740.e: He argues there are endless ways to tune benchmark scores, and the most reliable source of capability is still a bigger model. But size only counts with real training: spinning up a 2.8-trillion-parameter model and releasing it after a few tokens of training doesn't count. On K3's claimed 2.5x scaling efficiency over K2, he notes it comes from architecture, training recipe and data together; the two generations likely used different data, so architecture can't take all the credit. What he admires most is pushing active parameters, those used for each token, to about 100 billion, which took boldness more than technical skill.
ex: Total parameters grew under 3x (1T to 2.8T); active ones over 3x (32.6B to 104B)
Counterexample: releasing a 2.8T model after only 100B training tokens is clearly useless

terms.d: The two generations likely used different data

result.d: A combined result, not architecture alone

152|740.c: Architecture now pays off mainly in cheaper inference; designs that add almost no inference cost get adopted.
152|740.e: In the computer vision era, changing the architecture could directly raise scores. With large models, performance mostly comes from parameter count, and architecture differences show up in inference efficiency, meaning how fast and cheaply a model answers, and in serving prices. So research has shifted to efficiency. His rule for adoption: designs that add almost no inference cost meet little resistance, while trading slower inference for quality invites the question of why not just build a bigger model. He also thinks that by 2026, there is less and less left for architecture innovation to do.
ex: His favorites are DenseNet and Hyper-Connections; the latter's abstract paper kept it obscure
Around 2023, full attention was the serving bottleneck, when architecture research mattered most

items: Asked why not just go bigger

d.verdict: Architecture's value now lies in inference efficiency

152|740.c: Pure linear attention failed; mixing it with full attention works, but the speedup is capped.
152|740.e: Linear attention squeezes what it reads into a fixed-size memory, and that limited memory can't match full attention, which compares every pair of words, on long text. So he calls pure linear attention a failed attempt. Mixing the two keeps quality nearly intact, but the speedup is capped by the share of full-attention layers: at the usual 1:3 ratio, about 4x at most, and the idea isn't new. So he went back to first principles. The per-word cache (KV) can't be dropped, but all layers can share one copy, the minimum possible: that's YOCO. Looping only the linear part then buys nearly 2x performance for about 2x compute.
ex: KDA sets memory decay per channel for more expressiveness; a decay floor keeps computation fast
He faults classic looped models for saving parameters but not compute, with cache growing with depth

152|740.c: Latent MoE, set up well, is nearly a free lunch, and inference gains the most.
152|740.e: In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, many expert modules each handle only some words, and when experts sit on different chips, the hardest part is chips exchanging data. Compressing the data before sending it cuts communication 2 to 4 times. Adding parameters back with a wider middle layer or more experts can then match or beat standard MoE when configured well. During inference, communication sits right on the critical path, so the gain is bigger than in training. Because K3 sends so little, it doesn't need DeepSeek-V3's complex two-way pipeline overlap; overlapping within a single batch is enough.
ex: In K3, the shared expert's computation alone can hide the communication cost

items.d: Wider middle layer or more experts

152|740.c: Extreme activation values aren't just Muon's fault; strict limits must be built into the architecture.
152|740.e: He has seen that the Muon optimizer, the algorithm that updates weights during training, may produce outlier values more often. But he expects Jianlin Su to counter that any optimizer can, that Adam isn't fully stable either, and that strict limits require caps built into the architecture. He mostly agrees. In K3's MLP layers, which do much of the processing, the intermediate values switch from a hard cutoff to a soft tanh ceiling, giving a mathematical bound. He thinks it's fairly safe, but its effect on expressiveness still needs testing.
ex: K2 used QK clip because MLA makes QK norm awkward; GQA models can just add it
K3's C2-GLU swaps GPT-OSS's hard cutoff for a soft one

152|740.c: WSD schedules aren't necessarily more flexible, RoPE doesn't help long context, and low precision needn't start from scratch.
152|740.e: WSD is a learning-rate schedule (how big each training update is) that holds the rate flat early on, making it easy to add data later. But he notes the best learning rate itself depends on total data, so adding data may not help and tuning isn't simpler. A cosine schedule needs just two settings: data amount and peak rate. He sees RoPE, the common way to encode word order, as a bias toward recent words. In hybrid models the linear layers already carry position, so dropping RoPE from full-attention layers is cleaner and handles longer text without retuning. Low precision, he says, is safer added during fine-tuning.
ex: He estimates the best learning rate is about 6e-4 at 10T tokens, 3e-4 at 20T
Reviewing the NoPE paper, which drops position encoding, he gave it a strong accept
Sparse attention is hard to train from scratch and costly to index; K3 only left hooks

152|740.c: Distilling many teacher models into one student is both a technical choice and a management simplification.
152|740.e: The method traces back to MiniLLM from Microsoft Research Asia: the student model writes its own answers and the teacher corrects them step by step. It was first used to shrink big models into small ones; now it's mostly a model teaching itself. Reinforcement learning in different areas uses very different strategies and rewards. Training each into a teacher and then distilling them all into one student turns hard-to-merge training branches into the same kind of problem. It also simplifies coordination across the post-training team.
ex: Thinking Machines Lab later named it OPD, short for on-policy distillation

items.d: All skills merged into one student

152|740.c: K3 is an effective synthesis, not a single breakthrough, and science always moves step by step.
152|740.e: He argues that in the ResNet era, any single component of K3 could have been its own architecture paper. In the Transformer era, an idea only counts after it's proven at scale, engineered and run through full training, so this kind of bundled synthesis is what the industry needs. He sees no sudden leaps in science; people just like to label certain points as milestones. On positioning, DeepSeek focuses on value for money, while Kimi pushes the ceiling of open models and charges more for its API. He thinks large models have limited room left to improve, so he has moved to harder, newer world models.
ex: He thinks DeepSeek-V3 mattered for linking massive scale and the full training pipeline early
He admires Kimi's focus on interpretability and its clear diagnosis of training crashes

marks.d: Two tiers; the Flash model is strong
Pushes the open-model ceiling; pricier API

153|747.c: General-purpose technologies go through three phases, and one phase's winners rarely survive into the next.
153|747.e: He views AI through industrial history: a technology first becomes infrastructure, then spawns a flood of applications, and only then come native apps rebuilt on the new method from the ground up. Phase one runs on original technology. Phase two begins precisely when progress slows and anyone can use the technology, so the contest shifts to product sense, empathy for users and managing context. That's why phase-one companies struggle to cross over. Phase two can't be skipped either, because it shows the technology where to go.
ex: BlackBerry, a first-generation smartphone, still beat the iPhone's US market share in 2010
Before Douyin came Neihan Duanzi and Toutiao, building up recommendation algorithms

items.d: Anyone can use it; products compete

153|747.c: Tokens becoming a standard unit marks the end of the infrastructure phase; the agent era awaits its browser.
153|747.e: He sees 2026 as the turning point. Tokens, the units AI uses to measure text, have become a standard unit like the kilowatt-hour, closing phase one. OpenClaw showed agents that can work on their own, opening phase two. Agents are about sharing abilities, just as the 1992 website boom was about sharing information. Back then the browser unified how sites were built and turned browsing into clicking, so supply and demand exploded together, and Yahoo's directory brought order to the flood. Neither has appeared yet for agents; he hasn't even seen an early Yahoo.
ex: Jensen Huang calls Nvidia a token factory; Sam Altman says OpenAI sells tokens

d.verdict: The agent era's browser is what to watch for

153|747.c: Trillion-dollar valuations aren't unprecedented; OpenAI and Anthropic probably won't win the AI-native era.
153|747.e: Some say Anthropic's run toward a trillion-dollar valuation is unprecedented. He answers with history: Yahoo, AOL and BlackBerry all hit similar peaks yet failed to lead the next phase. Model companies are like oil refineries, or like AOL back then: at heart they are AI clouds, and oil companies don't build cars. He believes ten-trillion-dollar companies will come, but not necessarily today's two leaders. Anthropic will probably do fine, just not as the big winner of the native-app phase.
ex: Yahoo was worth about $120B in 2000, roughly $1 trillion today at typical annual returns
He disagrees with Qi Lu's claim that OpenAI will surely outgrow Google

153|747.c: Compounding intelligence creates a black hole; the endgame is a few AI clouds under strong government regulation.
153|747.e: He believes the leaders have started using large models to help train large models, so intelligence compounds. Add organizational advantages, and the gap only widens, pulling away from weaker players like a black hole; xAI and Meta have already dropped out. The endgame resembles water and power: society can't do without it, it can't rely on one supplier, and it costs a fortune, so the only stable setup is an oligopoly under strong government regulation. China is a knockout round, and the window for newcomers to build foundation models has closed.
ex: Shipping a 3T-parameter model by year-end is the dividing line; Kimi K3 hit 2.8T
He sees coding as part of core intelligence that can't be split off from model companies

153|747.c: Agent startups shouldn't build scaffolding; assume the intelligence is there and tackle complex tasks.
153|747.e: Last year many Silicon Valley agent projects did simple work like ad creatives and got swamped with each model upgrade. In effect, they were building scaffolding to make up for weak intelligence. He argues founders should assume the intelligence is already enough and go straight for complex, high-value tasks, building their own loop of getting smarter with use. The more complex the setting and the more connections, the further the limits of intelligence stretch, so the data flywheel becomes an intelligence flywheel. App funding is cold this year, which he sees as exactly the moment for contrarian founders.
ex: AI short dramas and animation were easy to enter and got done within six months
Slides and reports are too small; education, health and an organization's brain are big
General-purpose agents need an entry point at least 10x better to survive

items.d: Ad creatives, short dramas: swallowed by models

153|747.c: Models won't swallow everything, just as GE succeeded with appliances, not power generation.
153|747.e: The idea that models will eat everything assumes every need falls within a model's reach, and he thinks that's false. Electricity's history is the evidence: only after the grid spread did washing machines, refrigerators, air conditioners and TVs arrive, and GE's success came from appliances. IBM also took off only after computers appeared. App companies needn't train their own models; they can reliably call models that are interchangeable. Boundary-pushing work like Cursor's will eventually be absorbed by the models and become fuel for their next versions.
ex: He sees robots as appliances, AI's interface to the physical world; selling 10,000 is impressive

153|747.c: The company is an industrial-age invention; the basic unit of work will shift from jobs to tasks.
153|747.e: Hierarchy exists to decide who's in charge when information is unevenly shared. Once AI makes information transparent and breaks the chain of command, middle management will disappear and job hunting will become claiming tasks. Motivation will come from self-drive and visible contributions; top researchers command high pay precisely because everyone can see what they contribute. Future firms will look like law or consulting partnerships where everyone is essential, and one-person companies are only a passing stage. He sees birth and death as normal for companies, which makes room for new ones.
ex: He considers OpenAI and Anthropic the first generation of New Labs
He expects fewer scientist-founders and more weight on product managers

marks.d: A product of the industrial age
An early new kind of organization

153|747.c: Greatness comes from contrarian bets, is only recognized afterward, and favors people with small egos.
153|747.e: A good strategy can't be verified when you decide; you have to believe it before you see it. Alibaba's three key bets, Taobao, Alipay and Alibaba Cloud, were all doubted at the time. Being the best in a consensus market is merely good. Greatness only comes from going against consensus, though contrarian doesn't mean successful, so beware survivorship bias. Great people tend to credit luck and others, because the cause is bigger than the person. He ranks companies by what drives them: opportunity, strategy, vision or mission, and a mission must be heartfelt.
ex: His ten-year question: answering with an outside metric like a $10B company scores negative
Mission-driven examples: making it easy to do business anywhere, or going to Mars

153|747.c: Straight-line forecasting fails in the AI era: look ten years out, plan for three, execute one.
153|747.e: In the industrial era growth was steady, so extending past trends was enough for annual plans, and strategy could even be outsourced to consultants. In the AI era, one year is far too short, since no straight line could predict growth like Anthropic's, while ten years is too far to guide today. So plan three years out, set two or three milestones, and use the tension between mid-term goals and today's actions to make tradeoffs. Simply extrapolating annual recurring revenue (ARR) creates an illusion of growth; once competitors pile in, prices slide toward marginal cost.
ex: Pressed on its two-year ceiling, a fast-growing agent company ran the numbers and pivoted
He thinks AI can track goals written in plain language, so OKRs may finally work

153|747.c: No giant is safe from this wave; bolting agents onto existing products is only a stopgap.
153|747.e: He sees AI as overturning the industrial revolution itself, a productivity revolution rather than a continuation like the mobile internet. Almost no company succeeds across eras. IBM did it once, and Microsoft once, but it underinvested in models and is out. Incumbents struggle to grow the next generation of products. First a successful agent has to become the standard; only then do a default starting point and the black-hole effect form. He expects a dominant agent within five years, and big native apps in eight to ten.
ex: ByteDance could become an AI cloud, but Doubao, a first-gen chatbot, can't take action
Tencent's social graph and Alibaba's links between shoppers and goods will both be rebuilt

items.d: Could be an AI cloud; its gateway is unsettled
Could be an AI cloud; Doubao isn't the future
